en: Preface to the True Lineage of the Chan School:
There was a Great Sage in Central India known as the Lord Śākyamuni. He was prophesied by Dīpaṃkara in ages long past as the successor for this Bhadrakalpa.
For forty-nine years, he revealed and transformed the teachings, receiving sentient beings and benefiting all living things.

His compassionate salvation was immeasurable and his benevolence universally encompassing. Wherever his voice and teachings reached—throughout oceans of lands as numerous as motes of dust—the light of the Twin Trees ceased its radiance, yet the *Bhūṣaṇa-mudrā* remained with Kāśyapa.
At Shaoshi, the single transmission was established; at Bodhidharma, the foundation of the Mahāyāna was laid.
This Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, transmitted outside the scriptures, is the origin of the Chan school.
Subsequently, after six transmissions it reached Caoxi. Thereupon, the branches and sub-branches spread far and wide, filling the world.

Were it not for the textual records of these events, how could one know of their needle-like penetration into the profound essence, their lightning-fast triggering of the subtle mechanism, and their revelation of the wondrously luminous true nature? This was the monk Daoyuan of Wu.

Regarding all the works contained within the *Chuan deng lu* (Records of the Transmission of the Lamp), Emperor Zhenzong of the Song dynasty issued an imperial decree to Yang Yi, the Hanlin Academician, to provide a preface and serve as the general editor.
Subsequent to this work are the *Guang deng*, *Xu deng*, *Lian deng*, and *Pu deng*; although each is detailed in its own way...
Although they differ slightly, there is nothing that does not serve to clarify this one great matter.

During the Song dynasty, there was a monk named Ji who, troubled by the vastness of the *Wudeng Huiyuan*, composed the *Wudeng Huiyuan* (The Essential Source of the Five Lamps) to benefit future students;
this was a most noble aspiration. Nevertheless, later generations still regarded it as difficult to penetrate and master, which was their [point of] concern. This is because...
These are the words and phrases from the intermediate opportunities [of the teaching]. Those that are steep and perilous stand ten thousand fathoms high like a sheer cliff;
those that are shallow and mundane are but half a nostril. Some enter the sea to count its sands; others chase sheep and are moved at the forked path.
These are the works of the Chan master Rujing of Jiaxing Prefecture during the present dynasty, who possesses the true lineage of the Zen school. May he be spared from calamity.
Chan Master Cankong received the essential instructions from [Master] Hulinsi at Hulin. He subsequently withdrew into seclusion within the walls of Zhenru Monastery in Jiahe.
Scholars and sages from all quarters looked toward him with admiration, and those who came to pay their respects were always so numerous that the doorsteps were constantly covered with shoes.
Yet, lamenting that the karmic conditions for the Five Lamps (Wudeng) were steep and perilous, he remarked: "For those of superior capacity, the truth is right before one's face."
I have accordingly compiled this. It covers ten days of instruction in their entirety.

For those of middling and inferior capacity, who face silver mountains and iron walls where even a hair’s breadth is as vast as ten thousand miles, I have transcribed and abridged these teachings—from the time of a certain Buddha down to the successor of a certain person—totaling several generations and several hundred people, arranged into several fascicles.
This is intended so that everyone may understand them clearly, thereby serving as a cause for their own realization. Furthermore...
The Dream Divine Teaching, titled *The True Lineage of the Chan School*, has been carved into woodblocks and circulated. How magnificent this is!
Once the book was completed, [the Master] arrived at my door carrying his staff to request a preface. Alas, I am already in my dotage;
how could I possibly suffice to compose a preface for this book? Nevertheless, looking up with reverence—
Since the Buddha-dharma was first transmitted to China during the Yongping era of the Han dynasty, the Chan school has pervaded the entire world.
From the Buddhas and patriarchs down to those who have received its transmission, it has passed from the single lamp to the inexhaustible lamps.
Up to the present day, two thousand years having elapsed, there have been [successive masters] in every generation.
The Golden Wheel [of Sovereignty] deeply believed and thoroughly understood this, giving rise to joyful inspiration and causing the golden ramparts to resound with brilliance.

Reaching unto our Great Ming’s Founder, the August Emperor Taizu Gao, who was sagely, divine, martial, and civil, he ruled over both the Chinese and the barbarians, establishing stupas and raising victory banners.
The Imperial Edicts are celestial verses that elevate the people to the realm of benevolence and longevity and bring the world to a state of harmonious prosperity.

Emperor Taizong Wenhuang, succeeding to the throne to maintain the legacy of his ancestors, was reverent, enlightened, and contemplative, his brilliance extending to the four quarters of the universe.
The Sage Ruler governs through non-action; he composes verses in praise and hymn. The Buddha’s radiance shines forth.

We reverently consider how Your Majesty succeeded to the Great Jewel, a sage of gentle and respectful virtue, who exerts himself with vigor to seek good governance, bringing the four seas into harmonious union.
The Buddha-Sage has returned; the Buddha-Dharma is protected from without; devas and humans offer harmonious praise; and the entire realm enjoys peace and prosperity.
I, a white-haired subject, have requested leave to retire in old age.

Though I have received boundless grace for which I can find no way to repay it, I have found no time for rest. Recently, I was able to survey the authentic lineage of the Chan school, for which I am deeply moved by joy and gratitude.

At some future time, there will surely be those who present this volume to Your Majesty’s discerning gaze, much like the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) compiled during the Jingde era.

However, I do not know who was commissioned by imperial decree to preside over the general compilation and revision, and who concurrently composed the preface and introduction. Although I am old, I am still able [to provide this].
With joyful veneration and reverent silence, they awaited his sublime voice.
On the day before the New Year’s Eve of the third year of the Hongzhi era of the Great Ming (the year of Gengxu),

[this was written by] the Jinshi-degree recipient, Grand Master for Splendid Honor, Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, Imperial Guardian of the Crown Prince, and Minister of the Ministry of Rites.
Preface to the *Zhengmai* (The True Lineage) of the Chan School, composed by the eighty-two-year-old Zou Gan of Hangzhou, formerly serving concurrently as the Left Shushi of the Left Springfang,
retired from office by imperial decree.

Originally, the afflictions and fevers of the triple world incinerate all that is easily ignited; yet the one thing that eternally sustains life persists without extinction throughout billions of kalpas.
If you seek to become a Buddha, nothing is more urgent than realizing the mind. The mind is fundamentally perfected, and its nature is originally wondrous enlightenment.

As many as the sands of the Ganges River all possess the Tathāgata; the myriad paths and thousand trails all return to concentration and wisdom. If you seek the Buddha outside the mind, how [can you ever find him]?
Some treat the dust of heterodox cooking as the nature of porridge; others seek the ultimate truth abroad, blowing sand into their skulls to make a meal.
To be able to cause Bodhi to penetrate through and the mani-jewel to shine brightly, clarifying the source and expanding the lineage to enlighten the śramaṇas—this is indeed difficult.
Yet, from our Śākyamuni Buddha down to the Patriarch Bodhidharma, the sublime path was widely proclaimed; it has already been made manifest in the Western Regions.
The teachings were clearly expounded and gradually spread to the Eastern Lands. Therein, the doctrine of non-triplicity was revealed and the gate of non-duality was opened.

The joy of dhyāna became ever more manifest, and the patriarchal style flourished widely. It guided and enlightened the multitude of delusions and cut off all false imaginings; thus, the myriad paths converged in a single return.

First, it is due to Prajñā (Wisdom). From this arose the Dharma-eye of the Mí-yáng and Yún-mén schools, extending to the five schools of Cáo-dòng and Líng-jì, each of which attained Buddhahood and became patriarchs.
They had dharma heirs spanning one, two, or even several generations—up to ten or a hundred generations—who likewise transmitted their lineages and branches.
Thus, lamp followed lamp in succession, and bowl passed to bowl in inheritance. Listen to this!
The Master’s transmission was to investigate the intent of other monks. This is like holding up a bright mirror that reflects forms upon encountering objects;

it is like administering an efficacious medicine that treats illnesses according to their specific conditions. At home, he wielded the torch of wisdom to illuminate sentient beings on the path of delusion; among men, he steered the vessel of compassion.
To ferry the multitudes across the ocean of enlightenment—this is the purpose for which this orthodox lineage of the Chan school was established.

As for "Chan," it is called a "school" (*zong*) because it is the realization and verification of the pearl of the wondrous mind. As for "lineage" (*mai*), it is called "orthodox" (*zheng*) because it eliminates heterodox paths outside the Way.

The public cases (*gongan*) are made clear, and the stages are distinguished; the overgrown weeds of scriptural texts are cut away, and the entanglements of words and letters are severed. It extensively adopts the sudden...
The *Jianzhuan miaoyan* (Gradual Sublime Sayings) alone propagates the profound meaning of the dialogues; it is truly the "Southern Chariot" for the realm of Chan and the "Arsenal" of the Zen school.
As for Master Yan, he has captured its brilliant splendor, casting its contents into vessels and bowls, carving them upon woodblocks, and printing them for the world.
I solicited funds from others and labored for several years until, in a single day, I completed my studies; my heart was truly filled with joy.

I questioned those who were ignorant and deluded, yet my own ignorance remained vast and empty like a waveless sea; it was easy to sink into the ocean of suffering, and I had not yet glimpsed the seal of realization within True Suchness (Tathatā).

My aspirations were still burdened by the dust and grime of worldly defilements. As for regarding the South as sacred and the North as foolish, turning one’s back on the North to face the South—this is a great awakening.
One may enter. Facing north with one's back to the south, those who are dull-witted and lacking in clarity—such as this student of the Buddha—have attained the essential realization of Mahākāśyapa;
why must they necessarily be members of the monastic order to emulate Fēnggān’s loquaciousness?
Preface to the *Chan Zong Zheng Mai* (The True Lineage of the Chan School) by Xu Dunxing of Min Prefecture, composed in the early autumn of the Yisi year of the Wanli era.
It cites that in the Gengwu year of the Jingtai era, the monk Konggu went to Mount Xiujī to study Chan; this mountain is located to the west of Hangzhou.

At Hushang. Previously, the Master had been accumulating conditions for his propagation of the Dharma in our prefecture. One night, while conversing in the mountain hermitage, [Hushang] was able to attend closely to the Master’s forge.
One day he asked the Master, "What is the meaning of the 'exposed pillar'? The Master remained silent for a long while and said, "This is that which cannot be spoken of."
He departed from that assembly. Subsequently, in the Gengyin year of the Chenghua era, the Master passed away at the age of forty-six.

He had also been critically ill and revived once more; during this interval while he was bereft of his protector, he first devoted himself single-mindedly to the Pure Land, encouraging others to recite the Buddha’s name.
He accumulated two hundred hu of rice by chanting one name for every grain of rice, and for three years he provided for the assembly. He also printed several tens of thousands of images.

I have been engaged with this for fifteen years, yet it remains unfinished to this day. Recently, while in Hangzhou, I happened to read the *Wudeng Huiyuan* (Compendium of the Five Lamps), though I did not manage to complete the volume.

Now, by chance, I have obtained the opportunity to read it through; seeing that my late teacher, Master Konggu, had personally added punctuation and commentary to it, how fortunate I am to encounter this!
A mixture of emotion and trepidation welled up within me. However, as the karmic conditions for this text are steep and perilous, I must proceed with great care.
The volumes of these texts are vast and extensive. Among them, those of superior capacity grasp the meaning immediately upon encountering it;

they are like ten suns shining at once, which is to say, the high radiance descending upon a secluded valley, or a long wind traversing the great void. As for the rest—the followers of middling and inferior capacities—[the path is otherwise].
A silver mountain and an iron wall; a hair’s breadth becomes ten thousand miles. Neglecting one's own person, one gives rise to false understanding and considers it established.
For this reason, I have set my mind to transcribing and compiling [these texts] for easy consultation. Some may say: "I have set aside my brush due to a hand ailment for forty years;
decrepit and senile, I am no longer fit to handle pen and ink. To all such claims, I reply: No. (Bing year)
On the first day of the middle month of the twelfth lunar month, I began transcribing [the texts] by day and reviewing them by night.
Upon reaching the passage concerning Du Hong’s visit to Chan Master Wuzhu, when a crow cawed in the courtyard tree, he attained realization—what is called "finding the point of entry."

"It was not through my own awakening. Because of this, he further strengthened his resolve and said to himself, "If it were not for the inspiration and exhortation provided by my late teacher while he was still alive, how could there be the achievements of today?
He then reflected again, "The essential collection of teachings has indeed accorded with the Buddha’s intent.
What title should be given to this compilation? That night, as if hearing a divine voice, he heard it say, "The True Lineage of the Chan School. Upon waking, he marveled at this. First...

The Buddha said: "You listen to the Dharma with a conditioned mind; this Dharma is also conditioned. Observing it in this way, one finds that the spirit (*ātman*) is the self (*ātman*), and the self is the spirit.

Dream and non-dream are two yet one. How much more so when considering the very life-vein of the Buddhas and Patriarchs since the beginning of the assembly—what we today call the true lineage of the Chan school.
For this reason, I have carefully set forth these inverted reflections on the application of the mind.

It was not to be so. Others remarked, "If this collection is not transmitted, it will be as good as non-existent. Thereupon, he urgently commanded that those of like mind and virtue at Xingsheng Monastery transcribe it into volumes.
He solicited contributions from those who share his *siddhānta* to fund the carving of the printing blocks, so that its transmission might be widely disseminated. At that time...
On the first day of the eleventh month of winter in the year of Jisi (1489) during the Hongzhi era of the Great Ming,
Ruji of Jiahe respectfully records this preface on the Ancient Opening of the Illumination: Reading the True Lineage of the Chan School—
The Coming West of Bodhidharma.
Master Mazu addressed the assembly, saying in brief: "Bodhidharma came from the West to transmit the Dharma of the Supreme Vehicle, the One Mind, so as to bring you all to awakening.
He further cited the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* to seal the mind-ground of sentient beings."
Guizong Heshang said, "It is not that the ancient worthies of old lacked understanding; they were men of noble character who did not conform to the common run.
People of the present day cannot achieve self-reliance and instead waste their time in vain. Yongquan said, "Understanding..."
In general, you must know how to penetrate through language; if your realization is not complete, I can guarantee that you will remain in the cycle of birth and death. Why is this so?
It is because the outflows of consciousness have not yet been exhausted. You need only exhaust them in this very moment, and only then will you achieve true establishment.

When there was something to discuss, Zhaozhou Zen Master said: "Brothers, do not stand for long. If there is something to discuss, let us talk; if there is nothing, sit beneath your robes and bowls and exhaustively investigate the principle.
Zen Master Huanglong Nan told Ciming: "This mind of mine is not yet settled; I beg you to point it out for me."
Ciming said, "Since it is thus, let us sit and deliberate.
[He] deeply investigated the grand regulations.
The ancient Chan Master Jianfu once studied under Daguang Xuanfu and Yan’ya, yet none of them satisfied his mind. Thereupon...
He remained silent throughout the entire day, deeply investigating the grand regulations of the former masters. One day, while reading the words of Yunmen,
he suddenly attained awakening and found the point of entry.
Chan Master Dahuī said: "I left home at the age of thirteen and have known of this matter since early on.
Although I was in a village temple, I constantly sought to purchase the recorded sayings of various masters to read them.
Though I had not yet fully mastered their principles, I took great pleasure in the words of Yunmen and Muzhou. You all must first find a point of entry; once you have found that point of entry..."

"Head! You must not let the old monk down. (He said at length: "I have told you clearly and plainly, yet you still do not understand; how much less could you grasp it if I were to conceal it from you?"
Gradually, there was the monk Kaikō Kokuku, who asked: "Please tell me of your master’s realization, so that it may serve as a standard for this degenerate age. Kokuku replied:
"I visited Nan'oku Koko and various other masters of wisdom; they all instructed me to investigate Zhaozhou’s 'Mu' (No). After a long time..."
I had no sense of realization. However, upon casually encountering the living function of the patriarchs within the *Wudeng Huiyuan*, my mind gradually began to open and expand.
"I have already recognized the functional pivot of the ancients," I said. I asked again, "May I read the *Renyantianmu* and the *Biyanyiji*?"
Śāriputra said, "It may be so.
Vimalakīrti said, "This Dharma cannot be attained through seeing, hearing, perceiving, or knowing; yet it is not apart from seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing."
It cannot be attained. Upon reaching this point, you must know that there is a single path of life. If you recognize this path of life, the Dharma will reside within you;
though the speed of realization may differ, the result remains the same.
The Elder said, "This plot of land has been entrusted to you for a long time already; I shall stand here waiting for you to grasp it.
The Ancient Pagoda Master said, "Those of sharp faculties attain liberation at that very moment;
those of dull faculties may take three or five years, but not more than ten. If you do not awaken, I will send you to the Hell of the Plucked Tongue. *Investigate!*
Mazu was constantly practicing seated meditation at Mount Heng. Nan Yue once instructed him by using the example of polishing a brick to make a mirror, saying:
"If you cling to the form of sitting, you do not understand its principle. The Patriarch said: "To cling to it is to lose the proper measure; one will inevitably fall into [delusion]."
[He was like one] on a deviant path; let him be free and at ease, for his essence has neither going nor staying. Miaoxi said: "I only want you to have Chan while walking and Chan while sitting;
whether speaking or remaining silent, moving or still, may your essence remain tranquil. Everywhere else, they say one must first achieve stillness before awakening;

I, however, say one must first awaken before achieving stillness. I dare not deceive you: when unawakened, the mind-consciousness flies about in confusion; once awakened, it becomes perfectly settled."

If you do not understand the Great Principle, Master Deshan said: "Even if you were to pass through the belly of a Buddha, you would still only be one who can 'practice'—you have never encountered the true person.
As soon as you meet that good person, you will immediately recognize the light at the gateway of the six sense organs."
Yingxiang said, "Recite the *lùbù* (proclamation) from within your mouth; these are hidden words and wondrous phrases, brilliant and fresh.
But alas, you yourself have no share in them. O benevolent one, these are merely the spittle of others. Yuantong said, "If the eye of the Way is not yet clear, what use is there?
You must earnestly investigate this when you have nothing else to do. Xuansha said, "If the eye of the Way is not clear, it is the root of birth and death."
Regarding the statement that "the source must not be broken," Master Huanzhu said:
"The various venerable masters of previous generations never once spoke of 'working on the kung-fu' (making effort). Only..."
This is a single *pāyattika* offense, intended to bring about realization upon hearing these words.

Furthermore, it is said that when the ancients applied their minds to studying this Way, they spoke of it as "applying effort" (*gongfu*). This description is most appropriate, yet students generally treat this term [as a mere technicality].

Regarding the question, "Seeking realization at the point of inquiry," it is said that people of old questioned because they were deluded; therefore, they sought entry into realization through their inquiries.

Upon obtaining even a single word or half a phrase, they took it as the subject for investigation, striving until they attained thorough penetration. This was not like the people of today who ask recklessly and answer off the cuff, only to invite ridicule.
The meaning of this "Selected Collection" (Jianji) is as follows:
because the *Wudeng Huiyuan* (Compendium of the Five Lamps) is vast and difficult to read, it contains many kōans (jiyuan) that are steep, perilous, and rise like cliffs ten thousand fathoms high.
Those of superior capacity can grasp it at a glance, while those of middling or inferior capacity are left at a loss.
For this reason, I have selected only those passages that are clear and straightforward so that people may easily understand them; my choices were not fixed, but rather compiled into this volume.

For instance, in the *Huìyuán Běnjí* (Original Collection of the Huìyuán Era), regarding several individuals such as Chan Master Fǎróng of Niútóu Mountain, they are all collectively titled "Chan Master Dàyī, the Fourth Patriarch," with their dharma heirs branching out from him.
Prior to this, within the *Zhengmai* (Orthodox Lineage), each of the Fourth Patriarchs was marked with a secondary branch extending from the main trunk; others may be inferred by analogy.

The sermons delivered in the hall (*shàngtáng*) are extremely pertinent to people; I have therefore briefly added headings according to my humble judgment, much like a historical chronicle, to facilitate their investigation.
This compilation, titled *Jiyi Wudeng Huiyuan*, has been produced by eliminating the superfluous and adhering to the essential; I have not dared to make any alterations whatsoever.

Among the accounts of miraculous circumstances at birth and the records of visits and dialogues, I have not dared to include those that were overly prolix. Nevertheless, there are instances where the material has been condensed for the sake of brevity.
The point of engagement.
To experience the karmic conditions and observe the karmic conditions, one must look at where the master poses the question and how the student answers. How is it so? How is it so?
That is not so; there is naturally a point of entry. Once one has found this point of entry, how could there be anything steep, perilous, abrupt, or obscure?
One should apply it as appropriate to the occasion.
Whenever a "Critique" (評) is appended to a kōan (機緣), it refers to the critical commentary (評唱) by Master Yuanwu.

If a "Verse" (頌) is appended, it indicates that such a verse exists within the *Sunggu Lianzhu* (Jeweled Necklace of Verses on Ancient Cases), or that although it appears in a collection of kōans or verses, it was not included in the *Huiyuan* (會元).

If the meaning and phrasing are perfect and subtle, it shall be marked as "Added and Collected" (增收). As it is said, "A crane looks toward the eminent stream," one should establish great resolve; one must not be careless or hasty.

One must thoroughly investigate and mutually elucidate the various collections of ancestral verses on ancient cases, the *Biyan ji* (Blue Cliff Record), and the *Rentian yimu* (Eye of the Human and Heavenly Eye);
this has been the consistent precedent throughout past and present.

Someone said: "The *Wudeng Huiyuan* (Compendium of the Five Lamps) is the very marrow of the Buddhas' and patriarchs' minds. Who would dare recklessly distinguish between superior and inferior, such that its selections and exclusions lack fixed criteria?
I replied: "Do you not see that the *Wudeng* [Record] was the work of the five schools? It is now being made into a 'Compendium' (*huiyuan*)."
In the *Biyanji* (Blue Cliff Record), only one hundred ancestral cases were selected.

As for the *Chanzong songgu lianzhu tongji* (Comprehensive Collection of Linked Pearls of Zen Ancestral Verses), more than four hundred people composed verses and compiled them. Did they not know that there were seventeen hundred virtuous teachers?
It is like being at the point of death; one must seek a remedy that provides immediate efficacy. This is my own abbreviated collection.

There is no other reason. Whenever I see my fellow students, I fear they will not look at this because it is too voluminous; I am truly concerned that the Great Dharma might become obscured and diminished.
Therefore, I have strenuously compiled this work so that it may be easily consulted and mastered, enabling those who enter the gate of awakening.
Would they not then consider me not to be in the wrong? This is precisely what Master Zhenglu’an meant when he said: "Whether they understand me or condemn me, let it be only this collection."

The True Lineage of the Chan School, Volume One:
The Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Śākyamuni Buddha [Verse]: Immediately upon his birth, he pointed one finger toward heaven and one finger toward the earth, and walked seven steps.
After taking seven steps, he looked around in the four directions and said, "In the heavens above and on the earth below, I alone am the Honored One. (Later Yunmen said:

"If I had seen him at that time, I would have struck him dead with a single blow and fed him to a dog, just to ensure peace throughout the world. [Commentary] [Verse]: One day the World-Honored One ascended the seat. When the great assembly had gathered and settled, Mañjuśrī struck the gavel and said:
"Observe closely the Dharma of the Dharma-King; such is the Dharma of the Dharma-King. Thereupon, the World-Honored One descended from his seat.
In the past, when Mañjuśrī arrived at the assembly place of the Buddhas, he encountered the Buddhas each returning to their own abodes.
There was only a single woman sitting near that Buddha, having entered into samādhi. Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Why is it that this person is permitted to sit near the Buddha while I am not? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "You need only awaken this woman and cause her to emerge from samādhi."
He emerged from his meditative absorption. "Ask her yourself," [the Buddha] said. Mañjuśrī circumambulated the woman three times and snapped his fingers once;

he then supported her and carried her up to the Brahma Heaven, yet despite exhausting all his supernatural powers, he could not bring her out. The World-Honored One said, "Even if there were hundreds of thousands of Mañjuśrīs, they likewise would be unable to bring this woman out of her concentration.
Below here, past lands as numerous as the sands of forty-two Ganges Rivers, there is a..."
The Bodhisattva Wuming was able to bring this woman out of her samādhi.

In an instant, the Mahāsattva Wuming emerged from the earth, prostrated before the World-Honored One, and the World-Honored One commanded Wuming to come forth. Wuming then returned to the woman’s side and snapped his fingers once.

The woman then emerged from meditative concentration. [Verse: World-Honored One, because King Prasenajit asked whether conventional truth exists within ultimate truth—if one says it does not exist, then wisdom should not be dual;
if one says it does exist, then wisdom should not be unitary.

"As for the meaning of 'one' and 'two,' what is its significance? The Buddha said, 'Great King, in the past, under the Dharma of the Buddha Dragon-Light (Nāgaprabha), you once asked about this very meaning.
Now I have nothing to say, and you have nothing to hear. This absence of speaking and absence of hearing is what is called the meaning of one and the meaning of two.
[Verse: World-Honored One, because of the question from a non-Buddhist, you were asked: 'What Dharma did you preach yesterday? You replied: 'I preached the Dharma of concentration.'"
The non-Buddhist said, "What dharma did you teach today? [The Buddha] replied, "The indeterminate dharma. The non-Buddhist said, "Yesterday you taught the determinate dharma;
why do you teach the indeterminate dharma today? The World-Honored One said, "Yesterday was determinate; today it is indeterminate. [Verse: The World-Honored One.
Because a rishi possessing the five supernatural powers (pañcābhijñā) asked: "The World-Honored One possesses six supernatural powers, while I possess only five.
What is that one power? The Buddha called to the rishi of the five powers, who responded, "Yes. The Buddha said, "What is that one power? You ask me. [Verse:
The World-Honored One, because the Bodhisattva Universal Eye (Samantacakṣus) wished to see Samantabhadra but could not find him, even entering [samādhi] three times...
In concentration, he surveyed the trichiliocosm, yet could not find Samantabhadra anywhere; he then returned and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Simply give rise to a single thought within the stillness of samādhi, and you shall see Samantabhadra.
Thereupon, as soon as Wanshan (Universal Eye) gave rise to a single thought, he saw Samantabhadra riding upon a six-tusked white elephant in the sky. [Verse] The World-Honored One, because of...
On the day of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, Mañjuśrī had spent the summer retreats in three places. Kāśyapa intended to strike the gavel to expel him;
as soon as he raised the gavel, he saw hundreds of thousands of millions of Mañjuśrīs. Kāśyapa exhausted all his supernatural powers, yet he could not lift the gavel.
The World-Honored One then asked Kāśyapa, "Which Mañjuśrī do you intend to expel? Kāśyapa was speechless. [Verse: The World-Honored One, because of Long-Nail...
The brahmin sought to debate the meaning of the Dharma, making a prior agreement, saying: "If my thesis falls, I shall cut off my own head. The World-Honored One asked:
"What is the fundamental tenet of your thesis? The brahmin replied: "My tenet is that not a single thing is accepted.
The World-Honored One asked: "Is this view itself accepted? The brahmin flung his sleeve and departed. Having traveled halfway, he realized his error and said to his disciples: "I must return."
"Go! Behead yourself to apologize to the World-Honored One. His disciple said, "Before the assembly of devas and humans, it would be fortunate indeed to achieve victory;
why then behead yourself? Zhì replied, "I would rather be beheaded before those who possess wisdom than achieve victory before those who lack it.
He then sighed and said, "In my doctrine, I have failed in both respects. This view, if accepted, is a coarse gateway to defeat. This is the view [of the self].
"I do not accept it; my position is subtle at the point of defeat. No one among gods, humans, or those of the two vehicles knows where my meaning falls into error;
only the World-Honored One and the great Bodhisattvas know where my meaning falls. Returning before the World-Honored One, he said, "My argument has fallen into defeat at two points;
therefore, I shall cut off my head to apologize. The World-Honored One said, "In my Dharma, there is no such thing as this. You..."

They turned their hearts toward the Way; thereupon, together with five hundred followers, they all simultaneously threw themselves at the Buddha’s feet to leave the household life and attained the fruit of Arhatship.

[Verse] World-Honored One, once there was a non-Buddhist who asked: "I do not ask about speech, nor do I ask about silence. The World-Honored One remained silent for a long while. The non-Buddhist praised him, saying:
"The World-Honored One is of great kindness and great compassion; he has dispelled the clouds of my delusion and enabled me to attain [enlightenment]."
He entered, performed a prostration, and departed. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "By what principle did the outsider gain such conviction that he praised [the teaching] and departed?
The World-Honored One said, "It is like a fine horse that moves at the mere sight of the shadow of the whip. [Verse: One day the World-Honored One commanded Ānanda.

"The time for the meal is approaching; you should enter the city with your alms bowl. Ānanda assented. The World-Honored One said, "Once you have taken up your bowl, you must follow the ritual of the seven Buddhas of the past.
Ānanda then asked, "What is the ritual of the seven Buddhas of the past?
The World-Honored One called out, "Ānanda! Ānanda assented. The World-Honored One said, "Go with your bowl. The World-Honored One.
Because there was a bhikṣu who asked: "In the Dharma of the World-Honored One, I see that while there is a place for abiding, there is as yet no place for realization.
What will the World-Honored One show me? The World-Honored One said: "Bhikṣu [Name], what will you show me? This is your question."

[Verse] The World-Honored One, on account of the brahmin Kāla, exercised his supernatural power and, with his left and right hands, held up two *saṃyūka* trees to offer as an act of worship to the Buddha.
The Buddha called out to the rishi, and the brahmin responded, "Yes. The Buddha said, "Put it down."
The Brahmin then lowered the flower from his left hand. The Buddha again called out to the immortal, "Lower it.
The Brahmin then lowered the flower from his right hand. The Buddha again called out to the immortal, "Lower it.
The Brahmin said, "World-Honored One, both my hands are now empty; what more do you command me to lower? The Buddha said, "I am not commanding you."
"Cast away those flowers. You should cast away the six external objects, the six internal faculties, and the six intermediate consciousnesses all at once.
When there is nowhere left to abandon, that is your place of liberation from birth and death. At these words, the Brahmin realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

[Verse] At the assembly on Vulture Peak, there were five hundred bhikṣus who had attained the four dhyānas and possessed the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), yet they had not yet attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).
Using their supernormal power of knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*), each beheld their own past:
having killed their fathers, harmed their mothers, and committed various grave offenses. Within their own minds, each harbored doubts and was unable to enter into realization of the profound Dharma.
Then Mañjuśrī, receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power, took up a sharp sword in his hand and approached the Tathāgata with it.
The World-Honored One said to Mañjuśrī: "Stop, stop! You should not commit such a transgression. Do not harm me. If I am to be harmed, let it be for the sake of goodness that I am harmed.
Mañjuśrī, from the very beginning you have had no self or person; it is only because of your internal mind that you perceive them as existing."
When the notions of "self" and "person" arise within the mind, the self is inevitably harmed; this is precisely what is called "harm. Thereupon, five hundred bhikṣus praised him in unison, saying:
"Mañjuśrī, the Great Sage of Wisdom, has profoundly penetrated the very source and bottom of the Dharma.

Though he personally grasps a sharp sword and presses it against the body of the Tathāgata, the sword and the Buddha are likewise identical. They are of one single mark and not two; they are without marks and without arising. This is...

The middle [section] asks: "What is killing? [Verse: The World-Honored One struck a skull and asked Jīvaka, "To which realm was this person reborn? He replied, "Reborn in the human realm. He struck another and asked, "To which realm was this person reborn?
He replied, "Reborn in the heavens. He struck yet another; Jīvaka was at a loss for an answer. [Verse: The World-Honored One, based on his past causes.
Draping his hair over the mud, he offered flowers to Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
Seeing where the hair had been spread, Dīpaṃkara signaled for the assembly to withdraw and pointed to the ground, saying, "In this spot, a Brahma-shrine (stūpa) should be erected.

At that time, there was an elder among the assembly named Bhadra who took a measuring-staff and, planting it at the indicated spot, declared, "The construction of the Brahma-shrine is complete. Then the devas scattered flowers and praised him, saying, "May..."
"You possess great wisdom. [Verse] World-Honored One, because of the seven virtuous women who were wandering in the Śītavana cemetery, one woman pointed to a corpse and said, "The corpse is here;
where has the person gone? Another woman said, "How? How? Sisters, observe closely! Each of them attained realization.
Moved by this, Śakra devānām indra scattered flowers and said, "I pray only that the noble sisters will tell me what you require."
"I shall provide for you for the rest of my life. The woman said, "In my home, the four requisites and the seven treasures are all fully provided.
I require only three things: first, a single rootless tree; second, a patch of ground where neither sun nor shade exists;
third, a mountain valley that does not echo when one calls into it. Śakra said, "I possess everything that is required. As for these three things—"
[Śakra] said, "I truly have nothing. The woman said, "If you have nothing, how can you understand how to save others?
Śakra was at a loss; he then went together with her to inform the Buddha. The Buddha said, "Kauśika, even my great disciples, the Arhats, do not understand this meaning.
Only the great Bodhisattvas understand this meaning. [Verse: To the east of the city there was an old woman who [offered food] to the Buddha.
They were born together, yet he did not wish to see the Buddha. Every time the Buddha approached, he would immediately turn away to avoid him.

Nevertheless, wherever he looked toward the east or west, everywhere was the Buddha. He then covered his face with his hand, only to find that within the palms of his ten fingers, everything was likewise the Buddha.
[Verse] When Aṅgulimāla went to the gate of a householder’s home carrying his alms bowl, it happened that the woman of the household was just...
There was a woman in difficult labor whose child and mother had not yet separated. An elder said, "Gautama’s disciple, you are a most holy one;
what dharma do you possess that can spare her from the perils of childbirth? Yaśoda replied to the elder, "I have only recently entered the Path and am not yet aware of this dharma.
Wait while I return to ask the World-Honored One, and I shall come back to inform you. Upon his return, he related the matter in detail to the Buddha. The Buddha told Yaśoda: "You..."
"Go quickly and report this, saying: 'Since I have followed the Dharma of the Worthy and Holy Ones, I have never killed a living being.
Aṅgulimāla, having received the Buddha’s words, went swiftly to inform her. Upon hearing this, his wife gave birth at that very moment. [Verse: The World-Honored One arrived before the Cāpāla Shrine.
He commanded Mahākāśyapa to share his seat and sit beside him, then wrapped him in his saṃghāṭī robe and said:
"I entrust the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to you in secret; you must protect and uphold it, and transmit it to future generations. [Verse:
As the World-Honored One was about to enter nirvana, the Great Being Mañjuśrī requested the Buddha to turn the Wheel of Dharma once more. The World-Honored One rebuked him, saying: "Mañjuśrī, I—"
He dwelt in the world for forty-nine years and never spoke a single word. You requested that I turn the Wheel of Dharma once more;
did I ever turn the Wheel of Dharma? [Verse] At the assembly of his parinirvāṇa, the World-Honored One rubbed his chest with his hand and addressed the multitude, saying:
"You all should carefully contemplate my body, which is the color of purple-polished gold. Gaze upon it until you are fully satisfied; do not let yourselves fall into regret later.
If you say that I have entered parinirvāṇa, you are not my disciples; if you say that I have not entered parinirvāṇa, you are likewise not my disciples.
At that time, the assembly of ten billion beings all attained realization.
The First Patriarch, Venerable Mahākāśyapa [Verse]: Seeing the World-Honored One at the assembly on Vulture Peak, he held up a flower to show the multitude.
At that time, the assembly remained silent; only Kāśyapa broke his countenance with a smile. The World-Honored One said:
"I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa, the subtle and wonderful Dharma-gate of the true mark which is formless. It does not rely on words or letters."
The Outer Separate Transmission. Entrusted to Mahākāśyapa (the verses differ slightly from the ancient versions).

The Second Patriarch, Venerable Ānanda [Verse]: One day he asked Kāśyapa, "Elder brother, apart from the golden-threaded *kaṣāya* robe that the World-Honored One transmitted, what else did he transmit separately?
Kāśyapa called out, "Ānanda! Ānanda responded, "Yes? Kāśyapa said:
"Knock down the banner-pole in front of the gate!
When the Venerable Fourth Patriarch Upagupta was guiding beings in the world, those who realized the fruits of the path were most numerous; he would, on average, deliver one person at a time.
He placed one tally inside the stone chamber; that chamber was eighteen cubits long and twelve cubits wide, and it became completely filled with them.
Finally, there was the son of a householder named Gandhamādana, who came to pay his respects to the Venerable One and sought to leave the household life.

The Venerable One asked, "Have you left the household life with your body, or have you left the household life with your mind? He replied, "I have come to leave the household life not for the sake of body or mind.

The Venerable One said, "If it is not for the sake of body or mind, then who is it that leaves the household life? He replied, "As for leaving the household life, it is because there is no 'self' and no 'mine.
Because there is no self and no mine, the mind does not arise or cease. That the mind neither arises nor ceases is itself the eternal Way. Thus he spoke.

The Buddha is also eternal; the mind has no form or characteristics, and its essence is likewise so. The Venerable One said: "You shall attain great awakening; the mind will naturally reach full realization.
You should rely upon the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, and continue to uphold the lineage of the Sages."
The Eighth Patriarch, Venerable Buddhānandi [Verse]. The Ninth Patriarch, Puṇyamitra, asked the Patriarch:
"If parents are not my kin, who is the most intimate kin? If the Buddhas are not my Way, who is the most supreme Way?
The Patriarch answered in verse: "That which you speak is more intimate than the mind; parents cannot be compared to it. That which you practice accords with the Way; the Buddhas..."
The mind is it. To seek outwardly for a Buddha with form is not like you. If you wish to recognize your original mind, it is neither joined nor separate.
When the Tenth Patriarch, Venerable Xi, arrived at a forest grove, Pūrṇayaśas stood before him with palms joined. The Patriarch—
The Master asked, "From where have you come? Śa said, "My mind does not go. The Master said, "Where do you dwell? He replied, "My mind does not stay. The Master said, "Are you not settled?
He replied, "All Buddhas are likewise so. The Master said, "You are not the Buddhas. He replied, "The Buddhas are also not [the Buddhas].
The Master knew he was a vessel for the Dharma and immediately granted him the tonsure and ordination. He transmitted the Dharma to him, speaking this verse: "The True Body..."
Spontaneously true; because it is true, its explanation possesses principle. Having realized the truly true Dharma, there is neither practice nor cessation.
The eleventh patriarch, the Venerable Punyayaśas, subsequently traveled to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, where there was the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa.
He went forward to pay his respects and asked, "I wish to recognize the Buddha; which one is he? The Patriarch said, "If you wish to recognize the Buddha, it is that which you do not recognize.
He asked, "Since I do not recognize the Buddha, how can I know it is him? The Patriarch said, "Since you do not recognize the Buddha, how can you know it is not him?
He said, "This is the meaning of the saw. The Patriarch said, "That is the meaning of the wood. The Patriarch then asked, "What is the meaning of the saw?"
Baizhang said, "I will go out with you on equal terms. Maming turned his horse and asked, "What is the meaning of 'wood'? Baizhang replied, "You have been explained by me.
At these words, Maming attained sudden and thorough enlightenment.
The Fourteenth Patriarch, Venerable Nāgārjuna, arrived in South India. The people of that country mostly placed their faith in meritorious deeds.

The Patriarch preached the Dharma for them, whereupon they said to one another, "When a person possesses meritorious deeds, they are foremost in the world; yet to speak merely of 'Buddha-nature'—who can actually perceive it?
The Patriarch replied, "If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, you must first eliminate your *asmimāna* (self-conceit). The people asked, "What is Buddha-nature?"
"Large or small? The Patriarch replied, "Neither large nor small; neither broad nor narrow; no merit and no retribution; neither death nor birth.
Hearing these superior principles, they all returned to their original resolve. The Patriarch then manifested a body of sovereign mastery from his seat, like the orb of the full moon;
the entire assembly heard only the sound of the Dharma, but could not see the Patriarch’s form. Among that assembly was the son of an elder named...
Kāṇadeva addressed the assembly, saying, "Do you recognize this sign? The assembly replied, "We have never beheld such a sight with our own eyes; how would we dare to identify it?
Kāṇadeva said, "This is the Venerable One manifesting the essential form of the Buddha-nature to show us. How do we know this?
It is because, through the samādhi of formlessness, his physical appearance is like the full moon. The meaning of the Buddha-nature is vast, empty, and luminous. Thus he spoke.
When he had finished, the wheel-mark vanished and he returned to his original seat, where he spoke this verse: "The body manifests the form of the full moon to represent the essence of all Buddhas;
the preaching of the Dharma has no fixed form, serving to discern that which is neither sound nor color. Upon hearing this verse, the assembly suddenly attained the realization of non-arising.
The Fifteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kanadeva [Verse]: He went to visit the Great Being Nāgārjuna.
As he was about to reach the gate, Nāgārjuna, knowing him to be a man of wisdom, first sent his attendant to place a bowl filled with water before the seat. When the Venerable saw it, he...

He immediately cast a single needle into it and proceeded; they joyfully reached a state of accord. When the Patriarch arrived at the kingdom of Kapilavastu, there was an elder named Brahmā-Śuddhodana.
One day, fungi grew upon the trees in his garden, and their flavor was most exquisite.
Only the elder and his second son, Rāhula-bhadra, took them and ate them; once taken, they grew back immediately, and when they were finished, they grew again.
He was reborn again, yet none of his other relatives were able to see him. His grandfather, knowing the cause from his past life, went to his house.
The elder then asked for the reason, and the grandfather said: "In the past, you once made offerings to a bhikṣu. However, this bhikṣu’s insight into the Path was not yet clear;
because he had received the offerings of the faithful in vain, his retribution was to become a wooden fungus. Only you and your son have offered with sincere devotion."
Only those who have been nurtured may partake of it; others cannot. He then asked the elder how old he was.
The elder replied, "I am seventy-nine. Thereupon, the Patriarch spoke a verse: "If one enters the Way without penetrating its principle, He returns to this world to consume the faithful offerings.
When you reach eighty-one, This tree will no longer grow. Having heard the verse, the elder was even more deeply moved and filled with admiration, saying, "Disciple..."
He was aged and infirm, unable to serve his teacher. He wished to relinquish his second son so that he might follow the teacher and leave the household life.
When the seventeenth patriarch, the Venerable Saṃghanandin, arrived at the kingdom of Mathurā while traveling to transform beings, he saw a youth in a mountain hut holding a round mirror.
The youth went straight before the patriarch. The patriarch asked, "How old are you? He replied, "One hundred years. The patriarch said, "You..."
[The Master] was still young in years. "How can you speak of a hundred years? The boy said, "I do not understand the principle; it is simply a hundred years.
The Patriarch asked, "Are you skilled in the pivot [of the teaching]? The boy said, "The Buddha said:

'If a person lives for a hundred years, yet does not understand the pivot of all Buddhas, it is not as good as living for a single day and attaining decisive realization. The Patriarch asked, "What does that which is in your hand signify? The boy said, "All..."
The Buddha is a great, perfect mirror, without flaw or obscuration within or without; two people may see it together, for their eyes and minds are alike.

When his parents heard their son’s words, they immediately relinquished him to let him leave the household life. The Patriarch took him to his original location, and after bestowing the full precepts upon him, named him Gayāśata.
At another time, hearing the sound of wind blowing through the palace bells, the Patriarch asked, "Are the bells ringing, or is the wind ringing?"
Śātavāhana said, "It is not the wind-bells that ring; it is my own heart that rings. The Patriarch asked, "And who is it that has this heart?
Śātavāhana replied, "Because all is utterly tranquil. The Patriarch said, "Excellent, excellent! Who else but you could succeed to my Way?
He then transmitted the Dharma-eye to him."
The nineteenth patriarch, Venerable Kumāralata, arrived at the kingdom of Central India. There was a mahāsattva named Jayata who asked:
"In my family, our parents have long been faithful to the Triple Gem, yet they are constantly afflicted by chronic illness. Whatever they undertake,"
Everything has turned out contrary to my wishes. Yet my neighbor has long followed the occupation of a *caṇḍāla*, yet his body is always vigorous and healthy, and whatever he undertakes succeeds.
How fortunate he is, and how undeserving of such misfortune I am! Zu said: "Why should you have any doubt? Furthermore, the retribution for good and evil occurs across three periods of time.

When ordinary people see only that the benevolent die young while the violent live long, or that the rebellious meet with auspicious fortune while the righteous suffer calamity, they immediately conclude [that there is no karmic consequence]."
"Causes and effects, as well as emptiness, sin, and merit—do you not realize that they follow one another like shadows and echoes, without the slightest deviation?
Even after passing through hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, they shall never perish. When Śāṇakavāsin heard these words, his doubts were suddenly dispelled. The Patriarch said:

Although you have already placed faith in the three karmas, you have not yet clarified that karma arises from afflictions (*kleśa*), afflictions exist because of consciousness (*vijñāna*), and consciousness depends upon non-awakening (*avidyā*).
This non-awakening depends upon the mind (*citta*). The mind is fundamentally pure; it is without arising or ceasing, without fabrication, without retribution, and without victory or defeat.
It is profoundly still and luminously aware. If you enter this Dharma-gate, you may become one with all Buddhas. One.

"All things—good and evil, conditioned and unconditioned—are like dreams and illusions. Śāṇakavāsin received these words and grasped their essential meaning; immediately, his latent wisdom was awakened.
The Patriarch then transmitted the Dharma-eye to him, saying in verse: "In the nature, there is originally no arising; It is spoken only in response to those who seek it.
Since nothing can be attained within the Dharma, Why harbor doubts about what is or is not resolved? He further said: "This is the realization of the nature of reality by the Tathāgata Subhūti."
[End of] sentence. You should propagate this for future students.
The twentieth patriarch, Venerable Jayata, was a native of Northern India. His wisdom was profound and deep;
he transformed and guided immeasurable beings. Later, he arrived at the city of Rājagṛha and propagated the Sudden Teaching. There, the assembly of students valued only dialectical debate. For...
The foremost among them was named Vāsula (translated as "Pervasive Practice"). He never lay down for even a single moment and performed prostrations to the Buddha during all six periods of the day.
Pure and free from desire, he was one to whom the assembly looked for guidance. When the Patriarch was about to ordain him, he first asked the assembly:
"This ascetic Vāsula is able to cultivate the Brahma-faring; can he attain the Way of the Buddha? The assembly replied: "Our teacher is diligent; why would he not [attain it]?"
"Very well," said the Patriarch. "Your teacher is far removed from the Way. Even if he were to practice asceticism for kalpas as numerous as dust motes, it would all be rooted in falsehood.
The assembly asked, "What virtues and conduct does the Venerable One possess that you should disparage our teacher? The Patriarch replied, "I do not seek the Way."
"I am neither inverted. I do not pay homage to the Buddha, nor do I treat him with contempt. I do not sit in perpetual meditation, nor am I indolent.
I do not eat only once a day, nor do I eat at irregular intervals. I am not content, yet I have no craving; that the mind has no expectations is called the Way.
When Pūrvavīta heard this, he gave rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), and with joy he offered praise. The Patriarch spoke again:
The assembly asked, "Did you understand my words? The reason I acted thus was because his desire for the Way was so earnest. Now, when a string is too tight, it snaps;
therefore, I did not praise him, but rather caused him to abide in a state of peace and joy and enter the wisdom of all Buddhas.
He then addressed Viśvāmitra, saying, "I have just now, before this assembly, rebuked you, O virtuous one. Did this not cause distress in your heart? Viśvāmitra replied, "I..."
I recall that seven kalpas ago, I was born in the Land of Constant Peace and Bliss under the teacher Jñānacandraviśuddha. He prophesied that before long I would realize the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāprabhāsa appeared in the world; because I was old, I leaned on a staff to pay my respects to him.
The teacher rebuked me, saying, "To honor the son while slighting the father—how can this be so base? At that moment, I thought to myself that I was without fault.

"Your transgression! I request that the Master instruct me on this. The Master said: "You prostrated to the Bodhisattva Mahāprabha while leaning a staff against the wall and drawing a Buddha’s face upon it.
Because of this arrogance, you lost two fruits of the path. Since I have taken responsibility for myself and repented my error, I have heard these various harsh words."
"Like the wind, like an echo—how much more so now that you have obtained the drinking of the unsurpassed nectar of immortality; how could you instead give rise to feverish affliction?
I only pray that, out of great compassion, you will instruct me with the wondrous Way. The Patriarch said, "You have long planted manifold virtues and shall succeed to my lineage.
Listen to this verse of mine: 'In a single word, one accords with the unborn; it is identical to the nature of the Dharma-realm. If one can understand it thus, one will penetrate all phenomena.'"
The principle has been concluded.
When the twenty-third patriarch, Venerable Helu, was seven years old, he was wandering through a village and beheld the vulgar sacrifices of the common folk.
He entered the temple and rebuked them, saying: "You recklessly instigate calamities and blessings to delude and confuse people. Year after year you waste livestock and slaughter animals."
The harm was extreme. Having finished speaking, the temple structure suddenly collapsed. Consequently, the local community called him the "Holy Child" (Shengzi).
There was a lion that took refuge with the Venerable One and asked, "I wish to seek the Way; what state of mind should I employ? The Patriarch said:
"You wish to seek the Way, yet you have no application of mind. The monk asked, "If there is no application of mind, who performs the Buddha-work?
The Master said, "If you have any application, it is not merit. If you have no action, that is itself the Buddha-work. As the sutra says:
"The merits I have performed are without the notion of 'mine'. Upon hearing these words, Siṃha immediately entered the wisdom of the Buddha.
The twenty-fourth patriarch, Venerable Siṃha, having attained the Dharma, traveled abroad and arrived at the kingdom of Kaśmīra.

There was one named Parika who had originally practiced dhyāna-vipaśyanā; thus, he possessed five groups of followers: those with meditative concentration, those with insight, those who clung to signs, those who abandoned signs, and those who remained silent.
The Patriarch interrogated and transformed them; the four groups were all silent and submitted in their hearts, but only the master of meditative concentration, Dharmadatta, remained.
When he heard that the fourfold assembly had been rebuked, he came in a state of indignation and frustration. The Patriarch said, "Virtuous one, you are practicing dhyāna; why have you come here?
Now that you have arrived here, how can you say you are practicing dhyāna? He replied, "Although I have come here, my mind is not disturbed.

Dhyāna follows the person who practices it; how could it have a fixed location? The Patriarch said, "Since you, Virtuous One, have come, your practice has also arrived. Since there is no fixed location," [the practice] is likewise present.
"Is it not that the person practices the concentration? The other said, 'It is because the person practices concentration; it is not that concentration practices the person.

When I come here, that concentration will be constantly practiced. The Master said, 'It is not that the person practices concentration; it is because concentration practices the person. When you come here of your own accord, who will be practicing that concentration?'"
He said, "Like a pure, bright pearl, with no obscurity within or without; if concentration (*samādhi*) is thoroughly penetrated, it must necessarily be like this.

The Patriarch said, "If concentration is thoroughly penetrated, it is indeed like a bright pearl. But as I now behold you, you are not of the class of pearls. He said, "That pearl is luminously transparent;
both within and without it is entirely settled. My mind is undisturbed, just like this purity. The Patriarch said, "That pearl has no interior."
[The Master] said, "Externally, O Benevolent One, how can you be fixed? Impure things do not move; this fixation is not purity.
Dharmada, having received the teacher’s awakening, his mind became brilliantly clear. Since the Patriarch had gathered the five assemblies, his fame spread far and wide. [Verse]:

Because the King of Kaśmīra took up his sword and went before the Venerable One, he asked, "Has the Master attained the emptiness of the aggregates? The Patriarch replied, "I have already attained the emptiness of the aggregates."

"Empty," [the Master] replied. The King asked, "Are you free from birth and death? The Patriarch said, "I am already free from birth and death. The King said, "Since you are free from birth and death, you may give me your head.
The Patriarch said, "This body is not mine; why begrudge my head? The King then brandished his blade and severed the Venerable’s head.
White milk gushed forth several feet high, and the King’s right arm immediately fell to the ground as well.
The twenty-seventh patriarch, Venerable Prajñātāra, was a native of Eastern India. While traveling to propagate the Dharma, he arrived at South India.
Its king was named Gandhāra; he venerated the Buddha-vehicle and honored him with offerings that surpassed those of all others.
Furthermore, he bestowed upon him a priceless jewel. At that time, the king had three sons: Candravairocana, Guṇavairocana, and...
Bodhitāra was the youngest of them, a bodhisattva. His grandfather wished to test what he had attained, so he took the pearls that had been offered and asked the three princes:
"These pearls are perfectly round and luminous; is there anyone who can equal them? The first prince and the second prince both said, "These pearls are the most honored among the seven treasures;
certainly none can surpass them. Were it not for the power of your majesty's Way, who could [do so]?"
He accepted them. The third prince said: "This is a worldly treasure; it is not yet supreme. Among all treasures, the Dharma-treasure is supreme.
This is a worldly light; it is not yet supreme. Among all lights, the light of wisdom is supreme.
This is a worldly clarity; it is not yet supreme. Among all clarities, the clarity of the mind is supreme. These various lights do not..."
It can illuminate itself, yet it must rely on the light of wisdom; it is through this light that it is discerned. Once it has been discerned, one knows it to be a pearl;

once it is known to be a pearl, its value as a treasure is clarified. If its value as a treasure were inherent, the treasure would not be a treasure by itself; if the pearl were discerned by itself, the pearl would not be a pearl by itself.

That the pearl is not a pearl by itself means that it must rely on the "wisdom-pearl" to discern the worldly pearl; if the treasure were not a treasure by itself, [it too would require such discernment].
This requires relying upon the jewel of wisdom to illuminate the jewel of the Dharma. Thus, when the teacher possesses the Way, that jewel immediately manifests;
when sentient beings possess the Way, the jewel of the mind is likewise so. The Patriarch praised his discernment and wisdom, and then asked again: "Among all things..."
"What thing is signless? He replied, "Among all things, that which does not give rise to signlessness. Again he asked, "Among all things, what is the highest?
He replied, "Among all things, the person-self (*pudgala-ātman*) is the highest. Again he asked, "Among all things, what is the greatest?
He replied, "Among all things, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is the greatest. [Verse] Because the Patriarch was invited by the King of East India...
During a vegetarian feast, the King asked the assembly, "Everyone here is reciting sutras; why alone does the Master not recite?
The Patriarch replied, "This poor monk, when exhaling, does not follow external conditions; when inhaling, he does not dwell within the aggregates or realms.
He constantly recites such a sutra—hundreds of thousands of millions of scrolls, not merely one or two."
The Great Master Bodhidharma was the third son of King Xiangzhi of South India.
His clan was Kṣatriya, and his original name was Bodhitāra. Later, he encountered the twenty-seventh patriarch, Prajñātāra, who arrived in his native land and received offerings from the king.
Recognizing the Master’s secret character, the king tested him by having him distinguish between the precious pearls bestowed upon his two elder brothers.
He elucidated the essential points of the mind. Subsequently, the Venerable One said to him, "Regarding all dharmas, you have already attained thorough penetration (*pramāṇa*).
Now, 'Dharma' carries the meaning of 'thorough penetration. It is fitting that you be named Dharma. Consequently, he changed his name to Bodhidharma.
The Patriarch then addressed the Venerable One, saying, "Now that I have obtained the Dharma, to which country should I go to perform the Buddha-work? I pray that you will grant me your instruction."

The Master said, "Although you have attained the Dharma, you must not travel far yet. Stay for now in the Southern Heaven and wait until sixty-seven years after my passing; then you shall go to China.
There, you shall administer the great medicine of the Dharma, directly reaching those of the highest faculties. Be careful not to travel too soon, lest you suffer decline under the sun.
Bodhidharma respectfully received these instructions and served at his side with diligent devotion for nearly forty years, never once neglecting his duties. When the time arrived...
The Venerable Śūṇatāta subsequently propagated the teachings in his native land. At that time, there were two masters: the first was named Buddhadasa, and the second was named Buddhasena.
Originally, they had studied the Hinayana dhyāna and contemplation with their teacher, Buddhabhadra. As for Buddhadasa...
Having encountered the Venerable Prajñātāra, he abandoned the Lesser Vehicle and turned toward the Great Vehicle, whereupon he and the Patriarch transformed beings together;

at that time, they were known as the "Two Gateways to Ambrosia. However, Buddhabhadra’s followers further divided into six schools. The first was the School of Manifest Characteristics (*Lakṣaṇavāda*).
The second was the School of Signlessness; the third, the School of Concentration and Wisdom; the fourth, the School of Preceptual Practice;
the fifth, the School of Non-Attainment; and the sixth, the School of Quiescence. Each clung to their own understanding and separately expanded the source of their conversion.

As monasteries rose up like rugged peaks and their followers became exceedingly numerous, the Patriarch sighed deeply and said: "If even one teacher among them has already fallen into the hoofprint of an ox, how much more so when such fragmentation and proliferation have arisen?"
These were divided into six schools. [The Master said,] "If I do not eliminate them, they will be forever entangled in false views. Having spoken thus, he subtly manifested his supernatural powers.

He proceeded to the school of the School with Characteristics (*sanimitta-vāda*), and so on, until he reached the school of the School of Quiescence (*śānta-vāda*). There, the respective masters, upon hearing the Teacher’s instructions, attained sudden and complete enlightenment.

Soon thereafter, the group of six disciples all vowed to take refuge [in the Triple Gem]. From this, the transformation spread throughout Southern India and its fame resounded across the five regions of the Indian subcontinent.
Over the course of sixty years, they delivered immeasurable multitudes. [Verse: Later, they encountered King Vikramāditya, who held the Triple Gem in contempt and disparaged it.

Consequently, he questioned the Venerable Prajñātāra (the head of the Formless School): "What is the Buddha? The Master replied: "To see one's own nature is to be the Buddha. The King asked: "Does the Master see his own nature?"
"No," [the Master] said. "I have seen my Buddha-nature. The King asked, "Where does this nature reside? He replied, "The nature resides in its functioning. The King asked, "What is this functioning?
I do not see it now. He replied, "It is functioning right now; it is simply that you yourself do not see it. The King asked, "Does it exist within me?
He replied, "If you were to function, there would be nothing that is not it. If you do not function, its substance is difficult to perceive. The King...
He asked: "When it is put to use, in how many places does it appear? He replied: "When it appears, there are eight instances. The King said:
"Please explain to me these eight instances of its appearance. Pāṭaliputra then spoke in verse: "In the womb it is the body; in the world it is the person.
In the eye it is called seeing; in the ear it is called hearing. In the nose it discerns fragrance; in the mouth it engages in discourse. In...
Holding it in his hand, he ran with it at his feet; it manifested everywhere, encompassing all *sāhasra* worlds, yet was withdrawn into a single atom.

Those who recognize it know it as Buddha-nature; those who do not recognize it call it a wandering spirit. Upon hearing these verses, the King attained immediate enlightenment, repented of his former errors, and offered his apologies.
The Patriarch thought that the conditions for China were now ripe and the time for his mission had arrived; he thus set sail across the vast ocean, making three [voyages].

Enduring the cold and heat of the journey, he arrived at the South Sea. It was indeed the twenty-first day of the ninth month in the seventh year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty, the gengzi year.
Xiao Ang, the Regional Inspector of Guangzhou, received him with the highest honors and submitted a memorial to Emperor Wu.
Upon reading the petition, the Emperor dispatched an envoy bearing an imperial decree to invite him. On the first day of the tenth month, he arrived in Jinling. The Emperor asked: "I am about to..."

"Since ascending to the throne, I have built monasteries, transcribed scriptures, and ordained monks beyond counting. What merit do these constitute? The Patriarch replied, "There is no merit whatsoever.
The Emperor asked, "Why is there no merit? The Patriarch said, "These are merely the minor fruits of the realms of humans and devas;
they are causes of outflow (*āsrava*). Like a shadow following a form, though they exist, they are not real. The Emperor asked, "What, then, is true merit? The Patriarch said:

Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect; its essence is inherently empty and still. Such merit is not to be sought through worldly means. [Commentary] [Verse]: The Emperor again asked, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths?
The Patriarch said, "Vast emptiness—there is no sage. The Emperor said, "Who is it that faces me? The Patriarch said, "I do not know. The Emperor did not attain realization.

(The *Sung-ku* [Verses on Ancient Cases], Part I, states: The Master then broke off a reed and crossed the river to reach Wei. Later, the Emperor raised this question with Master Chih, who said, "Your Majesty...")

"Do you recognize this person? Baizhang replied, "I do not. Baizhang said, "This is the Great Being Avalokiteśvara; he transmits the Buddha’s Mind-Seal. Baizhang said, "You should send an imperial edict for him. Baizhang continued, "Do not speak of an imperial edict from Your Majesty; even if people from the entire kingdom were to go, he would still not return.

Realizing his opportunity was not met, the Patriarch secretly returned north of the Yangtze River. Upon arriving at Luoyang, it was the first year of the Zhengguang era of Emperor Xiaoming of the Wei dynasty.
He took up residence at Shaolin Temple on Mount Song, where he sat facing a wall, remaining silent throughout the day. People...

No one could fathom him; he was called the Wall-Gazing Brahmin. [Verse] At that time, there was a monk named Shen Guang who had recently heard that the Great Being Bodhidharma was residing at Shaolin.
Thinking, "The Sage is not far away; I shall go to that profound realm," he went there and attended upon him morning and evening.
The Patriarch constantly sat upright facing the wall, and no instructions were heard. Shen Guang reflected to himself: "Those of old who sought the Way..."

"Beating the bones to extract the marrow; piercing the blood to relieve hunger; spreading one's hair to cover the mud; throwing oneself from a cliff to feed a tiger—ancients were like this. What person am I, then?
On the ninth night of the twelfth month of that year, it rained and snowed heavily.
Guǎng stood firm and did not move. By dawn, the accumulated snow had risen above his knees. The Patriarch, taking pity on him, asked: "You have stood long in the snow; what do you seek?"
Master Huiguang wept with compassion and said, "I only pray that the Upādhyāya will, out of his great kindness, open the gate of ambrosia to widely deliver all classes of beings.

The Patriarch replied, "The unsurpassed, wondrous Way of the Buddhas requires diligent effort over vast kalpas; one must be able to perform what is difficult to do and endure what is difficult to endure.

How can you, with such meager virtue and limited wisdom, and with a frivolous and arrogant mind, hope to attain the True Vehicle? Your diligent toil would be in vain. When Master Huiguang heard this from the Patriarch...
The Master exhorted him. [Huike] secretly took a sharp blade and severed his own left arm, placing it before the Master. The Master, knowing he was a vessel for the Dharma, said:
"When the Buddhas first sought the Way, they forgot their very forms for the sake of the Dharma. Now that you have severed your arm before me, your seeking is indeed permissible.
The Master then changed his name to Huike and asked: "May I hear the Dharma-seal of all Buddhas?"
The Patriarch said, "The Dharma-seal of all Buddhas is not obtained from others. Huik'e said, "My mind is not yet at peace; I beg the Master to bring it to peace for me.
The Patriarch said, "Bring forth your mind and I will bring it to peace for you. After a long while, Huik'e said, "I have searched for my mind, but it is utterly unobtainable. The Patriarch said:
"I have finished settling your minds for you. [Verse] Nine years later, wishing to return to India, he addressed his disciples, saying:
"The time has come; why do you not each speak of what you have attained? At that time, Dao Fu replied: "As I see it..."
"One does not cling to words and letters, yet one does not depart from words and letters to employ them as the Way. The Patriarch said, "You have obtained my skin.
Nini Tongzhi said, "What I now understand is like Ānanda seeing the land of Akṣobhya Buddha: having seen it once, there is no need to see it again."
The Patriarch said, "You have obtained my flesh. Daoyu replied, "The four elements are fundamentally empty;

the five aggregates do not exist, and in my field of vision, there is not a single dharma to be attained. The Patriarch said, "You have obtained my bone. Finally, Huik’e performed a prostration and stood in his place.
The Patriarch said, "You have obtained my marrow. He then turned to Huik’e and told him: "In the past, the Tathāgata..."
With the Eye of the True Dharma, it was entrusted to the Great Being Kāśyapa, passed down through successive transmission until it reached me.
I now entrust it to you; you must protect and uphold it. I also grant you this robe as a token of the Dharma. Each has its own symbolic significance, which you should understand.

[The disciple] said, "I pray that the Master will explain this. The Patriarch said, "Internally, the Seal of the Dharma is transmitted to accord with and realize the Mind; externally, the robe is bestowed..."
The *kāṣāya* robe was used to establish the fundamental tenets. In later generations, when people became shallow and insincere, doubts and suspicions arose in competition with one another:
"You are a man from the Western Heaven; they say you are a native son of this land. On what basis did you obtain the Dharma? By what do you certify it? You must now receive this robe and the Dharma.

In the future, it will be difficult for [the truth] to arise. Simply bring forth this robe along with my dharma-verses to manifest [the teaching]; thus, your transformation of beings will be unimpeded.

Two hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, the robe shall cease to be transmitted, while the Dharma will pervade the entire realm of saṃsāra. Those who clarify the Way will be many, but those who practice the Way will be few;

those who expound the principles will be many, but those who penetrate the principles will be few. There will be more than ten million who secretly accord with and secretly realize [the truth]. You...

"You must propagate [this teaching]. Do not slight those who have not yet awakened; with a single thought, they may turn their faculties toward the source and be identical to their original attainment.

Listen to my verse: 'I originally came to this land To transmit the Dharma and save deluded beings. One flower opens into five petals; The fruiting of the result is accomplished naturally. The Patriarch further said:
'I also have four fascicles of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* which I likewise entrust to you; this is the essential teaching on the Mind-ground of the Tathāgata."
Gate! I have caused all sentient beings to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter it. Since I arrived here, I have been poisoned five times. I have personally tested this myself:

when I placed a stone upon it, the stone shattered. Because I originally departed from South India to come to this Eastern Land and saw that the Great State of China possessed the majestic atmosphere of the Mahāyāna, I crossed the seas and deserts to seek you out for the sake of others, meeting with you at this opportune moment.
[The transmission] was not yet harmonized. [Huike] was as if dull-witted and stammering. Now that I have obtained your transmission, my intention is fulfilled. (A separate record states:
