When the Patriarch first resided at Shaolin Temple for nine years, he preached the Dharma for the Second Patriarch, teaching only: "Externally, cease all conditions; internally, let the mind be without breath. Let the mind be like a wall or a screen, and you may enter the Way. Huike spoke variously about the nature and mind, but never once accorded with the principle.

The Patriarch merely refuted his errors and did not explain the essence of the non-conceptual mind. Suddenly, Huike said, "I have already ceased all conditions. The Patriarch asked, "Have you not fallen into annihilationism? Huike replied, "It is not annihilationism. The Patriarch said, "This is the essence of the mind transmitted by all Buddhas; do not harbor further doubt.")
Having spoken thus, he sat upright and passed away. [Verse: He was buried at Xiongeri Mountain, and a stupa was erected at Dinglin Temple.

Three years later, Wei Songyun, while on an imperial mission to the Western Regions, encountered Sengzhuo on the Pamir Mountains. He saw him walking alone with a single shoe in his hand, striding lightly as he departed.
Songyun asked, "Where is the Master going? Sengzhuo replied, "I am going to the Western Heaven. Upon returning, Songyun related these events in detail when he reached the gate.
When the tomb was opened, there was only an empty coffin; a single pair of leather sandals remained. The entire court was struck with wonder and admiration.
By imperial decree, the sandals were taken from Shaolin Temple to be enshrined for veneration. Initially, when Emperor Wu of Liang met the Master, their karmic affinity had not yet been realized.

Later, upon hearing that the Master’s transformation was spreading in the Wei state, he wished to compose an inscription for the Master’s stele but lacked the leisure. Subsequently, he heard the account of Song Yun.
Thus it was accomplished. Emperor Daizong posthumously conferred upon him the title of Great Master Yuanjue (Perfect Enlightenment), and his stupa was named Kongguan (Contemplation of Emptiness).
The details regarding Great Master Huike’s attainment of the Dharma and the transmission of the robe are fully contained in the chapter on Bodhidharma.

Since the Master entrusted his transformation at Shaolin and returned to the West, he continued to propagate the profound wind of the Dharma and extensively sought dharma-heirs. [Verse] Reaching the second year of the Tianping era of the Northern Qi dynasty.

In that year, there was a layman over forty years of age whose name and lineage were not recorded. He came to pay his respects and asked the Patriarch, "I, your disciple, am afflicted by a wind-related ailment;
I beg the Master to help me repent for my transgressions. The Patriarch said, "Bring forth your transgressions, and I shall repent them for you."
The layman remained silent for a long while and then said, "I have searched for my transgression, but it cannot be found. The Patriarch said, "I have finished repenting your transgressions for you;

you should now dwell in accordance with the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. The layman said, "Now that I see the Master, I already know what the Sangha is; I only wonder what is meant by 'Buddha' and 'Dharma'. The Patriarch replied:
"This mind is the Buddha; this mind is the Dharma. The Dharma and the Buddha are non-dual; so too is the Sangha Jewel.
The man said, "Today I have finally realized that the nature of sin is neither within, nor without, nor in between. It is just as this mind is: the Buddha-Dharma is non-dual.
The Patriarch regarded him with deep esteem and immediately shaved his head, saying, "He is my treasure. He should be named Sengcan."
He received full ordination at Guangfu Temple. From that time on, his illness gradually improved. After serving him for two years, the Patriarch said to him:
"Bodhidharma came from afar from India and secretly entrusted to me the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, along with the robe of faith."
"I now entrust this to you; you must protect and preserve it so that it does not come to an end.
Master Sengcan first visited the Second Patriarch while still a layman. Having received ordination and the transmission of the Dharma, he lived in seclusion at Mount Wangong in Shuzhou.
During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Later Zhou, who suppressed the Buddha-dharma, the Patriarch traveled to the region of Taichou County.
He dwelt in the empty mountains, his residence never fixed, for more than ten years. At that time, no one was able to recognize him.
[Verse] In the twelfth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, the year of Renzi, there was a novice named Daoxin, fourteen years of age, who came to pay homage to the Patriarch, saying:
"I pray that you, O Upādhyāya, will out of compassion grant me the Dharma-gate of liberation. The Patriarch asked, "Who has bound you? He replied, "No one has bound me.

The Patriarch said, "Why then do you seek liberation? At these words, Huineng attained great enlightenment. He served the Patriarch for nine years, during which time the Patriarch repeatedly tested him with profound and subtle matters.
Knowing that his karmic conditions were ripe, he then entrusted him with the robe and the Dharma. The Patriarch’s *Xinxin Ming* (Inscription on Faith in Mind) says: "The Ultimate Way..."

There is no difficulty; it is simply that you dislike discrimination. Just do not harbor likes or dislikes, and all will be transparently clear. A difference of even a hair’s breadth results in a gap as vast as heaven and earth.
If you wish to attain realization in the present moment, do not maintain notions of favorability or opposition. To contend with such notions of compliance and resistance is the sickness of the mind.

Failing to recognize the profound essence, you labor in vain by merely contemplating stillness. Perfectly identical to the great void, there is neither deficiency nor excess. It is solely due to grasping and rejecting that this is so.
It is not so. Do not pursue that which has conditions; do not dwell in the patience of emptiness. With a single, even-mindedness, all is naturally exhausted.

Cease movement by returning to stillness; yet stillness itself further intensifies movement. To remain stuck in either extreme, how can one know the One Kind? If the One Kind is not penetrated, both sides fail in their function.
To dispel existence and non-existence is to follow emptiness and turn one’s back on emptiness. Excessive words and excessive thoughts only lead further away from accord. Cut off speech.

Cut off all deliberation; there will be nowhere it does not penetrate. Return to the root to attain the essential meaning; follow the illumination and you lose the source. A moment of returning-illumination surpasses the previous emptiness.

That the previous emptiness underwent transformation was entirely due to deluded vision. Do not seek the Truth; simply require the cessation of views. When these two views do not abide, be careful not to pursue them.
As soon as right and wrong arise, one becomes distracted and loses the mind. The two exist because of the one; the one also...
Do not cling. When the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault. Where there is no fault, there are no dharmas; where there is no arising, there is no mind.
If the capacity can cause objects to cease, then objects will follow the capacity and sink away. Objects exist because of the capacity for objects; the capacity exists because of objects.

If you wish to know these two segments, they are originally one emptiness. This one emptiness is identical to the two, equally encompassing the myriad phenomena. Seeing neither essence nor coarseness, how could there be partiality? This is the Great Way.

The essence is vast; there is neither ease nor difficulty. With narrow views and doubt, one becomes increasingly anxious and increasingly sluggish. To grasp it is to lose the proper measure and inevitably enter a deviant path.
To let it be naturally is for the essence to have neither departure nor abiding. To follow one's nature accords with the Way; to roam freely brings an end to affliction.
To fixate the mind violates the truth; to be muddled and heavy is not good. Do not weary your spirit; what use is there for partiality? If you wish to attain the One Vehicle, do not harbor aversion.
The six sense objects are not inherently evil; they are identical to perfect enlightenment. The wise remain in non-action, while the foolish bind themselves.

There is no dharma apart from the Dharma, yet they delusively cling to it with their own minds. To employ the mind by means of the mind—is this not a great error? Delusion gives rise to stillness and turmoil, while awakening is free from likes and dislikes. All dualistic extremes arise from one’s own deliberations.
They are like dreams, illusions, or flowers in the sky—what need is there to grasp at them? As for gain and loss...
Right and wrong—let them all be cast aside at once. If the eyes do not sleep, all dreams vanish of their own accord; if the mind does not vary, the myriad dharmas are as one.
This oneness of suchness is profound and mysterious; in its state of stillness, one forgets all conditions. Viewing the myriad dharmas as equal, one returns to spontaneity.

When that which causes [the distinction] is extinguished, it can no longer be compared to anything. In the cessation of movement there is no movement; in movement there is no cessation. Since both are unestablished, how could there be "one"?
It is so. Reaching the ultimate limit, no rules or regulations remain; the mind accords with equality, and all activities cease.

Doubts are completely purified, and right faith becomes upright and straight. Nothing is retained; there is nothing to be remembered. Empty clarity illuminates itself without taxing the power of the mind.
This is not a place of discursive thought, difficult for the conscious intellect to fathom. In the *tathatā* dharma-realm, there is neither other nor self. It is urgent.
It is in accord; it is simply called non-duality. Where there is no duality, all are identical. There is nothing that is not encompassed. The wise of the ten directions all enter this school.
This school is neither constricted nor expansive; a single thought-moment is ten thousand years. It is neither existent nor non-existent, yet it is present before the eyes of the ten directions.

The smallest is identical to the largest, as all boundaries and limits are forgotten and severed. The largest is identical to the smallest, as no outer periphery is seen. Existence is itself non-existence; non-existence is itself...
This is existence. If it were not thus, there would be no need for guarding at all. One is all; all is one. If you can simply be like this, why worry about not reaching completion?
The mind of faith is non-dual; non-dual is the mind of faith. The path of language is cut off; it is neither past, future, nor present.

Master Daoxin was born with extraordinary qualities. From his youth, he aspired to the school of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and the various gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*) appeared to him as if they were the result of past cultivation.
Having inherited the legacy of his patriarch, he concentrated his mind without sleep; for nearly sixty years, his side never touched his mat.

Later, while residing at Mount Póshān, students gathered around him like clouds. One day, while traveling to Huangmei County, he encountered a young boy on the road whose physical features were most remarkable.
Xiu was extraordinary compared to ordinary children. His grandfather asked him, "What is your surname? He replied, "I have a surname, but it is not an ordinary one.
The grandfather asked, "What is it? He replied, "It is Buddha-nature. The grandfather asked, "Do you have no surname? He replied, "Because nature is empty, there is none.
The grandfather silently recognized that he was a vessel for the Dharma and immediately instructed his attendant to go to Xiu’s mother and request permission for him to leave the household life.
Because of their past karmic ties, the mother showed no sign of reluctance and eventually gave him up as a disciple. He was subsequently entrusted with the Dharma and the robe.
One day, he addressed the assembly, saying: "In my travels through Mount Lu during the Wude era, I ascended its peak and gazed toward Mount Poutou.
There I saw purple clouds like a canopy, beneath which white vapors split into six horizontal paths. Do you understand this, or not? The assembly remained silent.
Hongren said, "Could this be a case where, after you, Master, a separate branch of the Buddha-dharma will emerge? The Patriarch replied, "It is well.

Later, in the *guimao* year of the Zhenguan era, Emperor Taizong, having heard of the flavor of the Master's Way and wishing to behold his dignified presence, issued an imperial decree summoning him to the capital.

The Patriarch submitted a memorial declining the honor three times in succession, ultimately refusing on the grounds of illness. On the fourth occasion, the Emperor dispatched an envoy with the command: "If it is indeed..."
He did not move. The messenger immediately seized his head and brought it back to the mountain to convey the imperial decree. The Master then extended his neck toward the blade;

his countenance remained solemn and composed. The messenger was struck with wonder and returned to report the circumstances to the Emperor. The Emperor’s admiration increased all the more, and he bestowed upon him precious silks so that the Master’s resolve might be fulfilled.
Master Hongren was a native of Huangmei in Qizhou. [Verse:
Formerly, while serving as a "pine-planting path-guard" at Mount Poutou, he once requested of the Fourth Patriarch, "May I hear the Way of the Dharma? The Patriarch said, "You are already old;
even if you were to hear it, would you be able to transform others extensively? If you should come again, I may yet wait for you. He then departed and walked by the water's edge.

She saw a young woman washing clothes and bowed to her, saying, "May I stay the night? The woman replied, "I have father and brothers; you may go seek them. She said, "If you agree, I shall immediately venture forth.
The woman nodded her head in assent, and she then turned her horse and departed. This woman was Zhou Shi’s younger daughter. Upon returning home, she soon became pregnant.
Her parents detested this greatly and expelled her. Having nowhere else to turn, she went daily to the village to hire herself out for spinning.
In the middle of the day, they stopped for the evening beneath a public shelter. Shortly thereafter, a son was born; considering him an ill omen, they cast him into a muddy harbor.
The next day, they saw him swimming upstream against the current, his physical form radiant and clear. Greatly astonished, they took him up.
When he reached the age of childhood, he followed his mother to beg for food, and the villagers called him "The Child Without Surname. One wise man encountered him and sighed, saying, "This child..."

Lacking seven characteristics, he had not yet attained the state of a Tathāgata. Later, encountering the Great Master with faith, he received the Dharma and succeeded him in propagating the teachings on Mount Pótóu.
During the Xiánhēng era, there was a layman surnamed Lú and named Huínéng, who came from Xīnzhōu to pay his respects.
The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? Lu said, "From Lingnan. The Patriarch asked, "What do you seek? Lu said, "I only seek to become a Buddha.
The Patriarch said, "People of Lingnan have no Buddha-nature; how can you become a Buddha? Lu said, "People may be from the north or the south, but how could the Buddha-nature be like that?
The Patriarch knew he was an extraordinary man and rebuked him, saying, "Go and work in the fodder shed! Lu bowed.
Having bowed his head and withdrawn, he entered the millhouse to perform labor among the pestles and mortars, working day and night without ceasing for eight months.

The Patriarch, knowing that the time for the transmission had arrived, addressed the assembly, saying: "The True Dharma is difficult to understand; it must not be left as mere memorization of my words.
You must take this as your own responsibility. Each of you should compose a verse according to your own inclination. If the meaning of your words accords with the profound essence, then..."
The monastic robes and the Dharma were all entrusted [to him]. At that time, there were more than seven hundred monks in the assembly.

Among them was the Elder Shenxiu, whose learning encompassed both the inner and outer teachings, and whom the multitude revered and looked up to. They all recommended him, saying, "If it were not for the Venerable Xiù, who else would dare to receive this?
Hearing the public acclaim, Shenxiu did not reflect further; he then inscribed a verse upon a wall in the hall, which said: "The body is the Bodhi tree; The mind..."
"It is like a bright mirror stand: at all times diligently wipe it clean, lest it be defiled by dust.

When the Patriarch was walking about and suddenly saw this verse, he knew it was composed by Shenxiu and praised it, saying, "If future generations practice according to this, they too shall attain supreme fruition.
He then ordered everyone to recite it. While Lu was at the mill, he suddenly heard the verse being recited and asked his fellow students, "What is this?"
The chapter and verses. A fellow student said, "You do not know. The Master is seeking a Dharma heir and has ordered each of you to compose a verse expressing your mind.
This is the one composed by Venerable Xiu; the Master has praised it with deep admiration and will surely transmit the Dharma and pass on the robe. Lu said:
"What is that verse? his fellow student asked as he recited it for him. After a long while, Lu said, "It is beautiful indeed, yet its meaning is not fully realized.

The fellow student rebuked him, saying, "How could a person of such mediocre capacity know this? Do not utter such delirious words! Lu replied, "Do you not believe me? I wish to compose a verse in response to yours.
The fellow student did not answer, but merely looked at one another and laughed. That night, Lu secretly told a young boy.
He was led down to the corridor. Master Lu himself held a candle and requested the Vice Prefect Zhang Riyong to write a verse beside Xiu’s verse, which read:
"Bodhi originally has no tree; / A bright mirror is likewise not a stand. / Originally there is not a single thing; / Where could dust and grime settle?
Later, when the Patriarch saw this verse, he said, "Who wrote this? They have not yet seen their nature. When the assembly heard this...
He spoke thus, but Lu did not look back at him. When night fell, the Patriarch went secretly to the rice-hulling shed and asked, "Is the rice white yet?
Lu replied, "It is white, but it has not yet been sifted. The Patriarch struck the millstone three times with his staff. Lu immediately beat the drum three times and entered the room.
The Patriarch said to him, "The Buddhas appear in the world for one great purpose; they guide beings according to their varying capacities."
Consequently, there arose the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and the three vehicles (*triyāna*), along with the principles of sudden and gradual [enlightenment], which served as the gateways for teaching.

Nevertheless, the unsurpassed, subtle, secret, perfectly luminous, and true *Dharmaparyāya*—the Treasury of the True Eye of the Dharma (*dharmadharmacakṣuskośa*)—was entrusted to the preeminent Venerable Mahākāśyapa.
It was transmitted successively through twenty-eight generations until it reached Bodhidharma, who arrived in this land. There, he found the Great Master Ke (Huineng) to inherit it.
Thus it has continued down to the present day. I now entrust to you this Dharma-treasure and the robe I have transmitted;
protect them well yourself and do not allow them to be severed. Listen to my verse: "When sentient beings come to sow seeds, The fruit arises from the ground.

Since non-sentient things have no seeds, That which lacks nature likewise does not arise. The Practitioner Lu received the robe and the Dharma while kneeling and addressed him, saying: "As for the Dharma..."
[He asked,] "To whom shall the robe be given? The Patriarch said, "In the past, when Bodhidharma first arrived, people did not yet believe him;

therefore, he transmitted the robe to manifest that he had attained the Dharma. Now that faith has matured, the robe is merely a source of contention. It shall stop with your person; it will no longer be transmitted."

"For now, we must remain hidden in seclusion, waiting for the time to go forth and transform others. As for those who receive this robe, their lives are as precarious as a thread hanging from a string.
Lu asked, "Where should we hide? The Patriarch said, "When you meet Hui, stop; when you encounter Hui, conceal yourself. After Lu had prostrated at his feet, he took the robe and departed.
That night he traveled south, and none of the assembly knew where he had gone.
When Master Huineng went to Mount Dong at Huangmei, Master Ren saw him once and recognized him in silence.

[Verse] Later, he transmitted the robe and the Dharma, instructing him to conceal them within his breast. After attending the four assemblies, he reached Nanhai, where he encountered Dharma Master Yinzong lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* at Faxon Temple.
The Patriarch stayed among the corridors and eaves; one evening, the wind blew the temple banner.
Regarding the banner: two monks were heard debating whether it was the banner that moved or the wind that moved. They exchanged arguments back and forth, yet neither had grasped the principle.
The Patriarch said, "Can one allow a layman to suddenly interject in such a high-level discussion? It is simply that the wind and the banner do not move; movement arises from the mind itself.
When Imprint Master (Yinzong) overheard these words, he was struck with wonder. The next day, he invited the Patriarch into his room and questioned him.

Regarding the meaning of the wind and the banner, the Patriarch explained it to him in full according to principle. Unconsciously rising to his feet, Yinzong said, "The practitioner is certainly no ordinary person.
Who is your teacher? The Patriarch, having nothing further to conceal, directly recounted the circumstances of how he had attained the Dharma.
Thereupon, Yinzong assumed the etiquette of a disciple and requested instruction in the essentials of Chan. He then addressed the fourfold assembly, saying, "Yinzong was formerly a mere commoner..."
Now, having encountered an incarnate Bodhisattva, he pointed to the layman Lu seated below and said, "This is the very person.

He was then invited to bring forth the robe of transmission he had inherited, which was presented for everyone to venerate. The assembly of eminent and virtuous monks shaved his head for him, and he received the full precepts from Vinaya Master Zhiguang at Faxon Temple.
Later, he returned to Caoxi and rained down the great Dharma rain for those who studied.
There were no fewer than a thousand [monks]. In the first year of the Shenglong era of Emperor Zhongzong, an imperial edict was issued stating:

"I have invited the two masters An and Xiu to provide for them with offerings within the palace. In my leisure from the myriad affairs of state, I have frequently investigated the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).

Both masters declined, saying: 'In the south there is Master Neng, who secretly received the robe and dharma of Great Master Ren; you may go to him to inquire. He then dispatched the inner attendant Xue..."

Jian dispatched an imperial edict to invite him, saying: "I pray that Master Yuan will look upon me with compassion and hasten to the capital. Guishan Zuxian submitted a memorial declining on the grounds of illness, wishing to spend his final years among the forested foothills.
Jian said, "The virtuous Chan masters in the capital all say that if one wishes to realize the Way, one must practice seated meditation and cultivate meditative concentration."
"It has never been the case that one attains liberation without relying on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). I do not yet understand how the Dharma taught by the Master is so different.
The Patriarch said: "The Way is realized through the mind; how could it depend on sitting? A sutra says:
'If one sees the Tathāgata as either sitting or lying down, this is practicing a deviant path. Why? Because he comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; if there is neither arising nor ceasing."
"This is the Tathāgata’s pure meditation; all dharmas are empty and quiescent. This is the Tathāgata’s pure sitting; it is ultimately without realization—how much less can there be 'sitting'?
" Jian said, "When your disciple returns to the Sovereign, he will surely be questioned. I pray that you, Reverend, will out of compassion point out the essential core of the mind.
The Patriarch said, "The Way has neither light nor darkness; light and darkness are merely the meaning of alternation. Light and darkness are inexhaustible, and likewise..."
This is "existence" and "exhaustion. These names are established in mutual dependence. Thus, a sutra says: "Dharmas have no counterpart, for they do not depend on one another.

Jian said: "Brightness is used as a metaphor for wisdom; darkness is used to illustrate afflictions (*kleśa*). If those who cultivate the Way do not use wisdom to illuminate and shatter afflictions, by what means could they escape the birth and death that has no beginning?
The Patriarch said: "Afflictions are themselves bodhi; they are non-dual and non-distinct."
"Distinct. "If one uses wisdom to illuminate afflictions, this is the limited view of the Two Vehicles—the capacity of those such as the sheep and the deer.
Those of great wisdom and superior faculties do not act in this way. Jian asked: "What is the insight of the Mahāyāna? The Patriarch said:
"Luminosity and ignorance—these two natures are non-dual. This non-dual nature is itself the true nature. As for the true nature, it dwells within the foolish and ignorant."
It does not diminish; it does not increase among the worthy and holy; it is not disturbed while abiding in afflictions; it is not quiescent while dwelling in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
It is neither annihilated nor eternal; it neither comes nor goes; it is not in between, nor within or without. It is neither born nor extinguished;
its nature and characteristics are suchness (*tathatā*), eternally abiding and unchanging—this is called the Way (*mārga*). Jian said: "The Master speaks of 'neither born nor..."

"Extinction! How does this differ from the heterodox? The Patriarch said: "What the heterodox call 'neither arising nor ceasing' involves using cessation to stop arising, and using arising to manifest cessation;

thus, although it is cessation, it is not yet truly ceased, and although it is arising, it is called non-arising. What I call 'neither arising nor ceasing' is that which is fundamentally non-arising from the beginning and is likewise without cessation now.
This is why it differs from the heterodox. If you wish to know the essential point of the mind, simply..."

"Do not deliberate at all upon any good or evil. You will naturally enter the essence of the pure mind, which is profoundly still and eternally tranquil, with its wondrous functions as vast as the sands of the Ganges.
Having received this instruction, Jian was suddenly and completely enlightened. He paid his respects and took his leave to return to the capital.
One day, the Patriarch said to the assembly: "All of you, your own minds are the Buddha; do not harbor further doubt. Outside, there is not a single thing."
All that can be established arises from the fundamental mind producing ten thousand kinds of phenomena. Thus the Sūtra says: "When the mind arises, all phenomena arise;

when the mind ceases, all phenomena cease. If one wishes to accomplish the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), one must attain the Samādhi of the Single Characteristic and the Samādhi of the Single Practice.
If, in all places, one does not dwell upon characteristics and does not give rise to hatred or attachment toward those characteristics, nor harbor...

Regarding acceptance and rejection: not dwelling on matters such as gain and loss, success and failure, remaining at ease and tranquil, empty, harmonious, and serene—this is called the Samādhi of One Characteristic.

If, in all places—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—one maintains a purely direct mind, remaining unmoved within the site of enlightenment, truly accomplishing the Pure Land—this is called the Samādhi of One Practice.
If a person possesses these two samādhis, it is like having seeds in the earth.
Just as [the earth] can contain, nurture, and bring to fruition their actual results—being of one mark and one practice—it is likewise with this.
As I now preach the Dharma, it is like seasonal rain that universally moistens the great earth. Your Buddha-natures are like various seeds;
encountering this soaking moisture, they shall all sprout and grow. Those who receive my intent will certainly attain Bodhi; those who follow my practice will surely realize the Sublime.
Fruit. ○ In the first year of the Tianxian era, he addressed the fourfold assembly, saying: "I have been honored by receiving the robe and Dharma of Master Ren.
I now preach the Dharma for you, yet I do not transmit the robe to you. This is because your roots of faith are pure and mature, and you are certain and free from doubt."
"You are capable of great matters. Listen to my verse: 'The ground of the mind contains all seeds; The universal rain causes them all to sprout.
Once the essence of the flowers is suddenly realized, The fruit of Bodhi is spontaneously attained. Having spoken this verse, he further said:
'That Dharma is non-dual, and the mind is likewise so. That Way is pure and free from all marks. You must be careful not to contemplate purity, nor to empty the mind of it.'"
The mind is fundamentally pure; there is nothing to be grasped or rejected. Each person must exert their own effort. Go forth as you please, in accordance with conditions.
Once, a monk cited the verse of Chan Master Wo-lun, which says: "Wo-lun has skillful means; he can sever a hundred thoughts. When facing objects, his mind does not arise."
"Bodhi grows day by day. Upon hearing this, the Patriarch said, "This verse does not clarify the essential point of the mind.
If you practice according to it, it will only add to your fetters. He then showed them this verse: "If wisdom is able to eliminate all skillful means, Yet one does not sever the hundred thoughts;
When encountering objects, the mental states arise— How can Bodhi grow? The Patriarch preached the Dharma to benefit sentient beings for forty years. (The disciples recorded this.)
The catalog was titled the *Platform Sūtra* (Tánjīng) and became widely prevalent in the world. (The first volume of the *Huìyuán* ends here.

A collateral branch emerged from Chan Master Fǎróng of Niútóushān; at the age of nineteen, his learning encompassed the classics and histories, and he subsequently studied the extensive *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras.
He thoroughly understood the ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā*). One day, he sighed and said: "The classics of Confucianism and Daoism are not the ultimate Dharma;
the correct contemplation of Prajñā is the vessel for transcending the world. He subsequently retired to Mount Mao, where he surrendered himself to a master and shaved his head. [Verse:

Later, he entered Niutou Mountain and dwelt in a stone grotto on the northern cliff of Youqi Temple, where there was the marvel of hundreds of birds bringing him flowers. During the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, the Fourth Patriarch...
Observing the atmosphere from afar, he knew there was a person of extraordinary character on that mountain, and so he went in person to seek him out.
He asked the temple monks, "Is there any practitioner of the Way (*daoren*) here? They replied, "Among those who have left the household life, who is not a practitioner of the Way?
The Patriarch said, "Which one among them is the true practitioner of the Way? The monks were speechless. Another monk said, "About ten *li* from here into the mountains, there is a 'lazy' one..."
When Huiming saw him, he did not rise nor join his palms, asking, "Are you perhaps a man of the Way?

The Patriarch then entered the mountain and saw the Master sitting upright and composed, with no concern for anything around him. The Patriarch asked, "What are you doing here? The Master replied, "I am observing the mind."
The Patriarch said, "Observe: what is this person? What is this mind? The Master had no reply; he then rose, prostrated himself, and asked, "Great Virtue, where do you dwell in seclusion?
The Patriarch said, "This poor monk has no fixed abode; sometimes I go east, sometimes west. The Master said, "Do you know Chan Master Daoxin?
The Patriarch asked, "Why do you ask about him? The Master replied, "I have long admired his virtue and hope to pay my respects to him."
He went to pay his respects. The Patriarch said, "I am the Dhyāna Master Daoxin. The Master asked, "For what reason have you come here?
The Patriarch replied, "I have come specifically to visit you. Is there another place where you might rest? The Master pointed to the area behind him and said, "There is a separate small hermitage."
He then led the Patriarch to the hermitage. Upon circling the hermitage, he saw nothing but tigers and wolves. The Patriarch then raised both hands in a gesture of fear.
The Master said, "There is still this [fear] remaining. The Patriarch asked, "What is this? The Master was speechless.

After a short while, the Patriarch sat upon the stone where the Master had been sitting in formal meditation and wrote the character for "Buddha" (佛). When the Master beheld it, he stood transfixed with awe. The Patriarch said:
"There is still this [remaining]. The Master did not yet understand, so he bowed his head and requested an explanation of the essential truth.

The Patriarch said: "Indeed, the hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates all return to the single square inch of the mind. The wondrous virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all rooted in the source of the mind.

All gates of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, as well as supernatural powers and transformations, are entirely and inherently complete within you; they do not depart from your mind. As for all afflictions and karmic obstructions..."
Originally empty and still, all causes and effects are like dreams and illusions. There are no three realms from which to escape, and there is no bodhi to be sought.
Humans and non-humans are equal in their nature and characteristics. The Great Way is vast and open, transcending thought and deliberation.
Such a Dharma as this you have now attained; it lacks nothing. How does this differ from that of the Buddha? There is no other dharma. You need only...
Let the mind be free and at ease. Do not practice contemplative exercises; do not clarify the mind. Do not give rise to greed or anger;
do not harbor sorrow or anxiety. Be vast and unimpeded, moving freely in all directions. Perform neither good nor evil deeds. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—remain thus.
"Whenever one encounters conditions through the senses, it is all the wondrous function of the Buddha; there is joy and no sorrow, and for this reason he is called 'Buddha'.
The Master asked, "Since the mind is already complete, what is the Buddha and what is the mind? The Patriarch replied, "If it is not the mind, do not ask about the Buddha;
if you ask about the Buddha, it is not apart from the mind. The Master said, "Since you do not permit the practice of contemplation, when an object arises before you, how does the mind respond?"

Regarding "treatment" (remedy): The Master said, "Circumstances and conditions have neither good nor bad; good and bad arise from the mind. If the mind does not insist on naming them, from where would deluded feelings arise?
Since deluded feelings do not arise, the true mind is free to know all. You need only follow the mind with ease and freedom; there is no further need for remedies.
This is called the eternally abiding Dharmakāya, which is without change. I received the sudden teaching of Great Master Huicán."
"I now entrust this Dharma-gate to you. You must now receive my words with earnest attention and remain on this mountain alone.

Hereafter, there shall be five men of realization who will carry on your legacy and transform others. Having completed the transmission of the Dharma, the Patriarch returned to Shuangfeng and spent the rest of his life there.
From that time on, the master’s Dharma assembly flourished greatly. During the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty, when the disciples were short of provisions, the master went to Danyang to seek alms.

The mountain was eighty *li* away. He personally carried eighteen *dǒu* of rice, going there in the morning and returning in the evening, providing for three hundred monks without fail at the two meal times for three years.

One day, while Chan Master Zhiryan of Niutou was sitting in meditation, he beheld a strange monk. The monk was over ten feet tall, with a spirit that was exceptionally refined and a voice that was clear and resonant.
He said to the Master, "You have left the household life after eighty lifetimes; you ought to increase your diligent practice. Having spoken, he vanished.
Once, while the Master was in meditative absorption in a valley, the mountain waters suddenly surged in flood. The Master remained serene and unmoved, and the water [subsided] of its own accord.
He withdrew. Later, the Master went to visit Chan Master Rong and had his great matter clarified. Rong said to him, "I have received the true instructions of Great Master Xinxing;
that which I have attained has entirely vanished. Even if there were a dharma superior to nirvana, I would say it is like a dream or an illusion."
"A single speck of dust flying can obscure the sky; a single mustard seed falling can cover the earth. You have now transcended such views—what more need I say?
When Chan Master Tanchui of Zhongshan first visited Master Rong, Rong gazed at him and marveled at his extraordinary nature, then said to him:
"Form and sound are the lethal poison of non-arising; sensation and perception are the pitfall of the perfected man. Do you understand this, my son?

The Master remained silent and reflected deeply upon these words, whereupon he attained a great awakening to the profound principle. He subsequently withdrew from view on Mount Zhong for many years, spending his final days in a thatched hut with an earthenware vessel.
Chan Master Niutou Zhizhi visited Chan Master Fachih and was transmitted the True Dharma. From that time on, disciples from the region east of the Yangtze River all flocked to his gate.
Among them was one named Huizhong, whom the Master regarded as a vessel for the Dharma. The Master once showed him a verse, saying:

"My original nature is empty and non-existent; it is due to delusion that the notions of self and person arise. How can one still these deluded emotions? One must return and sit in the state of emptiness.
Zhong replied, "If emptiness and delusion are the true reality, where do 'self' and 'person' exist? There is no need to still deluded emotions; one should simply board the boat of Prajñā.
The Master knew he had attained realization and entrusted him with the affairs of the monastery. He then traveled according to conditions to transform and guide others.
Throughout his life, Chan Master Niutou Huizhong never changed his single robe. His only utensil was a single cauldron. He once had two storehouses filled with grain for the monks' offerings;

when thieves sought to steal it, tigers guarded it for him. When the district magistrate Zhang Xun arrived at the summit of the mountain to pay his respects, he asked the Master, "How many disciples do you have?
The Master replied, "There are three or five. Zhang Xun asked, "How can I see them? The Master...
He struck the meditation seat, whereupon three tigers roared and emerged. Xun retreated in terror. The Master had a verse on settling the mind that said:
"When both person and phenomena are purified, good and evil are forgotten; with a straightforward and true heart, this is the site of Bodhi."
When Chan Master Xuanting of Anguo first visited Chan Master Wei, he was standing in attendance.
A monk who lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* asked, "What is the meaning of 'dependent origination within true nature'? After a long silence, Master Wei remained still.

Master Xuanting suddenly replied, "Virtuous One, at the very moment you give rise to the thought of asking this question, that is dependent origination within true nature. Upon these words, the monk attained great enlightenment.
A monk asked Zen Master Tianzhu Chonghui, "Before Bodhidharma came to this land, was there still the Buddha-dharma?
The Master said, "Setting aside for a moment the time before he arrived, what is the matter right now? The monk said, "I do not understand; I beg the Master for instruction.
The Master said, "Ten thousand ages of eternal sky; a single day of wind and moon. The monk was speechless. The Master spoke again, "O *dārala* (junior brother)..."
"Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not. The Master said, "How is it from your own side? What does it have to do with whether Bodhidharma came or did not come?
His coming here was much like a fortune-teller; seeing that you did not understand, he broke open the lines of the divination for you.
As soon as 'good' or 'bad' fortune arises, if you were to take it as your own concern, you would see everything for yourself. The monk asked, "What is this?"
Regarding Jie Bu Di: The Master said, "From the moment you stepped out the gate, you were already off-center. Question: "When a deceased monk passes away, where does he go? The Master said:
"Beyond the mountain peaks, the heights are ever-accumulating with emerald green; across the flowing river, the bright moon’s color shines with radiance.
Question: "What is the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū? The Master said: "Throughout vast and great kalpas, [he has been here]."
"Formerly there was congestion; it was not the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū. What was it? [The student] asked, "Why is the Buddha-dharma not manifest before me?
The Master said, "It is precisely because you do not understand that the Buddha does not manifest before you. If you were to understand, there would likewise be no Buddha to be realized.
○ Question: "What is the meaning of [the Master’s] coming from the West? The Master said, "A white monkey carrying its young comes to the green..."
[The mountain] peaks [loom]. Amidst green calyxes, bees and butterflies carry flowers.
One day, a butcher came to pay his respects to Zen Master Xuansu of Helin, wishing to prepare an offering at the Master’s residence.
The Master went there with joy. The assembly all looked on in astonishment. The Master said, "The Buddha-dharma is equal; the worthy and the foolish are of one essence. It simply may be..."
As for those who seek deliverance, I go to deliver them. What further distinction could there be? [Verse: A monk knocked at the door.
The Master asked, "Who is this? He replied, "It is a monk. The Master said, "Not only a monk; even if a Buddha were to come, he would not find a place to stay.
[The monk] asked, "Why would he not find a place to stay? The Master said, "Because there is no place for you to lodge."
When Chan Master Weizze of Foguo first visited Chan Master Zhong, he attained a great awakening to the profound principle.
He then said: "Heaven and earth are without substance; I am without substance. Although they are without substance, they have never been without substance.
If this is so, then sages are like dreams and common people are like dreams; who, then, undergoes birth and death? The person of ultimate attainment is able to illuminate this alone."
"He can become the lord of all things; I know this well.

When Chan Master Daoqin of Mount Jing first devoted himself to Confucian teachings, at the age of twenty-eight he met Master Su, who said to him, "Observing your spirit and temperament, you are truly a treasure of the Dharma.
The Master was moved to realization and consequently requested to become his disciple.
Xuanzuo personally shaved his hair and then instructed him, saying, "As you travel along the current, stop whenever you encounter a path.
The Master then journeyed southward and reached Lin’an. Seeing a mountain to the northeast, he asked a woodcutter about it. The woodcutter replied, "This is Mount Jing."
He then settled there. A monk asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "There is a carp on the mountain;
there is dust on the ocean floor. [Verse] Mazu sent someone to deliver a letter. In the letter, he drew a circle. Mazu opened the seal.

Lord Cui Zhao asked, "I, your disciple, now wish to leave the household life; may I do so? The Master replied, "Leaving the household life is the business of a great man;

it is not something that generals or ministers can accomplish. At these words, the Lord attained realization. [Verse] In the third year of the Dali era of the Tang dynasty, Emperor Daizong issued an imperial decree.
Upon arriving at the imperial palace, he personally paid his respects. One day, while sitting with National Teacher Zhong in the inner courtyard, they saw the Emperor’s carriage approaching.
The Master rose to his feet. The Emperor asked, "Why does the Master rise? The Master replied, "How can you, O Donor, perceive me, a poor monk, within the context of the four modes of deportment?
The Emperor was pleased and said to the National Teacher, "I wish to bestow a name of honor upon this master. The National Teacher rejoiced.
Nevertheless, he received the imperial decree and was granted the title Guoyi (National One).
Once, when the monk Jizong of Huayan Monastery asked Master Yunju Zhi, "What is the meaning of 'seeing one's nature and becoming a Buddha'?
the Master replied, "The nature of purity is fundamentally serene and still; it is without movement and does not belong to existence or non-existence."

Regarding purity and defilement, long and short, acceptance and rejection—their essence is inherently *xiao-ran* (tranquil and detached). To perceive clearly in this manner is called "seeing one's nature.

Nature is the Buddha; the Buddha is nature. Therefore it is said: "Seeing one's nature is to become a Buddha. [The student] asked: "Since nature is already pure and does not belong to existence or non-existence, how can there be 'seeing'?

The Master said: "Seeing is seeing nothing. [The student] asked: "If there is nothing seen, how can there still be seeing? The Master said: *Note: The term xiao-ran (翛然) is used here to describe the state of being naturally free from conceptual constraints.*
There is also no locus of seeing. [The student] asked: "When one sees in this way, whose seeing is it? The Master said: "There is no one who can see.
[The student] asked: "Ultimately, what is the principle of this? The Master said: "Do you know? To falsely reckon that there is something is precisely to have a subject and an object."
This is what is called delusion. Following one's perceptions to give rise to conceptual understanding leads one to fall into birth and death. For one who sees with clarity, it is not so;

though they see all day long, they have never seen anything that can be named as a substance or characterized as a form. Since neither subject nor object can be apprehended, this is called "seeing one's nature.
[The student] asked: "Does this nature pervade all places? The Master said: "There is nowhere it does not pervade. [The student] asked: "Do ordinary people possess it?"
The Master said, "It was stated above that there is no place where non-seeing does not pervade; how could it be that ordinary beings do not possess this?
Why is it that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are not constrained by birth and death, while ordinary beings alone are entangled in this suffering? How could they have ever attained such pervasiveness?
The Master replied, "Ordinary beings, within the nature of purity, calculate in terms of subject and object; thus they fall into birth and death. As for the Buddhas and Great Beings..."
Within the nature of purity, one rightly knows that it does not belong to existence or non-existence, such that neither subject nor object is established. [The interlocutor] says:

"If this is how you speak, then there must be a person who either understands or does not understand. The Master says: "Since even 'understanding' cannot be apprehended, how could there be a person who understands?"
He asked, "What is the ultimate principle? The Master said, "I shall state it for you in brief:
within the nature of purity, there is neither ordinary person nor sage, nor is there anyone who has attained realization or failed to do so. 'Ordinary' and 'sage' are both merely names.

If one gives rise to conceptual understanding based on these names, one falls into birth and death. If one knows that provisional names are not real, then there is no one who actually corresponds to those names. Furthermore—
He said: "This is the ultimate point of culmination. To claim, 'I can realize it, but he cannot,' is a great illness.

To perceive distinctions between the pure and the defiled, or between the ordinary and the sage, is also a great illness. To form the understanding that there are neither ordinary beings nor sages belongs to the denial of cause and effect.
To perceive a pure nature in which one may dwell is a great illness; to form the understanding that there is no dwelling is also a great illness."

However, within the nature of purity, although there is no movement or agitation, it possesses unbreakable skillful means for application, as well as the arousal of kindness and the exercise of compassion.
At the very place where such arousal occurs, it is the entirety of the pure nature itself; this may be called "seeing one's nature and becoming a Buddha."
Jizong was filled with joy; he paid his respects and withdrew.
Chan Master Niaoke Daolin visited Dharma Master Fuli of Ximing Monastery in Chang’an to study the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the *Awakening of Faith*.
Fuli showed him the "Verses on Reality and Delusion" (*zhenwang song*) and instructed him to practice dhyāna. The Master asked: "How did you begin?"
[The Master] observed him. "How do you apply your mind? [The Master] prostrated himself, remaining silent for a long time. The Teacher performed three prostrations and withdrew.
It happened that Emperor Daizong had issued an imperial decree summoning National Teacher Guoyi to the capital; the Master then went to pay his respects to him and thereby received the True Dharma.
He returned to West Lake, where he saw a tall pine tree on Mount Qinwang with lush foliage, its branches curling like a canopy. He then took up residence upon it, and thus it became known as...
There was a disciple named Huìtōng who served as an attendant. One day, wishing to take his leave, the Master asked him, "Where are you going now?

He replied, "Huìtōng has left the household life for the sake of the Dharma. Since the Master has not deigned to grant me compassionate instruction, I am now going to various quarters to study the Buddha-Dharma.
The Master said, "As for the Buddha-Dharma, we have a little of it here as well. [Huìtōng] asked, "What is the Master’s [Dharma]?"
Regarding the Buddha-Dharma, the Master took up a tuft of cloth from his robe and blew upon it; Tong thereupon attained realization of the profound principle.
[Verse] Minister Bai Juyi asked: "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-Dharma? The Master said: "Commit no evil; practice all that is good. Bai said:
"Even a three-year-old child understands this. The Master said: "Though a three-year-old child..."
"You can speak it; an eighty-year-old man cannot practice it.

Master Shenxiu of the Northern School had been closely engaged in Confucian studies since youth. He was widely learned and possessed great erudition. Suddenly renouncing his attachments, he left the household life to seek teachers and inquire after the Way.
Encountering the Fifth Patriarch, whose primary practice was seated meditation, he sighed in admiration and submission, saying, "This is truly my teacher. He then made a vow.
The Master lived a life of austerity, performing his own tasks such as gathering firewood and drawing water while seeking the Way. Master Zu perceived this in silence and held him in high esteem.
The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "All Buddha-dharma is inherently present within one's own mind. To seek it outside the mind is like abandoning one's father and running away."
During the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, National Teacher Huian of Mount Song traveled to Huangmei to visit the Patriarch Huineng, whereupon he attained the essential point of the mind.
Later, two monks named Tanran and Huairang came to consult him. They asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "Why do you not ask about your own meaning? They asked, "What is the meaning of one's own self? The Master said, "You should contemplate the mystery."
[The Emperor asked about] "activity. [He asked,] "What is the secret activity? The Master indicated this by opening and closing his eyes.
Yet, even beneath these words, [Wuzhuo] knew where to turn. Wuzhuo then went directly to Caoxi. When Empress Wu summoned him to the capital, she treated him with the etiquette due to a teacher.
He was held in equal high esteem as the Zen Master Xiu. The Empress once asked the Master, "How old are you? The Master replied, "I do not remember. The Empress—

[The questioner] asked, "Why do you not record it? The Master said, "The body of birth and death is like a revolving cycle. Since a cycle has neither beginning nor end, what use is there in recording it?
Furthermore, this flow of the mind is continuous without interruption. To perceive the arising and ceasing of bubbles is merely deluded thought.
From the initial consciousness until the point when the signs of movement cease, it is exactly like this; how could one record it by year or month?"
Later, having heard this, they bowed their heads to the ground in submission and accepted it with faith.

Chan Master Daoming of Mount Meng, hearing that the Fifth Patriarch had secretly entrusted the robe and Dharma to Lu Xingzhe, immediately led several dozen companions to track his footsteps in pursuit.
Upon reaching Dayu Ridge, the Master was the first to see him; the others had not yet arrived.
When Lu saw that the Master had fled, he immediately threw the robe and bowl onto a flat rock and said, "This robe represents the seal of faith;
can it be seized by force? You may take it as you please. The Master then tried to lift it, but it remained as immovable as a mountain. Hesitating and trembling with fear, he then said:
"I have come to seek the Dharma, not for robes. I pray that the Practitioner will reveal it to me.
Lu said, "When you are neither thinking of good nor thinking of evil—at this very moment—what is the Original Face of Master Ming? At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment;
sweat poured from his entire body, and he prostrated himself in weeping salutation five times. He then asked, "Beyond these secret words and secret meanings..."
"Is there not yet another underlying meaning? Lu said, "What I have just told you is not a secret.
If you turn back and reflect upon your own true face, the secret will reside within you. The Master said, "Although I was among the assembly at Huangmei, I truly did not realize my own face.
Now that I have received your instruction on the point of entry, it is like a person drinking water—the coolness [is known by oneself]."
Nuan recognized him himself, saying, "The practitioner here is now the master of such-and-such a person. Lu said, "If it is so, then you and I share the same teacher at Huangmei.
Guard and uphold [the Dharma] well yourself."
Chan Master Daoshu of Shouzhou was nearly fifty years old when he left the household life. Upon meeting Chan Master Xiu, he realized the subtle truth beneath a single word.
He then selected Mount Sanfeng in Shouzhou to build a hermitage and reside there. There was often a "wild man" who wore simple, plain clothing and whose speech was strange and unconventional;
beyond his joking and laughter, he would manifest the form of a Buddha, as well as the forms of bodhisattvas, arhats, celestial immortals, and so forth.
Sometimes he emitted divine light, and sometimes he produced sounds. The master’s disciples beheld these things but none could fathom them.

After ten years had passed in this manner, [the apparition] suddenly vanished without trace or form. The master addressed the assembly, saying: "The rustic man has displayed many-colored conjurations to dazzle and delude people;
it required nothing more than for me, the old monk, to neither see nor hear him. His conjurations have reached their limit, but as for me, I neither saw nor heard."

[He was] known as Wujin (Inexhaustible). When Chan Master Jiangmozang encountered the flourishing propagation of the Northern School, he immediately went to him to serve as a disciple. Xiu asked him, "Your name is 'Subduing Demons. Yet here there are no mountain spirits or water monsters; what demons do you intend to subdue? The Master replied, "There are Buddhas and there are demons. Xiu said: [The Master continued: "If one has a Buddha, one has a demon. Xiu said: [The Master continued: "If one has no Buddha, one has no demon. Xiu said: [The Master continued: "When there is neither Buddha nor demon, what is it? The Master remained silent. Xiu said: "You have attained it. The Master said: "I have not attained it. Xiu said: "If you had attained it, you would have been able to speak. The Master said: "I have not attained it, yet I am able to speak. Xiu said: "This is truly the work of a man of great capacity. The Master then composed this verse: "Within the Dharma-gate of the One Vehicle, There is neither Buddha nor sentient being. If one says there is a Buddha, That is the demon of the Buddha. If one says there is a sentient being, That is the demon of the sentient being. When both Buddha and sentient being are absent, What is it that can be named? The ten thousand phenomena are originally empty; How could there be any arising or ceasing? To see the nature and realize the fruit— This is merely a temporary expedient. Xiu said: "Excellent! You have truly realized the Way. The Master then took his leave and went to Mount Luofu. There, he stayed for many years, practicing austerities. Later, when he returned to the capital, he resided at the Huayan Monastery on Mount Zhongnan. He passed away in the second year of the Yongtai era of the Tang dynasty, at the age of seventy-one. His remains were enshrined in a stupa at the monastery. His dharma heirs included the masters Daoyuan, Daowen, and others. His lineage flourished greatly thereafter. This concludes the record of Chan Master Jiangmozang. The Master’s name was Zhizhen; his secular surname was Li. He was a native of Changsha in Hunan. From childhood, he possessed a profound disposition and was naturally inclined toward the Way. At the age of twenty, he left home to study under Master Huizhao of Mount Nanyue. After receiving the full precepts, he traveled to various regions to seek out the teachings. Eventually, he arrived at the monastery of the Great Master Shenxiu of the Northern School and became his attendant. One day, while serving the master, he happened to overhear the master instructing a student: "The mind-ground is originally pure; it is only because of deluded thoughts that one fails to see its true nature. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, simply stop all thoughts. Upon hearing this, the Master suddenly attained great awakening. He then approached the master and said, "I have understood the meaning of the teaching. The master asked, "What is it that you understand? The Master replied, "The mind-ground is originally pure; it is only because of deluded thoughts that one fails to see its true nature. The master said, "You have indeed grasped my meaning. The Master then withdrew and practiced diligently. Later, he visited various teachers to resolve his remaining doubts. Finally, he settled at Mount Luofu, where he lived in seclusion for many years. His conduct was austere and his realization profound. He never sought fame or profit, and his reputation spread far and wide. When the Emperor heard of his virtue, he summoned him to the capital, where he was honored with the title of Chan Master. He taught extensively, guiding countless seekers. His final words were, "The Way is not something to be sought; it is simply the cessation of all seeking. Having spoken thus, he passed away peacefully. His disciples erected a memorial stele to commemorate his legacy. Thus ends the biography of Chan Master Jiangmozang. It is said that his teachings were vast and deep, and his influence lasted for generations. Those who encountered him were transformed by his compassion, and his name remains revered to this day. This is the end of the account. May all beings attain liberation through these records. Amity. Amity. Amity. Amity. Amity. Amity. Amity. Amity. Amity. Amity. Amity. Amity. Amity. Amity. Amity. Amity.
