"If you are Māra, you must dwell in the inconceivable realm. The Master said, "Even a Buddha is empty;
what realm could there be?
Chan Master Fuxian Renjian retired from his inquiries at Mount Song and lived freely amidst the outskirts and villages, calling himself the "Teng-teng-he" (the carefree harmonizer).
Furthermore, there is a song by Liaoyuan that circulates in the world.

Regarding the Monk Puo-zao-duo: [Verse] He lived in seclusion in a mountain valley of Mount Song. There was a temple there that was extremely efficacious; within its hall, only a single hearth was installed.
Offerings were made from far and near without ceasing, and many living beings were slaughtered for cooking. One day, the Master led his attendant monks...
He entered the temple and struck the hearth three times with his staff, saying: "Tut! This hearth is merely composed of clay and tiles.
From where does its sanctity come? From where does its spirit arise? Yet you thus slaughter living beings! He struck it another three times, and the hearth immediately collapsed and fell apart.
A moment later, a man appeared wearing a green robe and a tall cap; he prostrated himself before the Master. The Master said: "Is this it?"

The person said, "I am originally the stove deity of this temple. Having long endured the retribution of my karma, today I have received the teaching on the Dharma of Non-arising from you, Master, and have attained liberation from this place to be born among the devas.
I have come specifically to express my gratitude. The Master said, "This is your own inherent nature."

"It is not that I am speaking with forceful words. The deity performed a prostration twice and vanished. After a short while, an attendant monk asked, 'We have served the Master for a long time and have never received instruction.
What essential principle did the hearth-deity receive that he was able to be reborn in heaven?
The Master said, 'I simply told him that he was composed of clay and tiles; I had no other doctrine to impart to him. The attendant monk remained speechless. The Master [continued]:
The Master asked, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Why do you not understand your own inherent nature?
The attendant monks then prostrated themselves. The Master said, "Falling! Falling! Broken! Broken! Later, Zen Master Yifeng recounted this to National Teacher An.
National Teacher An sighed and said, "This man has realized that all things and the self are of one suchness; he may truly be called a bright moon."

He dwelt in emptiness; there was no one who did not see him. It is difficult to grasp the thread of his discourse. Feng asked, "I do not yet understand: what kind of person can grasp the thread of his discourse? An said, "One who does not know.
At that time, he was called "Puo-zao-duo" (The One Who Broke the Oven). A monk asked, "When every single thing is formless, how is it?
The Master said, "If you prostrate, then it is only you and not me; if you do not prostrate, then it is only me and not you."
The monk then prostrated in thanks. The Master said, "That which is originally possessed is not a thing; it is a non-thing. Therefore it is said:
'If the mind can transform things, one is identical to the Tathāgata.'"

Chan Master Yuangui of Mount Song visited National Teacher Huian and attained sudden enlightenment into the profound essence of the Way. He subsequently chose a site at Pangwu on the mountain to build a hermitage.

One day, a mountain deity requested the precepts. The Master immediately prepared a seat for him; once the five lay precepts had been conferred, the deity said, "My supernatural powers are second only to those of the Buddha.
The Master replied, "Of your ten supernatural powers, five are capable and five are incapable. As for the Buddha—"
"Ten statements: seven things you can do, three things you cannot. Shen suddenly straightened up, left his seat, knelt, and asked, "May I hear them?
The Master said, "Can you cause the Supreme Deity to turn back and make the Seven Luminaries travel from the east to the west? He replied, "I cannot.
The Master said, "Can you seize the Earthly Deities, melt the Five Peaks, and bind the Four Seas? He replied, "I cannot. The Master said, "This is what is called the five..."
He cannot. The Buddha can empty all phenomena and achieve the wisdom of all dharmas, yet he cannot immediately extinguish fixed karma.
The Buddha can know the nature of all beings and exhaustively understand the events of billions of kalpas, yet he cannot transform and guide those who lack the karmic conditions.
The Buddha can deliver immeasurable sentient beings, yet he cannot bring the realm of sentient beings to an end. These are the three things he cannot do. Fixed karma is likewise...
It is not firm or enduring; even the absence of conditions constitutes a single period. The realm of sentient beings is fundamentally without increase or decrease.
Throughout all time, there is not a single person who can master this Dharma. Where there is Dharma, there is no master; this is called "the non-existence of Dharma.

Where there is no Dharma and no master, this is called "mindlessness. As I understand the Buddha, there is likewise no supernatural power (*abhijñā*). It is simply that by means of mindlessness, one penetrates all phenomena as they truly are (*dharmatā*).
The deity said, "I am indeed shallow and ignorant; I have not yet heard the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). As for the precepts you have bestowed upon me, I shall faithfully practice them.
Chan Master Weizheng of Zhongnan Mountain [Verse]: Emperor Wenzong of the Tang dynasty was fond of eating clams.

Officials from along the coast used to present them to him in succession, which caused great exhaustion to the people. One day, among the imperial provisions, there was one that had been split open but would not close. The Emperor, because of this—
It was different. He immediately burned incense and prayed to it; then it opened, revealing the form and countenance of a Bodhisattva, complete with all the marks of a Brahma-like appearance.

The Emperor subsequently stored it in a casket of gold, sandalwood, and incense, covered it with fine brocade, and bestowed it upon Xingshan Temple, ordering the assembly of monks to gaze upon and worship it.
He then asked his ministers, "What auspicious omen is this? Some reported, "The Chan Master Weizheng of Taiyishan has a profound understanding of the Buddha-dharma."

He was widely learned and possessed a powerful memory. [The Emperor] requested that an imperial edict be issued to question him. The Emperor immediately promulgated the edict. When the Master arrived, the Emperor questioned him about the matter.
The Master said, "Your servant has heard that nothing occurs without a corresponding cause; this is merely to inspire Your Majesty’s faith. Therefore, a sutra says:"
"To those who are to be delivered by this body, he manifests this very body and preaches the Dharma for them.
The Emperor said, "The Bodhisattva’s body has indeed appeared, yet we have not yet heard him preach the Dharma. The Master asked, "Does Your Majesty perceive this as permanent or impermanent?
Do you believe it or do you not believe it? The Emperor replied, "This is a rare and marvelous thing; I believe it deeply. The Master said, "Your Majesty has already heard [the teaching]."

When the preaching of the Dharma was concluded, the Emperor’s heart was filled with joy and delight such as he had never before experienced. He issued an edict to all monasteries throughout the realm, commanding that an image of Avalokiteśvara be established in each, in order to express gratitude for this extraordinary blessing.
Chan Master Jingji of Mount Song [Verse]: A monk asked, "What is the practice of one who cultivates goodness? The Master said, "Carrying a cangue and wearing shackles.
The monk asked, "What is the practice of one who commits evil? The Master said, "Cultivating dhyāna and entering samādhi. The monk said, "My faculties are shallow."
"Please, Master, point directly. The Master said, "If you ask me about evil, evil does not follow from good; if you ask me about good, good does not follow from evil.
After the monk had remained silent for a long while, the Master asked, "Do you understand? The monk replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "The evil person has no thoughts of goodness;
the good person has no thoughts of evil. Therefore it is said: 'Good and evil are like floating clouds; both have no place of arising or ceasing. At these words, the monk...
Later, when Pòzuò Duò heard of this, he remarked, "This man has realized that all dharmas are non-arising.
When the Chan Master Wúzhù of Bǎotáng was asked by the Tang Prime Minister Dú Hóngjiàn, "I have heard from Master Jīn that there are three phrases of the Dharma-gate:
'no recollection,' 'no thought,' and 'do not delude. Is this so? The Master replied, "Yes. The official said, "Regarding these three..."

[The Master] said: "One or three? The Master replied: 'Non-recollection is called precept (śīla); non-thought is called concentration (samādhi); not being deluded is called wisdom (prajñā). When the single mind does not arise, one possesses precept, concentration, and wisdom;
it is neither one nor three. The Official asked: 'In the last phrase, the character for "delusion" (妄)—is it the "wàng" with the radical for "heart" (心)?
The Master said: 'It is the one with the radical for "woman" (女). The Official asked: 'Is there a scriptural authority for this? The Master said: 'The *Dharmapada*.'"
The Sūtra says: "If one gives rise to a mind of diligent effort, this is delusion, not diligence. If one can keep the mind from being deluded, diligence will be boundless.
Upon hearing this, the Master’s doubts were completely dispelled. The Master asked again, "Do you still instruct people by means of the three phrases?

The Master replied, "For a beginner practitioner, one must first cause them to cease discursive thought and settle the waves of consciousness. When the water is clear, the reflection appears; thus they awaken to non-thought."
The essence is quiescently manifest; even non-thought does not arise. At that time, a crow was cawing in the tree in the courtyard. The Master asked, "Do you hear it? The Master replied, "I hear it.
After the crow had gone, he asked again, "Do you hear it? The Master replied, "I hear it. The Master said, "The crow has gone and there is no sound;
why do you say you hear it? The Master then addressed the assembly at large: "A Buddha appears in the world but rarely; the True Dharma..."
It is difficult to hear. Each of you listen attentively. Hearing is non-existent as hearing; it is not related to the nature of hearing. It is fundamentally unarisen; how could it ever cease?
When there is sound, it is the object of sound that arises of itself; when there is no sound, it is the object of sound that ceases of itself.
Yet this nature of hearing does not arise following sound, nor does it perish following sound. To awaken to this nature of hearing is to escape being turned by the sensory object of sound.
You should know that hearing is without arising or ceasing; hearing is without coming or going. The official, together with his subordinates and the great assembly, bowed their heads and asked again:
"What is called the 'Primary Meaning' (paramārtha)? From what sequence does one enter the Primary Meaning? The Master said:
The ultimate truth (paramārtha) has no sequence, nor does it have entering or exiting. In the conventional truth (saṃvṛti), everything exists; in the ultimate truth, it is non-existent.
The nature of the lack of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva-svabhāva) of all phenomena is called the ultimate truth. The Buddha said: "That which has existence is called the conventional truth;
that which lacks intrinsic nature is the ultimate truth. Gong said: "As the Master has revealed, this is truly inconceivable."

The Tripitaka Master Jñānagupta from the Western Regions attained awakening upon hearing the words of the Sixth Patriarch. Later, while traveling to Mount Wutai, he saw a monk sitting in meditation within a hermitage.
The Master asked him, "What are you doing sitting here all alone? The monk replied, "I am practicing the contemplation of stillness. The Master asked, "Who is it that contemplates?"
"What is this 'stillness'? A monk bowed and asked, "What is the principle of this? The Master said, "Why do you not observe yourself and become still for yourself?
The monk was at a loss. The Master asked, "Whose lineage did you come from? He replied, "Chan Master Xiu. The Master said:
I am of the lowest caste among the heterodox paths of the Western Regions; I do not fall into such views. To sit here blankly and vacantly—what benefit would that be for the Way?
When Chan Master Fahai of Shaoyang first met the Sixth Patriarch, he asked: "Regarding 'this very mind is Buddha,' I pray you will deign to provide an instruction and illustration."
The Patriarch said: "If the preceding thought does not arise, that is the mind; if the succeeding thought does not cease, that is the Buddha.
To manifest all phenomena is the mind; to be free from all phenomena is the Buddha. Were I to explain this in full, it would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.

Listen to my verse: 'To realize the mind is called wisdom; To realize the Buddha is concentration. When concentration and wisdom are held in equal balance, The mind becomes pure within itself. Awakening to this Dharma-gate Is due to you.'"

Regarding the nature of habitual tendencies: their fundamental essence is non-arising. To cultivate both simultaneously is the correct practice. The Master accepted this with faith and praised it in verse:

"The very mind is originally the Buddha; Failing to realize this, one remains self-subdued. I know that the causes of concentration and wisdom Are cultivated together, free from all external objects."
When Chan Master Zhicheng of Jizhou first visited Master Xiu, he later went to Caoxi to resolve his doubts. The Sixth Patriarch asked, "How does your teacher instruct the assembly?
The Master replied, "He has often instructed the great multitude to settle the mind and contemplate stillness, sitting upright for long periods without lying down.
The Patriarch said, "To settle the mind and contemplate stillness is a sickness, not Chan; to sit for long periods and constrain the body—what benefit is there for the principle?"
"Listen to my verse: 'Since birth, sitting and never lying; after death, lying and never sitting. Originally but stinking bones—why establish merit or fault?
The Master asked, "I do not yet understand, Great Master: with what do you instruct people? The Patriarch said, "If I were to say that I have a dharma to give to others, I would be deceiving you.
I merely untie your bonds according to the occasion, provisionally calling it 'samādhi. Listen to my verse:"
He said: "The self-nature precept is entirely without mind; the self-nature wisdom is entirely without obstruction. The self-vajra is neither increasing nor decreasing;
the coming and going of the body is fundamentally samādhi. Upon hearing this verse, the Master repented and apologized, immediately vowing to take refuge [in him].
He then presented a verse, saying: "This illusory body of the five aggregates—how can an illusion reach its ultimate end? Turning toward True Suchness, the dharmas are still not pure."
Chan Master Xiaoliao of Biandan Mountain had a stupa inscription composed by Chan Master Hule Cheng. Its brief summary states: "The Master resided at Biandan Mountain and was styled Xiaoliao;
he was the direct successor of the Sixth Patriarch. The Master attained the mind that is no-mind and realized the appearance that is no-appearance.
That which is no-appearance is the myriad phenomena that dazzle the eyes; that which is no-mind is the blazing activity of discrimination. He severed all..."

To speak of "one resonance": a resonance cannot be transmitted; yet it is transmitted through practice. To speak of "the ineffable": the ineffable cannot be exhausted; yet one exhausts it through error.

The Master attained the "non-existence of non-existence," yet he did not fail to exist within that non-existence. I, now, employ the "existence of existence," yet I do not exist within that existence.
This existence that is not existent means that coming and going do not increase; this non-existence that is not nonexistent means that *nirvāṇa* is not extinction. Alas!
While the Master dwelt in the world, Caoxi was illuminated; when the Master entered nirvana, the Dharma-boat sank. The Master’s discourse on the unspeakable filled the universe;
he revealed the vehicle of definitive meaning to deluded disciples. The mountain colors of Biandan still hang over this place;
in the empty valley, the name "Xiaoliao" remains.
Chan Master Fada of Hongzhou had recited the *Lotus Sūtra* three thousand times.

Later, he prostrated before the Sixth Patriarch and said, "I only pray that the Honored One, in his great compassion, will briefly explain the meaning and principles within this sūtra. The Patriarch asked, "In your recitation of this sūtra, what do you take as its central tenet?
The Master replied, "I am a person of dull faculties; from the beginning, I have merely followed the text in my recitation. How could I know its essential purport? The Patriarch said:
"Try reciting it for me once; I shall explain it for you. The Master then recited the sutra aloud.
Upon reaching the "Expedient Means" chapter, the Patriarch said, "Stop. This sutra fundamentally takes the appearance of the world through causes and conditions as its primary theme.
Although it employs many kinds of parables, they do not exceed this point. What are these causes and conditions? They are simply the one great matter. This one great matter is..."
This is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. You must be careful not to misinterpret the meaning of the sutra.

If you see others say that "opening, showing, awakening, and entering" belong solely to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and that we have no share in it—if you interpret it thus, you are slandering the sutra and disparaging the Buddha.

Since he is already a Buddha, he has already perfected knowledge and vision; what need would there be for him to further "open" them? You should now believe that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is simply...
Your own mind has no separate essence; it is simply that all sentient beings obscure their own luminosity for themselves.

Greedily craving sensory objects, they are disturbed by external conditions and internally agitated, willingly submitting to being driven about. Thus, you must labor to rouse them from samādhi and speak to them with various bitter words of admonition.
He exhorted him, saying, "Rest and sleep; do not seek outwardly. You are no different from the Buddha; therefore, it is said that you 'open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
If you merely weary yourself with fixating on thoughts, claiming them to be your daily practice, how is this any different from a cow that loves its own tail?

The Master said, "If that is so, then one need only understand the meaning; there is no need for the labor of reciting the scriptures. The Patriarch said, "What fault is there in the scriptures? How could they possibly obstruct your mindfulness?"
"It is simply because delusion and enlightenment depend on the person; loss and gain are determined by you. Listen to my verse: When the mind is deluded, it is turned by the *Lotus Sūtra*;
When the mind is enlightened, it turns the *Lotus Sūtra*. If one recites for a long time without clarifying oneself, One becomes an enemy to the meaning of the text.

Without thoughts, every thought is correct; With thoughts, every thought becomes deviant. When neither existence nor non-existence is reckoned, One forever rides the white ox cart. (etc. The Master [Nanyue] understood from this.
The essential meaning [of this] was such that he never ceased reciting and upholding it.
When Chan Master Zhītōng of Shòuzhōu first studied the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, he did so approximately one thousand times, yet he could not comprehend the Three Bodies and Four Wisdoms.
He went to pay his respects to the Sixth Patriarch to seek an explanation of their meaning. The Patriarch said: "As for the Three Bodies: the Pure Dharma Body, you..."
This is your nature. The Perfect Reward Body is your wisdom; the thousand billion Transformation Bodies are your practice.
If you were to separate from your original nature and speak of the three bodies apart from it, they would be called "bodies with no wisdom.

If you realize that the three bodies have no self-nature, they are called the four wisdoms of Bodhi. Listen to my verse: "The original nature possesses the three bodies; through illumination, they are perfected."
The four wisdoms do not depart from seeing and hearing conditions; they transcendently lead one to the stage of Buddhahood. I shall now explain this for you;
believe it with earnest faith and you will never again be deluded. Do not follow those who run about in pursuit, who spend their whole days speaking of Bodhi.

The Master asked: "May I hear the meaning of these four wisdoms? The Patriarch said: "Since you have already realized the three bodies, you naturally understand the four wisdoms. Why ask further? If one were separated from the three bodies,"
A Separate Discourse on the Four Wisdoms: This is called having wisdom but no body. That which is "having wisdom" thus becomes "non-wisdom.
Furthermore, a verse is spoken: The nature of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is pure; The Wisdom of Equality has a mind free from ailment; The Wisdom of Wondrous Observation sees without effort;
The Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks is identical to the Perfect Mirror. The five, eight, six, and seven [consciousnesses] transform as fruit and cause; they function only through their application.
Names and phrases have no substantial nature. If one leaves no lingering attachment toward the place of transformation, then amidst all profuse activity, one dwells eternally in the *nāga-samādhi*.

(Regarding the transformation of consciousness into wisdom, the teachings state: the first five consciousnesses are transformed into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is Done; the sixth consciousness is transformed into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation; the seventh consciousness is transformed into the Wisdom of Equality; and the eighth consciousness is transformed into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.)

"Although the six and seven [consciousnesses] transform within the causal stage, and the five and eight [consciousnesses] transform upon the fruition stage, it is merely their names that change, while their essence does not. The Master bowed in gratitude and praised him with this verse:

"The three bodies are originally my own essence; The four wisdoms are fundamentally the clarity of my mind. Body and wisdom merge without obstruction; Responding to things, they take form as they will.

To initiate cultivation is entirely deluded movement; To cling to a state is not true refinement. Through the Master’s instruction, wondrous wisdom is realized; At last, the name of defilement is extinguished."
One day, Chan Master Zhiche of Jiangxi traveled a great distance to pay his respects to the Sixth Patriarch.

He asked, "I, your disciple, have often read the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, yet I do not yet understand the meaning of 'permanent' and 'impermanent. I beg the Master’s compassion to explain this briefly for me. The Patriarch said:
"That which is impermanent is the Buddha-nature; that which is permanent is the discriminating mind regarding all dharmas of good and evil.
[The monk] said, "What the Master has said greatly contradicts the scriptural texts. The Patriarch said, "I transmit the Buddha’s Mind-Seal; how could I dare to contradict the Buddha’s scriptures?
[The monk] said, "The scriptures state that the Buddha-nature is permanent, yet the Master says it is impermanent. As for the various dharmas of good and evil..."
"Even up to the bodhicitta, all are impermanent. Yet the Upādhyāya claims they are permanent; this is a contradiction that causes the student to become increasingly confused.
The Patriarch said, "Regarding the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, in the past when I heard the Bhikṣuṇī Anantarakṣā recite it once, I immediately gave a lecture upon it.
Not a single word or a single meaning failed to accord with the scriptural text—even for your sake [I have done so]."

"In the end, there is no second teaching. The student said, "My understanding and capacity are shallow and dim. I pray that the Master will explain this to me in detail. The Patriarch said, "Do you understand?
If Buddha-nature were permanent, what further need would there be to speak of good and evil dharmas?
Even until the end of kalpas, not a single person would ever give rise to the bodhicitta. Therefore, my teaching of impermanence is precisely the Buddha’s teaching of true permanence."
This is the Way. Furthermore, regarding all dharmas, if the mind were impermanent, then every individual thing would possess its own self-nature (*svabhāva*), thereby undergoing birth and death;
consequently, the truly eternal nature would have places where it does not pervade. Therefore, when I speak of "eternity," it is precisely the meaning of true impermanence as taught by the Buddha.
For the sake of ordinary people and non-Buddhists who cling to false eternity, and for the various followers of the Two Vehicles, the Buddha [taught this].
People mistakenly reckon the permanent as impermanent; together, these constitute the eight inversions.
Therefore, within the definitive teachings on Nirvāṇa, such biased views are refuted, and the true permanence, true bliss, true self, and true purity are clearly expounded.

You now rely on the words while turning your back on the meaning, misinterpreting the Buddha’s final, perfect, and subtle instructions by taking impermanence to mean annihilation and permanence to mean fixed death.
"Even if you were to read it a thousand times, what benefit would there be? At this, Xingchang suddenly felt as if he had awakened from a drunken stupor and spoke a verse:
"Because I guarded against impermanence, the Buddha taught the nature of permanence. One who does not know the skillful means is like one picking up pebbles at a spring pond.
Now, without applying effort, the Buddha-nature appears before me. It was not bestowed by my teacher, nor have I attained anything myself. The Patriarch said:

"You have now attained thorough penetration; you should be named Zhiche (Thorough Penetration). The Master performed a bow of thanks and departed. (The Master's surname was Zhang and his name was Xingchang).
One day, Chan Master Zhichang of Xin Prefecture went to visit the Sixth Patriarch. The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? What do you seek?
The Master replied, "I recently paid my respects to Great Penetration (Dagong) Master, who instructed me on the principle of seeing one's nature to achieve Buddhahood. However—"

He resolved his doubts. Upon arriving in Jizhou, he met a person who pointed out the way to him, instructing him to seek out the Venerable Master. He prostrated himself with the wish that the Master would compassionately accept him.
The Patriarch asked, "What words did he say? Try reciting them for me; I shall provide you with verification.

The Master said, "When I first arrived there three months ago, I had not yet received any instruction. Because my longing for the Dharma was so intense, I entered the abbot’s quarters alone during the middle of the night and paid my respects."
He bowed and pleaded with grief. Daotong then said, "Do you see empty space? He replied, "I see it. Daotong asked, "Do you see any form or characteristic in empty space?
He replied, "Empty space has no shape; how could it have any characteristics? Daotong said, "Your original nature is like empty space.
Turn back and contemplate your own nature; there is not a single thing to be seen. This is called right view. No [further words].

When a single thing can be known, this is called true knowledge. There is no blue, yellow, long, or short; one simply perceives the fundamentally pure source, the perfectly luminous essence of awakening.
This is what is called "seeing one's nature and attaining Buddhahood," and it is also called the "World of Ultimate Bliss" and the "Wisdom and Vision of the Tathāgata.
Although students hear these explanations, they are still not yet fully resolved. I beg the Venerable Master to grant us instruction so that we may be free from doubt.
[Zhi] said, "The teacher’s explanation still retains views and cognition; that is why you have not yet understood. I shall now show you a verse, which says:
'Not seeing a single dharma, yet maintaining the view of non-existence, Is much like floating clouds obscuring the face of the sun.

Not knowing a single dharma, yet clinging to the knowledge of emptiness, Is like lightning flashing within the vast void. When such views and cognitions arise in an instant, One mistakenly identifies them [as the truth].'"
"How could you ever have understood skillful means? You should, in a single thought-moment, realize your own error. Your own numinous light is constantly manifest.

Upon hearing this verse, the Master’s mind was suddenly opened; he then composed a verse himself, saying: "Groundlessly giving rise to conceptual understanding, Seeking Bodhi by clinging to appearances, Maintaining a single thought of awakening— How can this surpass one's former delusion?
The source-body of self-nature’s enlightenment, Is wrongly obscured by following after reflections."
Wandering in flux, he has not entered the room of the Patriarchs; he is utterly bewildered as he pursues both extremes.

Zen Master Zhidao of Guangzhou first visited the Sixth Patriarch and asked, "Since I left home to become a monk, I have studied the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* for over ten years, yet I have not clarified its great meaning.
I pray that the Master will grant me instruction. The Patriarch said, "In what respect have you not [clarified it]?"
He finished speaking. [The Master] said, "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are the nature of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss.
[Nanyue] expressed doubt regarding this. The Patriarch asked, "How do you doubt it? He replied, "All sentient beings possess two bodies."
This refers to the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The form-body is impermanent; it has arising and ceasing. The dharma-body is permanent;
it is without cognition and without awareness. As the Sūtra says: "When arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction (*nirvāṇa*) is bliss. I do not yet know which body this extinction pertains to.
In which body does one experience pleasure? If it is the physical body (*rūpakāya*), then at the time of its dissolution, the four great elements disperse and it is entirely suffering;

since suffering cannot be called pleasure, [pleasure is not found there]. If it is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) in its state of quiescent extinction, then it would be identical to grass, wood, tiles, or stones—who would then experience pleasure?

Furthermore, the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) is the essence of arising and ceasing, while the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are the function of arising and ceasing. Thus, the one essence and the five functions are both subject to arising and ceasing.
This is the eternal. When arising, function emerges from the essence; when ceasing, function is withdrawn back into the essence.

If rebirth were permitted, then the class of sentient beings would neither be interrupted nor extinguished. If rebirth were not permitted, they would eternally return to quiescent extinction, becoming identical to insentient objects.
In this way, all dharmas would be suppressed and constrained by nirvana, such that they could not even—

[Daowu] said, "If one is born, what joy is there? Zu said, "You are a son of the Śākya; why do you practice the heterodox views of annihilationism and eternalism, and discuss the Dharma of the Supreme Vehicle?
According to your understanding, you claim that apart from the physical body (rūpakāya), there is a separate dharmakāya that is free from birth and extinction."

They seek quiescence and further infer the permanence and bliss of *nirvāṇa*. To say that there is a body and a recipient [of sensation] is to cling to birth and death and to be addicted to worldly pleasures.

You should now know that for all deluded people, the Buddha teaches that they mistake the combination of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) for their own self-nature, and differentiate all phenomena as external objects. Thus, they love life and hate death, with every thought-moment shifting and changing.

Flowing on, they do not realize that all things are like dreams and illusions, falsely undergoing the cycle of saṃsāra; they mistake the eternal bliss of nirvāṇa for the aspect of suffering, seeking and striving throughout their days.
Out of compassion for them, the Buddha reveals the true bliss of nirvāṇa, in which not even a single moment possesses the characteristic of arising.
The *kṣaṇa* (moment) has no characteristic of extinction; there is nothing further to be extinguished through arising and ceasing. This is the manifestation of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa*).
At the time of this manifestation, there is also no measure of manifestation. This is what is called "eternal bliss. This bliss has no experiencer, nor is there anyone who does not experience it.
How could there even be the names of "one substance" and "five functions," let alone speak further of *nirvāṇa*? [This is] the prohibition and subduing.

To claim that all dharmas shall never arise again is to slander the Buddha and destroy the Dharma. Listen to my verse: The unsurpassed Great Nirvana is perfectly luminous, eternally tranquil, and illuminating.
The ignorant and foolish call it death; non-Buddhists cling to it as annihilation. Those who seek the two vehicles regard it as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
All these belong to the conceptualizations of the emotional mind, the very root of the sixty-two views. They falsely establish what is empty and illusory.
What is called "name"? What is the meaning of "reality"? Only those of transcendent capacity penetrate it without grasping or rejecting.

By knowing the phenomena of the five aggregates and the self within the aggregates, one sees that all external manifestations of forms and every characteristic of sound are equal to dreams and illusions.

One does not give rise to views of ordinary or holy beings, nor does one form a conceptual understanding of nirvana. With the two extremes and the three temporal limits severed, one should always respond to the various faculties.
While employing [means], do not give rise to the thought of employment. While discerning all phenomena, do not give rise to the thought of discernment.
When the kalpa-fire burns the ocean floor and the wind-driven mountains strike one another, the bliss of true, eternal quiescence—the mark of nirvāṇa—is thus.

I now speak these words by force, so as to cause you to abandon false views; do not follow the literal meaning of my words, for I permit you to know but a small portion. Upon hearing the verse, the Master leaped up.
He rose, performed a prostration, and withdrew.
Chan Master Zhijue of Yongjia [Verse]: Having extensively investigated the Tripiṭaka and mastered the profound and wondrous Dharma-gate of Tiantai *zhiguan* (cessation and contemplation).

Throughout the four modes of deportment, he constantly practiced meditative contemplation in secret. Later, inspired by the Zen Master Lang of Zuoxi, he traveled together with the Zen Master Ce of Dongyang to Caoxi.
Upon his initial arrival, he shook his mendicant’s staff, circumambulated the Patriarch three times, and stood there resolutely still.
The Patriarch said, "Now, a śramaṇa is endowed with three thousand dignified demeanors and eighty thousand subtle practices.

From what direction have you, O Venerable One, come, giving rise to such great conceit? The Master said, "The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift. The Patriarch said, "Why do you not realize non-arising?
Why do you not understand that there is no swiftness? The Master said, "To realize is itself non-arising; to understand is fundamentally without swiftness. The Patriarch said, "..."

"So it is, so it is. At that time, the great assembly was without exception struck with astonishment. The Master then performed his salutations with full decorum and took his leave after a short while.
The Patriarch said, "Is your return too soon? The Master replied, "Since I am fundamentally unmoving, how could there be such a thing as 'soon'?
The Patriarch asked, "Who knows this is unmoving? The Master replied, "It is you, O Benevolent One, who give rise to discrimination. The Patriarch said, "You have thoroughly attained the unborn."

The Master asked, "If there is no birth, how can there be intention? The Patriarch said, "If there is no intention, who is it that makes distinctions? The Master said, "Even making distinctions is not intention.
The Patriarch sighed in praise, saying, "Excellent, excellent! Stay for one night. At that time, he was called "Awakened in One Night" (Yi-xiu-jue).
The Master composed the *Song of Realizing the Way* (*Zhengdao ge*) and the *Collection from Yongjia* (*Yongjia ji*).
Chan Master Benjing of Sikong Mountain [Verse]: During the Tang Dynasty, Emperor Xuanzong summoned the Master to the capital and issued an edict for him to reside at Bailianting.

Subsequently, he summoned renowned monks and eminent scholars from both monastic districts to attend the Inner Court Dharma Hall to expound the principles of the Buddha-dharma together with the Master.
At that time, Chan Master Yuan raised his voice and said to the Master: "Now, facing the Sacred Sovereign, we are to evaluate the essential tenets; one ought to be direct..."
The questioner replied directly, without resorting to elaborate words: "According to what the Master perceives, what constitutes the Way? The Master said, "A mindless state is the Way.

Yuan asked, "Since the Way arises because of the mind, how can you say that a mindless state is the Way? The Master said, "The Way is fundamentally nameless; it is because of the mind that it is named 'the Way.
If the mind were not present, the Way would not exist as such. Since the mind, when thoroughly investigated, is found to be non-existent, upon what could the Way rely?"
"What is established? Both are equally false; they are all merely provisional names. Yuan said, "Does the Chan Master see that body and mind exist? Is this the Way?
The Master replied, "The body and mind of this mountain monk have been the Way from the very beginning. Yuan said, "Just now you said that no-mind is the Way."
Now you further say that body and mind are the Way; is this not a contradiction? The Master said: "No-mind is the Way. When the mind is extinguished, the Way is non-existent.
Mind and the Way are one and the same; therefore, it is said that no-mind is the Way. Body and mind are fundamentally the Way, and the Way is fundamentally body and mind.
Since body and mind are fundamentally empty, the Way is likewise exhausted at its source and does not exist. Yuan said: "This is what Master Guan’s Chan says."
"His physical form was very small, yet he understood this principle. The Master said, "Virtuous One, you see only my physical appearance;
you do not see my formlessness. That which you see is merely what you perceive. The Sūtra says: 'All that has form is entirely illusory.
If one sees all forms as non-form, then one sees the Way. If one takes form to be real, one will not succeed even after the exhaustion of kalpas.'"
Jian Dao Yuan said, "I now request the Master to explain the signless (animitta) based upon signs (nimitta). The Master replied, "The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states:
'The four great elements have no master; the body likewise has no self. To be free from the view of "mine" is to be in accord with the Way.

Venerable sir, if you believe the four great elements have a master who is the self, or if you harbor a view of self, you shall not realize the Way even after the exhaustion of kalpas. Yuan heard this and was moved.
The man’s voice faltered and his complexion changed; he hesitated and withdrew from his seat. The Master had a verse that said: “The four elements have no master and are like water;
Meeting curves or encountering straightness, there is neither self nor other. In both purity and filth, no mind arises; Whether obstructed or flowing, how could there ever be two intentions?
When encountering objects, simply be like water without a mind; Acting freely in the world—what matters can there be? He further said: “One great element is thus; what of the four?”
The same applies to the Great [Elements]. If one realizes that the four great elements have no master, one immediately awakens to the state of no-mind.
If there is no-mind, one naturally accords with the Way. Chan Master Zhiming asked: "If you say that no-mind is the Way, then tiles and pebbles also have no mind;

they too should be the Way. He further said: "Body and mind are fundamentally the Way. Since the four modes of birth and the ten classes of beings all possess body and mind, they too should be [the Way]."
The Master said, "Virtuous One, if you interpret this through the understanding of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, you are worlds apart from the Way;
you are one who seeks seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, not one who seeks the Way. As the Sutra says: 'There are no eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, or mind.

When even the six sense faculties do not exist, upon what could seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing be established? Since they are fundamentally non-existent when traced to their source, where could they possibly abide?"
"How can the mind not be the same as grass, trees, tiles, and pebbles? Mingdu remained silent and withdrew. The Master had a verse that said:

"Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are without obstruction; Sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and phenomena are always in samādhi. Like a bird flying through the sky, simply so it goes; Without grasping or rejecting, without hatred or love.
If you understand that where things respond there is fundamentally no mind, Only then can one be named Avalokiteśvara."
(The subsequent dialogue between the Chan Master and his close attendants is omitted here due to its length.

When Chan Master Xuancè of Wuzhou was traveling, he arrived at Hesuo. There was a Chan Master named Huáng who had once visited Huangmei and considered himself to have attained correct meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
The Master knew that Huáng’s realization was not yet authentic, so he went to him and asked: "You sit here..."
"What are you doing? Huáng replied, "I am entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The Master said, "When you say you are entering meditative concentration, is there a mind or is there no mind?
If there is a mind, then all wriggling creatures should likewise attain concentration. If there is no mind, then all grasses and trees should also attain concentration.
Huáng said, "When I am truly entering meditative concentration, I do not perceive the existence of either a mind with thought or a mind without thought."

The Master said, "Since you do not perceive a mind of existence or non-existence, this is constant samādhi; how could there be entering or exiting? If there were entering or exiting, it would not be the Great Samādhi.
Huang was speechless. After a long while, he asked, "Whom did your Master succeed? The Master replied, "My teacher is the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi.
Huang asked, "What does the Sixth Patriarch take to be dhyāna-samādhi? The Master replied, "My teacher says: 'That which is wondrously profound and perfectly round...'"

"Quiescence: its essence and function are suchness (*tathatā*). The five aggregates (*skandha*) are fundamentally empty; the six sense objects (*viṣaya*) do not exist. There is no emerging and no entering;

neither fixed nor distracted. The nature of dhyāna has no abiding; it is the quiescence of dhyāna that is free from abiding. The nature of dhyāna has no arising; it is the thought of dhyāna that is free from arising.
The mind is like space, yet even the measure of space does not exist. Upon hearing this teaching, Huáng went to Caoxi to request a resolution of his doubts and obscurations.
The Patriarch’s intent and the Master’s realization were in profound accord, and Huihuang finally attained awakening.
Regarding Chan Master Zhìhuáng of Hebei [Verse]: when he first visited the Fifth Patriarch, although he had frequently sought clarification, he remained stuck in gradual practice.
He then went north of the River to build a hermitage where he sat in long-term meditation for over twenty years, never showing a trace of indolence.
Later, encountering the inspiration of Master Ce, he went to visit the Sixth Patriarch. The Patriarch, taking pity on his journey from afar, bestowed upon him an opening resolution.
Under these words, the Master attained a sudden and thorough realization; the state of mind he had cultivated during the preceding twenty years left no trace whatsoever.
National Teacher Huizhong of Nanyang [Verse]: One day he called to his attendant. The attendant responded. This was repeated three times; each time the attendant responded.
The Master said, "I thought it was I who had failed you, but it was actually you who had failed me. [A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What was the National Teacher’s intention in calling to the attendant?

Zhaozhou replied, "It is like a person writing characters in the dark; though the characters are not formed, the traces of the brushstrokes are already manifest. Ascending the hall, he said: "Those who study the Chan school should follow the Buddha..."

Regarding the teachings: those of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) that realize the single vehicle (*ekayāna*) accord with the source of one’s own mind; those of non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*), however, do not allow for mutual agreement, being like parasites within a lion’s body.
Now, if one who acts as a teacher for others pursues fame and profit and opens up divergent paths, what benefit is there for oneself or others?

It is like a master craftsman whose hands are not injured by his adze; it is like the load carried by a fragrant elephant, which a donkey cannot endure. A monk asked, "How can one attain Buddhahood? Question: "Is seeing the emptiness of the ten directions the Dharma-body? The Master said: "To seek it through conceptualization is a perverted view. Question:
"If the mind itself is Buddha, may one still cultivate the myriad practices? The Master said: "All the sages possess the two kinds of adornment; how could they deny cause and effect? He further said:

The Way is far-reaching. To speak of the Way while having something to gain from the teaching is the howling of a jackal;
to speak of the Dharma without anything to gain is called the lion’s roar. [Verse] Ascending the hall: Green vines entwine themselves, climbing straight to the summit of the cold pine.

The visitor asked, "How can you, Master, equate this bubble-like, illusory body with the essence of the Dharma? The Master replied, "Why have you fallen into such heterodoxy?"
Dao asked, "Where is it that I have entered onto a false path? The Master said, "Have you not seen what is taught in the scriptures:

The Patriarch said, "My friend has come from afar with great hardship. Do you bring your original nature? If you have this original nature, you should recognize its master; try to explain it to me. The Master replied:
"Taking non-abiding as the foundation—this very seeing is the master. The Patriarch said, "How can this śrāmaṇera speak so recklessly?

He then struck him. Under the staff, the Master reflected, saying, "A great spiritual friend is difficult to encounter throughout kalpas; now that I have met one, I must not let this opportunity pass."
"How could I begrudge my own life? From this day forth, I shall serve you. [Verse] On another day, the Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying:

The Patriarch said, "I told you that it has no name and no character, yet you immediately called it the 'fundamental source' and 'Buddha-nature. The Master bowed and withdrew. The Patriarch said, "This child, hereafter—"

"Even if one were to cover one's head with a bundle of reeds, one would still only become a follower of the school of intellectual understanding (Fayan said: 'The ancients' bestowals of prediction were never mistaken.
To establish intellectual understanding as the core doctrine today is precisely what Heze did'). The Master subsequently went to the Western Capital to receive the precepts.

During the Jǐnglóng era of the Tang dynasty, he returned to Caoxi to examine the Great Tripitaka. Within it, there were six points where he harbored doubts, which he questioned of the Sixth Patriarch. First:
Question: Regarding the precepts, concentration, and wisdom: what is the substance of the precepts employed? From where is concentration cultivated? By reason of what does wisdom arise?
Why is what is seen not flowing through? The Patriarch said: Concentration is simply to settle the mind; the precepts are used to restrain one's conduct.

Within the nature, there is constant illumination by wisdom; thus one sees for oneself and knows deeply. Second Question: That which was originally non-existent now exists—what is this thing? That which was originally existent... [The text ends here.]
"Now there is no 'non-existence' of anything. To recite the sutras while not seeing their meaning is truly like riding a donkey and yet searching for another donkey.

The Patriarch said: "The evil karma of the preceding thought was originally non-existent; the good arising in the succeeding thought now exists. If you constantly practice wholesome deeds in every thought-moment, the human and heavenly realms will not be far off for future generations.
You are now listening correctly to my words; I am precisely that which was originally non-existent and now exists. (Third)

Question: "Does one extinguish birth by means of extinction? Does one extinguish extinction by means of birth? If one does not understand the meaning of birth and extinction, what is seen will be like being deaf and blind.

The Patriarch said: "To extinguish birth by means of extinction is to cause people not to cling to their nature (*dharmatā*). To extinguish extinction by means of birth is to cause the mind to depart from its objects.
Yet, this does not immediately leave the two extremes; it merely removes the disease of birth and extinction. The fourth question: "First, there is sudden [enlightenment]..."

"Gradual first, then sudden; gradual first and sudden later. Those who do not realize the nature of the sudden and the gradual are constantly confused and distressed within their minds. The Patriarch said: "To hear the Dharma is sudden within the gradual;
to awaken to the Dharma is sudden within the gradual. To practice the path is gradual within the sudden; to realize the fruit is sudden within the gradual. Sudden and gradual are constant causes;
within awakening, there is no confusion or distress. The fifth question: "Is it wisdom after concentration, or concentration after wisdom?"

Concentration. Regarding which arises first—concentration or wisdom—is what constitutes the correct practice? The Patriarch said: "Always give rise to a pure mind; within concentration there is wisdom, and toward objects there is no [discursive] mind.
Within wisdom there is concentration; when concentration and wisdom are equal, there is nothing prior. Cultivating them together, one's own mind is rectified. The sixth question:
Is it the Buddha first and the Dharma later, or the Dharma first and the Buddha later? What is the fundamental source of the Buddha and the Dharma?
"From where does it arise? The Patriarch said: "In speaking, the Buddha comes first and the Dharma second; in listening, the Dharma comes first and the Buddha second.
If one discusses the fundamental source of the Buddha-Dharma, it arises from within the minds of all sentient beings.
Twenty years after the Patriarch’s passing, the sudden teaching (Dunzhi) of Caoxi fell into decline in the regions of Jingzhou, Wu, and Songyue, while the gradual school flourished in Qin.

Luo: The Master entered the capital in the fourth year of the Tiānbǎo era. It was only then that the two schools (the Southern School of Sudden Enlightenment and the Northern School of Gradual Teaching) were definitively established;

The National Teacher asked, “What was your intention just now? The Master replied, “To whom could I have explained it? The National Teacher said, “I am asking you.”
"You," the Master said. "Where did you see me? [Verse] The Master asked again: "After a hundred years, if someone asks about the ultimate matter, what will you say?
The National Teacher said: "Fortunately, he is already pitiable; why must you insist on seeking a talisman for protecting the body?

“I am illuminated by it without interruption. Do you believe this? The Master said, “I do believe it, yet I do not know whether the light and the jewel are the same or different.
Zhe said, “The light is the jewel; the jewel is the light. How can there be such names as ‘same’ or ‘different’?
The Master said, “When the eyes and ears encounter sounds and forms, do they proceed independently, or is there an interpenetration? Zhe said, “They proceed independently.”
"Let us set this aside for a moment. To what dharma do you point as the substance of sound and form? The Master said, "According to what you have said, there is no sound or form to be found.

Zhe said, "If you realize that the substance of sound and form is empty, you will also believe that the various faculties, such as the eyes and ears, as well as ordinary and holy beings, are equal and like an illusion.
Their divergent movements and mutual interplay—their underlying principle is clear. The Master, because of this...
Having thus attained realization, he paid his respects, took his leave, and departed.
During the Dazhong era, Chan Master Zongmi of Guifeng was summoned to the imperial court and bestowed with purple robes. The Emperor repeatedly questioned him regarding the essentials of the Dharma.
The court officials turned toward him with devotion; only the Chancellor, Lord Pei Xiu, entered deeply into the inner sanctum, receiving his teachings and serving as a lay protector.

Because masters of the Chan and doctrinal schools were mutually disparaging one another, the Master consequently composed the *Chan-yuan zhu-quan ji* (A Collection of Explanations on the Source of Chan).

He transcribed and recorded the various texts, explanations, and verses concerning the fundamental principles of the Chan gate as described by different houses, compiling them into a single canon (some say it consists of one hundred fascicles).
To be bequeathed to future generations. ○ Its preface states in brief: "Zen" is a term from India; in its full form it is *dhyāna*.

Here it is translated as "cultivation through contemplation" (*sīwéi xiū*), and also as "meditative concentration" (*jìnglù*). These are all general designations for meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

The "source" is the original enlightened nature of all sentient beings; it is also called Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), and it is also called the realization of the mind-ground, which is termed wisdom. Cultivation..."

The names are fixed. Concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) together are termed *dhyāna*. This nature is the fundamental source of *dhyāna*; therefore, it is called the "Source of Dhyāna" (*chanyuan*).

It is also called *dhyāna* (or *zhanna*). Regarding "principle and practice": this fundamental source is the principle of *dhyāna*, while forgetting emotions and acceding to it is the practice of *dhyāna*;
hence, it is called "principle and practice. However, among the various works compiled here, most discuss the principle of *dhyāna* while little is said of its practice.
...practice. Therefore, I have provisionally titled this work "The Source of Chan" (Canyuan). Nowadays, there are those who identify true nature alone as Chan;

this shows they do not comprehend the essential meaning of principle and practice, nor do they distinguish between the phonologies of China and India. However, it is not that there is a separate essence of Chan apart from true nature.

It is simply that when sentient beings are deluded regarding true nature and conjoin with sensory dust, they are termed "distracted. When they turn their backs on sensory dust and conjoin with true nature, only then is it termed [Chan].
Regarding meditative concentration (*dhyāna*): if one discusses its fundamental nature directly, it is neither true nor false, neither opposed nor conjoined, and neither fixed nor distracted.
Who would speak of "meditation" in this regard? Furthermore, this true nature is not only the source of the gate of meditation, but is also the source of all phenomena;
therefore, it is called the *dharmatā*. It is also the source of sentient beings' delusion and awakening; therefore, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha* and the *ālayavijñāna*.
(From the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*): It is also the source of the myriad virtues of all Buddhas; therefore, it is called "Buddha-nature. (From the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and others):

It is also the source of the myriad practices of Bodhisattvas; therefore, it is called the "Ground of the Mind" (*citta-bhūmi*). (From the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*): The myriad practices do not transcend the six *pāramitās*.
Meditation (*dhyāna*) is merely one among these six, specifically the fifth. How could it alone be designated as the true nature (*tathatā*) and termed a single practice of meditation?

Ah! Yet among all practices, the single path of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) is the most divine and wondrous. It is capable of giving rise to the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) inherent in one's nature.
All sublime functions, the myriad practices, the myriad virtues, and even supernatural powers and radiance—all emerge from concentration.
Therefore, those of the Three Vehicles who seek the Holy Path must necessarily cultivate meditation; apart from this there is no gate, and apart from this there is no road. As for mindfulness...

When a Buddha seeks birth in the Pure Land, they likewise cultivate the sixteen contemplations of meditation (*dhyāna*), as well as the *nien-fo samādhi* (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi), the *pratyutpanna samādhi*, and others.
Furthermore, the true nature (*tathatā*) is neither defiled nor pure; there is no distinction between ordinary beings and sages.

However, within the gate of meditation (*chanmen*), there are levels of shallow and deep, with distinct gradations. It is said that those who practice while harboring heterodox views, rejoicing in higher realms and loathing lower ones, are practicing the meditation of external paths (*tīrthika*).
To cultivate with both aspiration and revulsion while correctly believing in cause and effect is the dhyāna of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

To cultivate after awakening to the principle of the partial truth of the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*) is the dhyāna of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). To cultivate after awakening to the ultimate truth manifested by the emptiness of both self and phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is the dhyāna of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*).

(The four aforementioned categories all possess distinctions regarding the four formless realms and the four spheres of emptiness. If one suddenly awakens to the fact that one’s own mind is originally pure...
Fundamentally, there are no afflictions; the nature of untainted wisdom is inherently complete from the beginning. This mind is itself the Buddha, ultimately without distinction.

To practice in reliance upon this is the meditation of the Supreme Vehicle. It is also called the Tathāgata’s Pure Meditation, the Single Practice Samādhi, and the Samādhi of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
This is the root of all samādhis. If one can maintain mindfulness...

Through the cultivation of mindfulness, one naturally and gradually attains hundreds of thousands of samādhis. This is the very Chan that has been transmitted successively from master to disciple within the lineage of Bodhidharma.
Before Bodhidharma’s arrival, the interpretations of various schools were all based on the four dhyānas and eight samāpattis;
eminent monks who practiced them all attained their respective functional powers. Only later did Nanyue and Tiantai instruct practitioners to rely upon the principle of the three truths.

Although the teachings and meanings of practicing the three types of cessation (*śamatha*) and the three types of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) are most perfect and subtle, their methods of entry and the sequence of their stages are nonetheless merely the various characteristics of the aforementioned meditative practices.
Only that which was transmitted by Bodhidharma is sudden and identical to the Buddha-body, standing far apart from all other gateways;
therefore, those who study this school find its essential meaning difficult to grasp. To grasp it is to become a sage and swiftly realize *bodhi*; to lose it is...

This would lead to perversion and cause one to swiftly enter the mire and darkness. Therefore, the ancestors changed their ways to prevent such loss, transmitting it from one person to another for a time;

once later generations had something to rely upon, they allowed thousands of lamps to illuminate together. However, as the Dharma remained long and became corrupted, those who committed errors grew numerous.

Consequently, among those who study the sutras and śāstras, instances of doubt and slander are likewise numerous. To examine the origins: the Buddha taught both sudden and gradual teachings, and Chan opened both sudden and gradual gates.

These two teachings and two gates correspond perfectly with one another. Yet today, the lecturers emphasize exclusively the meaning of the gradual, while the Chan practitioners propagate exclusively the sudden school.
When Chan and lecturing meet, they are as far apart as Hu and Yue; (Zongmi) I do not know what deeds were performed in past lives [to result in this].

Having perfumed this mind, though he himself was not yet liberated, he sought to untie the bonds of others. For the sake of the Dharma, he risked his very body and life; his compassionate heart was more urgent than his physical spirit. (As the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:

"If one is bound oneself and claims to be able to untie the bonds of others, such a thing is impossible. Yet he could not bring himself to stop; this was verified as being due to the difficulty of changing long-standing habitual tendencies.

He constantly lamented that people and the Dharma had diverged, and that the Dharma was becoming a sickness for people. Therefore, he separately compiled commentaries on the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras, extensively opening up the gates of precept and meditative concentration.
This is the Gateway of Wisdom. It reveals that sudden enlightenment relies upon gradual cultivation and demonstrates that the Master’s teachings accord with the Buddha’s intent.
Since the meaning has been shown in detail from beginning to end, the text is vast and difficult to navigate. Though those who study it extensively are many, those who maintain their resolve are few;

all the more so when one’s traces involve names and forms—who can distinguish gold from brass? They merely exhaust themselves without yet perceiving the resonance of the occasion. Although the Buddha’s teaching increases his compassion, [this situation remains].

This was his practice. Yet, he reflected that self-attachment and views were difficult to guard against; he therefore abandoned the multitude and entered the mountains to cultivate concentration and balance his wisdom.

For ten years, he continuously stilled his thoughts. Within his tranquil wisdom, the subtle habitual tendencies became manifest as they arose and ceased, along with the various meanings of the Dharma.
Arranged and manifested within the empty mind: like fine dust swirling in the sunlight through a window opening, or like reflections shimmering clearly at the bottom of a limpid pool.
How could this compare to the deluded meditation of those who stubbornly maintain silence, or the frantic wisdom of those who merely seek out the texts?

Nevertheless, because one originally attains realization of one’s own mind to discern the various teachings, one must earnestly apply oneself to the Heart-Teaching (*citta-tattva*); and it is precisely for the sake of discerning these various teachings that [this work] is composed.

Thus, one understands the cultivation of the mind and reverently adheres to the teachings and their meanings. As for the "Teachings" (Jiao), these are the sūtras and śāstras compiled by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
As for "Chan," these are the verses and gāthās composed by various spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).

The śramaṇa Daoyi was constantly practicing seated meditation at Mount Heng. The Master, knowing him to be a vessel for the Dharma, went to him and asked, "Virtuous One, what do you intend by sitting in meditation?

"Can a tile be made into a mirror? The Master said, "Since grinding a tile cannot produce a mirror, how can sitting in meditation make one a Buddha?
The monk asked, "How then is it so? The Master said, "It is like a bullock pulling a cart. If the cart does not move, do you strike the cart or do you strike the bullock?
The Master spoke again: "What you study in sitting meditation—is it to study sitting as a Buddha? If you study sitting meditation, meditation is not..."

Facing all objects, their mind is neither still nor distracted; neither grasping nor dispersing, they transcend everything. With no obstruction regarding sounds or forms, they are called a "Way-person" (*daoren*).
Regarding good and evil, right and wrong, they employ neither; they neither cling to a single dharma nor reject a single dharma. This is called...

To be a person of the Mahāyāna means not being bound by anything—whether good or evil, emptiness or existence, defilement or purity, conditioned or unconditioned, mundane or supramundane, merit or wisdom.

This is called the Buddha-wisdom. When all attachments regarding right and wrong, beauty and ugliness, principle and non-principle, and all conceptual views and emotions have been exhausted, one cannot be fettered; being sovereign everywhere is called the first arousal of the bodhicitta.
The Bodhisattva then ascends to the stage of Buddhahood. Question: "If one now receives the precepts, purifies body and speech, and has already perfected all virtues, will one attain liberation?
The Master said: "One attains a small measure of liberation, but has not yet attained liberation of mind, nor liberation in all places.
Question: "What is liberation of mind, and what is liberation in all places? The Master said: "Seeking nothing."
Regarding the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, one does not even seek merit, wisdom, knowledge, or understanding.

When both defiled and pure mental states are exhausted, one neither clings to this state of non-seeking as being "correct," nor does one dwell in that state of exhaustion. One does not rejoice in heaven or fear hell;
being unimpeded regarding bondage and liberation, the body, mind, and all places are termed "liberation. Do not say that there is even a fraction of precept remaining in the body.

To think that purity of speech and mind constitutes full realization is ignorance; you do not yet know that the gates of precepts, concentration, and wisdom—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—and the untainted liberation have not yet been touched by even a hair’s breadth.
You must exert yourself and press forward with fierce inquiry. Do not wait until your ears are deaf, your eyes grow dim, your face is wrinkled, and your hair has turned white;
until the suffering of old age has overtaken your body, and you are entangled in the bonds of sorrowful attachment, with tears streaming from your eyes and your heart filled with terror. One—
Having no basis for support, one does not know where one is going. At what point will it be that one cannot even manage one's own hands and feet?
Even if one possesses merit, wisdom, fame, and gain, none of these can provide salvation, because the eye of the mind has not yet opened;

one merely dwells upon various sensory objects without knowing how to reflect back upon oneself, and thus fails to see the Buddha-way. All the karmic conditions of one’s good and evil deeds throughout this lifetime will then manifest before one.
Suddenly, whether with joy or fear, the five aggregates of the six realms appear simultaneously before them.
Fully arrayed and magnificent dwellings, boats, ships, carriages, and litters all manifest with brilliant radiance; these are all produced from the greed and attachment of one’s own mind.
All evil environments are transformed into sublime realms. Following wherever the intensity of greed and attachment leads, and guided by the karmic consciousness, one undergoes rebirth accordingly.

There is not the slightest portion of freedom. Whether one is a dragon or a beast, noble or base, none of these distinctions are ultimately fixed. Question: How does one attain a portion of freedom? The Master said:
"If you can attain it now, then you have attained it. When confronted by the five desires and the eight winds, let the mind be free from grasping or rejecting.

When stinginess, envy, greed, attachment, and the sentiment of 'mine' are exhausted, and both defilement and purity have vanished, the mind is like the sun and moon in the sky—shining without being conditioned."

The mind should be like wood or stone; yet, moment by moment, it must be as if one were saving one's head from fire, or like a fragrant elephant crossing a river—cutting through the current and passing over without further doubt or stagnation. Such a person cannot be contained by either heaven or hell.
Now, when reading sutras or examining the teachings, all words and phrases must be turned back and brought to meet oneself. Yet, all these verbal instructions merely clarify that which is right now.
The nature of enlightened awareness is simply that it is not turned by any objects of existence or non-existence; this is your teacher.
It can illuminate and shatter all objects of existence and non-existence; this is the vajra-wisdom, which possesses a state of autonomous independence.
If you cannot understand it in this way, even if you were to recite the twelve Vedas, you would only achieve the arrogance of overestimation. Instead, [you will fall].

This is slandering the Buddha; it is not true cultivation. To simply distance oneself from all sounds and forms, yet neither dwell in that distancing nor dwell in intellectual understanding—this is true cultivation.

Reading scriptures and examining the teachings may be considered a good thing according to worldly standards, but when reckoned among those who clarify the principle, these are people who are obstructed;
even those on the Tenth Ground cannot escape this, as they flow back into the cycle of birth.
The River of Death. However, the teachings of the Three Vehicles all treat the maladies of greed, hatred, and so forth.

If at this very moment, in every thought-moment, there are maladies such as greed and hatred, you must first treat them. There is no need to seek out meanings, phrases, or intellectual understanding; such understanding belongs to greed.
Greed transforms into illness. Now, simply remain detached from all dharmas of existence and non-existence, and likewise detached from detachment itself.
By passing beyond these three propositions, you will naturally be no different from the Buddha. Since you are yourself the Buddha, why worry that the Buddha does not understand your words?
I fear that you are not yet a Buddha, for you are bound by the existence and non-existence of all phenomena and have not attained freedom.

Because your realization of the Principle has not been established, you are first possessed of merit and wisdom, which carry you away like a lowly servant serving a noble. It would be better to first establish the Principle;

only then will you possess merit and wisdom. If you truly desire merit and wisdom, you can produce them at any moment: you could take a handful of earth and turn it into gold, or take a handful of gold and turn it into earth, or transform the waters of the ocean.
[He] turned milk into ghee; he shattered Mount Sumeru into fine dust; he gathered the waters of the four great oceans into a single pore.
He rendered a single meaning into immeasurable meanings, and rendered immeasurable meanings into a single meaning. I humbly pray that you will honor [this].

Once, when the Master had finished preaching the Dharma and the assembly was descending from the hall, he called out to them. The assembly turned their heads, and the Master said: "What is this? (Yaoshan)
(These are known as the "Hundred-Fathom Hall" phrases. Whenever the Master performed manual labor or took up tasks, he invariably preceded the assembly.
His leaders could not bear this and secretly removed his tools, requesting that he cease. The Master said, "I have no virtue; why should I compete with others for toil?
Since his tools were searched for everywhere and not found, he likewise forgot to eat. Thus there arose the saying: "If one does not work for a day, one does not eat for a day."
It has spread throughout the world.
Chan Master Nanquan Puyuan initially studied the ancient regulations of the Xiangbu school and investigated the *Vinaya* texts and their precepts.

He subsequently traveled among various lecture halls, attending lectures on the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, and the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and *Śata-śāstra*. He refined his understanding of profound meanings and later sought instruction from the Great [Master].
In his quiet chamber, he suddenly forgot the trap [of conceptualization] and attained the Samādhi of Līlā (Free Play).
One day, while serving congee to the assembly of monks, Mazu asked, "What is this in the bucket? The Master said, "Old man, shut your mouth! Why do you speak such words? Mazu then desisted;
none of the other fellow practitioners dared to question him further. [One day] he ascended the hall [to preach]. "Dīpaṃkara Buddha..."
The Way is thus understood. If the various phenomena arise from what the mind’s characteristics conceive, they are false and unreal. Why? Because the mind itself does not exist;

how then could it give rise to various phenomena? They are like forms and shadows, or like discriminating within empty space, or like a person attempting to capture sound and place it in a box, or like blowing air into a net to make it full. Therefore, the Elder Masters said: "It is not the mind."
It is not the Buddha; it is not an object. Rather, I shall instruct you, my brothers, in the practice of the path.

According to the teachings, Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages dwell in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi and attain the secret Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas. They naturally acquire all meditative concentrations, liberations, and the wondrous functions of supernatural powers.
Reaching all worlds, they universally manifest form-bodies, or manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment.

Awakening, turning the Great Dharma Wheel, and entering Nirvana—causing immeasurable [beings] to enter a single pore, expounding a single phrase of the sutra for immeasurable eons without its meaning being exhausted, and teaching and transforming immeasurable billions of sentient beings so that they realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)—if this is still called "ignorance regarding the knowable" (*jñeya-āvaraṇa-moha*), it is an extremely subtle ignorance regarding the knowable.
It is utterly at odds with the Way; it is a great difficulty, a great difficulty! Be careful! Be careful!

The monk asked, "What is 'solitude is not within'? Nan-yü said, "To perceive sounds and forms is not the work of a true adept.
The monk then asked Changsha. Changsha stared at him with wide-open eyes. When the monk repeated his question, Changsha closed his eyes to show him.

The Master said, "Too worldly. The monk then pressed his palms together. The Master said, "Too monastic. The monk was speechless. [Commentary] [Verse] The Master and Huigui.
Zhong and Magu went together to pay their respects to National Teacher Nanyang. On the road, the Master drew a circle and said, "If you can speak of this, then you may go.
Zhong sat down right within the circle; Magu performed a woman’s bow. The Master said, "In that case, you shall not go.
Zhong asked, "What kind of mental activity is this? The Master then called out to them and they returned together, never going on again.
[The Master] pays homage to the National Preceptor. [Verse: While the Master was performing manual labor on the mountain, a monk asked, "Where does the road to Nanquan lead?
The Master picked up his sickle and said, "This thatch-sickle of mine was bought for thirty coins.
The monk said, "I am not asking about the thatch-sickle; where does the road to Nanquan lead? The Master replied, "It works perfectly well for me. ○ A monk asked:
"One cannot attain 'this very mind is Buddha,' nor can one attain 'neither mind nor Buddha. What is the Master's intention?
The Master said, "Virtuous One, simply believe that 'this very mind is Buddha' and you are finished. What more is there to say about attaining or not attaining?
