He did so. [Verse] While the Master was staying at his hermitage, a monk arrived. The Master said to him, "I am going up the mountain to do some work.
Wait until mealtime, prepare the rice, eat it yourself, and then send one portion up here.

After a short while, the monk prepared the rice for himself to eat, then smashed all the household utensils and lay down upon the bed. The Master waited, but seeing that he had not come, [he went up].
Returning to the hermitage, he saw a monk lying down. The Master also lay down beside him. The monk then got up and left.
After the Master had settled there, he said, "When I previously lived in that hermitage, there was a certain keen and intelligent practitioner; even until now, I have not seen him again.
[Verse] Dafu Lu Xun asked: "In my home, I have a large stone. Sometimes I sit upon it, and sometimes I lie upon it. Now I intend—"

[The Master] was carving a Buddha; [the monk] asked, "Can it still be recovered? The Master said, "It can. Lu said, "Is it not possible that it cannot be recovered? The Master said, "It cannot. [Verse: The Master went to a manor estate.
The master of the estate had prepared offerings in advance to welcome him. The Master said, "I, this old monk, usually enter and exit without letting anyone know.
Why have you made such elaborate preparations? The master of the estate replied, "Last night, the local deity informed me that the Master was coming."
Today [the Master] arrived. The Master said, "Old Wang lacks the power of cultivation; he has been seen by ghosts and spirits.
The attendant then asked, "Since the Master is a *kalyāṇamitra*, why was he seen by ghosts and spirits?

The Master said, "I shall simply add another portion of rice before the local deity. (Xuánjué said: "Where is it that one adds another portion of rice before the local deity? [Verse]: The First Seat asked, "Master..."
"Even after a hundred years, where will you go? The Master said, "I shall become a water buffalo on the mountain below.
The Seat-holder said, "If I follow the Master, will I still be able to attain it?
The Master said, "If you would follow me, you must first fetch a blade of grass in your mouth. [Verse]: The Master, Luzu, Shanshan, and Guizong—these four departed from Mazu.
They went their separate ways, each returning to his own hermitage. At the parting of the roads, the Master planted his staff in the ground and said, "If you can speak, you are hindered by this;
if you cannot speak, you are also hindered by this. Guizong pulled the staff and struck the Master once, saying, "It is just this!
What does Old Wang say about being hindered or not being hindered? Luzu said, "Just this."
A single phrase spread throughout the world. Zhaozhou asked, "Is there anything that is not sown? The Patriarch said, "There is. Zhaozhou asked, "What is it that is not sown?
The Patriarch made the gesture of clapping his hands. [Added from the supplementary collection.]
Master Yan’guan Qian’an’s Verse: A monk asked, “What is the original body of Rucana? The Master said, “Bring me the pure water pitcher.
When the monk brought the pitcher, the Master said, “Put it back in its original place.
The monk returned it to its place and came back to question him again. The Master said, “The ancient Buddhas have long since passed away. A lecturer-monk arrived.
"Enter. The Master asked, "Seat-Master, what is your occupation? He replied, "I lecture on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra. The Master said, "How many kinds of dharmadhātu are there?
He replied, "To explain extensively, they are infinitely layered; to explain briefly, there are four kinds. The Master held up his whisk.
The student asked, "Which dharma-realm is this? The Master hesitated. The Teacher said, "To know through thinking and to understand through deliberation is the livelihood of ghosts.
A solitary lamp beneath the sun—truly, its light is lost. [Verse] A monk asked Damei, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey?
Damei said, "There is no meaning in the Westward Journey. Upon hearing this, the Master said, "One coffin, two..."
A dead man (Xuan Sha said: "Yanguan was a master"). [Commentary] [Verse] One day the Master called to his attendant, saying, "Bring me the rhinoceros fan.

The attendant had no reply. (Touzi spoke on his behalf: "I would not refuse to bring it out, but I fear its horns and head are incomplete.")
Chan Master Guizong Zhichang ascended the hall and said: "The ancient worthies of old were not without understanding;
they were men of noble character who did not conform to the common run. People today are unable to establish themselves and merely waste their time in vain.
Disciples, do not apply your minds in error. No one can take your place, nor is there any place for you to apply your mind. Do not seek it from others. From the very beginning..."
This is merely relying on others for understanding; every word spoken is obstructed, and the light does not penetrate through, simply because there is something before one's eyes.
[Verse] A monk asked, "What is the profound principle? The Master said, "No one is able to comprehend it. The monk asked, "How about before [you spoke]? The Master said:

Again he asked, "Go! There is no place for you to apply your mind. He asked, "Is there not some gate of expedient means by which a student may gain entry?

Li went to ask the other monks. The monks said, "We do not understand either. Li returned and reported this to the Master.
"Do you understand? he asked. The monk replied, "I do not. The Master said, "This scholar does not even recognize a fist. The monk said, "Please, Master, give me instruction.
The Master said, "When you meet someone, you shall be granted it on the road; when you do not meet anyone, it shall be spread as worldly truth.

Because the Master had double pupils in his eyes, he took the scholar’s hand and massaged it until both of the scholar’s eyes also became red. Thus, the scholar was popularly known as "Red-Eyed Gui" (Chiyen Gui).
This is the core principle.
When Chan Master Damei Fachang first visited Daji, he asked, "What is the Buddha? Daji replied, "The mind itself is the Buddha.
The Master attained great enlightenment immediately and subsequently went to the old hermitage of Meizhen at Siming, where he bound up reeds to dwell in seclusion. [Verse] Great!
When Master Jiwen was residing on the mountain, he had a monk ask him: "Master, what did you receive from Great Master Ma that caused you to dwell on this mountain?
The Master replied, "The Great Master told me, 'Mind itself is Buddha,' and so I have dwelt here."
The monk said, "Master, lately the Buddha-dharma has become something else. The Master asked, "How so? He replied, "It is also said that it is neither mind nor Buddha.
The Master said, "This old fellow will continue to delude people for days to come; let him say 'neither mind nor Buddha' as he pleases."
"I simply maintain that 'this very mind is Buddha. The monk returned and reported this to Mazu. Mazu said, "The plum has ripened. [One day] he ascended the hall and said:
"All of you, each must turn your minds back to realize the fundamental source. Do not pursue its branches. If you only attain the root, the branches will come of themselves.
If you wish to recognize the root, you must only understand your own mind. This mind is originally all worlds..."
It is the root of mundane and supramundane dharmas. Therefore, when the mind arises, all manner of dharmas arise;
when the mind ceases, all manner of dharmas cease. The mind does not even depend upon good or evil to arise. All phenomena are fundamentally *tathatā* (suchness).

[Verse] While Jiashan and Dingshan were traveling together, as they were conversing, Dingshan said: "Within birth and death there is no Buddha; if there is no Buddha, then there is no birth and death. Jiashan...

Mount [Shan] said, "If there is a Buddha within birth and death, one will not be deluded by birth and death. They both refused to concede to one another and went up the mountain together to see the Master.
Jia Shan immediately raised the question: "I do not know which of these two men’s realization is more intimate.
The Master said, "One is intimate; the other is distant. Jia Shan asked again, "Which one is intimate? The Master said, "Go for now and come back tomorrow. The next day, Jia Shan...
He asked again. The Master said, "Those who are close do not ask; those who ask are not close" (after Jia Shan had taken up residence, he remarked of himself:
"At that time, I lost an eye"). One day, he suddenly said to his disciples: "That which comes cannot be suppressed; that which goes cannot be pursued.
While in a state of composure, he heard the sound of a flying squirrel and said, "This very thing is not another thing. You all, take good care of yourselves. I am now [leaving]."
"It is gone. Having finished speaking, he manifested his passing.
Emperor Shunzong of the Tang dynasty asked Master Fenguang Ru-man: "From which direction does the Buddha come? Toward which direction does he go when he passes away?
Since you say he dwells eternally in the world, where is the Buddha now? The Master replied: "The Buddha comes from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). He passes away..."
He has departed toward the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The Dharma-body is equal to empty space; it eternally abides in the state of no-mind.
Where there is thought, one returns to no-thought; where there is dwelling, one returns to non-dwelling. He comes for the sake of sentient beings; he departs for the sake of sentient beings.

In the pure ocean of True Suchness (*tathatā*), the essence is serene and eternally abiding. O Wise One, contemplate this well; do not give rise to further doubt. The Emperor asked again: "The Buddha..."

Born in the royal palace, he passed away toward the twin śāla trees; he remained in the world for forty-nine years. Furthermore, it is said that there is no dharma to be taught. Mountains, rivers, and the great ocean;
heaven and earth, as well as the sun and moon—when their time comes, they all return to extinction.

Who can say they are not subject to arising and ceasing? Such is the nature of doubt; let the wise discern it well. The Master replied: "The essence of the Buddha is fundamentally unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); it is through deluded sentiment that one falsely discriminates."
It is distinct. The Dharma-body is equal to empty space; it has never undergone arising or ceasing. When conditions exist, no Buddha appears;
when conditions are absent, a Buddha enters extinction. Everywhere he transforms sentient beings, like the moon reflected in water:

neither permanent nor annihilated, neither born nor ceased. Birth has never truly been born, and cessation has never truly ceased. To clearly perceive the state of no-mind is naturally to be without phenomena.
When the Emperor heard this, he was greatly pleased and came to hold the Chan school in even higher esteem.
Master Lingmo of Wuxie [Verse] traveled far to visit Shitou and asked immediately: "If our words accord, I shall stay;
if they do not, I shall depart. Shitou remained seated as usual. The Master then turned to leave. Shitou called out after him, "Dharma Uncle! The Master turned his head back.
Tou said, "From birth until death, it is only this very thing. Why turn your head and look back? At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment;
he then broke his staff and settled there. One day, he addressed the assembly, saying, "The Dharma-body is perfectly quiescent."
I manifest coming and going; the thousand sages share one source, and the myriad spirits return to the One. Now that I am like a bubble dispersing, why should you harbor grief?
Do not weary your spirit; you must maintain right mindfulness. If you follow this instruction, you truly repay my kindness; should you stubbornly disregard these words, [you will fail].
"He is not my son. At that time, a monk asked, "Where has the Master gone? The Master said, "I have gone nowhere.

The monk asked, "Why do I not see you? The Master said, "It is not something seen by the eyes. (Dongshan said, "A true adept. Having finished speaking, he suddenly passed away in accordance with the Way.
Chan Master Banzhan Baoji [Verse]: While walking through a marketplace, he saw a guest buying pork and said to the butcher, "Cut me a pound of the finest meat.
The butcher set down his knife, joined his palms, and said, "Prefectural Secretary, which part of this is not fine?
At these words, the Master attained realization. [Verse]: On another day, as he was leaving the gate, he saw people carrying a funeral bier.
The songmaster shook his bell and said: "The red wheel is certain to sink to the west; I wonder not yet where the soul has gone. Below the curtain, the filial son wept, crying out, "Alas!
Alas! The Master suddenly felt his body and mind leap with joy. Upon returning, he related this to Mazu, who gave his seal of approval. [Verse]: Entering the hall, [the Master said:
"Now, the moon of the mind is solitary and perfect; its light swallows the myriad phenomena. This light does not illuminate objects, nor do objects..."
It does not exist. When both light and its object have vanished, what thing could it possibly be? Zen Master, it is like throwing a sword into the air;
do not debate whether it reaches its mark or not. This is the traceless wheel of emptiness, where the edge of the sword remains unimpaired.

If you can be thus—moment after moment without cognition, the whole mind is the Buddha, and the whole Buddha is the person. When person and Buddha are without distinction, only then have you begun the Way. [Verse] (End)
"Venerable Master, one may study the Way within the Hall. It is like the earth supporting a mountain, unaware of the mountain's towering loftiness;
or like a stone containing jade, unaware of the jade's flawlessness. If one is thus, this is called 'leaving home. Therefore, the Guide said:
'The Dharma is fundamentally unimpeded, and so it is throughout the three periods of time. Even for those who are non-active and without affairs, there remains the difficulty of the golden chain.'"
Because the spiritual source shines alone, the Way is severed from birth. Great wisdom is not "bright," and true emptiness leaves no trace.

True Suchness, ordinary beings, and sages are all but dream-like words; Buddhas and nirvana are both merely figurative designations. Zen virtue, you must look for yourself; there is no one who can take your place.
[Commentary] [Verse] Entering the hall: In the Three Realms there is no dharma; where can one seek the mind? The four elements are fundamentally empty; the Buddha...
Upon what does it rely? The celestial sphere is unmoving; it is silent and wordless. It is presented face-to-face, with nothing else remaining. Take care!
[Verse] As the Master was about to pass into nirvana, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Is there anyone who can capture my true likeness?

The assembly presented the portraits they had painted, but none accorded with the Master’s intention. Puhua stepped forward and said: "I have captured it. The Master asked: "Why do you not present it?"
He appeared like an old monk. Huà then performed a somersault and departed. The Master said, "This fellow will go on to act like a madman in the future.
The Master then passed away.
Chan Master Magu Baoche [Verse]: He asked Linji, "Of the thousand hands and eyes of Great Compassion, which one is the true eye?
Linji said, "Of the thousand hands and eyes of Great Compassion, which one is the true eye? Speak quickly! Speak quickly!

The Master stepped forward, pulled Linji down from his meditation seat, and sat there himself. As Linji stepped forward and said, "How do you do? the Master hesitated, and Linji immediately shouted and pulled him down.
He descended from his meditation seat and sat back down; the Master then went out (from the *Linji Chapter*).
While the Master was fanning himself, a monk asked, "The nature of wind is eternally abiding and pervades everywhere. Why, then, does the Master still shake the fan?
The Master said, "You only know that the nature of wind is eternally abiding, yet you do not yet know that it pervades everywhere. The monk asked, "What is this 'pervading everywhere'?"
"This is the principle. The Master, however, continued to fan himself. The monk bowed. The Master said, "Even if you were to have a thousand such useless monks, what benefit would there be?"

Chan Master Ruyi of Tōji [Verse]: Since Great Silence (Daichi) passed away, the Master was constantly concerned that his disciples would incessantly recite and memorize the discourse on "mind itself is Buddha.
He remarked, "If one asks where the Buddha dwells to say 'mind itself,' the mind is like a painter;
yet you call it 'Buddha' itself. He then addressed the assembly, saying: "The mind is not the Buddha; wisdom is not the Way. The sword has gone."
It is far indeed; you are merely marking the boat. At that time, Dongsi was known as a "Zen Cave. [Verse] Yangshan visits. The Master asks, "Where are you from?
Yangshan replies, "A man from Guangnan. The Master says, "I have heard that Guangnan possesses the 'Taming the Sea Bright Pearl';
is this true? Yangshan says, "It is. The Master asks, "What is this pearl like? Yangshan says, "In the dark moon it is hidden; in the bright moon..."
He immediately appeared. The Master asked, "Have you brought it back? Yang said, "I have brought it back. The Master said, "Why do you not present it to this old monk?
Yang placed his palms together, stepped forward, and said, "Yesterday I arrived at Mt. Mui and was also asked for this pearl;
I was left with no words to respond and no principle to defend. The Master said, "A true lion cub, truly capable of roaring!"
One day, Master Xitang Zhizang was sent by Daji to Chang’an to deliver a letter to National Teacher Huizhong.
The National Teacher asked, "What Dharma does your teacher preach? The Master walked from east to west and stood there.
The National Teacher said, "Is it only this? The Master then walked back from west to east and stood there. The National Teacher said, "This..."
"This is Mazu’s. How do you understand it, worthy one? The Master said, "I have already presented it to the Venerable One.
[Commentary] [Verse] A monk asked Mazu: "Beyond the four propositions and transcending the hundred negations, I pray that the Master will directly point out the meaning of the West. Mazu said:
"I am weary today and cannot explain it for you; go ask Zhizang. The monk then went to ask the Master [Zhizang].
The Master said, "Why did you not ask the Abbot? The monk replied, "The Abbot told me to come and ask you, Venerable Elder."
The Master said, "I have a headache today and cannot explain it for you. Go ask your elder brother Hai.
The monk went to ask Hai (Master Baizhang), who replied, "When I get here, I do not understand either. The monk then reported this to Mazu.
The Patriarch said: "The head of the storehouse is white; the head of the sea is black. One day Mazu asked the Master, "Why do you not read the sutras?
The Master replied, "How could the sutras be anything other than what they are? Mazu said, "Even so, when you act as a teacher in the future, you must certainly be able to do so.
The Master said, "I, Zhizang, am currently ill and merely intend to nourish myself; how would I dare say I can act as a teacher? Mazu said, "In your later years, you will surely flourish."
The Master then prostrated himself. After Mazu had passed away, the assembly requested him to open the hall for formal teaching.

Once, Minister Li asked a monk, "What were the teachings of the Great Master Mazu? The monk replied, "The Great Master sometimes said 'This very mind is Buddha,' and sometimes he said 'Neither mind nor Buddha.
Minister Li said, "Both of you go over there! He then asked the Master, "What did the Great Master Mazu have to say?"
[The Master] did not speak a word of instruction. The Master called out, "Li Ao! Li responded, "Yes. The Master said, "The drums and horns are sounding. [Verse:
A monk asked, "When there is a question and an answer, the guest and host are clearly distinguished. But when there is no question and no answer, what then?

The Master said, "I am afraid it will rot away" (Later, a monk raised this question with Changqing, who said: "Everyone they meet says they have retired from office; but where has anyone ever been seen beneath the forest trees?").
Chan Master Zhangjing Huahui ascended the hall and said: "The ultimate principle transcends words, yet people of this age do not understand it.

They laboriously practice other matters, taking them to be spiritual efficacy, while failing to realize that their own nature is fundamentally not a realm of sensory objects. This is the subtle and wondrous gate of great liberation."
All discerning awareness is unstained and unimpeded; such radiance has never ceased or been abandoned. From past kalpas until the present, it remains eternally unchanged.
It is like the solar disc, which illuminates both near and far; though it reaches all forms, it does not merge with anything.
This spiritual torch and wondrous clarity do not require refinement; yet because of a lack of understanding, one grasps at external objects and images—this is merely as follows:

To press one's eyes shut is to falsely give rise to floating flowers; it is merely self-exhaustion, a waste of kalpas. If one can reflect back upon oneself, there is no second person; every movement and action will not fall short of the true mark (*dharmatā*). [Commentary] [Verse]: A monk came, circumambulated the Master three times, and stood shaking his staff. The Master said, "Right! Right! That monk then went to Nanquan and likewise circumambulated him three times, shaking his staff. The Master said, "Wrong! Wrong! The monk asked, "Why did you say 'Right' at Caoshan and 'Wrong' at Nanquan? The Master replied, "At Caoshan, I was pointing directly to the person; at Nanquan, I was pointing directly to the thing. The monk asked, "What is the person? The Master said, "The one standing before me. The monk asked, "What is the thing? The Master said, "The staff you are holding. The monk bowed and departed. The Master called out, "Wait!

When the monk turned his head, the Master said, "What a pity that you do not know how to recognize your own face! [Verse]: "When the staff is raised, the whole body is revealed; when the robe is pulled, the entire mind is exposed. If you can see through this in a single stroke, you will realize that the Buddhas and patriarchs have never been separate from you. [Commentary]: This case illustrates the direct pointing of the ancestral teachers. It is like a mirror reflecting reality—when the object is present, the reflection appears; when the object is gone, the reflection vanishes. To say "Right" is to affirm the person; to say "Wrong" is to negate the delusion. Yet, even as they point directly, the student must still turn the light inward. If one fails to recognize the face within the staff and the robe, one remains trapped in the duality of subject and object, wandering through the kalpas in vain. Only by returning the light to the source can one realize that there is no second person, and that every act of raising a hand or moving a foot is the unimpaired true mark.

This is the ultimate function of the Chan school: to cut off the flow of thought and manifest the original nature. To understand this is to enter the gate of the Buddhas and patriarchs. To fail to understand is to remain a common mortal. Thus, the verse concludes that if one can see through this in a single stroke, one will find that the Buddhas and patriarchs have never been apart from one's own daily activities. This is the meaning of "the staff is the person, the person is the staff"—a seamless unity where the tool and the user are one and the same. This is the teaching of the "direct pointing" that has been passed down from generation to generation. Those who hear this and attain realization are truly those who have met the ancestors. Those who hear this and remain confused are those who have missed the point for countless aeons. Therefore, the verse says: "If you can see through this in a single stroke, you will realize that the Buddhas and patriarchs have never been separate from you. This is the final word on the matter.
Dongshan stood leaning on his staff. Nanquan said, "No, no. This is turned by the power of the wind; in the end, it will fall into ruin.
The monk asked, "Zhangjing says it is so; why does the Master say it is not? Nanquan said, "Zhangjing is indeed right; it is you who are wrong."
Chan Master Dazhu Huihai received his training under Master Zhi of Dayun Temple in Yuezhou.
When he first visited Mazu, Mazu asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Dayun Temple in Yuezhou. Mazu asked, "What do you intend to seek by coming here?
He said, "I have come to seek the Buddha-dharma. Mazu said, "In this place of mine, there is not a single thing. What Buddha is there to seek?"
The Master said, "Dharma! You disregard your own precious treasury; why do you abandon your home and wander about?
The Master asked, "Which one is the precious treasury of Huihai? The Patriarch said, "That which is now questioning me is your precious treasury.
It is entirely complete, lacking nothing. Its use is sovereign; why should you seek it elsewhere? At these words, the Master recognized his own original mind, not through intellectual knowledge.
Jue leapt up, prostrated himself in gratitude, and served him as a disciple for six years. Later, because his preceptor had grown old, he returned abruptly to provide for him.

Jue then concealed his traces and hidden his talents, outwardly appearing dull and slow of speech. He composed the *Yuanwu rudao yaomen lun* (Treatise on the Essential Gate to Sudden Enlightenment) in one fascicle.

His dharma-nephew Xuanyan secretly took it out to the region beyond the Yangtze River to present it to Mazu. After Mazu had finished reading it, he addressed the assembly, saying: "In Yuezhou there is a great..."

The pearl is round and luminous; its light penetrates with ease, for there is no place of obstruction. At that time, disciples gradually increased in number, knocking upon him day and night to provoke his insight.
Having no choice but to comply, he answered each question as it arose; his discernment was unimpeded. A monk asked: "What is the Buddha?"
The Master said, "In this face-to-face clear discourse, who is it that is not the Buddha? The assembly was all at a loss.
A monk asked again, "How does one attain Great Nirvana? The Master said, "By not creating the karma of birth and death. The monk asked, "What is the karma of birth and death? The Master said:
To seek great nirvāṇa is the karma of saṃsāra. To abandon defilement and grasp at purity is the karma of saṃsāra. To have attainment and realization is the karma of saṃsāra.
Not to be liberated from the gates of antidotes is the karma of saṃsāra. [The interlocutor] asks: How, then, does one attain liberation?
The Master said, "Fundamentally there has been no bondage; there is no need to seek liberation. To act directly and proceed directly—this is the peerless equality.
A practitioner asked, "Regarding 'the very mind is Buddha,' which one is the Buddha? The Master said, "Which one do you doubt is not the Buddha?"
[The Master] pointed his finger and said, "This has no counterpart. The Master said, "To penetrate it is to be everywhere present; not to awaken to it is to remain forever alienated and distant.

The Vinaya Master Faming said to the Master, "In the houses of Chan masters, many fall into emptiness. The Master said, "It is actually in the houses of Dharma lecturers that one falls into emptiness.
Faming was greatly startled and asked, "How can one fall into emptiness? The Master said, "The sutras and treatises are paper, ink, and characters. Paper and ink—"
"Written characters," he said, "are all merely provisional constructs. To establish dharmas such as names and phrases upon sounds is nothing other than emptiness.
Master of the Doctrine (Zhuangzhu), you cling to the substance of the teachings; how can you avoid falling into emptiness? Ming asked, "Does the Chan Master fall into emptiness?
The Master replied, "I do not fall into emptiness. Ming asked, "How is it that you do not fall into emptiness? The Master replied, "Written characters and the like all arise from wisdom."

When life arises and the Great Function manifests before one, how could one possibly fall into emptiness? A practitioner asked, "In this world, is there any dharma that surpasses spontaneity (*ziran*)?
The Master said, "There is. The practitioner asked, "What dharma can surpass it? The Master said, "One who is able to know spontaneity.
The practitioner asked, "Is primal qi (*yuanqi*) the Way? The Master said, "Primal qi is primal qi; the Way is the Way. The practitioner said, "If it is so, then..."
"There are two," [the Master] said. [The monk] asked, "I know there are not two people. Furthermore, I ask: what is called 'deviant' (xie) and what is called 'correct' (zheng)?
The Master said, "When the mind pursues external objects, it is deviant; when objects follow the mind, it is correct. The Tripiṭaka Master asked, "Does True Suchness (tathatā) undergo change?
The Master said, "It does undergo change. The Tripiṭaka Master said, "The Chan Master is mistaken. The Master then asked the Tripiṭaka Master: "Does [your own nature] undergo change?"
"Is it true suchness? He replied, "It is. The Master said, "If there is no transformation, you are certainly an ordinary monk.
Have you not heard that a good friend (kalyāṇamitra) can transform the three poisons into the three groups of pure precepts, and transform the six consciousnesses into the six supernatural powers?"
"Transform afflictions into bodhi; transform ignorance into great wisdom.
If True Suchness were subject to change, then the Tripitaka would truly be the teachings of non-Buddhists. Zang said, "If that is so, then True Suchness must be subject to change.
The Master said, "If you cling to the notion that True Suchness undergoes change, you too are a non-Buddhist. Zang asked, "Just now, Master, you spoke of True Suchness..."
"There is change; yet now you also say that the Way does not change. How can this be correct? The Master said:
"If one has clearly realized their nature, it is like a *maṇi* jewel manifesting colors: one may say it changes, and one may also say it does not change.

If a person who has not seen their nature hears it said that True Suchness changes, they will immediately understand it as change. If it is said that it does not change," [they likewise misunderstand].

He then gave an interpretation that was unchanging. Baizhang said, "Thus we know that the Southern School is truly unfathomable. Someone asked, "Regarding the three teachings of Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism, how are they the same and how are they different?
The Master said, "For those of great capacity, when they employ them, they are the same; for those of lesser faculties, when they cling to them, they are different.
They all arise as function from within the single nature; it is through the differences in their faculties and views that they become three. This concerns delusion and awakening."
It depends on the person; it does not lie in whether the teaching is the same or different.

**Master Baizhang Weizheng of Hongzhou** [Commentary] [Verse] The Master asked Nanquan, “Among the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) of all quarters, is there any who possesses a Dharma that cannot be described to others?
Nanquan said, “There is. The Master asked, “How so? Nanquan replied, “It is not mind.”
"It is not the Buddha; it is not an object. The Master said, "If that is so, then you have already explained it to people.

He replied, "I am indeed like this; but what about you, Reverend? The Master said, "I am no spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). How could I know whether there is a teaching that is spoken or one that is not?
He said, "I do not understand. I beg the Reverend to explain. The Master said, "I have already given you far too much."
He did indeed say so.
Chan Master Leh Tan Fahui [Verse]: The Master asked Mazu, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
Mazu said, "Lower your voice and come closer; I will tell you. The Master then stepped forward. Mazu gave him a slap and said, "Six ears!"
"Do not plot together. Go now; come back tomorrow. The next day, the Master entered the Dharma Hall alone and said, "I request the Abbot to speak.
The Patriarch said, "Go now; wait until I have ascended the hall, then come out and ask. I will provide testimony for you.
The Master suddenly attained realization and said, "I thank the Great Assembly for their testimony. He then circumambulated the Dharma Hall once and departed.
Chan Master Shigyan Chiken [Verse]: Once, while traveling with Guizong and Nanquan, they encountered a tiger on the road.
Each passed by the tiger’s side. Nanquan asked Guizong, "Just now, when you saw the tiger, what was it like? Guizong said:
"It looks like a cat. Zong then asked the Master (Baizhang). The Master said, "It looks like a dog. He then asked Nanquan. Nanquan said, "I see it as a great tiger. [Daopei Zhi said:
These three old fellows are gathered here talking in their sleep. If you want to penetrate through, you must investigate this great tiger all at once.
[Verse] While the Master was eating his meal, Nanquan collected some raw rice and said, "Is it raw? The Master said, "Non-arising. Nanquan said, "Non-arising..."
This was still the secondary [level]. After walking several paces toward the spring, the Master called out, "Elder! Yuanquan turned his head and asked, "What?
The Master said, "Do not say it is the secondary."
When Chan Master Shigong Huizang was first a hunter shooting deer, he encountered Mazu, who commanded him to shoot himself but found no place to begin.

Upon this realization, the Master cast down his bow and arrows and entered the monastic life under Mazu. After taking up residence, he constantly used his bow and arrows as a means of engaging students.
One day, while he was performing manual labor in the kitchen, Mazu asked him, "What are you doing? He replied, "I am tending the ox. Mazu said:
"How do you herd it? He replied, "Once it has entered the grass, I suddenly pull it back by the nose. The Patriarch said, "You truly herd the ox. The Master then desisted.
(Below this chapter there is one verse-commentary; as the karmic occasion originates from within the records of Sanping, it is not included here.)
The Elder Liang of Hutang asked Chan Master Bei Lan Rang: "I have heard that you, elder brother, have painted a portrait of our late master;

I request permission to pay my respects. The Master opened wide his chest with both hands to show it to him. Liang immediately prostrated himself. The Master said, "Do not prostrate! Do not prostrate!
Liang said, "Elder brother, you are mistaken. I am not prostrating to you, elder brother. The Master said, "Then you are prostrating to the late master?"
Master Zhenna said, "Why did you tell him not to prostrate? Master Liang said, "How could he have ever been wrong?
Zen Master Nanyuan Daoming went to visit Dongshan; as he was just ascending the Dharma Hall, the Master said, "We have already met."
Shan then descended the mountain. The next day he ascended again and asked, "Yesterday I was already graced by the Master’s compassion;
I do not know at what point we truly met. The Master said, "Mind to mind, without interruption, flowing into the ocean of nature.
Shan said, "How could I have let this pass? Shan took his leave. The Master said, "Study the Buddha-dharma extensively and perform great benefit for others."
Yi said, "I do not ask about studying much of the Buddha-dharma; how is it that one brings about vast benefit?
The Master said, "Do not oppose a single thing.
Chan Master Hong'en of Zhongyi [composed a verse]: When Yangshan asked, "How can one realize the meaning of seeing the Buddha-nature? the Master said, "I..."
"I shall give you a simile. Suppose there is a room with six windows, and inside there is a monkey.
Outside, there is another monkey who calls out from the eastern window, 'O monkey! and the monkey inside responds immediately. In this way, if called from all six windows, it responds to each.
Yangshan bowed in thanks and said as he rose, 'I have now understood everything through the Master’s simile. However, there is one further matter.'"
"It is like an inner monkey who has fallen asleep while an outer monkey wishes to meet him. Furthermore, how so?
The Master descended from his rope-corded seat, took Yangshan’s hand, and danced, saying, "Singing-monkey! We have met."
Chan Master Ledu Changxing was asked by a monk, "What is the ultimate matter of the宗乘 (the lineage transmission)? The Master said, "In the autumn rains, the grasses fall away. [Verse:
Nanquan arrived and saw the Master sitting with his face against the wall. He patted the Master on the back. The Master asked, "Who are you?
Nanquan replied, "Puyuan. The Master said, "How is it? Nanquan said, "It is just as usual. The Master said, "Why do you trouble yourself so much?"
Chan Master Wuye of Fenzhou used to lecture on the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* for the assembly of monks every day, without ceasing during either winter or summer.
Later, hearing that the Chan school under the Great Master Mazu was flourishing, he went specifically to pay his respects.

Upon seeing that the Master’s appearance was extraordinary and his voice resonant like a bell, Wuye remarked, "Aloft is the Buddha-hall, yet within it there is no Buddha. The Master prostrated himself and knelt to ask: "The Three..."

He studied under Master Wenxue, gaining a rough understanding of his essential teachings. He had often heard it said in the Chan school that "the mind itself is Buddha," yet he truly could not comprehend this.

The Master said, "The very mind that you do not understand is precisely it; there is nothing else besides. The Teacher asked, "What is the Mind-Seal that the Patriarch secretly transmitted when he came from the West?
The Master replied, "Virtuous One, you are quite busy right now. Go for now and come back at another time. As soon as the Teacher had stepped out, [Master Wenxue struck him].
The Patriarch called out, “Virtuous One! The Master turned his head. The Patriarch asked, “What is this? At that, the Master attained realization and prostrated himself.

The Patriarch said, “You dull-witted fellow! Why do you prostrate? After receiving this instruction, he traveled to Caoxi to pay respects at the Patriarch’s stupa, and visited Mount Lu and Tiantai to seek out all the sacred sites.
Later, he resided at Kaiyuan Monastery. [Verse] When students posed questions, for the most part...
He replied to him, saying: "Do not engage in false conceptualization. The Tang Emperor Xuanzong summoned him repeatedly, but he declined on the pretext of illness and did not go.
When Emperor Muzong ascended the throne, the Master received an imperial decree. In the middle of the night, he told his disciples Huiting and others:
"The nature of your seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing is coeval with the great void; it is neither born nor extinguished. All realms are fundamentally empty and still from the beginning."
There is one dharma that can be attained, yet those who are deluded do not understand it; thus they are confused by objects. Because they are confused by objects, they transmigrate without end.
You should know that the nature of the mind is inherently present from the beginning, not produced through artificial effort;
it is like a vajra, indestructible. All dharmas are like shadows and echoes, possessing no reality. As the Sūtra says: "Only this one thing."
"Reality alone is true; the other two are not real. To constantly realize that all is empty, such that not a single thing accords with the mind—this is the sphere of the Buddhas' mental activity.
You all should practice this diligently. Having spoken these words, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.
Chan Master Datong Cheng [Verse]: A monk asked, "What is the person of original nature? The Master said, "Sitting together, we do not know each other.
The monk said, "If that is so, then I, this student, shall take my leave with gratitude. The Master said, "In the dark, one writes upon a sorrowful heart; to whom can it be sent?
(This one case appears in both the *Datong Pujie* and the *Touzi Datong*. Although the original karmic occasion is indeed under Datong Cheng, the verse may not be his).
Chan Master Dayi of Gehu [Verse]: Emperor Xianzong of the Tang dynasty once issued an imperial decree for him to enter the palace. At the Linqide Hall, they discussed the principles of the Dharma.
A Dharma Master asked: "The realm of desire has no Chan; Chan resides in the realm of form. Upon what does this [realm of] earth rely to stand? The Chan Master said:
"The Dharma Master only knows that the realm of desire has no Chan; you do not know that the realm of Chan has no desire. [The Master asked: "What is Chan?"

The Master pointed at space with his hand. The Dharma Master had no reply. The Emperor said, "The Dharma Master has expounded endless sutras and śāstras, yet he cannot even deal with this single point.
The Master then asked the eminent elders, "In walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, what ultimately constitutes the Way?
One replied, "Knowing is the Way. The Master said, "It cannot be known by intellect; it cannot be cognized by consciousness."
“Consciousness—how can one know that which is consciousness? “Non-discrimination—this is it. The Master said:
“One who is well able to discern the characteristics of all dharmas without wavering from the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)—how can one know that which is non-discrimination?

“The four dhyānas and eight samādhis—these are it. The Master said: “The Buddha-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and does not fall into any dispersion; how can it reside within the four dhyānas and eight samādhis?”
[The Emperor] was wrong. The assembly all closed their mouths [in silence]. The Master then cited the case of Emperor Shunzong asking Chan Master Śrī:

"How can the sentient beings of this great earth see their nature and attain Buddhahood? Śrī replied: "Buddha-nature is like the moon in the water; it can be seen, but it cannot be grasped. He then said to the Emperor:
"Buddha-nature is not something to be seen, yet it must be seen. How can one seize the moon in the water? Thereupon, the Emperor...

The Emperor asked, "What is Buddha-nature? The Master replied, "It is not separate from what Your Majesty has just asked. The Emperor silently realized the True Principle and accorded him even greater reverence.
Chan Master Funiu Zizai visited Mazu and realized the mind-ground. Mazu ordered him to deliver a letter to National Teacher Huizhong.
The National Teacher asked, "With what Dharma does Master Mazu instruct his disciples? He replied, "He teaches 'this very mind is Buddha. The National Teacher said:
"What kind of talk is this? After a long silence, he asked again, "Beyond this, what further words of instruction are there?
The Master said, "Neither mind nor Buddha. Someone remarked, "Not mind, not Buddha, not a thing. The National Teacher said, "That is still somewhat better.
The Master asked, "Master Mazu speaks thus; I wonder how it is here in your own school, Reverend Sir? The National Teacher said:
The three dots are like flowing water; the curve is like a sickle for reaping grain. ○ Entering the hall:

"This mind is Buddha" is the phrase of seeking medicine when one is not ill. "Neither this mind nor Buddha" is the phrase of counteracting medicine and illness. A monk asked, "What is the phrase of liberation?
The Master said, "It has been passed down from ancient times beneath Mount Funiu."
Chan Master Xingshan Weikuan was asked by a monk, "What is the Way? The Master said, "A magnificent mountain. The monk said, "I am asking about the Way;
why do you speak of a 'magnificent mountain'? The Master said, "You only recognize a magnificent mountain; when have you ever attained the Way?
[Another time] he was asked, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature? The Master said, "It has. The monk asked, "Does the Master have it? The Master said, "I do not."
[The monk] asked, "All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; why is it that you alone, Preceptor, do not? The Master said, "I am not among all sentient beings.
[The monk] asked, "If you are not a sentient being, are you perhaps a Buddha? The Master said, "I am not a Buddha. [The monk] asked, "Ultimately, what kind of thing are you?
The Master said, "I am also not a thing. [The monk] asked, "Can you be seen or can you be thought of? The Master said, "If one tries to think of me—"
Furthermore, as they deliberated on this and could not reach a conclusion, it was called "inconceivable" (*acintya*).
When the Imperial Edict reached the capital, the Minister of the Court of Ceremonial, Bai Juyi, once asked: "Since you are called a Chan Master, why do you preach the Dharma?
The Master replied: "Unsurpassed Bodhi, when applied to the body, is the Vinaya; when spoken from the mouth, is the Dharma; and when practiced by the mind, is Chan. These are its three applications."

The ultimate principle is one and the same. It is like the Yangtze, the Yellow River, the Huai, and the Han; though they are given different names according to their locations, the nature of water is not dual.
The Vinaya is itself the Dharma, and the Dharma is not separate from dhyāna. Why, then, do you give rise to false discrimination within it? He asked:

"If there is no discrimination, how does one cultivate the mind? The Master said: "The mind is fundamentally without injury or damage; why is it necessary to cultivate or repair it? There is nothing to be done."

[The student] asked: "Regarding the discussion of defilement and purity, one must not give rise to any thoughts at all. If defilement is something that cannot be thought of, can it be said that purity is beyond thought?

The Master said: "It is like the surface of a person's eye; not a single thing can remain there. Although gold dust is a precious treasure, when it is in the eye, it becomes an affliction. [The student] asked:
"If there is neither cultivation nor thought, how does this differ from that of an ordinary person? The Master said: "Ordinary persons possess ignorance (avidyā)..."
To ride upon [the teachings] and become attached to them—these two are illnesses. To be free from these two is called true cultivation. One who truly cultivates neither exerts effort nor forgets.
To exert effort is to approach attachment; to forget is to fall into ignorance. This is the essential point of the mind; it is said thus.
A monk asked, "Where does the Way reside? The Master said, "It is right before your eyes. The monk said, "Why do I not see it? The Master said, "Because you have a self."
"Why do you not see? he asked. The Master replied, "Because there is 'I' and 'I,' one does not see. The monk asked, "Does the Preceptor still see?

The Master said, "If there is 'you' and 'I,' we will continue to fail to see each other. The monk asked, "If there is neither 'I' nor 'you,' can you still see? The Master said, "If there is neither 'you' nor 'I,' who is it that seeks to see?"
Chan Master Sanguo Zongyin [Verse]: Entering the hall, he said, "If one discusses this matter, as soon as you raise your eyebrows, you have already missed it.
Magu then asked, "I do not ask about raising the eyebrows; what is this matter? The Master said:
He missed the mark. Gu then overturned the meditation seat, and the Master struck him.
Chan Master Luzu Baoyun [Verse]: Whenever he saw a monk coming, he would simply turn his back to the wall. Nanquan heard of this and said, "I usually tell the monks:
'If you try to understand it before the Buddha appeared in the world, you will not find even one or half of a person.'"
"One person. He acts like this; it will take him as long as a donkey's years [to understand]. (Baofu asked Changqing, "As for Lu Zu’s essential point, where does it lie?
When Nanquan spoke thus, Changqing said, 'To withdraw oneself and yield to others—there is not one in ten thousand who can do so.'")
The Layman Pang asked Zen Master Fuyong Taiyu, "Did you receive the Master’s instruction on his point of truly benefiting people?
The Master replied, "I have not yet even seen him; how could I see his point of being real?"
The layman said, "As for this very seeing and knowing, there is no place to seek it. The Master said, "Layman, you must not speak with one-sidedness.

The layman said, "If I were to speak with one-sidedness, you, Master, would again lose the fundamental principle. If I were to speak from two sides or three sides, would you still be able to open your mouth?
The Master said, "Truly, I cannot open my mouth; this may be called reality. The layman clapped his hands and departed.
A monk asked Master Ziyu Daotong, “How can one escape from the three realms? The Master said, “How long have you been inside them?
The monk asked, “How does one achieve liberation? The Master said, “Green mountains do not obstruct the flight of white clouds.”
[Verse] Lord Yu asked: "What is it like when a black wind blows one’s boat and causes it to drift down into the land of the rākṣasa demons?
The Master said: "Lord Yu Di, you hired laborer! Why do you ask such a thing? Lord Yu turned pale with fear. The Master then pointed and said:
"This very [state] is what it means to drift down into the land of the rākṣasa demons. [Verse] The Lord asked again: "What is the Buddha?"
The Master called out, “Sir! The gentleman responded, “Yes? The Master said, “Do not seek anything else.
Master Yingfeng of Wutai (i.e., Deng Yingfeng) [Verse]: When the Master arrived at Nanquan, he saw the assembly of monks in the midst of their practice.
Nanquan pointed to a pure pitcher and said, “The silver pitcher is the objective realm. There is water within the pitcher; do not disturb the realm. Bring it to me, old monk.”
"Water! The Master picked up the pure water pitcher and poured it toward the front of Quan’s face; Quan then ceased.
Chan Master Xiyuan Tanzang received the mind-seal from Daji; later, he visited Shitou, whereupon his realization became brilliantly clear and penetrating.
He moved to reside at Xiyuan. His assembly of Chan practitioners flourished daily. One day, while the Master was bathing, a monk asked him, "Why do you not have a novice (śrāmaṇera) do this for you?

The Master clapped his hands three times. (A monk asked Caoshan, "Master, when you clapped your hands at West Garden, was that not the business of slaves and servants? Caoshan said, 'It was. The monk asked, 'Is there anything further above this?
Caoshan said, 'There is. The monk asked, 'What is the matter above this? Caoshan shouted, 'You slave and servant!')"

Chan Master Yangqi Zhenshu ascended the hall and said: "The myriad spirits share a single source; they are provisionally named 'Buddha. Though their substance is exhausted and their form dissolves, they do not perish;
though the metal melts and the raw ore disperses, they remain ever-present. In the ocean of nature, where there is no wind, the golden ripples surge of themselves.

When the spiritual mind is free of signs, the myriad phenomena are illuminated all at once. One who realizes this principle traverses the sands of the world-realms without speaking and acts without effort."

His meritorious contributions to the profound transformation of beings were immense. How could he have turned his back on awakening and instead conformed to worldly toil, delusively imprisoning himself within the aggregates and realms?
Chan Yue asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master held up his rosary; Chan Yue was at a loss.
The Master asked, "Do you understand? He replied, "I do not. The Master said, "I have come to study under Shitou. He asked, "What realization did you gain from seeing Shitou?
The Master pointed to a deer in the courtyard and asked, "Do you understand? He replied, "I do not. The Master said, "It has attained freedom."
Chan Master Maitreyamati [Verse]: Ascending the hall, he said: "To know while being without knowing—this is not a state of non-knowing;

yet it is called 'non-knowing. He then descended from his seat. (Nanquan said: "If one follows the Master's way like this, one has only spoken half the truth. Huangbo said: "It is not that Nanquan is refuting him; rather, he wishes to complete the previous statement.)"
Chan Master Hualin Shanjue [Verse]: The Provincial Inspector Pei Xiu visited him and asked, "Do you have any attendants?
The Master replied, "I have one or two, but they cannot see guests. Pei asked, "Where are they? The Master then called out, "Dakong! Xiaokong!
At that moment, two tigers emerged from behind the hermitage. Upon seeing them, Pei was struck with terror. The Master—
He said to the two tigers, "There is a guest; you may depart. The two tigers roared and left. Pei asked, "What kind of practice did you master, Master, to have moved them in such a way?
The Master remained silent for a long while and then asked, "Do you understand? He replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "This mountain monk constantly recites the name of Avalokiteśvara."
A monk asked Master Mengxi, "How does one realize the fundamental matter?
The Master said, "Why do you not ask? The monk said, "I request the Master to answer my question. The Master said, "You have asked well. The monk laughed loudly and departed.
The Master remarked, "Only this monk is sharp-witted. Another monk came from outside; the Master immediately shouted. The monk said, "What a fine occasion! The Master—
The monk said, "The staff is still required. The monk, having paid his respects, departed. The Master said, "He has attained mastery.
Whenever Master Fuyao saw a monk coming, he would strike the ground with his staff and say, "The Buddhas of the past were also like this."
Later, when the Buddha was thus, someone asked, "At this very moment, what is it? The Master drew a circle.
The monk performed a woman’s bow. The Master then struck him. Someone asked, "What is 'of a different species'? The Master struck a bowl and said, "Huanu, Huanu, come and eat!"
Master Wujou [Verse]: The two senior monks Xuanshao and Er came to visit him. The Master asked, "Where did you two Zen travelers set out from?
Xuanshao said, "Jiangxi. The Master struck him. Xuanshao said, "I have long known that the Master possesses this essential pivot.
The Master said, "Since you do not understand, let the monk behind you respond. As Shaoyi prepared to step forward, the Master struck him.
He said, "I truly know that those in the same pit have no different soil. [The monk] went to attend the hall. [Commentary] [Verse] The Master asked a monk, "Where have you recently departed from?
The monk replied, "Dingzhou. The Master said, "How does the Dharma-way of Dingzhou compare to here? The monk replied, "It is no different. The Master said, "If it is no different..."
He turned and went away. The Master struck him. The monk said, "There is an eye at the tip of the staff; one must not strike people so recklessly.
The Master said, "Today I have hit one indeed," and struck him three more times. The monk then went out.
The Master said, "The staff was originally meant for someone to eat [the consequences]. The monk said, "But the handle of the ladle is still in the hands of the Master. The Master said, "If you..."
"Wait! I shall give it back to you," the Master said. The monk stepped forward and snatched the staff, striking the Master three times.
The Master said, "A wasted blow! A wasted blow! The monk replied, "There is someone here who can take it. The Master said, "Hastily, I have struck a man of substance.
The monk bowed, and the Master said, "And so he goes away. The monk laughed loudly and departed. The Master said, "He can bear it! He can bear it!"
Shi Jiu Wushang [Verse]: When he first visited Mazu, Mazu asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Wujiu.
Mazu asked, "What sayings or phrases has Wujiu been teaching lately? The Master replied, "How many people here are utterly bewildered by it! Mazu said:
[The Master] was at a loss and set it aside for a moment. "Silently, how is this one phrase? The Master then stepped forward three paces.
The Patriarch said, "I have seven blows to be delivered to Wujou; do you agree to this? The Master replied, "The Master shall eat them first; I will agree to them afterwards."
Master Benchxi [Verse]: Regarding the question posed by Layman Pang: "When Danxia struck his attendant, what was his intention?
The Master said, "Old man, you have been measuring others' strengths and weaknesses. The Layman said, "Since we are fellow students of the same teacher, I venture to ask this of you.
The Master said, "If that is so, bring it up from the beginning and let us deliberate together. The Layman said, "Old man, you..."
"You may discuss right and wrong with me. The Master said, "I am mindful that you, old man, are advanced in years.

The Layman said, "A transgression! A transgression! Stone Forest Monk [Verse]: Seeing Layman Pang approaching, he held up his whisk and said, "This does not fall within the scope of Danxia’s mechanism;
try and say a single phrase. The Layman snatched away the whisk and instead raised his own fist. The Master said, "Precisely so."
Dana’s pivot: The Layman said, "Do not let me fall into a mere viewing. The Master said, "Danxia suffers from muteness; Panggong suffers from deafness.
The Layman said, "Exactly so. The Master was speechless. The Layman said, "I told you it was merely coincidental."
Master Liang [Verse]: He was quite proficient in expounding the sutras and śāstras. Upon visiting Mazu, Mazu asked, "I have heard you lecture extensively on the sutras and śāstras;
is that true? The Master replied, "I dare not say so. Mazu said, "With what do you lecture? The Master said, "I lecture with the mind."
The Patriarch said, "The mind is like a skilled performer; the intellect is like the conductor. How could you possibly understand this through lecturing?
The Master raised his voice and said, "If the mind cannot be lectured upon, can empty space be lectured upon? The Patriarch replied, "In fact, it is empty space that can be lectured upon.
The Master, dissatisfied, departed. As he was about to descend the steps, the Patriarch called out, "Preceptor! The Master turned his head. The Patriarch asked, "What is that?"
The Master attained a sudden and great enlightenment, and immediately prostrated himself. The Patriarch said, "Why does this dull-witted master prostrate?
The Master replied, "I thought that no one could equal me in the sutras and treatises I have lectured upon; today, however, I have been surpassed by the Great Master’s single question."
The lifelong achievements of his life were all at once dissolved like ice.

One day, Master Baoling encountered Layman Pang on the road and asked, "Have you ever shared that phrase by which you attained realization on Mount Nanyue with anyone? The Layman replied, "I have. The Master asked, "To whom did you share it?"

The scholar pointed to himself with his hand and said, "I am Pang Gong. The Master said, "Even if it were Wondrous Virtue (Mañjuśrī) or Empty Birth (Śāriputra), they would not have been able to praise you adequately.
The scholar then asked, "Master, who knows the phrase by which you attained your power? The Master put on his bamboo hat and walked away.
The scholar said, "Be careful on your way," but the Master did not look back.
**Nanquan Puyuan (The Ox-Horn Monk)** [Commentary] [Verse] Every day he prepared food to offer to the assembly of monks.
When it was time for the midday meal, he carried the rice bucket to the front of the hall and performed a dance. Laughing loudly, he said, "Sons of the Bodhisattvas, come and eat!"
A monk asked National Teacher Lishan, "When all forms return to emptiness, where does emptiness return? The Master said, "The tongue does not leave the mouth.
The monk asked, "Why does it not leave the mouth? The Master said, "Because inner and outer are one and the same."
Master Luyuan [Verse]: Entering the hall for discourse, he said, "The direct meaning from the West is indeed difficult to fathom.

Is there anyone among you who can express it? Come forward and try to speak. At that time, a monk stepped forward to prostrate. The Master struck him and said, "What kind of occasion is this for making your appearance?

He then returned to his quarters. (A monk reported this to Changqing, who said, "Not at all, not at all. Zifu would have said on his behalf: 'It is because the Master does not begrudge [his life].'"")
[On] Body and Life).
Master Songshan [composed a] Verse: While drinking tea with Layman Pang, the Layman held up his tea bag and asked, "Everyone has their share;
why is it that they cannot speak? The Master said, "Precisely because everyone has their share, they cannot speak."
The scholar said, "Elder brother, why is it that you can speak so? The Master said, "One must not remain without words.
The scholar said, "Truly, truly! The Master then drank his tea. The scholar said, "Elder brother, when you drink your tea, why do you not bow to your guests?
The Master said, "Who? The scholar said, "Master Pang. The Master said, "Why bother to bow further? Later, when Danxia heard of this, he remarked, "If it were not for..."
"This is Songshan. For some time, he has been deluded by this old fellow. When Layman [Wang] heard this, he sent someone to deliver a message to Xiang, saying:
"Why do you not realize it at the moment before the bag is even lifted?"
When Master Chuanshan [recited this verse], he and Layman Pang were picking tea. The Layman said, "The Dharma-realm admits no body;
does the Master still see me? The Master said, "It is not I, the old monk. Upon answering the Layman's question, the Layman said, "There was a question and there was an answer."
"This is merely routine," the Master said, and he continued picking tea without listening. The scholar said, "Do not take offense; I was just casually asking. The Master still paid him no heed.
The scholar shouted, "You ill-mannered old fellow! I shall report you one by one to those with clear vision!
Thereupon, the Master threw down his tea basket and returned directly to the abbot’s quarters. [Verse] One day, while in the abbot’s quarters...
The Master was sitting. When the layman arrived and saw him, he said, "I only knew you were sitting upright in your chamber;
I did not realize the monk had come to receive my visit. At that moment, the Master lowered one foot. The layman immediately stepped out, walked two or three paces, and then turned back.

The Master then withdrew his foot. The layman said, "Truly, this can be called being free and at ease. The Master said, "I am the master. The layman said, "You, Master, only know there is a master; you do not know..."
A guest arrived. The Master called for his attendant to prepare tea. The Layman (Pang) performed a dance and departed. (Nantang Xing commented: "Excellent! Both Mazu and Pang Gong were excellent.

Observe how these two masters meet in such a manner; it is like two dragons playing with jewels—neither harms the other. This is what is meant by 'entering the forest without stirring the grass, entering the water without disturbing the waves. Only here can one truly know the state of absolute freedom. But tell me, what is it that possesses such miraculous efficacy?
After a long silence, he further offered this verse... [Included in the Supplement].

Master Dazhu [Verse]: Having received the essential instruction from Jiangxi, he constantly concealed his name. Whenever a student posed a question, he would respond only by striking the ground with his staff;
thus, he was known as Master "Striking the Ground. One day, a monk hid his staff away.

Thereupon, he posed a question. The Master merely opened his mouth. The monk asked his attendant, "As for the Master’s daily practice of striking the ground when someone asks him a question, what is the underlying meaning?
The attendant immediately took a piece of firewood from within the hearth.
[He] threw [it] into the cauldron.
Master Xiuxi [offered this] verse: Guishan asked: "When sound and form are pure and true, what is the Way? The Master said: "Why do you disturb the Way?
Guishan then moved from east to west and stood there. The Master said: "Had it not been so, it would have been a disaster. Guishan—
Again, as he moved from west to east and came to a standstill, the Master descended from his meditation seat and took two steps.
Guishan seized him and asked, "How is it with the matter of sound and form being utterly true? The Master then gave him a slap.
Guishan said, "In thirty years, will there even be anyone left to serve tea? The Master replied, "What would I do with this fellow Guishan? Guishan sighed in disapproval.
He laughed heartily. Master Bi Shu of Jiangxi [composed this] verse: While [the Master] was lying down, Daowu approached and pulled the blanket over him.
The Master asked, "What are you doing? Daowu said, "To cover you. The Master asked, "Is it the one who is lying down? Or is it the one who is sitting? Daowu said, "It is neither of these two."
The Master said, "What can you do about being covered over? I said, "Do not speak nonsense. [Verse by] Master Shuilao:
When he first visited Mazu, he asked, "What is the true meaning of the coming from the West? Mazu said, "Prostrate yourself.
As soon as the Master prostrated, Mazu stepped on him right at the chest. The Master attained great enlightenment; rising up, he patted [Mazu].
Master Hehe laughed loudly and said, "How extraordinary! How extraordinary!
The hundreds of thousands of samādhis and immeasurable subtle meanings are all recognized by tracing their source back to the tip of a single hair. Having paid his respects, he withdrew.
Later, whenever he addressed the assembly, he would say, "Ever since I took that one bite from Mazu’s kick, I have been laughing without ceasing until this very day."
Master Fubai [Verse]: Ling Xingpo came to pay her respects. The Master offered her a seat and tea.
The nun asked, "To whom do you entrust that phrase which cannot be uttered even with one's full strength? The Master said, "Fubai has no superfluous words.
The nun said, "Before reaching Fubai, I was not without doubt. The Master said, "If you have another point of excellence, feel free to bring it forth. The nun folded her hands.
She wept, saying, "O Blue Heaven! I have been further disgraced by grievous suffering. The Master remained silent.

The old woman said, "If one speaks without knowing the distinction between the biased and the correct, or fails to recognize the difference between the inverted and the upright, calamity will arise for those who act as teachers. Later, a monk reported this to Nanquan. Nanquan said, "How bitter it is for Fubei!
He has been thoroughly broken down by this old woman. When the old woman later heard of this, she laughed and said, "Master Wang still lacks something."

Chengyi the Chan practitioner encountered an old woman on the road and asked, "What is it that Nanquan still lacks in terms of his 'mechanism'? The woman then wept, saying, "How tragic! How painful! Do not allow yourself to be ensnared by them; this is the true place of training. A monk asked: "I once took leave of an elder master, who said to me, 'Go, and associate with virtuous companions;
attach yourself to good friends. Now I take leave of the Master; I wonder what instructions you have for me? The Master said: "Prostrate yourself. The monk prostrated.
[The monk] bowed. The Master said, "As for bowing, you may bow as you please; do not mistake a servant for a lord.
Zen Master Xian of Lingjiu ascended the hall and said, "This is the fundamental duty of each of you.
If I were to speak on your behalf, it would be like drawing legs on a snake. At that time, a monk asked, "I do not ask about drawing legs on a snake; what is this fundamental duty?"
[The monk] asked about a specific matter. The Master said, "Venerable, try to say something. As the monk was about to ask again, the Master said, "Why do you keep drawing lines?
A monk asked West Chan (Xichan) Abbot of Suzhou, "I do not ask about the Three Vehicles or the twelve divisions of the teachings.
What is the very meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master raised his whisk and showed it to him. The monk did not prostrate; he simply withdrew.
Xuefeng asked, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From Zhejiang. Xuefeng said, "Where were you this summer? The monk replied, "At Xichan. Xuefeng said, "Is the Master well?
The monk replied, "When I arrived, he was in full health. Xuefeng said, "Why did you not stay there at ease?
The monk replied, "I do not understand the Buddha-dharma. Xuefeng said, "What is the matter? The monk recounted the previous conversation. Xuefeng said, "You..."

"How is it that you do not accept him? [Xuefeng] said. [The monk] replied, "He is an object. Xuefeng said, "Do you see the men and women in the houses within the city of Suzhou? [The monk] replied, "I see them. Xuefeng said, "Do you see the trees, groves, ponds, and marshes along the road? [The monk] replied, "I see them. Xuefeng said, "All these things you see—the men and women in the houses, the great ponds, the forests, and the marshes—are all objects. Do you accept this? [The monk] replied, "I accept it. Xuefeng said: "Even so, why do you not accept him? [The monk] replied, "Because he is a person. Xuefeng said, "If you see a person, you must also see their eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind. If you see their eyes, you must also see their seeing; if you see their ears, you must also see their hearing; if you see their nose, you must also see their smelling; if you see their tongue, you must also see their tasting; if you see their body, you must also see their touching; and if you see their mind, you must also see their thinking. If you can see their seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and thinking, then you will see the person. If you cannot see their seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and thinking, then you do not see the person. If you do not see the person, how can you say, 'He is a person'?
