"As for the mere act of raising the whisk—why do you not accept it? The monk then prostrated and said, "I have spoken thoughtlessly;
I beg the Master’s compassion. Feng said, "The entire universe is this single eye.
Where will you sit and squat within it? The monk was speechless.
Dafu Lu Xing [Commentary] [Verse]: He asked Nanquan, "Master Zhao is truly extraordinary; he understands that heaven and earth share a single root and all things are one body.
Nanquan pointed to the peony in the courtyard and said, "Dafu, when people of this age see this single flower, it is like being in a dream.
(This kōan is recorded in the *Huìyuán* according to the chapter on Nanquan.)

The Lay Practitioner Gan-zhi [Verse]: One day he entered Nanquan’s hall to prepare for a vegetarian feast. Huangbo was serving as the head seat (shouzuo). The practitioner requested that alms be distributed.
The head seat said, “Between the two gifts of wealth and Dharma, there is no distinction. Gan said, “If you speak thus, how can you deserve my offering? He then took it out.
A moment later he re-entered and said, “Please grant me the gift of wealth. The head seat said, “Between the two gifts of wealth and Dharma...”

The offerings were equal and without distinction; Gan then proceeded to distribute the *dakṣiṇā*. [Verse: On another day, he entered the monastery to provide gruel and invited Nanquan to perform the recitations.
Nanquan struck the gavel and said, "I request the assembly to recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* for the sake of the marmot and the white ox.
Gan brushed his sleeves and departed. After the meal, Nanquan asked the steward, "Where has the Master gone?"
Zuo said, "I would have gone right then and there. Quan immediately smashed the cooking pot.
Chan Master Chang of Guannan was asked by a monk, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? The Master raised his staff and said, "Do you understand?
The monk replied, "I do not understand. The Master then struck him. Whenever the Master saw a monk come to pay his respects, he would mostly drive him away with his staff.
Some said, "It is delayed by one hour. Others said, "The drum of Guannan has been struck," yet among their contemporaries, few sang in response or harmonized with them.
When Chan Master Xuanzhen of Shuangling first asked Wudeng, "Why is it that the tracks of the Bodhisattva without supernatural powers are difficult to find?
Wudeng said, "Only those who walk the same path know. The Master asked, "Does the Master know? Wudeng said, "I do not know."
The Master said, "Why do you not understand? I replied, "Go away; you do not recognize my words. Later, the Master realized the essential meaning under Yanguan.
Chan Master Jiansong of Mount Jing had a junior disciple named Hongxin, who prided himself on his scholarly exegesis. The Master said to him:
"The True Dharma of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is direct and transcends all verbal explanation. Your calculation of the sands of the ocean—what benefit does it provide for the ultimate principle?

If you can simply refrain from harboring cognitive views and extinguish external conditions, becoming free from all mental activity, that is your true nature. Yin was at a loss; he then paid his respects and took leave to travel to various regions.
Upon reaching Mount Gui, he finally awakened to the profound essence and subsequently became a successor of Master Guishan.
Chan Master Lingxun of Furong [Verse]: When the Master took his leave of Guizong, Guizong asked, "Where are you going?
The Master replied, "I am going back to the South. Guizong said, "You have been here for many years; now that you are packed and ready to depart, come back and let me speak some Dharma for you.
The Master finished his preparations and went upstairs. Guizong called, "Come closer! The Master approached. Guizong said, "The time..."
"Han! Be well on your way. The Master took these words to heart and immediately forgot his former understanding.
When National Teacher Daemao of Silla ascended the hall, he said: "If you wish to recognize the Teacher of all Buddhas, recognize him within the mind of ignorance.
If you wish to recognize the eternally abiding, undecaying nature, recognize it in the midst of the constant transformation of all phenomena."

Chan Master Zhìtōng of Wǔtái (who styled himself the "Great [Divine] Buddha") [Verse]: Originally under Guījōng, one night he suddenly cried out repeatedly, saying, "I have attained great enlightenment!
The assembly was startled by this. The next day, when he ascended the hall and the assembly had gathered, Guījōng said, "The monk who attained great enlightenment last night, come forward.
The Master stepped forward and said, "This humble one. Guījōng asked, "What principle have you seen that you speak thus?"
He attained great enlightenment. "Try to explain it to me," [Zhaozhou] said. The Master replied, "A nun was originally made of woman. Zong was struck with wonder. The Master then took his leave.
Zong saw him off at the gate and handed him his straw hat. The Master took the hat, placed it on his head, and walked away without looking back.
At the time of his death, he composed a verse: "Raising my hand, I grasp the Southern Dipper; Turning my body, I lean against the Northern Polestar. I have emerged from the heavens."
Looking outward: who among you is a person like me?
Master Tianlong of Hangzhou ascended the hall and said: "Great assembly, do not wait for this old monk to come up; if you wish to come up, come up; if you wish to go down, go down.
Each of you possesses the ocean of the nature of the Flower Treasury (Huazang Xinghai), fully endowed with merit and unimpeded radiance. Each and every one...
Excerpt: Bai Juyi, the Prefect of Hangzhou, had long studied under Foguang. He attained the heart-dharma and simultaneously received the Mahāyāna Vajra Jewel Precepts (and so forth).
Whenever he held office, he frequently sought out the ancestral Way, studying without a fixed teacher.
The Monk Puhua of Zhenzhou [Verse]: He served as a disciple of Panshan, who secretly transmitted to him the true instructions. Yet he feigned madness and spoke without restraint.
After Panshan passed away, he traveled to spread the teaching in the northern regions. Whether in cities or among burial mounds, he would shake a single bell and say:
"If it comes from the bright side, I strike the bright side; if it comes from the dark side, I strike the dark side; if it comes from the four quarters and eight directions..."
Xuánfēng struck him. Xūkōng came forward and struck him in succession. One day, Línjì ordered a monk to seize him and asked, "What if he does not come in this manner at all?
The Master pushed him away and said, "Tomorrow there is a vegetarian feast at Dàbēi Monastery. The monk returned and reported this to Línjì.
Línjì said, "I have always suspected this fellow; whenever he meets someone, regardless of their status, he simply shakes [his sleeves]."
A single sound of the gong. [Verse] One day, Linji was sitting in the monks' hall together with the Elder Mudata of Heyang.
They were discussing how the Master (Linji) daily acted like one driven by wind and madness in the marketplace, and whether he was an ordinary person or a sage.
Just then, the Master entered; Linji immediately asked him, "Are you an ordinary person or a sage? The Master replied, "First, tell me: am I an ordinary person or a sage?"
"Saint! Jì shouted. The Master pointed his finger and said, "The bride of He-yang; the grandmotherly Zen of the wooden pagoda;
Linji, that little fellow—he alone possesses a single eye. Jì said, "This thief! The Master said, "Thief! Thief! and then went out.
Chan Master Liangsu of Shouzhou [Verse]: He went to visit Magu. When Magu saw him coming, he took up a hoe and began weeding.

When the Master reached the spot where Magu was weeding, Magu paid him no mind at all and returned to his quarters, closing the door behind him. The next day the Master went again, and Magu closed the door once more.
The Master then knocked on the door. Magu asked, "Who is it? The Master replied, "Liangsu. As soon as he had uttered his name—
Suddenly, he attained realization and said, "Preceptor, do not deceive me, Liangsui.
Had I not come to pay my respects to you, Preceptor, I would have been led astray by the sutras and treatises for the rest of my life. Gu then opened the door to meet him.
Upon returning to his lecture hall, he said to the assembly, "What all of you know, Liangsui knows entirely; what Liangsui knows, none of you know."
When Chan Master Huichao of Shushan went to pay his respects at Dongshan, the Master said, "You have already established yourself in one place;
why have you come here again? Dongshan replied, "Liang-jia is helpless before my doubts; I have come specifically to see the Master.
The Master called out, "Liang-jia! Dongshan responded, "Yes. The Master asked, "What is it? Dongshan was speechless. The Master said, "A fine Buddha indeed, but he simply lacks—"
Guangyan. A monk asked Chan Master Chuwai of Qianzhou, "Regarding the three vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings, one attains the wondrous through the realization of their principle;
are the intent of the patriarchs the same as this, or are they different? The Master said, "One must discern beyond the six propositions; one must not be turned by sounds and forms. The monk said:
"What are the six phrases? The Master said, "Speaking; silence; neither speaking nor silent; all of these; none of these.
How would you handle it? The monk had no reply.
The Tang Emperor Xuanzong asked Chan Master Hongbian of Jianfu Temple, "What is called 'precept' (śīla)? He replied, "To guard against wrongdoing and cease evil is called precept.
The Emperor asked, "What is 'concentration' (samādhi)? He replied, "When the six sense faculties encounter objects, the mind does not follow after conditions;

this is called concentration. The Emperor asked, "What is 'wisdom' (prajñā)? He replied, "When both mind and objects are empty, and one’s illumination and awareness are free from delusion, this is called wisdom."
The Emperor asked, "What constitutes skillful means? He replied, "Skillful means is the gate of provisional ingenuity that conceals reality and covers up appearances.
To provide guidance for those of middling and inferior capacities by employing indirect methods to lead and instruct them is called 'skillful means.

Even to say to those of superior faculties, 'Set aside skillful means and speak only of the Unsurpassed Way,' is itself a discourse of skillful means. This extends even to the profound words of the Patriarchs, which forget all merit."
He said, "There is no trace of even the means for emergence. The Emperor asked, "What constitutes the Buddha-mind?
He replied, "Buddha is a term from the Western Heaven; in the language of Tang, it means 'Awakened. It refers to a person possessing wisdom and illuminating awareness as the Buddha-mind.

'Mind' is another name for the Buddha, which has hundreds of thousands of different designations, yet its essence is but one. It has no form or shape; it is neither blue, yellow, red, nor white; it is not male..."
The characteristics of female and so forth—whether among devas or non-devas, humans or non-humans—manifest as devas or humans, and can appear as male or female.

Being neither beginning nor end, without birth and without extinction, it is therefore called the nature of numinous awakening. Just as Your Majesty responds to the myriad affairs of state every day, this is precisely Your Majesty’s Buddha-mind.
Even if a thousand Buddhas were to transmit it together, they would not consider there to be anything else to be attained.

The Emperor asked, "What if there is someone nowadays who recites the Buddha's name? He replied, "When the Tathāgata appeared in the world, he served as the Teacher of Gods and Humans and as a Good Spiritual Friend (kalyāṇamitra).
He taught the Dharma according to their respective capacities: for those of superior faculties, he revealed the Supreme Vehicle so they might suddenly awaken to the ultimate principle;
for those of middling and inferior faculties, who were unable to understand it all at once, the Buddha, for the sake of Vaidehī, provisionally opened the sixteen [visualizations]."

The Gate of Contemplation (*guanmen*) causes the practice of *nianfo* (mindfulness of the Buddha) to result in rebirth in Sukhāvatī. Thus, a sutra states: "This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. Outside of the mind there is no Buddha;

outside of the Buddha there is no mind. The Emperor asked: "If some people uphold the sutras and practice *nianfo*, while others uphold mantras (*dhāraṇī*) seeking the Buddha, how should these be regarded?
He replied: "The Tathāgata’s various expositions and praises are all for the sake of the Supreme Vehicle (*ekayāna*). It is like the myriad rivers [all flowing into the sea]."
"Rivers all flow toward and take the sea as their source. In this same way, all these various differentiated numbers return to the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).

The Emperor asked, "Since the Patriarch has already attained the seal of mind-to-mind transmission (*cittamudrā*), how is it that the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* speaks of 'dharmas that can be obtained'? He replied:
In the Buddha’s single transformation, there is truly not a single dharma given to others; he merely shows all people that their respective self-natures are one and the same Dharma-treasury.
At that time, when the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara merely certified Śākyamuni’s original dharma and there was nothing to be attained, he then accorded with Dīpaṃkara’s original intent.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "There is no self and no person; there are no sentient beings and no life-spanners. This dharma is level."

[The Master replied: "I cultivate all wholesome dharmas without dwelling upon their marks. The Emperor asked: "Since you, Chan Master, have realized the meaning of the Patriarchs, do you still prostrate to the Buddha and recite the sutras?
He replied: "For a śramaṇa or a śākyaputra, prostrating to the Buddha and reciting the sutras is simply the constant dharma of maintaining the tradition."

There are four types of retribution. Nevertheless, one should cultivate the body in accordance with the Buddha’s precepts, seek out wise teachers, gradually practice the myriad deeds, and tread the path traversed by the Tathāgata.
The Emperor asked: "What is meant by 'sudden realization,' and what is meant by 'gradual cultivation'? He replied: "To suddenly clarify one's own nature is to be of the same rank as the Buddhas;
yet, because there are defiled habits from time immemorial, one must rely on gradual cultivation as an antidote to bring [the mind] into accord."
The function of the arising of nature is like a person eating rice: one does not become full after a single mouthful.
On that day, the Master debated for seven *ke* (hours), was granted a purple robe, and was titled Chan Master Yuanzhi.
When Master Yangshan arrived for an audience with Master Langzhou Gudī, the Master said, "Go away; you have no Buddha-nature.
Yangshan placed his palms together, stepped forward three paces, and responded with an "Amen" (Eh). The Master smiled and said, "From where did you obtain this samādhi? Yangshan replied:
"I received my name from Danyuan and attained the ground at Guishan. The Master asked, "Are you not then a son of Guishan?
Guishan said, "In terms of worldly truth, it is not that I am not; however, regarding the Buddha-dharma, I do not dare [claim such].
Guishan then asked, "From where did you, Reverend, obtain this samādhi? The Master replied, "I obtained this samādhi from Zhangjing. Guishan sighed and said, "Not..."
Inconceivable! It is difficult for those who come to find a place of rest.
Master Gaoji of Hezhong Prefecture [composed this] verse: While traveling on the Road of the Arhats, he encountered an old man riding an ox.
The Master asked, "Where does the Road of the Arhats lead? The old man patted his ox and said, "Speak! Speak! The Master shouted, "This beast!"
Sheng’ou asked, “Where does the path of the Arhats lead? The Master, however, patted the ox and said, “Speak! Speak!
Sheng’ou said, “Even if it were so, you still lack hooves and horns. The Master then struck him, and Sheng’ou patted the ox and ran off. [Added from other collections.]
Master Bimokshan (Bimioban) [Verse]: He always carried a wooden fork. Whenever he saw a monk come to pay his respects, he would immediately place it around the monk’s neck and say:
"Which demon taught you to leave the household life? Which demon taught you to travel as a pilgrim? If you can speak, you die under the fork;
if you cannot speak, you die under the fork. Speak quickly! Speak quickly! Among his disciples, few were able to respond.
When Master Tong of Mount Huo visited the Teacher, as soon as he saw him, he did not prostrate but instead leapt into his arms.
The Teacher patted Tong three times. Tong rose, clapped his hands, and said, "Brother, you have deceived me for three thousand li;
you have deceived me for three thousand li! and then he departed.

**Master Zhilin of Hunan [Verse]:** He would constantly revile Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, calling them both mere malevolent spirits. Holding a wooden sword in his hand, he claimed to be subduing demons.
As soon as he saw a monk coming to pay his respects, he would cry out, "A demon has come! A demon has come! and brandish the sword wildly before returning to his quarters.
This continued for twelve years. Afterward, he set aside the sword and remained silent. A monk asked, "For twelve years..."
[The monk] asked, "Why did you subdue the demons previously? The Master said, "Thieves do not strike the homes of the poor.
[The monk] asked, "Twelve years later, why did you not subdue the demons? The Master said, "Thieves do not strike the homes of the poor."
A monk asked Zen Master Qi’an of Huangzhou, “How does one recognize one’s own Buddha? The Master said, “When a single leaf is bright, it cannot be exhausted;
when the melody of the pines and wind ceases, there is no one to lament. The monk asked, “What is one’s own Buddha? The Master said:
The swift horse galloping before the grass is truly difficult to exhaust; to reach the ultimate subtlety, one must still follow the path of the beast.

The Venerable Master Chen of Muzhou maintained the precepts with rigorous discipline and was learned in the Tripitaka; he traveled to various regions and attained realization of the essential meaning under Huangbo.
Later, at the request of the fourfold assembly, he resided at Guanyin Yuan. His followers constantly numbered over a hundred, and this continued for several decades.
[Verse] When students came to challenge him, he would answer immediately according to their questions; his phrasing was steep and perilous, as it did not follow conventional paths.

Consequently, those of shallow capacity often mocked him, yet only those of profound learning and quick intellect revered and submitted to him. Thus, seekers from all quarters flocked to him in admiration, all regarding him with the utmost respect.
He was previously known as Chen the Straw Sandal Maker. Later, he returned to Kaiyuan Monastery and lived in a room weaving straw sandals to support his mother;

thus he earned the nickname "Chen the Straw Sandal Maker. Whenever he saw a monk lecturing, he would call out, "Preceptor! The preceptor would respond, "Yes? The Master would then say, "A fellow carrying a single board!
[Verse] One evening, during the late assembly, he addressed the multitude, saying: "All of you here—have you yet attained a point of entry? If not,"
"You must find a point of entry; you need to find a point of entry. If you find a point of entry, you must not, hereafter, betray this old monk.
At that time, a monk came forward and bowed, saying, "I shall never dare to betray the Master.
The Master said, "You have already betrayed me. He added, "I have told you clearly, yet you still do not understand."
[The Master] said, “Indeed! How much more so when one covers it up for the future! [Verse: When the Master saw a monk, he said, “This is a case already resolved;
I grant you thirty blows. The monk said, “I am like this. The Master said, “Why does the *vajra* at the entrance of the three gates raise its fist?
The monk said, “Even the *vajra* is like this. The Master then struck him. A monk asked, “What is the path that leads upward? The Master said:
"What difficulty is there in the essential Way? [The student] said, "I request the Master to speak of it. The Master said, "The third and the first; the middle nine and the lower seven. [Verse]:
When asked about removing one layer by means of another layer, that is not what I am asking. When one does not remove one layer by means of another layer, how is it?
The Master said: "Yesterday morning I planted eggplants; today I plant winter melons. [Question]: A certain person asked, "I am both a lecturer and a practitioner."
[The student] asked, "When one does not understand the meaning, what should be done? The Master said, "It is truly as it is; you must repent.
[The student] said, "I beg the Master for instruction. The Master said, "If you had not questioned me, I would have remained silent with my mouth shut. Since you have questioned me..."

The Marrow. ○ Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "This nature is originally pure and replete with myriad virtues.

The King of the Empty Mind is profound and subtle, difficult to fathom. Formless and signless, he possesses great supernatural power; he can extinguish a thousand calamities and bring to fulfillment ten thousand virtues.
Although his essential nature is empty, he is able to bestow the Dharma rules. When observed, he has no form; when called upon, he has a voice.

He serves as the Great General of the Dharma, transmitting the scriptures of the Mind-precepts. Like the flavor of salt in water or the presence of blue in lacquer, he is definitively present, though not [visible].
Seeing its form, the mind-king is likewise: dwelling within the body, entering and exiting through the gate of the face, responding to objects according to circumstances, sovereign and unimpeded;
all that it does is accomplished. Realizing the fundamental consciousness-mind, with this consciousness-mind one sees the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha, and this Buddha is the mind.
In every thought-moment, there is the Buddha-mind; the Buddha-mind recollects the Buddha. If you wish to achieve success early, restrain yourself with the mind of precepts and maintain purity.

The Vinaya purifies the mind; the mind itself is the Buddha. Apart from this sovereign mind, there is no other Buddha. Those who seek to attain Buddhahood must not defile themselves with a single thing.
Although the nature of the mind is empty, the essence of greed and anger is real. Upon entering this Dharma-gate, one attains Buddhahood while sitting upright.
Having reached the other shore, one obtains the *pāramitās*. A true seeker of the Way should observe their own mind and know that the Buddha resides within. Do not...
Seeking outwardly, one finds that mind is Buddha and Buddha is mind. When the mind is clear, one recognizes Buddha; when one understands thoroughly, one recognizes the mind.
Apart from the mind there is no Buddha; apart from Buddha there is no mind. That which is not Buddha cannot be fathomed; it is incapable of being grasped.

Clinging to emptiness and stagnating in quiescence, one drifts and sinks therein. The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not find peace of mind in this; the Great Beings who have clarified their minds awaken to this profound resonance. Body—[text ends].
The nature of the mind is wondrous; its function never changes. Therefore, the wise let the mind rest in its natural freedom.

Do not say that the mind-king is empty and devoid of intrinsic nature, for it can cause the physical body to act either erroneously or correctly. It is neither existent nor non-existent, appearing and disappearing without fixed certainty.

The nature of the mind transcends emptiness; it can manifest as both ordinary and sagely. For this reason, I exhort you: take care to guard and be cautious yourself. Every moment of action returns [to the source].
Furthermore, it is not swept away or submerged. The pure mind-intelligence is like the gold of the world; the Dharma-treasury of Prajñā resides within both body and mind.

This unconditioned Dharma-jewel is neither shallow nor deep. All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have realized this original mind; those who encounter it through the right conditions do so beyond the distinctions of past, future, and present.

Fearing that the administrative official might discover his situation and find it inconvenient, the Master took his leave and went into hiding at a village temple. After three years had passed, he suddenly heard a youth reciting the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra.
When the text reached the passage, "To those who should be saved by the body of a bhikṣu, he immediately manifests in the body of a bhikṣu," he experienced a sudden and great awakening.
He then burned incense and prostrated from afar, saying, "I now know with certainty that my late teacher’s final words were never in vain."

He set out. From that time on, he could not understand [the teaching] and instead resented his former master. Once the former master had passed away, he thought, "Only Shishuang is the legitimate grandson;
he will surely provide proof. He then went to visit Shishuang. Upon seeing him, Shishuang asked, "Since leaving Daowu, where have you been?"

The Master rose and stepped forward, saying, "I request the Master to speak a turning word. Baoshuang said, "Have you not heard it said:
'I will not speak of life, nor will I speak of death'? The Master then recounted the circumstances of his realization while at the village temple, and finally prostrated himself in worship.

Chan Master Lucheng was asked by a monk, "What is formlessness? The Master replied, "The mountains are green and the waters are blue. A monk came for an interview.
The Master looked at him with his eyes. The monk said, "This is a mechanical device; it has no application within my own sphere. The Master snapped his fingers three times.
The monk circumambulated the meditation seat once and stood in his place. The Master said, "Go to the hall. Just as the monk was about to leave, the Master let out a shout.
The monk then looked back at him with his eyes. The Master said, "Truly, it has no application. The monk bowed.
One day, Zen Master Shengshan Sengmi was hoeing the tea garden with Dongshan.

Mount [Shan] said, "You think that those who possess physical strength are [the ones who attain it]. Grand Master Pei asked a monk, "When one makes offerings to the Buddha, does the Buddha eat them?

As they were coming down [the mountain], Yanguan asked the Master, "What about when one comes down all at once? The Master said, "Close your bowl. Yanguan approved of this.

I do not do it this way. You do not do it this way; I, however, do it this way. The monk again prepared to advance.

The Master said, "The clay ox steps forward at every stride. A monk asked, "When nothing can encompass it everywhere, what then?
The Master said, "At midnight, the stone man has no shadow; though he moves crosswise and lengthwise, one cannot discern his source or destination."
Chan Master Jia Shan Shanhui ascended the hall and said: "Since the time of the Patriarchs, people have misunderstood the transmission.
To this day, they take the words and phrases of the Buddhas and Patriarchs as models for teaching others. If one acts in this way, one instead becomes a madman or a person devoid of wisdom.
He [the Patriarch] merely pointed it out to you: that the absence of dharmas is itself the Way; the Way has not a single dharma; there is no Buddha to be realized."
The Way can be attained; there is no dharma to be grasped, and no dharma to be abandoned. Therefore, the old monk says: "Before one's eyes there is no dharma, yet the meaning lies before one's eyes.
This is not a dharma of the present moment. If you seek to learn from the Buddhas and patriarchs, such a person has not yet possessed the eye. Why?

Because all such things belong to that which is relied upon, and thus one does not attain self-mastery. It is fundamentally because birth and death are vast and boundless that consciousness [is deluded].
By nature, there is no portion of freedom. To seek a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) across thousands of miles, one must possess the correct eye.

Seek liberation from erroneous views; definitively examine the birth and death before you: do they truly exist, or do they truly not exist? If anyone can definitively attain this, I grant you permission to emerge.
Those of superior capacity clarify the Way upon hearing these words; those of middling or inferior capacity must labor through successive stages.
Running about aimlessly! Why do you not settle upon what must certainly be grasped within birth and death? Where else could you harbor doubts regarding the Buddhas or the Patriarchs?

A person of wisdom would laugh at you for trying to substitute someone else for your own birth and death. If you do not understand, listen to one more verse: "Toiling to uphold the dharma of birth and death."
Seek only from the presence of the Buddha. To be deluded regarding the correct principle before one’s eyes is like seeking bubbles by striking fire.

Later, when he went to reside at Dàtōng, he ascended the hall and, citing the occasion of his first meeting with Cùwéi, said to the assembly:

Next, he moved to Qingping. Entering the hall, he addressed the assembly: "Venerable elders, those who have left the household life must first comprehend the Buddha’s intent.

If one comprehends the Buddha’s intent, it matters not whether one is a monk or a layperson, male or female, noble or humble; one simply attains peace and happiness according to the abundance or scarcity of one's own household.
Venerable elders, you have all long dwelt within the monasteries and traveled extensively to consult the venerable masters. Now, how do you comprehend the Buddha’s intent?"
"Intend! Come forth and let us deliberate together. Do not harbor empty pride; otherwise, in the end, nothing will be accomplished and your life will pass in vain.

If you have not yet realized the Buddha’s intent, then even if water gushes from your head and fire issues from your feet—even if you burn your body and scorch your arms, possess great wisdom and eloquence, gather a following of a thousand or two thousand, and preach the Dharma like clouds and rain until the heavens—"
Flowers fall in disarray; this merely constitutes a heterodox teaching. To contend over right and wrong is to remain far removed from the Buddha-dharma.

Zen Master Zhaoshan Guangren ascended the hall. When the assembly had gathered, the Master said from before his seat, "Do you have anyone who can bring forth a question that does not belie the eyes of a lifelong traveler?
Is there such a one? The assembly was silent. The Master said, "If there is none, I shall ascend the seat.
He then ascended the seat. A monk came forward and bowed. The Master said, "Let it be that you have failed me; but what about the great assembly?"
Having said this, he returned to his quarters. The following day, a monk asked him to clarify the meaning of his previous words:
"How was that? The Master said, "At the time of the meal, there was rice for you to eat; after nightfall, there was a bed for you to sleep on. Why have you been pressing me so relentlessly all along?
The monk bowed, and the Master said, "Suffering! Suffering! The monk said, "I beg the Master to point it out directly. The Master then extended his foot and said, "Stretch [it]."
"Contracting [the mind] is entirely up to you; let the old monk be as he is. (End of Volume Five of the *Huìyuán*).
Chan Master Jūhuì of Dàguān Mountain [composed this] verse: A monk asked, "If Daomou was indeed the Patriarch, is he not the Patriarch?
The Master said, "He is not the Patriarch. The monk said, "If he is not the Patriarch, why did he come here? The Master said, "It is only because you do not realize it. The monk said—
"Once the offering has been made, what then? The Master said, "Only then will you know it is not the Patriarch. He ascended the hall and said:

"The temporal teachings of a single generation are merely for the purpose of adjusting the hands and feet of people of this time. Even if one were to strip them away until the very bottom, they would only result in a person who has 'finished the business' (a person of affairs)."
This must not be treated as a matter for the patched robe (the Zen practitioner). Thus it is said: "Forty-nine years of teaching did not exhaust its clarity;
it cannot be pointed out. When you arrive here, what should you do? If you continue to prattle on, I fear you will only bring about your own ruin. Be careful.

Chan Master Jiufeng Daogyan [Verse]: He once served as the attendant to Shishuang. When Shishuang passed away, the assembly requested the Head Seat to succeed him as abbot. The Master addressed the assembly, saying, "One must first understand the meaning of our late teacher before one may do so. The Head Seat asked, "What was the late teacher’s meaning? The Master replied, "The late teacher said: 'Rest! Cease! Be cold and still! At this, the Head Seat had a sudden realization. The Master then said, "If you can say a single word, I will hand over the Dharma to you. The Head Seat said, "I have nothing to say. The Master said, "If you have nothing to say, then you have understood the late teacher’s meaning. The Head Seat then bowed. The Master then handed over the Dharma to him. Later, when the Head Seat was about to pass away, he told his disciples, "When Jiufeng was my attendant, he gave me the robe and bowl. You should go and repay his kindness. His disciples went to the Master and informed him of the situation. The Master said, "The old fellow has finally let me down. He then composed a verse: "Thirty years ago, I was a fool; Thirty years later, I am still a fool. The fool is not different from the wise; The wise are not different from the fool. The fool and the wise are one and the same; Where is there any distinction between them? Upon finishing the verse, he passed away. The Master then performed the funeral rites for him. Later, when the Master was about to pass away, he instructed his disciples, "After I am gone, you must all go to the place where the Head Seat is staying and pay respects to him. His disciples asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "He is the one who truly understands the late teacher’s meaning. The disciples then went to the Head Seat and paid their respects. The Head Seat asked, "Did the late master leave any instructions for you? The Master replied, "He left no instructions. The Head Seat said, "If you had received any instructions, you would have been able to stay here and receive my offerings. Since you have none, you must go elsewhere to seek sustenance. The Master then departed. The Head Seat subsequently passed away. The Master then returned to Jiufeng and took up residence there. One day, while walking in the garden, he suddenly called out to his attendant, "Attendant! The attendant replied, "Yes, Master? The Master said, "The wind is blowing the flowers; where do they fall? The attendant said, "They fall upon the ground. The Master said, "Attendant, you have fallen into the common crowd. The attendant then asked, "Master, where do they fall? The Master said, "They fall into the midst of the clear stream. The attendant then asked, "What is the clear stream? The Master said, "It is the place where the waves never cease. The attendant then asked, "What is the place where the waves never cease? The Master said, "It is the place where the spring never dries up. The attendant then asked, "What is the spring that never dries up? The Master said, "It is the place where the moon is reflected in the water. The attendant then asked, "What is the moon reflected in the water? The Master said, "It is the place where the sky is bright and clear. The attendant then asked, "What is the sky that is bright and clear? The Master said, "It is the place where the sun rises. The attendant then asked, "What is the rising sun? The Master said, "It is the place where the dawn breaks. The attendant then asked, "What is the breaking dawn? The Master said, "It is the place where the night ends. The attendant then asked, "What is the end of the night? The Master said, "It is the place where the morning begins. The attendant then asked, "What is the beginning of the morning? The Master said, "It is the place where the world awakens. The attendant then asked, "What is the awakening of the world? The Master said, "It is the place where all beings attain enlightenment. The attendant then asked, "What is the attainment of enlightenment? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any delusion. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of delusion? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any seeking. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of seeking? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any grasping. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of grasping? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any attachment. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of attachment? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any duality. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of duality? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any separation. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of separation? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any coming or going. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of coming or going? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any birth or death. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of birth or death? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any beginning or end. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of beginning or end? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any past, present, or future. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of past, present, or future? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any time. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of time? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any space. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of space? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any form. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of form? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any name. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of name? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any concept. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of concept? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any thought. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of thought? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any mind. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of mind? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any consciousness. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of consciousness? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any perception. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of perception? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any sensation. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of sensation? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any feeling. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of feeling? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any desire. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of desire? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any attachment. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of attachment? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any clinging. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of clinging? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any grasping. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of grasping? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any letting go. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of letting go? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any holding on. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of holding on? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any binding. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of binding? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any liberation. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of liberation? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any bondage. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of bondage? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any freedom. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of freedom? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any restriction. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of restriction? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any obstruction. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of obstruction? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any hindrance. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of hindrance? The Master said, "It is the place where there is no longer any barrier. The attendant then asked, "What is the absence of a barrier?
