Chan Master Linji Yixuan of the Linji School at Mount Nanyue [Verse]: Initially, while in the assembly of Huangbo, his practice was pure and singular.
At that time, Muzhou served as the First Seat (Dharma-seat Elder). He asked, "How long have you been here, Senior Monk? The Master replied, "Three years. Muzhou said, "Have you ever..."
"Have you ever made an inquiry? the Master asked. "I have never made an inquiry," the monk replied. "I do not know what to ask.

The monk said, "Why do you not ask the Abbot, 'What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma'? The monk then went to ask him; before he had even finished speaking, the Master [had already responded].
Huangbo struck him. The Master came down from his seat. Baizhang said, "How was your inquiry? The Master said, "Before I had even finished asking my question, you struck me;
I do not understand. Baizhang said, "Just go and ask again. The Master asked once more, and Huangbo struck him again.
This happened three times; he asked three times and was struck three times. The Master said to Baizhang, "I have already received your encouragement to inquire about the Dharma."
"Time and again I have received the Master’s staff, yet I have lamented my own karmic obstacles for failing to grasp the profound meaning. I shall now take my leave. Baizhang bowed and withdrew.

Before leaving, Baizhang went first to Huangbo and said: [The Master] said: "If you are going, you must first take leave of the Master before you depart. Baizhang bowed and withdrew. [Baizhang] arrived at Huangbo’s place first and said:
The Master asked of the Elder Huashang, "Although you are but a junior, you are truly extraordinary. If he comes to take his leave, use skillful means to receive him;
in the future, he will become a great tree that provides shade for all people under heaven. The next day, the Master took his leave of Huangbo.
Huangbo said, "There is no need for him to go elsewhere. Go directly to Daoyi at Tancheng in Gaoyang; he will surely explain it for you. The Master arrived there.
Daguyu. Guyu asked, "Where have you come from? The Master said, "I have come from Huangbo. Guyu asked, "What words did Huangbo say?
The Master said, "Three times I asked him about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma, and three times I was struck.
I do not know whether I was at fault or not. Guyu said, "Huangbo’s compassionate heart was so earnest that he brought you to a state of thorough exhaustion."
He came back here again to ask whether there was a fault or not.
At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment and said, "So, it turns out Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is nothing more than this. Yuyou grabbed him and said, "You bed-wetting little devil!
Just now you were asking if there was a fault or not, and now you say Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is nothing more than this. What principle have you seen?"
"Quick way! Quick way! The Master struck Daoyu three times under the ribs. Daoyu pushed him away and said, "Your teacher is Huangbo; it is none of my business.
The Master took his leave of Daoyu and returned to Huangbo. Upon seeing him, Huangbo asked, "This fellow comes and goes; when will there ever be an end to it?
The Master replied, "It is only because your compassionate heart is so earnest. Having finished his greetings, he attended [Huangbo].
As he stood there, Huangbo asked, "Where have you been? The Master replied, "Yesterday I received the Compassionate Command of the Abbot, ordering me to go to Dagu.
Huangbo said, "What words did Dagu speak? The Master recounted the previous conversation. Huangbo said, "That old fellow Dagu is too talkative.
Wait until he comes back, and I will give him a thorough beating. The Master said, "What need is there to wait? Strike him right now! Thereupon, he followed after [Huangbo].
Yunyan said, "This madman has come here to pull at a tiger’s whiskers. Linji then gave a shout.

Baizhang then struck him. The Teacher caught the staff and pushed him over. Baizhang called for the *karmadāna*: "Help me up!
When the *karmadāna* helped him up and said, "How can you tolerate this madman’s rudeness? as soon as Baizhang rose, he struck the *karmadāna*. The Teacher then continued hoeing the ground.

He said: "In all other regions they perform cremation; here, we bury people alive. (Miaoshan asked Yangshan, "What was the meaning behind Huangbo’s striking the rector? Yangshan replied, "The real thief has run away.")
(Those who steal will eat the staff. One day, while the Master was sleeping in the Sangha hall, Huangbo entered as usual and struck the head of the wooden board once with his staff.
The Master raised his head, saw it was Huangbo, and went back to sleep. Huangbo struck the head of the board once again.
He went up to the upper room and saw the Head Seat meditating. He said, "The junior monks in the lower room are meditating, yet you are here indulging in discursive thoughts.
The Seat replied, "What are you doing, old man? Huangbo struck the head of the meditation board once more and then departed.
(Miaoshan raised this as a question for Yangshan, asking, "What was Huangbo’s intention? Yangshan said, "Two colors, one match. [Verse] As the Master was planting pine trees, Huangbo...
He asked, "What is the purpose of planting so many pines in the deep mountains? The Master said, "First, to provide the mountain gate with a scenic setting;
second, to serve as a landmark for future generations. Having spoken, he struck the ground three times with his mattock.
Huangbo said, "Even so, you shall receive thirty blows from me. The Master struck the ground three times again and gave a long sigh.

Huangbo said, "My school has reached you; it shall flourish greatly here. (Miaoshan raised this question to Yangshan: "At that time, Huangbo entrusted his lineage to Linji alone; was there anyone else? Yangshan replied, "There was.")

Yangshan said, "I have heard that it exists, but because the era is so remote, I do not wish to mention it to you, Master. Miaoyan said, "Even so, I still wish to know. You simply go ahead and tell me. Yangshan said, "One person points the way; the command is carried out throughout Wu and Yue. When it encounters a great wind, it stops.
Once Huangbo entered the kitchen and asked the head cook, "What are you doing? The cook replied, "I am sorting the rice for the community monks' meal.
Huangbo asked, "How much is eaten at one sitting? The cook replied, "Two shi and five dou. Huangbo said, "Is that not too much? The cook... [replied].

[The Master] said, "I am still afraid there is too little. Huangbo then struck him. [Baizhang] brought his head up to show it to the Master (Nanquan). The Master said, "I shall test this old fellow for you.

As soon as they arrived, Baizhang stood in attendance. Huangbo recounted the previous conversation. The Master said, "The rice steward does not understand; please, Preceptor, provide a substitute phrase for him.
Huangbo said, "Just bring it up. The Master said, "Is that not too much? Huangbo said, "Tomorrow he shall eat another serving."
Dun said, "What do you mean by 'tomorrow'? Eat right now! He then gave Ba a slap.
Ba said, "This madman comes here again to stroke the tiger's whiskers. The Master let out a shout and went out. (Later, Guishan raised this case and asked Yangshan.)

“What was the intention of these two venerable elders? Yangshan asked. Baizhang said, “What about you, Master? Yangshan replied, “Raising a son, one finally knows a father’s compassion. Baizhang said, “Not so. Yangshan asked, “And what about you, Father? Baizhang said, “It is much like inviting a thief to ruin the family.
When the Master took his leave of Huangbo, Huangbo asked, “Where are you going? The Master replied, “Not south of the River; I shall go north of the River. Huangbo struck him.
The Master seized his staff and gave him a slap. Huangbo laughed loudly and called to his attendant, “Bring...”
When the Zen board and desk arrived from the late master Baizhang, the Master said, "Attendant, bring some fire! Huangbo replied, "Not so;
you simply take it away. In the future, it will cut off the tongues of everyone under heaven.
The Master then rode a letter to Mount Miao to visit Yangshan. During their conversation, Yangshan said, "Brother, in the north there is one who..."
At the residence, the Master said, "How could such a thing be? Yang replied, "Just go; later there will be one person who will assist you.
This person will have a head but no tail; he will have a beginning but no end" (this was a prediction regarding Puhua).
Later, when the Master resided at Linji in Zhenzhou, his disciples gathered like clouds. One day, he said to the two senior monks, Puhua and Ke Fu: "I wish to..."
"Upon this, I establish the school of Huangbo. You two, first, go and expose me. The two men respectfully descended.
Three days later, Puhua came back up and asked, "What did you say three days ago, Master? The Master struck him.
Three days later, Ke Fu came up and asked, "Why did you strike Puhua the other day, Master? The Master struck him as well.
In the evening, he gave a small discourse (xiaochan), saying: "Sometimes the person is taken away but the environment is not;

sometimes the environment is taken away but the person is not; sometimes both person and environment are taken away; and sometimes neither person nor environment is taken away" (the questions and answers are fully contained in the *Kefu Zhang*). A monk asked:
"What is the true Buddha, the true Dharma, and the true Way? I beg the Master for an explanation. The Master said:
"The Buddha is the purity of the mind; the Dharma is the luminosity of the mind; the Way is the pure light that is unimpeded everywhere.
These three are one; they are all empty names without substantial reality. For one who is a true practitioner of the Way, the mind is uninterrupted from moment to moment. From [this point]..."

The Great Master Bodhidharma came from the Western Land solely to seek a person who would not be deluded by others. Later, he met the Second Patriarch, and with a single word, the matter was resolved;
only then did he realize that all his previous efforts had been in vain. This is where I, this mountain monk, see it today.
This is no different from the Patriarchs and Buddhas. If you gain realization within the first phrase, you are fit to be a teacher to the Patriarchs and Buddhas.
If you gain realization within the second phrase, you are fit to be a teacher to humans and devas. If you gain realization within the third phrase, you will not even be able to save yourself.
A monk then asked, "What is the first phrase? The Master said, "The Seal of the Three Essentials is opened; the vermilion dot is narrow."
Before there is even room for deliberation, the distinction between host and guest is established. [The student] asks: "What is the second phrase? The Master says:
"How could one with wondrous understanding fail to question Wuzhuo? How could Upagupta fail to match the power that cuts the current? [The student] asks: "What is the third phrase? The Master says:
"Just look at the puppeteer on the stage manipulating the puppets; all depends entirely on the person inside. He then said: "In general, when performing and expounding the School..."
The Vehicle. Within a single phrase, one must possess the three gates of mystery; within each gate of mystery, one must possess the three essentials.
There is the provisional and the real; there is illumination and function. How do you all understand this? The Master said to the monks:
"At times, a single shout is like the precious sword of the Vajra King; at times, a single shout is like a crouching lion; at times, a single shout is like..."
The probing pole and the shadow-grass: sometimes a single shout is not used as a single shout. How do you understand this?
When a monk hesitated, the Master gave a shout. Addressing the assembly: Those who study the Way must be extremely careful. It is like the meeting of host and guest.
Thereupon, discourse and exchange ensued. Sometimes he manifested forms in response to things; sometimes he functioned with his entire being;
sometimes he displayed joy or anger through skillful means; sometimes he appeared as half his body; sometimes he rode upon a lion, or sometimes he rode upon an elephant king.

When a truly authentic student let out a shout, he first produced a lacquer basin. The Good Knowledge (the Master) failed to discern it as an objective condition and thus entered into that other's realm.
Above, he makes a display; the student then shouts at him again. The former person refuses to let go. This is a terminal illness, incurable.
It is called "the guest looking for the host. Or, perhaps the *kalyāṇamitra* does not bring forth his own substance, but simply seizes [the student] according to the point of the student's question.
When the student is seized, they refuse to let go even unto death. This is...
The host observes the guest. There may be a student who presents a single pure object before a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
If the spiritual friend recognizes this object and seizes it to cast it into a pit, the student says, "Excellent, O spiritual friend! The spiritual friend then says, "Alas!
You do not distinguish between good and evil. The student then prostrates; this is called the host observing the host. Or...
There was a student who, wearing a cangue and shackles, came before a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). The spiritual friend further placed another kind of cangue and shackle upon him.
The student rejoiced; neither could distinguish between them, and they called this "the guest viewing the guest. Venerable Sir, this is what I, a mountain monk, have brought forth.
All of these are for the purpose of discerning demons and distinguishing [the true from the false], so that one may know what is deviant and what is correct.

The Master asked Luopu, "From the beginning until now, there has been one who practices the staff and one who practices the shout. Which of these is more intimate? Luopu replied, "Neither is intimate. The Master said, "What is the point of intimacy?
Luopu then shouted. The Master struck him. [Verse]: Entering the hall, he said: "There is a person who, for kalpas, remains on the road, never departing..."

[The Master] turned his back. He said, "Tell me, which one is in front? Which one is behind? Do not act as Vimalakīrti;

The Master said, “You all learn my shouting from me. Now I ask you: suppose there is a person coming from the East Hall...”

Addressing the assembly: "Sometimes I first manifest illumination and then function; sometimes I first function and then manifest illumination; sometimes illumination and function are simultaneous."

At times, illumination and function do not occur simultaneously. There are those for whom illumination comes first and function follows; there are those for whom function comes first and illumination follows.
When illumination and function are simultaneous, it is like driving the ox of the plowman away and snatching the food from the hungry man, or breaking the bone to extract the marrow.

[Verse] The Master asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From the place of Cui Chan. The Master said, "Have you brought back Cui Chan’s shout? The monk said, [silence].
[The monk] said, "I did not bring it with me. The Master said, "If that is so, then you have not come from Cui Chan's place.
The monk then gave a shout; the Master then struck him. [Verse] Addressing the assembly: I hear that they shout in the front corridor and they shout in the back quarters.
My sons, do not shout blindly or shout recklessly. Even if you could shout until Xinghua were cast into the void and then dashed down—there would still be not a single [point].
"His breath has ceased. Wait until he recovers and rises; then I shall tell you that it is not yet finished. Why?
Because I have never scattered genuine pearls within a purple silk curtain for you all. What is the point of this reckless shouting and wild bellowing?
[Verse]: When Yunju was residing at Sanfeng, the Master asked him: "If one temporarily borrows a question to serve as a 'shadow-grass' (a preliminary probe), how is it? Yunju—
[The monk] was speechless. The Master said, "I think you, Reverend, could not have answered this question. It would have been better to bow and withdraw.
Twenty years later, Jue remarked, "Reflecting on it now, at that time I need not have said, 'Why bother?
Later, when the Master sent a fundraising official to visit the Master [Baizhang], the Master asked, "When you were staying at Sanfeng Hermitage, I asked you a question and you could not answer."
"Have you been able to say it yet? The Master related the previous story. The Teacher said, "For twenty years at Yunju, I have only been able to say 'Why bother?
Xinghua is not like that; how could he compare to saying 'No need'?

"Completely not entering; not understanding, completely not entering. [The monk] said, "In no way is it like this.

Chan Master Baoshou Zhao (First Generation) [Verse]: A monk asked, "What is it like when the myriad objects of perception come to invade?
The Master said, "Do not concern yourself with them. The monk bowed. The Master said, "Do not touch them; if you touch them, I shall break your waist. [Verse]:

While the Master was sitting in the abbot’s quarters, a monk came to pay his respects. As the monk was making his inquiry, the Master said, "The hundreds of thousands of sages are all entirely contained within this very place."
The monk said, "As for what the ancients said: 'The great trichiliocosm is a bubble on the sea'—I wonder from where this single *changfang* (room) comes?
The Master said, "The thousand sages are present in the world; who can testify to this? The Master then threw down his whisk.
The monk moved from west to east and stood there. The Master struck him. The monk said, "If one had not studied long, how could one know the ultimate point?"
The Master said, "Thirty years from now, these words will circulate widely. [Verse] Zhaozhou arrives; the Master is on his meditation seat, sitting with his back turned.
Zhaozhou spreads his sitting mat and prostrates. The Master rises and enters the abbot's quarters; Zhaozhou folds up his mat and departs.
[Verse] A monk was asked by the Master, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From the Western Mountain. The Master said, "Did you see the monkeys? He replied, "I saw them.
The Master said, "What tricks did they perform? He replied, "I saw nothing; not even a single trick could they perform.
The Master then struck him. [Verse] Hu Dingjiao came for an audience. The Master asked, "Are you not Hu Dingjiao? He replied, "I dare not [say so]. The Master said, "..."
"Can you drive a nail back into empty space? Huo replied, "I ask the Master to break it open for me.

Later, Huo went to Zhaozhou and recounted the previous story. Zhaozhou asked, "Why were you struck by him? Huo said, "I did not know my fault."
"Where is it? Zhaozhou said, "Right here in this single seam; even now, one cannot do anything about it. At these words, Hu attained awakening.
Zhaozhou said, "For now, let us nail up this seam."

"What is the authentic proof of the Way? The Master said, "What are you saying? The Seat-holder asked again. The Master struck him with his sitting mat and said, "You lacquer bucket!

The Master raised his staff. The monk turned around and made a gesture as if to receive the blow. The Master said, "Running downhill, one does not stop; such a swift opportunity is hard to encounter.
He then struck him. The monk said, "You thief! and departed. The Master then cast down the staff.
Subsequently, another monk asked, "Just now, why did you allow that monk to get away? The Master said, "It was because he saw the former Master coming."
Dajue Wufu went to visit Linji. As soon as Linji saw him, he held up his whisk. Dajue spread out his sitting mat. Linji threw down the whisk.
Dajue folded up his sitting mat and said, "I am going to the hall. At that time, the assembly of monks said, "Could it be that this monk is a personal acquaintance of the Master?
He does not prostrate, nor does he receive a blow. When Linji heard this report, he ordered an attendant to call the one who had just arrived.
A newcomer arrived. The Master followed the attendant to the Abbot’s quarters. Nanquan said, "The assembly says that you have come to visit the Elder, yet you neither prostrate nor receive a blow.
Are you perhaps an old monk's relative? The Master then said, "I take my leave," and went down.
[Verse] After the Master had taken up residence, a monk asked, "What is the primordial body? The Master replied, "Its head rests on Mount Heng, its feet [in the sea]."

His single robe and meager food were all because his sacred mind had not yet attained full penetration;

therefore, he hurried along on his travels to resolve profound mysteries, to propagate and spread the teachings, to consult extensively with those who possessed prior knowledge, and to draw near to those of high virtue—doing so solely to continue the Buddha-mind.
Lamp. To perpetuate the ancestral lineage, to exalt the holy seed, to guide those of later capacity, and to benefit both self and others—never forgetting the traces of the predecessors.
Is there anyone present now who can deliberate on this? If there is, come forward; let us all deliberate together.

A monk asked, "What is the phrase for guiding a beginner? The Master said, "Are you a wandering monk? [The monk] asked, "What is the phrase for discerning the patchwork robe? The Master said, "You have been wearing it for thirty years."
The phrase regarding the Sangha. The Master said: "The sun rises in the west at dawn. [The student] asked: "What is the phrase for when the true command is being exercised? The Master said:
"Bringing it from a thousand miles away to present one's original face. [The student] asked: "What is the phrase for establishing heaven and earth? The Master said:
"In the continent of Uttarakuru, long-grained rice grows; those who eat it have neither greed nor anger. Then he said: "Take these four turning phrases."
To examine the monks of the world: as soon as you step forward, they have already examined you. A monk asked, "What is the place where a student exerts effort?
The Master said, "Jiaozhou strikes the Great Image. The monk asked, "What is the place where a student turns about? The Master said, "Jiaozhou strikes the Great Image."
The Master said, "The Iron Ox Watering at Shanfu. A monk asked, "What is the point where the student is intimately close? The Master said, "Playing with lions in Xihe.
He then said, "If a person can understand these three phrases, they have already discerned the Three Mysteries (Sanxuan). There are further words of the Three Essentials (Sanyao) remaining;
you must truly realize them, for this is no ordinary matter. I shall provide a verse for the assembly on the matters of the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials."

Difficult to distinguish. When one attains the meaning and forgets the words, the Way is easy to approach. A single phrase clearly encompasses the myriad phenomena; on the Double Ninth, in the ninth month, the chrysanthemums bloom anew.
Ascending the hall: Every single word must possess the three mysteries (*san-xuan*). Each mystery must possess the three essentials (*san-yao*).

There is illumination and there is function. Sometimes illumination comes first and function follows; sometimes function comes first and illumination follows; or illumination and function occur simultaneously.
Furthermore, sometimes illumination and function do not occur simultaneously; first there is illumination and then function. Let me consult with you on this:
if function comes first and illumination follows, you must indeed be a person of some caliber to handle it. But when illumination and function are simultaneous, how will you respond?
Illumination and function do not occur at the same time; how then do you intend to find a place to settle? A monk asked, "What is the guest within the guest?

The Master said, "Joining palms before the hermitage, he questions the World-Honored One. The monk asked, "What is the host within the guest? The Master said, "Facing each other, there is no companion.
The monk asked, "What is the guest within the host? The Master said, "Massive clouds stretch across the sea; he draws his sword..."
He stirred up the Dragon Gate, saying: "What is the Lord within the Lord? The Master said: "Three heads and six arms, supporting heaven and earth;
the wrathful Nātha smashes the Imperial Bell. Ascending the hall, he said: "Fenyang has three secrets, which monks find difficult to discern.
If you further intend to ask 'How is it?', I will strike you over the head with my staff. At that time, a monk asked: "What are the three secrets? The Master then—
[The Master] struck him. The monk prostrated. The Master said: "I shall now offer you a verse for all at once. The First Secret: Receiving and guiding is without fixed time;
Eloquent words cannot fully describe it— Clouds parting to reveal the moon in the blue sky. The Second Secret: Radiating light to distinguish the worthy and the wise;

Inquiring and answering with a heart to benefit living beings— Uprooting the wedge from within the eye. The Third Secret: Spoken by the barbarian from the Western Land; The water of the Ji flows past Xin."

[The Master] said, "In the northern lands, they use *bin* iron. Furthermore, he asked: 'Is there anyone here who understands? If you understand, come forth and convey a message; I wish to know the extent of your realization.
Do not merely do as you have been told, memorizing words and phrases to pass for your entire life—what benefit is there in that?
Do not stand here long; take care. [Verse: A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master [said]:...
He said, "A fan of blue silk is sufficient for wind and coolness. [Verse] He ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, saying:

"Now, one who expounds the Dharma must possess the ten kinds of wisdom that accord with reality. If one does not possess these ten kinds of wisdom that accord with reality, one cannot distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, nor differentiate the monastic from the lay.
One would be unable to serve as eyes for gods and humans to determine right from wrong—like a bird flying through the sky with broken wings, or like an arrow..."
When the arrow is shot, the string snaps; because the string has snapped, the arrow does not hit the mark. Because the wing is broken, it cannot fly through the air.
When the string is strong and the wing is firm, the arrow pierces both [the target and the air]. What is "the ten wisdoms being identical with reality"? Point them out for all you venerable elders:
first, identity of substance; second, identity of the Great Matter; third, total identity as fellow practitioners; fourth, identity of true resolve; fifth, identity of pervasiveness.
1. Universal pervasiveness; 2. Identical endowment; 3. Identical gain and loss; 4. Identical birth and killing;
5. Identical roaring voice; 6. Identical entry. It is further asked: With what kind of person does one enter identically? With whom does one roar the same sound? What is this "birth and killing"?
What thing is identical in gain and loss? Which one is identical in endowment? And what is it that is identical in universal pervasiveness?
Who shares the same true resolve? Who can join as a fellow practitioner? Which one shares in the Great Matter? What thing shares the same substance?
Is there anyone who can point it out? Those who can point it out do not begrudge their compassion; those who cannot point it out have not yet attained the eye of study.
You must discern this with urgency; you must recognize right from wrong, for the face is present before you—it will not remain standing long.
Take care.
Chan Master Guisheng of Ye County [Verse]: He traveled to visit Shoushan. One day, Shoushan held up a bamboo stick and asked, "If you call it a bamboo stick, you encounter resistance;

Chan Master Yungcong of Guyin (also known as Shimen Cong) first attended upon Master Heng of Baizhang.

While observing the summer retreat, Baizhang ascended the hall and cited the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, saying: "Perfect enlightenment has no name or mark; wherever conditions arise is the site of practice. Thereupon, the Master stepped forward.
Question: "What is perfect awakening that is without name or mark? Zhao said: "Do you see the pillar? The Master asked:
"What is the site of enlightenment (dōjō) that accords with conditions? Zhao said: "Today is the opening of the summer retreat. [Verse: Next, he visited Shoushan. He asked:
"When a student has personally reached the Jewel Mountain, what is it like when returning empty-handed? Shoushan said: "A torch before every door."
The Master attained great enlightenment upon hearing these words. He presented a verse, saying: "I am now twenty-seven years old; Seeking the Way, I have traveled far and wide.
Today I rejoice at this encounter, Yet, for all intents and purposes, we do not know one another. Later, he arrived at Dayang, where Master Xuan asked, "Where have you recently departed from?
The Master replied, "Xiangzhou. Dayang asked, "What is the phrase that is not separated [from reality]? The Master said, "The Master."
"Being the abbot is no easy matter. Yang said, "Just sit and drink tea. The Master then went to join the assembly.

The coiled dragon’s strength lets out a loud cry; later in the evening, its spiritual essence becomes even more abundant.

Greeting those who have come. If you can utter the third phrase, you will still not be able to save yourself. Ascending the hall, he said: "The spring scenery is mild and warm;
the spring rain is universally moistening. All things sprout their buds—where is there that does not receive this grace?
But tell me, how do you express the power of receiving this grace? After a long silence, he said: 'A drop of spring rain is as slippery as oil.'"

The Master replied, "From Hanshang. Shoushan held up his fist and said, "Is there such a thing as this in Hanshang?
The Master said, "What kind of 'clanging bowl' is this? Shoushan said, "Blind! The Master said, "Exactly so," gave a single clap, and departed. On another day, Shoushan asked again, "Student..."
"When one has personally reached the Jewel Mountain, what is it like to return empty-handed? The Master said, "A torch before every door.
At these words, the Teacher attained great enlightenment and said, "I no longer doubt the tongues of the old monks throughout the world.

[Zhaozhou] raised the matter of his late teacher, saying, "Do not take offense at having just offended you. The Master then gave a shout. He asked again, "When did you arrive at Fenyang?
Xue said, "I arrived at such-and-such a time. The Master said, "I have heard your name since I was in Zhejiang;
I thought your understanding was truly like this. How then can your reputation be spread throughout the world? Xue then prostrated himself and said, "It is my fault."
A monk asked, "What is 'taking away the person but not the environment'? The Master said, "The white chrysanthemum has just bloomed under the warmth of the double ninth;
the young lord of a hundred years does not encounter spring. The monk asked, "What is 'taking away the environment but not the person'?

The Master said, "Throughout the great earth there is no news; in solitude, one freely assumes the true. The monk asked, "What is 'taking away both person and environment'? The Master said, "Grass..."
The wild man changed color. Both the ordinary and the holy were equally empty. [A monk] asked, "What is it to have neither the person nor the environment usurped?
The Master said, "The clear breeze and the bright moon; the rustic old man smiles as they draw near. Ascending the hall, he said: "The bell tolls and the drum beats;
the magpies chirp and the crows caw. For all of you, I have preached Prajñā and finished lecturing on Nirvāṇa. Do you believe this yet?"
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva manifests great spiritual powers before all of you. If you do not believe this, he will depart for other lands to save those in suffering and benefit living beings.
Ascending the hall [to teach], he speaks of the gradual; returning to the ordinary, he accords with the Way. Discussing the sudden, he says: [The text ends here.]

Leaving no trace of the Emperor’s presence—this is the direct approach. Even if one were to discuss its suddenness and return to its constancy, it would still be a matter of suppressing [the mind] to achieve it.
Chan Master Bajiao Guquan [Verse]: He visited his fellow student Chan Master Ciming. Ciming asked, "White clouds hang across the valley mouth;
from where has the man of the Way come? The Master looked left and right and said, "Where was the fire last night that burned out the ancient..."
Renfeng Ming said, "Not yet; speak further. The Master made the sound of a tiger. Renfeng struck him with his sitting cloth (*zuoju*), and the Master caught it.
He pushed Renfeng onto the meditation seat (*chánchuáng*). Renfeng then made the sound of a tiger again.

The Master laughed loudly and said, "I have encountered more than seventy virtuous teachers (*shànzhīshí*), but today for the first time I have met a true master (*zuojiā*). When Ciming moved to reside at Foyan, the Master went there once again.
He went to visit him, stayed for a short while, and then returned. He composed a verse to send to him, saying: "It has been half a year since we parted;
I know not with whom you have been discussing Chan. Amidst the same exquisite scenery within Mount Xiang, you yourself guide your followers while I sleep."
When Chan Master Tiansheng Haotai arrived at Langye, Langye asked, "To bury troops and engage in combat is not yet the mark of a master.
With a single horse and a solitary spear, I invite you to meet me. The Master pointed at Langye and said, "If the general does not lead with courage, he brings misfortune upon his entire army.
Langye struck the Master once with his sitting cloth; the Master also struck Langye once with his sitting cloth. Langye caught him and said, "That previous sitting cloth—"
[The Master] said, "This is the practice of this mountain monk. Where does the *sanzu* (upper seat) fall? The Master said, "I humbly pray that you will partake.
Xiaotuo Kai said, "At the fifth watch, rising before dawn, there are still those traveling by night.
The Master said, "Drawing the bow after the thief has fled. Xiaotuo Kai said, "Please sit and drink tea. **Verse:** A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "Black lacquer."
Holy Monk. Chan Master Fushan Fayuan (styled Yuanlugu Gong). [Verse] A monk asked: "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said: "A pile of bones rising from level ground. ○ When the Duke Ou-yang Wen-chung heard of the Master’s extraordinary brilliance, he went to his quarters. Before long...

There was one who treated him with unusual deference. While playing *qi* (go) with a guest, the Master sat beside them. Wenzhong suddenly gathered up the board and requested that the Master expound the Dharma by means of the game.
The Master immediately ordered the drum to be beaten and ascended the seat, saying: "If we discuss this matter, it is like two families playing a game of *qi*."

What does this mean? When opponents know one's intent, one must not yield in the moment of action. Only when one can string together five points and supplement them with three, while also maintaining a single path through, will it be successful.
There is a certain class of people who only know how to secure their own position by closing the door; they do not understand how to seize the corner or break through the pass.
Their stubborn positions and tiger-mouths are displayed simultaneously, yet once the game is broken, their efforts are in vain. Therefore it is said: "The fat borders are easy to obtain."
A slender belly is difficult to seek; when one thinks of acting, one often loses the connection. With a coarse mind, one repeatedly strikes one's head.

Cease boasting of being a master of the state; do not vainly speak of being an immortal. Whether winning the game or losing the pieces is not the point; tell me, when black and white have not yet been distinguished, where does that first move fall?
After a long silence, he said: "From of old, there are nineteen paths; how many people are lost and how many attain enlightenment?"
Wenzhong sighed with admiration and said to his colleagues with composure: "At first, I suspected that Chan discourse was merely empty and exaggerated.

Today, having seen this old man’s karmic conditions and what he has attained and cultivated, I realize that were it not for an awakening and clarity within the mind-ground, how could such wondrous principles exist?
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The Buddhas appearing in the world establish gates of transformation; they do not depart from the wisdom-eye of the three bodies."
It is like the three eyes of Maheśvara. Why? One eye is so tightly shut that not even a drop of water can pass through; it is difficult for the ordained and the laity to distinguish.
One eye is wide open across the great earth; the ten directions are unobstructed. One eye casts a single glance over high and low, and all myriad species look up together.
Nevertheless, if one is a monk of the true lineage, only when meeting on a common road with another who possesses the peerless, penetrating True Eye can one truly succeed. Thus it is said:
According to the Way, the Buddhas of the three periods do not know that it exists; yet the "tawny cat" and the "white ox" do know it exists.
But tell me, what is it that the tawny cat and the white ox know exists? Do you wish to understand? Deep autumn: rain upon the curtains of a thousand homes;
setting sun: the wind of a flute on a tower. In his later years, the Master retired to Huisheng Rock. There he composed the *Xuzu Miaoyi* (The Profound Meaning of the Patriarchs and Buddhas).

The nine bands are: the Band of the Buddha’s True Dharma Eye; the Band of the Dharma-Treasury of the Buddha; the Band of the Vertical Penetration of Principle; the Band of the Horizontal Penetration of Phenomena; the Band of the Interlacing of Principle and Phenomena;
the Band of the Curling and Hanging Down; the Band of Wondrous Harmony and Simultaneity; the Band of the Golden Needle and Twin Locks; and the Band of Constant Reality in Equanimity.
Once the students had transmitted and recited these, the Master said: "If one were to rely on the Perfect and Ultimate Dharma Gate, there would originally be ten numbers. Now..."
These nine strands have already been explained for you all. Is there yet another strand that you can perceive?

If you can perceive it with intimacy and clarity, then please come forward and explain it to the assembly. If you can explain it clearly, I will grant you the previously mentioned nine strands and the perfectly luminous eye of the Way.
If it is not intimate and your explanation does not correspond to the truth, then rely solely upon my words.
To understand it for oneself in such a manner is called slandering the Dharma. "What do you all say to this? The assembly remained silent. The Master rebuked them and departed.
Chan Master Baoying Zhao ascended the hall and said: "Throughout the twelve periods of the day, I allow you one moment of 'cessation of study'—this is itself study."
In the Buddha-dharma, Ānanda—though foremost in extensive learning—was nonetheless expelled by Kāśyapa and was not permitted to participate in the Council.
Only then did he realize that his cleverness, vast scholarship, memory, and conceptual recollection were outward-directed pursuits; they had no connection whatsoever with the awakened, numinous mind.

Trapped within the husk of the five aggregates, he could not penetrate through them; when things accorded with his desires, joy arose, and when they opposed his desires, anger arose, thereby obscuring [his true nature].
Deeply entrenched, they bind themselves and fetter themselves, finding no liberation. They drift through birth and death;

the six sense organs become their affliction, and they are oppressed by manifold sufferings, lacking any autonomy. Yet they allow their deluded minds to act as masters within this state. Great men, seize the opportunity early!
(He lets out a shout and says: "Investigate!"
A monk asked Chan Master Dàchéng Huìguǒ, "What is it like when one brushes away the dust and sees the Buddha? The Master said, "To brush away the dust is already a deviation;
to see the Buddha is an error. The monk asked, "If it is not like this at all, what then? The Master said, "An error."
When Chan Master Danying Daguan of Jinshan first visited Chan Master Dayang Huiyan, he asked: "Dongshan specifically established the categories of 'partial and correct' and 'ruler and minister.
What matter does his intention clarify? Huiyan replied: "The state of affairs before one's parents were born.
The Master asked: "How does one realize this? Huiyan said: "Midnight is perfectly bright; at daybreak, nothing is revealed. The Master was left bewildered and subsequently went to visit Guoyin.
[The Master] recounted the previous conversation. Yinyuan said, "Dayang did not say it was wrong; he simply had a narrow mouth.

He could not finish speaking even with his mouth full. I, the old monk, am not like that. The Master asked, "What is the matter before one's parents were born? Yinyuan said, "A brick from the latrine.
The Master asked, "What is 'midnight is perfectly bright, yet at dawn it is not revealed'? Yinyuan said, "A peony flower."
Later, as he was putting a sleeping cat away, the Master became increasingly suspicious and alarmed. One day, during a communal work assignment, Wuye asked him, "Are you carrying firewood today?
The Master replied, "Yes. Wuye said, "Yunmen once asked a monk, 'The person carries the firewood; the firewood carries the person. How do you understand this? The Master had no reply.

Yinyoung said, "This matter is like a person learning calligraphy: those who can accurately replicate the strokes and characters are skilled; those who cannot are clumsy. This is because they have not yet been able to forget the rules.

One must reach the point where the brush forgets the hand, and the hand forgets the mind—only then will it be possible. At this, the Master attained silent realization. After a long while, he said, "As Shitou said:
'To cling to phenomena is fundamentally delusion; to accord with principle is likewise not awakening. Yinyoung asked, "What do you think of that?"

The Master spoke of medicine. Huineng said, "It is talk of medicine. Huineng rebuked him, saying, "You take illness for medicine; how can that be right? The Master said, "In affairs, it is like a box finding its lid;
in principle, it is like an arrow with a straight shaft and sharp point. How could there be anything more wondrous than this?

Yet you still consider it illness; I truly do not yet understand your meaning. Huineng said, "Even reaching such 'wonder,' one has merely clarified the relationship between principle and phenomena (li-shi). As for the Patriarch..."

The intended meaning is such that it cannot be reached by intellectual consciousness; how much less can phenomena and principles exhaust it? Therefore, the World-Honored One said: "Principles obstruct right knowledge and vision;
phenomena obstruct the continuity of birth and death. The Master, as if suddenly awakening from a dream, asked: "How should one utilize this?"
Yinyuan said, "If speech does not leave the old nest, how can one transcend the entanglements? The Master sighed and said, "As soon as it touches the lips, it falls into conceptual thought;
all such things are dead ends and are never the living path. He addressed the assembly, saying, "As soon as it touches the lips, it falls into conceptual thought;
all such things are dead ends and are never the living path. Even if you manage to break through and escape, you are still mired in samsara. Do not—"
This would mean you have failed your lifelong purpose and lived this life in vain. Do you wish not to fail your lifelong purpose?
He picks up his staff and strikes once, saying: "You must not be deceived by this staff; look!
This staff pierces through the skulls of all of you and leaps right into your nostrils! He strikes again. *Upasarga* (The Preface)

In the Hall, when the great assembly had gathered and settled, a monk just emerged to pay his respects. The Master said, "If you wish to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should contemplate the conditions of time and season.
The monk then asked, "What are the conditions of time and season? The Master immediately descended from his seat. Question:
"What is 'taking away the person but not the environment'? The Master said: "At home, there is no longer news of a return; the road is long and empty."
There was a "Plaque for Yearning for One's Hometown. [A monk] asked, "What is 'seizing the environment but not seizing the person'?

The Master said, "The vast ocean is made to dry up until its bottom is revealed; the green mountains are ground down until they become dust. [The monk] asked, "What is 'seizing both the person and the environment'? The Master said:
Heaven and earth are still empty of the sun and moon of Qin; mountains and rivers no longer see the sovereign and ministers of Han.

[The questioner] asked, "What is meant by 'the human realm and the environment are both not taken away'? The Master said: "The oriole sings through the thousand forests, flowers fill the ground; travelers wander for three months, grasses invade the sky."
Chan Master Zhenshou Ren ascended the hall and said: "Clearly and brightly there is no awakening; to have a dharma is delusion.

When the sun rises without clouds, it shines universally across the heavens. When there is no film before the eyes, space is fundamentally free of flowers. Do not speak erroneously before those who lack wisdom. *Chán* (Investigate!)"
When Chan Master Yongqing first questioned Guyin, he asked: "The ancients said, 'Tomorrow there is a meal at Dabe Temple.
What is the meaning of this? Guyin replied: "The sun rises and one sits in the shade; the weather is cold and one does not lift one's head. Later, when the Master entered the room, Guyin asked:
"How do you understand that previous occasion? The Master said: "If one understands it, one enjoys it while on the journey; if one does not understand..."
When [the Master] said, "This is merely the circulation of worldly truth," [Niu-tou] replied, "Not yet; speak further. The Master shook his sleeves and departed.
The Layman Li Zunxū, the Prince Consort, visited Guyin and asked about the matter of leaving the household life.

Guyin answered him with the public case concerning Duke Cui Zhao’s question to Master Jingshan. Upon these words, the Duke attained great enlightenment and composed a verse, saying: "To study the Way, one must..."
This is an iron man. To place it upon the palm of one’s hand is to discern it instantly; he proceeds directly toward unsurpassed Bodhi, taking no account of any right or wrong.
Layman Yinggong Xia Song had personally attained realization at Guyin and daily roamed with the old bhikṣu. Once, while at Shanglan...
When Chan Master Puchu arrived, the Duke asked, "When the hundred bones fall apart and scatter, which one is the Elder’s own self?

Lan replied, "I left Qiyang on the twentieth day of last month. The Duke ceased questioning. Lan, however, asked in turn, "When the hundred bones fall apart and scatter, which one is the Duke’s own self?
The Duke then gave a shout. Lan said, "The shout is certainly not lacking, but after all, which one is it?"
"This is something for you, Sir, yourself. The Master replied with a verse: "Do not mistake the foremost function before the wind; where in the great void can thought be lodged?
If this mountain monk wishes to convey the message, it is when the moon rises over ten thousand miles of cloudless sky.
Lan said, "This too is merely playing with the spirit."
When Chan Master Huayan Daolung first visited Master Shimen Che, he asked:
"The ancients said, 'If one can find peace and ease wherever one is, one naturally accords with the ancient tracks. Although these words exist, how is it when the mind of doubt has not yet ceased?
Shimen replied, "One must know [the Way] before one can find peace and ease wherever one is. It is like a person living in a prefecture or county who, whether hearing or..."
He saw all manner of wonders and marvels, yet he always treated them as ordinary; unaware of their existence, he remained at ease.
It was like a person living in a village who, upon encountering a little noise or spectacle, would speak of it with alarm and wonder. Under the Master’s words, he attained realization.
The Master fully transmitted to him the essential principles of Dongshan. Later, he became the successor of Guanghui. One day, Preceptor Cheng of Fuyan asked him:
The Chan Master had personally seen Shimen; why then did he instead succeed Guanghui? The Master said:
"When I met Guanghui, he wished to shave my head and asked me to bring him a stool. Guanghui said, 'Monk, I have a poem about the stool;
listen to it. He then said: 'Set it down and you will find peace and stability. At that moment, I gave my assent. Thereupon, I recounted what I had attained while at Shimen. Guang...
Hui said: "What Shimen has shown is like a hundred flavors of exquisite delicacies; it merely satisfies the person but cannot be eaten.
The layman Yang Yi, Duke Wen, whose courtesy name was Da-nian, was serving as the governor of Ruzhou when he first visited Guanghui.
Upon being received by Guanghui, the Duke asked: "A cloth drum is beaten at the front of the hall; who is the one who knows the music? Guanghui replied: "The wind that comes is clearly discerned."
The Duke said, "If that is so, then when Zen guests meet, they simply snap their fingers. Huì said, "A gentleman may be eight [feet tall].

The Duke responded, "Yes, yes. Huì said, "The grass-robbers have been utterly defeated. During a night conversation, Huì asked, "Director of the Secretariat, with whom have you recently had a discussion?
The Duke replied, "I once heard from the Abbot Liang of Yunyan that when two tigers bite each other..."
"How is it? Liang said. "The 'single unified mark' (*ekapiṇḍalakṣaṇa*). Guo asked, "I have been watching intently;
I do not know if saying it this way will suffice. Huì said, "It is not so here. Guo said, "Please, Master, give me another turn of phrase.
Huì made a gesture with his hand as if pulling up a nose and said, "This beast is still leaping about! At these words, Guo was suddenly liberated from all doubt.
There is a verse that says: An octagonal millstone runs through the void; A golden-maned lion transforms into a dog.
If you wish to hide your body within the Northern Dipper, You must join your palms behind the Southern Star. [Verse] The Master asked Guanghui:
"I have heard the Master say that all sinful karma arises from wealth and treasures, and thus you advise people to distance themselves from profit. Furthermore, regarding the South..."
"The sentient beings of Jambudvīpa take wealth as their lifeblood; states gather people through wealth. Within the teachings, there are two kinds of giving:
that of material wealth and that of the Dharma. How can you urge people to distance themselves from wealth? Huì replied, "The iron finial atop the flagpole. Gōng said: [and so forth].
The horse from Haitan is as large as a donkey. Huì said, "A chicken from Chu is not a phoenix from Mount Dan.
The Duke said, "Two thousand years since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, and the bhikṣus have little sense of shame. The Duke set forth one hundred questions and requested that Guǎnghuì answer them.
Huì answered each one in turn. The Duke asked Li Dūwèi, "What was accomplished by Śākyamuni through his six years of ascetic practice?"
The Commandant said: "When the carrying pole breaks, one knows the firewood is heavy" (Master Gong further elucidates his lineage’s secret realization sent to Li Hanlin).
Chan Master Cuiyan Zhen once studied under Ciming; he subsequently went to Jinluan, where he sat in summer retreat together with Attendant Shan.

Shàn was a senior disciple of Címíng; even Dàowū Zhēn and Yángqí Huì both submitted to his brilliance. The Master [Dàowū] prided himself on having personally seen Címíng and believed there was no one in the world who could satisfy him.
When Shàn conversed with him, he realized that [Dàowū] had not yet attained full penetration and laughed at him.
One day, while walking in the mountains, as their discussion reached its peak, Shàn picked up a piece of tile or rubble, placed it upon a flat rock, and said: "If you were to face this..."
"If you can produce a turning word for this, I will allow you to have personally seen Ciming. The Master looked left and right, intending to respond.

Shanshan scolded him, saying, "To hesitate while reflecting and to stop your mental activity means your emotional consciousness has not yet penetrated it; when have you ever even dreamed of it? The Master was filled with shame and trepidation, and immediately returned to Shishuang.
When Ciming saw him coming, he scolded him, saying, "A true practitioner on pilgrimage must know the proper timing; what is so urgent about this?"
The matter was not yet finished in the summer when he had already arrived here. The Master wept and said, "Because my elder brother Shan harbored a poisonous heart, it ultimately obstructed others;
that is why I have come to see you, O Honorable Monk. Ming suddenly asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?

The Master replied, "Cloudless, clouds arise upon the ridge; the moon exists, yet it sets in the heart of the waves. Ming glared at him and shouted, "With hair white and teeth gone, you still maintain such a view!"
[The Master] asked, "How can one escape birth and death? The Teacher [Wuzhuo] was startled and sought instruction. Ming said, "Ask me.

The Teacher repeated his previous words and questioned him. Ming shouted with a thunderous voice, "Cloudless peaks give rise to clouds; the full moon descends into the heart of the waves. At these words, the Teacher attained great enlightenment.
His spirit became clear and transcendent, and his wit and discernment were so swift that the monastic communities stood in awe of him. [Monk]
Question: "What is the place where a student turns his body? The Master said: "One wall; a hundred walls are harmonized. Question:
"What is the place where a student exerts effort? The Master said: "A thousand days of gathering firewood, burned in a single day.
Question: "What is the place where a student is intimate with the truth? The Master said: "The whole family is sent off to the ferryhead boat. [He] ascended the hall and cited a verse by Longya:
He said, "Studying the Way is like drilling for fire: when you encounter smoke, you must not yet stop. Only when the golden star appears will you have finally reached home.

Shending said, "Studying the Way is like drilling for fire: when you encounter smoke, you should stop immediately. Do not wait for the golden star to appear; it will burn your feet and then your head.
The Master said, "If we speak in terms of the sudden, Longya is still only halfway there. If we speak in terms of the gradual..."
Even the divine cauldron still has a measure of awakening remaining; regarding this, how can one proceed further? O virtuous ones, this year there are many fallen leaves;
from how many places have they been swept back home? Ascending the hall, he raised the following case: A monk asked Baling, "What is the Way?
Baling said, "A clear-eyed person falls into a well. Again, a monk asked Baoying, "What is the Way? Baoying said, "Before the Five-Phoenix Pavilion. Again, a monk asked...
Shoushan was asked, "What is the Way? Shoushan replied, "Three feet deep beneath one's feet. These are three turning words:
one phrase stands like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high; one phrase is rowing a boat on dry land; one phrase is the mutual interpenetration of guest and host.

Is there anyone among you who can discern them? Come forward and speak! If there is none, then for now practice the compassion of an Arhat, for it destroys the thieves of the fetters. Practice the [compassion] of a Bodhisattva...
The compassion of a Bodhisattva is for the sake of bringing peace to sentient beings; the compassion of a Tathāgata is for the sake of attaining the mark of suchness (*tathatā*).
Chan Master Zanyuan of Jiangshan left home at the age of three and became a monk at seven. At fifteen, he traveled abroad to visit Shishuang.
Upon entering the Master’s chamber, Ciming saw him and said, “Go, go, and attend to the stable! The Master then acted as a donkey.

Ming said, "He is truly a vessel of the Dharma. He appointed him as his attendant; for twenty years, he did not shrink from the cold or heat while carrying water and hauling firewood, personally undertaking all tasks in his quest for the Way.
Later, he appeared in the world at Tiantong on Mount Suzhou, Longhua, and Baiyun.

The Provincial Governor invited Master Zhigong to reside at his public monastery. Master Zhigong upheld the essential tenets of the school; his spiritual acumen was swift and sharp, and his realization was in accord with his practice, earning him the respect and admiration of all quarters.
Prime Minister Wang Anshi, deeply honoring the Master’s virtue and reputation, specially submitted a memorial requesting the imperial bestowal of ceremonial robes and a posthumous title.

Furthermore, the Master firmly declined the position of Chief Counselor and retired to build a hermitage among the Dinglin Mountains, where he lived in leisurely seclusion with the Master beneath the forest trees. Pure...
They conversed for the entire day. [The author] presented a verse to the Master, saying: "Not opposing things, the True Way is vast; Arising with every condition, one's own meditation is deep.
The faculty of the tongue is already pure—who could destroy it? Its traces are like space—how I have come to seek them! This, too, clarifies a rare event of this world.
In the first year of the Yuanyou era, the Master passed away. Prime Minister Wang wailed in grief at his stupa.
In praise of the Master’s true character, it is said: "Virtuous indeed is this man! His conduct is rigorous yet his countenance is serene; he understands speech yet is able to remain silent.

He does not rejoice in fame or honor, nor does he grieve over disgrace or defamation. He neither boasts nor exerts himself to overcome others. When people speak of their own virtues, whether they be monastics or laypeople, coming from the north or the south, he neither complies with them nor opposes them;
he neither resists nor suppresses them. He does not look at your flowers, but eats only his own fruit. Who could [match him]?
He succeeded him. "I have left behind these precepts.
Chan Master Da-ning Dao-kuan ascended the hall and said: "Taking non-thought as the school, taking non-abiding as the foundation, and taking true emptiness as the essence."
Wondrous existence functions as utility. Thus it is said: "The entire earth is true emptiness; throughout the dharma-realm is wondrous existence. But tell me, who is it that can employ this?
It is employed through the four seasons; the sun and moon are ever bright. The Dharma is fundamentally non-transmigratory; the Way has no fixed location.
It is sovereign according to conditions, rising and sinking along with phenomena. Whether in this land or another, entering the mundane or the sacred—though [it is thus]...
"It is indeed so. But tell me, how do you express the phrase 'entering a village, one follows its customs'? After a long silence, he said: 'The Sanskrit of the Western Heavens;
the Tang language of this Eastern Land. A monk asked, "What is the white ox on the open ground?
The Master stuck a pair of fire tongs into the brazier and said, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Its head is not lacking; its tail is not in excess."
Chan Master Daowu Wuzhen ascended the hall. "The lion cub roars; the dragon-horse colt leaps.

The mirror of the ancient Buddha is bright; the solitary moon over the three peaks is clear. He then performed a dance and descended from his seat. Ascending the hall again, he cited Dongshan’s words: [text continues].
On Mount Wutai, clouds steam rice; before the Buddha hall steps, it is a "dog-urine day. At the top of the banner pole, fried *zhui* seeds sizzle;
three monkeys toss coins at night. I, the old monk, am not like this: a three-faced *li-nu* cat treads upon the moon.
Two white oxen with smoke in their hands; a crowned blue hare standing by the courtyard cypress; a shell-shedding turtle flying up into the sky.
The old monk’s entanglements have all been seen through and exposed by you all. The old man Dongshan was truly extraordinary;
yet, even so, he could only take three or four steps, and did not go beyond seven jumps and eight leaps.
Tell me, where does the error lie? Today, this old monk will not spare his eyebrows and shall grant you all at once.
After a long silence, he said: "Excessive caution harms one's virtue; silence truly possesses merit. Let the vast ocean change as it may, I shall never speak for your sake.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The ancients said: 'To recognize it is still not to have it. This is truly difficult to comprehend. Earth..."
His jaw was prominent, his beard and mustache were thick, his eyes were deep-set, and his nostrils were large—truly strange.
Suddenly, he passed through the borders of Silla. A monk asked, "What is the first mystery? The Master said, "The light of Śākyamuni Buddha shines upon Ānanda’s shoulder.
The monk asked, "What is the second mystery? The Master said, "The solitary wheel surrounded by a throng of elephants. The monk asked, "What is the third mystery? The Master said... [text continues]
The Three Mysteries. A student asked, "The verse says: 'Tears flow like beads of dew toward the withered mulberry tree. What is the first essential?

The Master said, "It is best to clearly discern the coarse and the subtle. The student asked, "What is the second essential? The Master said, "A flash of lightning makes the heavens and earth shine brilliantly.
The student asked, "What is the third essential? The Master said, "Ancient pines grow old along the roadside. [He] ascended the hall for instruction and cited a monk’s case.
A monk asked Shoushan, "What is the Buddha? Shoushan said, "The new bride rides the donkey while her mother-in-law leads it.

The Sun. A secret treasury, profoundly hidden and formless; brought forth within the palm, it startles all people. How could those of the Two Vehicles, despite their diligence, hope to fathom it?

otherwise, the great earth, mountains, and rivers will tremble and quake.

Lamp. Outside the curtain, several stalks of green, withered bamboo. A question was asked: "How was it before the Buddhas appeared in the world?

(Also written as "Bamboo")—even this falls short of the trap and the snare. A single glance or a raised brow already constitutes a conceptualization; only by departing from these two paths can one accord with this essential principle.

Min patted [the master] and realized it, yet those who wish to explore the source of Chan find themselves ignorant of where to go. Hearing that the Way of Langya was held in high esteem by his contemporaries, he immediately hastened to his seat.

As instructed, he bowed twice to take his leave. Later, while residing at Changshui, whenever he received instruction, he would look upon the assembly and say:

"The Way is not attained through words or symbols; Chan is not known through deliberation or conjecture. To realize the meaning and penetrate the source requires no special artifice. Consequently, both schools held him in high esteem.

One night, they were building the abbot’s quarters. Yunwu asked, “What do you seek by coming here? The Master replied, “I seek the Dharma of the mind. Yunwu said, “The wheel of the Dharma has not yet turned;
the wheel of food must turn first. You are a young man with strong physical vigor; why not go begging for the sake of the assembly?
I have no leisure even to endure my own hunger, so how would I have the leisure to explain Zen to you? The Master did not dare disobey. Not long after, Yunwu moved to Cuoyan.
After the Master finished submitting his memorial, he went again to Cuiyan to seek instruction. Cuiyan said, "The Buddha-dharma has not yet reached you; it will only rot away. The snow is cold;
go and beg for charcoal for the assembly. The Master obeyed this command. When his duties were completed, he returned to the abbot's quarters.

Cuiyan said, "There is a vacancy in the Hall Administration; I shall trouble you with this now. The Master accepted it, but was unhappy, resenting that Cuiyan had not cleared the ground of his mind. He sat behind [the master].

The hoops of a wooden bucket he was carrying suddenly came apart, and he fell from where he stood. At that moment, the Master attained sudden enlightenment and clearly perceived the essential function of Yanguan.
He hurriedly adjusted his *kāṣāya* and went up to the dormitory hall. Yanguan met him with a smile and said, "Venerable Vinaya Master, rejoice!

Your great matter is now complete. The Master bowed twice and departed without uttering a single word. He served under him diligently for eight years, after which he emerged into the world at Cuoyan. At that time, the Head Seat...
He led his assembly out to welcome him and asked, "I do not ask about the Dharma-lineage of Deshan;

what is the Great Function of Linji? The Master said, "Where have you come from? As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him. As the monk was about to respond, the Master shouted, "Lead your assembly back!
From then on, the entire assembly was awed and submissive. A monk asked, "The myriad dharmas return to the One; where does the One return?"
The Master said, "The Yellow River has nine bends. [A monk] asked, "What is the first phrase? The Master said, "Reaching down, the hands pass the knees.

[Another occasion,] he ascended the hall and said: "If speech does not depart from the old nest, how can one escape the entanglements? A single cloud..."
It blocks the mouth of the valley; it has caused many to lose their way to the source. Therefore it is said: "Words do not unfold the matter;

speech does not meet the occasion. Those who rely on words perish; those who linger in phrases are deluded. You people here—relying upon what do you discuss and understand? After a long silence, he said:
"If you wish not to incur the karma of the Avīci Hell, do not slander the Tathāgata’s True Dharma Wheel. Ascending the hall, he said: "The Way is far."
How wondrous! Truth is present in every encounter. How distant is the Sage? If you embody it, it is divine. Thus, in the Sahā world, the Buddha’s work is performed through sound;
in the Gandhavatī world, the Buddha’s work is performed through fragrant food. Here at Cuoyan, [the Buddha’s work is performed...]

Within the mere inhalation and exhalation of breath, one makes offerings and serves all the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the past, present, and future, without missing even a single one.

To take this profound mind and offer it to the dust-motes and lands—this is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness. Ascending the hall, he said: "If you see that all marks are non-marks, then the mountains, rivers, and the great earth are entirely without fault.

A single grain of rice has never been hung upon even a single thread; yet with this, one can transform the great earth into gold and churn the long river into butter and curd.
Although it is so, there is no lack of wearing clothes and eating food; yet, as for the stench of sweat within the gate of the patch-robed monks, that has not even been dreamed of.
[He] ascended the hall and said: "Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are without obstruction—sound, fragrance, taste, touch..."
The Constant Samādhi. This is the realization of the Way of the patch-robed monks (*sōjū*). Mountains are mountains; waters are waters. When hungry, one eats; when weary, one sleeps.

One night he addressed the assembly, saying: "You lot, this group of young monks—you certainly do not know the Sūtras, Vinaya, or Śāstras;
you have entered the assembly to practice Chan, yet you do not understand Chan either. When the thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month arrives, how will you resolve it? The Master said:

"Truly, O virtuous Chan practitioners, the time since the Sage has passed away is remote, and the hearts of men have grown shallow. Looking at the monastic communities of today, they are even more so."

In whatever place they may be, they gather three hundred or five hundred disciples in vast numbers, considering their teaching to be flourishing solely because their meals are abundant and their quarters are comfortable.
Among them, there is not a single person who diligently strives for the Way;

even if there are ten or five such individuals, they run about hither and thither, half-ripe and half-raw. When they meet, they all say, "I understand! I understand! each claiming their own realization.
Each person claims to hold the jewel of the divine serpent; who would be willing to acknowledge their error?
Yet when it comes to being prodded and pressed by the staff, there is not one in ten thousand who can do so. How bitter, how bitter! As the saying goes: "The groves of Prajñā wither year after year;
the weeds of ignorance grow longer every day. Among these, the younger generation of recent times, as soon as they enter the assembly, immediately assume an air of self-complacency.
With hands folded in reverence, he accepts the offerings of others; wherever he goes, he does not select a single stalk of vegetables nor carry a single bundle of firewood.

His ten fingers do not touch water, and his mind is concerned with nothing but worldly affairs. Although this may bring him pleasure for a time, alas, it will burden him in the three miserable realms.
Have you not seen what is said in the scriptures: "It would be better to have glowing iron wrapped around one's body than to receive the robes of those who offer them with faith"?
"It would be better to pour molten copper into one's mouth than to accept food from a person of faith.

Elder, if you were to go there, even if the great earth were transformed into gold and the long rivers were churned into ghee and milk, to provide such offerings to you would not be considered excessive."
If this is still not it, then even for a drop of water or a thread of silk, you must wear fur and horns, pull the plow and drag the harrow, and only then can you repay him.
Have you not seen the Patriarch say: "If one enters the Way but does not penetrate its principle, they shall return their bodies to the offerings of the faithful"?
This is a definitive matter; it will never be in vain. Venerable seniors, time is precious; the moment does not wait for man.

Do not wait until the light of your eyes falls to the ground; then the field of black robes will have lacked even the merit of a single basketful of earth, and you will fall into the Iron Ring Mountains to suffer the torments of a hundred punishments.
Do not say that I did not warn you. Take care.

Chan Master Fang Rui of Langye ascended the hall and said: "The Creator has no intention to produce things, yet every thing comes into being of itself.

a skilled physician need not be encountered for the mind to become clear. Therefore, know that the wondrous wisdom and numinous light are not obtained through conditions."
Only upon reaching this point do I permit you to advance. Langye shall meet you in a different manner. Is there anything more?

[It is] attained. Zen Master Seongjong Juin of Seokbul-sa was asked by a monk: "What is birth from form? The Master said: "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth.

The Master said: "There is no interruption" (The Human and Heavenly Eye; the Eye of the Three Kinds of Birth; there is a verse by Shifo).
When Jingshu Jushuo Chan Master visited Daguan, he asked: "I have a superficial understanding of the sutras and treatises, yet I do not believe in Chan at all.

Guanzhen said, "What follows in the text is long. The Master said, "If that is so, then the Sūtra and Chan are of one essence. Guanzhen said, "The Buddha and the Patriarchs do not have two minds;
they are like a hand forming a fist, or a fist opening into a hand. Because of this, the Master attained realization and subsequently composed [this work].
The verse says: For over twenty years I have scrutinized you with suspicion; how many times have I tried to extinguish this mind of yours?

The lay practitioner Li Duanyuan, a regional military commissioner, had frequently read Chan texts since his childhood while residing in the state academy.

Although he later married and entered official service, he remained steadfast in his devotion to the ancestral Way. Consequently, he built a dwelling resembling a *ārāma* (monastery) in the rear garden and invited Daguan to reside there.

He consulted and studied with him morning and evening, forgetting even to sleep or eat. One day, Daguan looked at the official and said, "Were it not for the power of manifesting [through skillful means], how could you have reached this?"
"Alas! What can be done about having nowhere to enter? The Duke asked, "Are heaven and hell ultimately existent or non-existent?
I beg the Master to explain this clearly. Guoan said, "The Buddhas speak of existence within non-existence, like seeing flowers in the sky with one's own eyes.

Your Excellency seeks non-existence within existence, like grasping at the moon in water with your hands. It is truly laughable that you see a prison before your eyes and yet do not avoid it, while hearing [of such things] as being outside your mind."
The Grand Marshal wished to be reborn in heaven, yet he did not realize that joy and fear reside within the mind, and that good and evil constitute the external environment.

"If you, Grand Marshal, simply understand this mind, you will naturally be free from delusion. The Grand Marshal asked, "How does one understand the mind? Guishan said, "Do not deliberate upon either good or evil.
The Grand Marshal asked, "After ceasing such deliberation, where does the mind go? Guishan said, "For now, please return to your residence, Grand Marshal. The Grand Marshal said, "Only..."
"Where does the mind go after a person dies? Guanyou said, "If you do not know where life comes from, how can you know where death goes?

The official said, "As for life, I already know it. Guanyou asked, "From where does life come? The official was at a loss. Guanyou rose, thrust his hand toward the official's chest, and said, "It is right here!
What more do you intend to deliberate upon? The official said, "I understand. Guanyou asked, "How so?"

Chan Master Qionglong Yuan ascended the hall and said: "Fuzhen does not speak of Chan; with nothing to do, he sleeps until the sun is high.
If anyone asks about the meaning of the Patriarch, he strikes them two or three blows. O assembly, tell me: why is it so? It is because they would otherwise disturb this mountain monk’s sleep."
Master Xinghua Shaoling ascended the hall and said: "In the school of our ancestors, the Buddha-dharma does not exist; before the Hall of Virtue, benevolence and righteousness need not be discussed.
Although this is so, matters do not always follow a single path. I have heard it said that one’s parents are mournful and their toil in giving birth to us was great.
Desiring to repay this profound kindness, [one realizes] the vast heavens are inexhaustible. One’s hair, skin, and body must not be damaged or injured. This is from the *Analects*.

Such was the filial piety of Zhongni (the Master Kǒng). Yet, while revolving within the three realms, one cannot abandon the bonds of affection; only by casting aside such affection and entering the state of non-action does one truly repay their debt of gratitude.

Therefore, our Great Awakened World-Honored One practiced austerities on the Snowy Mountains, attained enlightenment at Magadha, and ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother—this was the filial piety of Śākyamuni. Having attained great liberation, he manifested great spiritual powers...
He passed through. Holding a golden staff in his hand and supporting a dragon-bowl in his palm, he went to the gates of hell and stood there in solemn contemplation.
There he saw his compassionate mother, weeping immeasurably. This was the filial piety of Maudgalyāyana. But what is the filial piety of Xinghua? After a long silence, he said:
"Today, Xinghua does not ascend to heaven, nor does he enter hell; within the Hall of Good Dharma, he is like a lamp."
On the royal throne, he preached the Dharma for his mother to repay her labors. He then asked, "Tell me, where is my mother now?
He continued, "In her lifetime, my mother accumulated abundant roots of goodness; there is no need to ask the Buddha, for she has certainly been reborn in heaven.
Among humans, a long life is rare in all ages; at ninety years, she was short by one. Having descended from the seat, he said, "I venture to trouble the assembly to burn a single incense stick."
Incense. It is used to assist this mountain monk in repaying his filial debt. Since she was the mother of this mountain monk, why do you trouble all of you to burn incense?

Have you not heard it said: "When a member of the eastern family dies, the members of the western family assist in the mourning"? [The Master] beat his breast with his hand and cried out: "Heaven! Heaven!"
Chan Master Zhihai Daoping ascended the hall and said: "This mountain monk does not understand the Buddha-dharma;

in guiding others, I have no fixed method. At times I half-open and half-close; at times I fully release and fully withdraw. It is like dropping a stone from out of nowhere amidst a crowd of ten thousand people;
if by chance one person is struck, they will suddenly realize that it flows everywhere."
