"It is contact. If you do not call it a fist, then it is the back. What would you call it? The Master was at a loss. After two years, he finally attained understanding;
yet he still engaged in debate without being refuted. Huángtáng grew weary of this and happened to converse with him when his arguments reached their sharpest point.
Dongjù said, "Stop! Stop! Talking about food can never satisfy a person. The Master was cornered and said, "I have reached this point with my bow broken and my arrows exhausted.
I pray that the Venerable will show me compassion and point out a place of peace and happiness. Dongjù said, "A single speck of dust flies up and obscures the sky."
"A single mustard seed falling would cover the earth. This is the place of peace and happiness; one simply must dread the many antiquated relics of the Senior Preceptor (Zhengji).
One must truly die away the entire mind that has existed since immeasurable kalpas before it can be so. The Master hurried out.

One day, hearing the administrative officer beating a novice, a sudden clap of thunder struck, and he attained great enlightenment. He hurried to see Huìtáng, forgetting to put on his sandals, and immediately began to praise himself.

[The Master] said, "Everyone in the world has merely 'participated' in Chan; I am one who has 'awakened' to it. The Abbot laughed and said, "To have attained the first rank in the selection of Buddhas—how could that be matched?
Consequently, he was given the title "Old Man Sishin" (Dead Heart). A monk asked, "What is Huanglong’s phrase for receiving people?
The Master said, "Opening one's mouth to scold someone. The monk said, "That which scolds is the phrase for receiving people; it is used to test a person."
[The Master] said: "A phrase. Furthermore, how is it? The Master said: "Simply recognize the one who is being reviled. Ascending the hall, he said:

"When a clear pearl is cast into turbid water, the turbid water cannot but become clear. When the recitation of the Buddha's name is applied to a distracted mind, the distracted mind cannot but become the Buddha.

Since the Buddha is not distracted, the turbid water naturally becomes clear. Now that the turbid water has become clear, to whom does the merit belong? After a long silence, he said: "Several times..."
Black winds toss the great ocean; never have we heard of a fishing boat capsizing [amidst them]. In the meditation hall, he asked a monk:
"The darkness of the final day of the month—suppose one were to apply five colors within that gloom and have hundreds of thousands of people look at those colors in the night.
Would any among them be able to distinguish blue, yellow, red, or white? The monk was speechless. The Master spoke on his behalf: "Every single one of them is blind."
The Master, because of King Zhengyan’s question, said: "I have heard that birth occurs through the conjunction of three conditions, and I have also heard of those who die and are reborn immediately.

Why, then, is there such a thing as being 'snatched from a womb' to be born? I am greatly perplexed by this. The Master replied: "It is like when you, Zhengyan, served as the Commissioner of Transport (Cao Shi)."
"Wherever one dwells, one immediately occupies that very position. The King asked, "Do you still have doubts? The Master said, "What more do you doubt?
At these words, the King attained realization.
Chan Master Huanglong Lingyuan Qing received the seal of his mind from Huaitang. He often said to people, "The reason students of today have not escaped birth and death lies in what?
It lies in the fact that their 'thieving mind' has not yet died. Yet, this is not their fault."
This is the fault of the teacher. It was like the Emperor Gaozu of Han, who deceived and killed Han Xin. Although Xin died, did his mind truly die?

As for the ancient students of the Way, they attained liberation from birth and death beneath a single word; where is the evidence of this? It lies in the fact that their "thieving mind" had already perished.
Yet, this was not something the student could achieve on their own; it was truly due to the subtle and profound skill of the teacher’s hammering. For example:

When Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty appeared in the Great Hall and beheld Hou Jing, he did not move a muscle or alter his tone; yet the heart of Jing was already withered and drained of all vitality.
Though the various accounts told of him are not without beauty, in essence, they are like the flowers painted by Zhao Chang:
though the likeness is lifelike, they are not real flowers. [The Master] ascended the hall and said: "The river moon shines; the pine wind blows. Throughout the eternal night, the clear sky..."
Who is it? Fog, dew, clouds, and rosy mists cannot conceal him. Even within this state, one says, "It would be better to go home.

But where does one return? The lotus leaves are round and round, as round as a mirror; the water chestnut tips are sharp and sharp, as sharp as an awl. Ascending the hall, he said: "The Ultimate Way is not difficult; it only dislikes picking and choosing.
Simply do not harbor hatred or love, and all will be transparently clear. When the Patriarch spoke these words, he was blind.
To shut out the eyes of all people in the world, to discern right from wrong, and to distinguish the black from the white—when a monk reaches this point, how can he clarify it?
"If you have not yet reached the end of the water, it is difficult to understand while sitting and watching the clouds arise."
When Chan Master Letan Caotang Qing first visited Chan Master Dayue Zhe of Daguai, he gained nothing.
Later, he visited Huanglong, who showed him the "wind and banner" koan. For a long time, he failed to reach a realization. One day, Huanglong asked, "How do you understand the 'wind and banner' koan?
The Master replied, "I have no way of entry; I beg the Master for a skillful means. Huanglong said, "Have you seen a cat catching..."
"O Mouse! Your eyes do not blink; your four paws rest firmly on the ground; your senses are directed forward; your head and tail are in a straight line; you aim and there is no miss.

If you, my son, can truly be thus—your mind free from distracting conditions—the six sense-faculties will naturally become still. If you investigate in silence, it is impossible that you will fail by even one part in ten thousand.
From then on, the Master withdrew from worldly distractions. After more than a year, he suddenly attained awakening and spoke in verse:
The Dragon said, "Sui sui sui. Xi xi xi. Sui sui sui; no one recognizes what follows after. When night falls, the bright moon ascends the solitary peak.
Originally, it was only this very thief. The Dragon accepted this and further told him: "Attaining the Way is not difficult."
To propagate the Way is difficult; yet propagating the Way depends upon oneself. To preach the Dharma for others is difficult; once it has been clarified, it lies in its diligent practice.
Generally speaking, when a patriarch preaches the Dharma, a single phrase contains the Three Mysteries, and within each Mystery there are the Three Essentials.
The disciple entered the abode of reality; having obtained his seat and donned his robe, he looked back at himself and went forth naturally, penetrating everywhere.

He remained in attendance upon the Master for another seven years before taking his leave to travel extensively through the monastic communities. A monk asked, "How was it before Niutou saw the Fourth Patriarch?
The Master said, "Jing three, Bian four. The monk asked, "How was it after he saw him? The Master said, "Ashy head, dusty face."
Fayan asked, "Ultimately, how is it? The Master said, "A total embarrassment. He ascended the hall and said: "Form and mind are not different;
self and other are without distinction. Raising his whisk, he said: "If you call this a whisk, you will enter hell like an arrow.
If you do not call it a whisk, you have eyes but are as if blind. Even if you manage to escape both extremes, you are still a black ox lying in stagnant water."
Chan Master Qingyuan Xin ascended the hall and said: "Thirty years ago, before I had studied Chan, when I saw mountains, they were mountains;
when I saw water, it was water. Later, when I encountered a teacher and attained a point of entry, seeing mountains, they were not mountains;
seeing water, it was not water. Now that I have attained a place of rest, I see mountains as simply mountains again."
The mountain. Seeing water, it is simply water. Great assembly, as for these three kinds of perspectives, are they the same or different?
If there is anyone who can discern this in both its black and white aspects, I grant that you have personally seen this old monk.
Chan Master Jia Shan Chun once had a creature carved from wood with the head of a lion, the hooves of an ox, and the body of a horse.
Every time he ascended the hall, he would hold it up and show it to the assembly, saying: "If you call it a lion, it has the body of a horse; if you call it a horse, it has the head of a lion."
Furthermore, it has the feet of an ox. Tell me, ultimately what would you call it? He commanded the monks to offer a response, but none succeeded.
The Master then presented this verse: With the majestic head of a lion, The feet of an ox, and the body of a horse; If one can enter the three paths, The profound gate will open layer upon layer.
Chan Master Shuangling Hua addressed the assembly from the high seat. "The green bamboos and yellow flowers are not external objects; the white clouds and bright moon reveal the whole of reality.
Every single thing is a possession of our own house; picked up at random by hand, it is no mere dust. He then raised his whisk and said:
Do you understand? To recognize it is as before, yet still not it. [The Master] struck the meditation seat and descended. Chan Master Guishan Xiaozhen ascended the hall and said:
"When one's ground is stable and secure, one’s transgressions fill the heavens. It is evident that one cannot lift one's feet;
when playing with spiritual powers, one wounds oneself where there is no wound. One specifically cannot set foot down. Now tell me, where does the fault lie?"
Where is it? Those who possess the eye for the study of the Way should come forth and engage in mutual discussion.
You must seek to see the mountain of your own original portion, rather than following divergent paths. Do not merely keep nodding your head to yourself, wasting your years and months.
At some future time, when the single blow of the hammer falls upon your crown, do not say you were not warned.
Chan Master Baofu Quan (a native of Zhangzhou) was by nature straightforward and courageous in his pursuit of the Way.

At the instance of Huitang’s raising of his fist, he attained a thorough realization of the fundamental source. His spiritual eloquence was swift and incisive. When Huang Shan谷 (Shan Gu) first entered the path, he asked Huitang, "Who here is capable of engaging in dialogue?
Huitang replied, "Quan of Zhangzhou. At that time, the Master was supervising laborers while clearing land for cultivation; Shan Gu accompanied Huitang [to visit him].
Daitō went to pay his respects and asked, "Do you know that the incense burner has given birth to a child?
The Master said, "Is it a boy or a girl? Huang hesitated, and the Master struck him. Daitō said, "It is not right to be so discourteous. The Master said, "This block of wood!
When would I wait to strike you? Huang laughed heartily. Later, he ascended the hall and, citing a verse by Hanshan, said: "My mind is like the autumn moon..."
The emerald pool is clear and pristine; nothing can be compared to it. How am I to describe it? The old monk says otherwise:
my mind is like a lantern; when the flame is lit, it is red within and without. Something can indeed be compared to it: tomorrow morning, the sun will rise in the east.

Those who transmitted [the teachings] took this as a joke. When Master Sishin saw it, he sighed and said, "If Brother Quan’s proclamations are such as these, he truly does not fail the entrustment of our late teacher."
Chan Master Huguo Xin ascended the hall and said: "In the three realms there is no dharma; where can one seek the mind?
If you wish to know the Master Huguo’s phrase of direct presence, look at this grove of bamboo before the gate."

One day, Master Chan Huanglong Ming ascended the hall. As soon as the assembly had gathered, the Master said, "I cannot continue to open my eyes and speak dreams," and he immediately descended from his seat.
Chan Master Daowu Yuan addressed the assembly from the high seat: "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing.
When the ancients spoke thus, it was like looking at a leopard through a tube; one sees but a single spot.

Even if one enters the forest without stirring the grass and enters the water without ruffling the waves, it is still like riding a horse across jagged ice. If you were a master at shooting down a soaring falcon, why would you not [act accordingly]?
"Scratching an itch on the head of a snake. One who possesses the true eye should try to discern this. After a long while, he said: "The embroidered mandarin ducks emerge from the golden needle.
The layman Huang Tingjian, a Grand Historian, possessed the karmic habituation of Prajñā; though holding a high office, he remained as tranquil as water. He moved in and out of [the world]...
In the Chan school, he had not yet found his direction and was fond of composing flowery verses.

He once visited Chan Master Yuan-tong Xiu, who rebuked him, saying, "A great man with such mastery of calligraphy—how can you willingly expend it on such things? At that time, Master Xiu was instructing Li Bashi on the matter of painting horses.
The Master (Chang) mocked him, saying, "Are you perhaps placing me back into the belly of a horse? Master Xiu replied, "You take your flowery..."
[He] said: "This stirs the lustful hearts of all people in the world; it does not stop within the belly of a horse—it only fears that it will lead one to birth in the *niraya* hells.

The Duke was struck with awe and repented, apologizing for his transgression. From then on, he ceased his literary pursuits and devoted himself solely to the Way. He composed a text of vows and strictly admonished himself against wine and carnal desire.
He took only morning gruel and midday meals. [Verse: He went to rely on Huìtáng and requested that he be pointed toward a direct and swift path.
Huìtáng said, "As for Zhòngní’s saying, 'My disciples, do you think I have anything hidden from you? I have nothing hidden from you,' how would you, the Grand Historian, usually explain this theory?
The Master attempted to respond, but Huìtáng said, "Not so, not so. The Master remained in a state of persistent confusion.
One day, while attending the assembly during a mountain walk, mountain rock chrysanthemums were in full bloom. Master Tang said, "Do you smell the fragrance of the *mugichwa* (cassia) flowers?

The Master replied, "I do. Master Tang said, "I have hidden nothing from you. The Master was suddenly enlightened and prostrated himself, saying, "How can the Abbot be so earnest with such a 'motherly heart' (*pobae*)?
Master Tang smiled and said, "I only wish for you to reach your home. [He then] went to visit Sisin Sin.
Chan Master Xin entered the room with the assembly. As he opened his eyes, he saw Zhang and asked, "New Elder, dead scholar!
When you are dead and burned into two heaps of ash, where will we meet? Zhang was speechless. Xin signaled for him to leave and said, "What you have attained under Huitang has not yet taken root.
Later, while serving as an official in Qian-nan, his power of the Way became even more eminent; in a state of non-thought, he passed away.
[He] immediately clarified the question posed by Sītiṅ and replied to him in a letter, saying: "In years past, I have repeatedly received your earnest exhortations.

For a long time I remained as if in a drunken dream, with things appearing only vaguely amidst shifting shadows. This was because my state of doubt was not yet exhausted and the root of my life-destiny had not been severed;

thus, I retreated in awe, like one gazing at a precipice. While traveling on the road in Qian-nan during my period of banishment, I woke from a midday nap and suddenly began to reflect upon [your teachings]."
How many people throughout the world have been deceived by old monks! Only Master Sishin refused to comply;
this was truly the foremost act of compassion. How fortunate we are beyond measure!

Upon reading the account that when Layman Shao was dispatched as the Governor of Hongzhou, he invited Huìtáng to inquire about the Way and attained silent realization, he composed a verse on seizing the vital point (*tōuki*), which says:
"By day I forgot to eat, by night I forgot to sleep; Holding the Dragon Pearl, I wished to ascend to heaven."
Instead, let go of everything within yourself. The four corners collapse to the ground, yet it is perfectly round. He presented this to the Hall Master (Huitang).
The Hall Master, deeply approving, said, "The layman Wu Xun, Secretary of the Secretariat, resides at Huitang. During a session in the inner chamber, Huitang said to him:

'I shall not question you regarding your lifelong studies, intellectual understanding, memory, or extensive learning. Speak a single phrase from before your parents were born. The official [Wu] hesitated."
The Abbot struck him with his whisk, and he immediately grasped the profound meaning.

Chan Master Ledtan Qian ascended the hall and said: "The numinous light shines through with clarity, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects. Its essence reveals the true and eternal, unbound by words and letters.
The nature of the mind is unstained; it is fundamentally perfected of itself. Simply leave behind delusive conditions, and you are the Buddha of Suchness."—Ancient Record.
People speak thus, yet they fail to realize it is a pitfall; it is like a shirt pressed against the skin that cannot be removed and cannot be passed through.
One must truly be a lion cub, standing upright ten thousand fathoms high, to be able to cut it off completely. Even so, this is the case.
This is also an old crow in a sack. [He] struck the meditation seat and descended from it.
Chan Master Kaixian Ying ascended the hall and said: "Climbing a mountain, one must reach the summit; entering the sea, one must reach the bottom.
Studying the Way, one must reach that place where even Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot speak. If it is not like this, you are all merely spirits clinging to the grass and wood."
"You devils who eat the spit and saliva of wild foxes—thus says the *Avataṃsaka*. It is like a potent medicine;
though it is bitter to the taste, it is necessary to cure the illness. A-ya! A-ya!"
Chan Master Xiangtian Fanqing was a native of Jiaxing. A monk asked, "For what purpose does the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion employ so many hands and eyes?
The Master said, "The wealthy feel that even a thousand mouths are too few. The monk asked, "Ultimately, what is the true eye? The Master said:
"From the beginning we have lived together, yet I do not know your name. Ascending the hall, he said: "Spring is already late; fallen flowers fall like a rain of red.
Whether travelers from north and south return or not, in the thousands and tens of thousands of groves the cuckoo cries. I have no home—where shall I go?
Throughout the lands of the ten directions, upon what can I rely? This old man has a true message: last night at the third watch, the moon [shone]."
At Chizhai Baqin Rui Chan Master first visited Chan Master Huanglong Nan. Huanglong asked, "Have you come for the sake of people's affairs, or have you come for the sake of the Buddha-dharma?
The Master replied, "I have come for the sake of the Buddha-dharma. Huanglong said, "If you have come for the sake of the Buddha-dharma, then right now we shall distinguish it."
[The Master] handed [the whisk] over and then struck it once with the whisk. The Master said, "Even you, Preceptor, must not disturb people. Long immediately took him as a worthy vessel.
Later, he followed Zhaojue and profoundly realized the profound mysteries. Ascending the hall, [he said]:

"In Buddha-worlds, the work of a Buddha is performed by means of a single speck of dust or a single hair, causing those who see a single dharma to be fully endowed with all dharmas. Therefore, I have provisionally set up this scaffolding."
There is a Buddha’s transformation within which takes silent, wordless stillness as the great Buddhist activity;
it causes those who study it to leave behind all marks, for this is precisely what is called the state of all Buddhas. Thus, I bestow this upon you three times with the fire-brush.

In another Buddha-land, yellow flowers and green bamboos constitute the Buddhist activity, causing those who behold these forms to see that form is itself emptiness. Furthermore, I entrust this to Maitreya.
The Buddha-jewel realm takes the emptiness of phenomena as its seat and manifests buddha-activities, so that practitioners do not cling to seeking a Buddha.

Having thoroughly investigated and realized this, there is a Buddha’s field of practice where buddha-activities are accomplished through the four kinds of offerings, so that those who know contentment may sever divergent thoughts.
It can be brought down; there is a wondrous domain of the Buddha characterized by all forms of speech.
Samādhi performs the Buddha’s work; it causes those who enter according to their capacities not to abandon either movement or stillness.

Thus, it serves as a channel to carry the great assembly. Now tell me: within this, is there any distinction of superior or inferior? After a long silence, he said: "Those who arrive must know they are masters. *Chān* (End)."
Chan Master Huili Chang ascended the hall and said: "The root and source of the Buddha-dharma cannot be realized and entered through anything other than right faith and wondrous wisdom.

The pivotal gate of the Patriarchs cannot be opened by anything other than great compassion and profound vows. When one possesses both faith and wisdom, the provisional and the real are practiced together, like gold within its ore.
When one fully embodies compassion and vows, good and evil can be distinguished, like the moon emerging from the clouds. Great assembly, only—"
"When one's parents have not yet been born, where can many parables be expressed? After a long silence, he said:
"Nine out of ten words may hit the mark, but they are not equal to a single moment of silence."
The Venerable Huìyuán traveled to Mount Lú and arrived at Dōnglín, where he frequently inquired about his own spiritual practice.

His peers, seeing that his appearance was coarse and his deportment awkward and uncouth, all mocked and ridiculed him. One day, while walking through the palace courtyard, he suddenly tripped and fell;
at that moment, he attained sudden and complete enlightenment. He composed a verse and had an attendant write it upon the wall, saying: "This one stumble, this one stumble!"
"Ten thousand taels of gold would indeed be enough to buy this: a hat upon his head and a bundle at his waist, with the clear wind and bright moon carried on the tip of his staff.
He departed from Donglin that very day. This was passed down to Zhaojue, who rejoiced greatly and said, "If a monk’s investigation of the Way is like this!"

Goodness cannot be added to it; it causes people to trace its course, yet in the end no one knows where it goes (the "Great Wisdom Armory" [Da-hui Wu-ku] claims this refers to the words of the realized master Deng Yung, but that is incorrect).
The Gentleman Su Shi, Inner Secretary, while staying overnight at Donglin Temple, attained a realization through a discussion with Zhaojue on the "discourse of the insentient.
At dawn, he offered this verse: "The sound of the stream is the broad and long tongue; The color of the mountains is surely the pure body.
Last night, eighty-four thousand verses were spoken; How shall I recount them to others hereafter?"
Toushuai Congyue was the first to lead the assembly at Daowu. Taking several monks with him, he went to visit Master Zhi of Yungai.

Before Zhi had spoken more than a few sentences, he fully understood what was within [Congyue’s] mind. He then smiled and said, "I observe that the Senior Seat’s character and bearing are extraordinary;
why is it that your speech and breath are like those of a drunkard? The Master’s face flushed red and sweat poured down as he said, "I pray that the Master..."
Without begrudging his compassion, Zhi spoke with him again, piercing him with a needle. The Master was utterly bewildered and subsequently requested to enter the room for instruction.
Zhi asked, "Have you ever seen the Venerable Fachang Yu? The Master replied, "I have read his recorded sayings; they are sufficient for my own understanding, so I have no wish to meet him.
Zhi asked, "Have you ever seen the Venerable Dongshan Wen? The Master replied, "A man from Guansi has no head."
"Brain! Dragging a cloth skirt and emitting the stench of urine—what excellence is there in that? Zhi said, "You should simply investigate within the stench of urine.
The Master followed these instructions and visited Dongshan, where he deeply grasped the profound essence. He then visited Zhi again.
Zhi asked, "Since you have seen the man from Guansi, how is the Great Matter? The Master replied, "If it were not for the Venerable Master’s instruction, I would have [remained lost]."
[He thought,] "Alas, I have wasted a lifetime. He then paid his respects and took leave. The Master subsequently visited Zhenjing.
Later, he emerged into the world at Luyuan. There was one named Qing Su who had long studied under Ciming; he resided in a single room and never associated with others.

One day, while the Master was eating lychees preserved in honey, Su happened to pass by the door. The Master called out, "This is a fruit from your native region, old man; you may share it with me. Su...
He said, "Since the passing of my former teacher, I have not received this food for a long time. The Master asked, "Who was your former teacher? Su replied, "Ciming.

I am merely fortunate enough to have served him for thirteen years. The Master then said with astonishment, "To be capable of serving as an attendant for thirteen years—how could it be anything other than having attained the Way?
He then offered him some leftover fruit and gradually drew closer to him. Su...
The Master asked, "Who is the person you have seen? He replied, "Dongshan Wensu. [Zhaozhou] asked, "Whom did Dongshan see? The Master replied, "Huanglong Nan.
[Zhaozhou] said, "Nan, a mere novice, has been with our late master for but a short time, yet his Dharma path has already spread so widely. The Master became even more perplexed and awestruck;
he then placed incense in his sleeve and went to pay his respects to Wensu. Wensu rose and avoided him, saying, "I am of meager merit. Our late master—"
He conferred upon him the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa). He did not permit [Hui]su to become a teacher. The Master [Dao]yi was even more respectful.

Su then said, "Out of pity for your sincerity, I am transgressing my late master’s prediction. Try telling me what you have attained throughout your life. The Master fully explained his insights. Su said, "You may enter the Buddha-way."
Yet he was unable to enter [the state of] Māra. The Master asked, "What do you mean? Su replied, "Have you not seen the ancients say:
'The final word is where one first arrives at the secure barrier'? After several months of this, Su was finally certified [as having attained realization].

The Master further cautioned him, saying: "What Wen has shown you are all correct knowledge and correct view; however, you left Wen too early and were thus unable to exhaust its subtlety. I shall now..."
"I shall clarify this for you so that you may enjoy its use and attain great mastery. In the future, do not by any means succeed me. Later, the Master succeeded Zhenjing.
A monk asked, "To lead an army and command generals, one must rely on the imperial tiger-token;
to lead a multitude and guide disciples, one must secretly wear the heart-seal of the Patriarchs. What is the Patriarchs' heart-seal? The Master said, "It cannot be spoken from the mouth."
[The student] said, "I have attained it. [The Master] said, "Is it merely this? Is there anything else? The Master said, "Do not take Zhi Dun’s crane and call it Wang Xizhi’s goose.
A question was asked: "What is the realm of Tuṣita? The Master said, "A single stream is the color of crushed indigo; a thousand peaks are as green as carved jade."
[The monk] asked, "What is it like to be a person within the realm? The Master said, "Seven hollows and eight protrusions—no one sees them; a hundred heads and a thousand faces—one knows them alone.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Night after night, one embraces the Buddha in sleep; morning after morning, one rises together with him.

Rising and sitting, we always follow one another; speaking and remaining silent, we dwell together. If you wish to know where the Buddha goes, it is simply this sound of speech. O Zen practitioners, great..."
Little Master Fu only knows how to embrace the bridge pillar to wash himself, or to hold the mooring rope while releasing the boat.

He takes what is struck from the printing block and casts it out from the mold. How could he know that a monk of true substance blocks the lairs of Buddhas and Patriarchs, breaks through the gates of mystery and subtlety, leaps out of the pits of annihilation and permanence, and does not rely on the realm of purity? Having nothing at all, he alone brandishes his two [hands].
Fists! Roaming across the seas, establishing a home and founding a nation—there are some fellows who also wish to sit motionless atop a hundred-foot pole.
Yet when the time comes to turn over, they cannot bring themselves to let go of their lives. Have you not seen how Master Yunmen said:
"Knowing this kind of matter, set it aside to one side; you must truly rouse your spirit and exert some effort."
If you can realize it before the primordial chaos was yet divided, you are still but a dull-witted fellow; how much less can you hope to savor its flavor upon the tongue of another?
There will never be an end to it. Do you Zen students wish to understand? What difficulty is there in raising one's eyebrows?
Clearly, not even a single hair-tip is seen. When the wind blows away the drifting clouds from the azure void, the moon rises over the green mountains.
"A single lump of mountain jade. He gave a shout and descended from his seat. [Verse]: Within the hall, he established three statements to test the students. The first was:
"One brushes away the grass and gazes at the wind, seeking only to see one's nature. Where, then, is the nature of the person right now? The second was:
Only by realizing one's own nature can one be liberated from birth and death. When the light of the eyes falls to the ground, how does one achieve liberation? Third, he said:
"If you can be liberated from birth and death, you will know the destination. When the four elements separate, where do you go? (Dongshan Wenlang and Baofeng Zhenjing).
Chan Master Foyun Fozhao Gaomo went to visit Chan Master Yuan Tongji. During their private interview, Ji raised the following case:
"A monk asked Touzi, 'When a person who has undergone the great death comes back to life, what then? Touzi said, 'Night travel is not permitted; one must arrive at dawn. What is the meaning of this?
The Master replied, "The kindness is too great to be repaid. Ji was greatly pleased and subsequently appointed him as the head of the assembly. That evening—

When he served as the *bifu* (the master of ceremonies) for the assembly, his responses were slow and his speech stammering; the assembly laughed at him, and the Master turned a flush of embarrassment.
The following day, while serving tea in the Sangha Hall, the tea ladle slipped from his hand and fell to the ground. Seeing the ladle bounce, he attained the *samādhi* of responding to stimuli.

Later, while relying on Zhenjing, he read a verse by the Patriarch which says: "The mind is identical to the realm of empty space; it manifests dharmas equal to empty space; it realizes the realization of empty space."
At that time, there was neither being nor non-being; he attained a sudden and great enlightenment. He would often say to others:

"On the twenty-first day of the eleventh month in the third year of the Shaosheng era, I realized the Chan of the 'square inch' (the mind). Ascending the hall, he said: "The meaning of the Patriarchs who came from the West is a separate transmission outside the teachings.
Without a vessel of great capacity, one cannot realize and enter it. Those who do realize and enter it are not constrained by words or letters."

Regarding what is called "that which is turned": sounds and forms are not that in which one is deluded, nor is there any distinction between Yunmen and Linji, nor any difference between Zhaozhou and Deshan.
Therefore, in proclaiming the Way, one must clearly understand that within words there are no words, and within no-words there are words.
If you can realize this point, it can be said that though you wear clothes all day long, you have never been stained by a single thread; though you eat all day long...
"Rice! I have never so much as chewed a single grain of rice; I am simply reviling the Buddhas and cursing the Patriarchs. What fault is there in that?
Nevertheless, if you wish not to incur the karma of the Avīci Hell, do not slander the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata. With a shout, he descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said, "Guizong knew how to slay the snake; Heshan knew how to beat the drum. The myriad phenomena and the entire cosmos all proceed from this very place.
He threw down the staff and said, "Return to the hall for tea. [Verse] The Master’s power of inquiry was profound and reached its depths;
his words did not conform to the times. Whenever he addressed the assembly, he would often cite: "In the eighth year of the Xining era, I presented my official documents..."
While at Fengxiang Prefecture, [the Master] reported that in his youth Mount Hua had collapsed for forty *li*, burying eighty village households.
"You younger generations," he said, "are like eggplants and gourds; when will you ever understand?
Someone asked, "On the precious lotus-flower throne, why is it always mundane truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)? The Master replied, "Foolish man! Does the Buddha-nature have two kinds?"
When Chan Master Ledu Zantang Zhun first visited Zhenjing, Zhenjing asked, "Where have you recently departed from?
The Master replied, "Dayang. Zhenjing asked, "Where did you spend the summer retreat? The Master replied, "Dawei. Zhenjing asked, "Where are you from? The Master replied, "Xingyuan Prefecture.
Zhenjing extended his hands and said, "How does my hand compare to the Buddha’s hand? The Master was at a loss. Zhenjing said, "Regarding your previous response—"
Each and every one is numinous and bright; each and every one is naturally authentic. Yet, as soon as you utter the words, "How is my hand like the Buddha’s hand?
it becomes an obstruction. Tell me, where does the sickness lie? The Master said, "I do not understand. Jing said, "Everything is already fully accomplished."
"Who else could I teach to understand? At these words, the Master was immediately relieved and at peace. He served his teacher diligently for ten years, following him wherever he went.

In the third year of the Shaosheng era, when Zhenjing moved to Shimen, the assembly grew even more numerous. Whenever monks came to question him, he would simply sit upright with eyes closed, offering no instruction.
When he saw students arriving, he would go to tend the vegetable garden; this became his constant practice. His fellow practitioner Gong addressed the Master as follows:
Zuo said, "Does this old man have no interest in the Way of the Dharma? One day, as he raised his staff to clear a channel, water splashed onto his robes;
he suddenly attained great enlightenment. Jing scolded him, saying, "Is this truly how you dare to act? From then on, Zuo’s traces became even more hidden, yet his fame increased all the more.
[End of entry]. ○ When the Master returned from Zhejiang to Lestam, he went to visit Chan Master Shen, who soon appointed him to share the teaching seat.

There was an attendant named Wuzhuo who, upon seeing the remains of a cooking fire that had been discarded, attained realization. He went to the abbot’s quarters to communicate his awakening, but Shen shouted at him and sent him out; consequently, Wuzhuo lost his resolve.

He hanged himself behind the latrine in the Yanshou Hall. Appearing and disappearing at no fixed time, the assembly feared him. When the Master heard of this, he went specifically to use the latrine at midnight.
Just as he was taking off his clothes, Wuzhu arrived carrying pure water. The Master said, "Wait for me to finish undressing. Once he had finished, [Wuzhu] presented the water.
Wu returned once more. Before long, as Wu was handing over the counting sticks (*zhōuzǐ*), the Master washed them clean and then called for the rinsing bucket to be removed.
Just as Wu reached out to take it, the Master seized his hand and asked, "Are you that attendant Wu? Wu replied, "Yes.

The Master said, "Is this the same 'awakening' you had back when you were in the Guest Prefect’s quarters, seeing something in the falling ember of a firebrand? This is what is meant by studying the Way through Zen meditation."
It simply requires knowing where the primary source of one's own life (the *mìngběn yuánchén*) resides. You have needlessly created this distinction between going and staying.
When you were in the Scripture Hall, you moved the Head Seat’s sandals; was that not what you realized at that time? Furthermore, while in the Guest Prefect’s quarters—
"Moving another person's pillow—was that not what you realized at that time?

Every night you were here drawing water and passing out tally-sticks—was that not what you realized at that time? For what reason do you not know where it has gone, yet remain here to disturb the assembly?
The Master pushed him violently; he collapsed like a stack of bricks being overturned. From this point on, he never appeared again.
Regarding "The Seer":
Zen Master Jingjue Ben was asked by a monk, "When like sounds respond to one another, how is it? The Master said, "A magpie crows upon the tree.
The monk asked, "When like energies seek one another, how is it? The Master said, "A fierce tiger roars before the cliff."
Chan Master Bao Ciying ascended the hall and said: "Coming up like this, a fierce tiger leaves the forest; coming down like this, a startled snake enters the grass.
Neither up nor down, the sun shines brightly. He gave a shout and said: "The waters of the Xiang River are clear and deep;
stepping out the door is the road to Chang'an."
Chan Master Baohua Jian ascended the hall and said: "In the practice of Chan, there is nothing extraordinary;

it simply requires that one's life-root be severed, one's state of doubt be shed, and the thousand eyes suddenly open. It is like a brilliant sun rolling up from the bottom of the great ocean, ascending through the celestial gates to illuminate everything beneath the four heavens.
All the myriad distinctions and thousandfold differences are simultaneously made clear, whereby one is able to grasp the vajra."
The King’s precious sword—moving freely in all directions, seven times released and eight times traversed—is used with sovereign ease; how joyful this is!

Yet, if one’s vision of the Truth is not genuine, and the images remain but faint, merely chasing words and following phrases, or being led by others’ instructions, one will never attain liberation, even in a donkey’s lifetime.
It would be better to stifle worldly attachments, straighten one’s backbone, summon some brilliance, and investigate until the teaching is thoroughly penetrated from every angle.

When a hundred matters are finished, a thousand are settled. Under waterside trees and forest groves, one nurtures the sacred embryo; thus, one does not receive the offerings of humans and devas in vain.
Even so, beneath the Gate of Reclining on Clouds, there is an iron threshold; you must exert yourself with even greater vigor.

One must leap over it to attain it; in the mere interval of deliberation, one falls into a pit or a ditch. [The Master] seized the whisk and pulled down the meditation seat, then descended from the seat.
Zen Master Guang of Jiufeng went to visit Master Zhi of Yungai and asked, "What was the underlying meaning when Xinghua struck Kebin?
Master Zhi stepped down from the meditation seat, extended both hands, and stuck out his tongue. The Master struck once with his sitting cloth. Master Zhi said:
"This is turned by the power of the wind. He then asked Chan Master Shishuang Lin, "What is your intention?
Lin struck his meditation mat once. Lin said, "A fine meditation mat, but you do not know where it lands.
He then asked Zhenjing, "What is your intention? Zhenjing also struck his meditation mat once. Zhenjing said, "He strikes you."
"Another blow! At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment. Later, he resided at Jiufeng, where he was revered by the assembly of monks.
Chan Master Huangbo Quan ascended the hall and, striking the meditation seat with his whisk, said: "With one blow, one pierces through the inexhaustible treasury;
all manner of precious treasures are found within our own house. Taking them up, we universally relieve the poor and destitute, so that they need not wander the path of lamentation."
As he walked along, he shouted, "Who is the one in poverty?
At that time, the Chan Master Juefan Qingliang Huihong had been lecturing on the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* at Xuancheng Monastery for over four years.
Qiye visited Zhenjing at Guizong. When Jing moved to Shimen, the Master followed him there.

Jing was concerned about the Master’s tendency toward intellectual profundity and would frequently cite Xuefeng’s remark that “Xuansha had not yet reached the ultimate” to provoke his doubts. Whenever the Master offered a response, Jing would say, “Are you speaking of principles again?
One day, he suddenly cast off all his lingering doubts and composed a verse, saying: “Lingyun saw it once and never saw it again.”
"Red and white branches, branch after branch, bear no flowers. How vexing are those guests on fishing boats; they come instead to wade for fish and shrimp on level ground.
Pure Vision (Jōken) expressed his joy at this. Later, while residing at Seiryō-ji, he addressed the assembly, citing the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra*:
"The Tathāgata said to Ānanda: 'You should smell this sandalwood in the incense burner. If even a single *zhu* of this incense is burned, the entire room [is filled with its fragrance]...'"
Within a distance of forty li from the city of Rājagṛha, everyone simultaneously smelled the fragrance. What do you think?
Does this fragrance arise from the sandalwood tree, does it arise from your nose, or does it arise from space?

Ānanda, if this fragrance were to arise from your nose, then as something produced by the nose, it would have to issue forth from the nose. Since the nose is not sandalwood, how could there be sandalwood within the nose?
Regarding "odor": you claim that one perceives odor through the nose. Yet, if the odor issues from within the nose, it would be illogical to say that one "perceives" it.
If it were produced in empty space, then since the nature of space is eternal and constant, the odor should also be eternally present; why then rely on burning this dried wood in a brazier?

If it were produced in the wood, then as the substance of the wood is burned to become smoke, if the nose were to perceive it, it ought to be enveloped by the scent of that smoke. Now, as the smoke rises—
[The Master said: "Empty. It has not yet reached a great distance; within forty *li*, how is it that [the fragrance] is already heard?

Therefore, one should know that the nose and the act of smelling have no location, and that both the act of smelling and the fragrance are illusory in their respective places. Fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
The Master said: "Entering this contemplation of the nose, one personally realizes non-arising (*anutpāda*). Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "As for the hearer..."
How does one hear? Is it heard by the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*), or is it heard by the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*), or is it heard by the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*)?

Guling only knew how to rub backs; when did the Bodhisattva ever clarify his mind? When one wishes to realize the Stage of Freedom from Defilement, one must have sweat break out over the entire body.

Chan Master Fanyi Xuechao of Wanyan ascended the hall and, holding up his staff, said:

The monster hides its tracks. Sometimes mind and phenomena are both forgotten, and the essence of illumination stands alone. Sometimes illumination and function occur simultaneously, with host and guest mutually employed.
[He] draws a line with his staff and says: "Under the Gate of Yanfu, nothing at all is employed. But tell me, what does Yanfu usually use?
[He] plants the staff on the ground, gives a shout, and descends from the seat. ○ He ascends the hall. Looking upward, he does not...

Chan Master Xuefeng Huikong ascended the hall and said: "Those who are sharp and quick act as soon as they are pointed out; those who are dull and stupid cannot be moved by being pushed or pulled.
When they act, everyone rejoices; when they do not move, everyone conceives aversion. As for me, the mountain monk now—"
"Transform this dull ignorance into swift intelligence! He snapped his fingers once and said: "That which previously could not be pushed out is now out;
that which previously would not dwell in the monastery now dwells there; that which previously loathed being a Buddha now acts as one;
that which previously loathed preaching the Dharma now preaches it. Setting aside for a moment whether it goes out or stays, or whether it dwells or does not dwell—dare I ask?"
He asked the assembly, "What kind of Buddha is it that you are becoming? Is it the Buddha Akṣobhya (Empty-King Buddha)? Is it the Buddha Dīpaṃkara (Lamp-Light Buddha)?
Is it the Buddha Śākyamuni? Or is it the Buddha Maitreya? Furthermore, what kind of Dharma is it that you are expounding? Is it the Fundamental Dharma? Or is it the Dharma of Non-Arising?"
"Is it a worldly dharma? Is it a world-transcending dharma? Is there anyone among you who has attained realization?
If there is, then this mountain monk’s work in appearing in the world is finished. If not, do not misrepresent me when you meet others. He let out a shout and descended from his seat.
Chan Master Ximing of Zhengfa opens the session at the end of the retreat and ascends the hall: "Leaves fall in profusion; heaven and earth announce early autumn.

This is clearly the meaning of the Western Patriarch—what need is there for further seeking? If you can understand it thus, you will finally believe that the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is fundamentally level and even.
The Great Gate of Liberation has never had a lock or key. It encompasses the universe and fills the void."

Emptiness is immeasurable and cannot be fathomed by the intellect. If one has not yet clarified this principle and does not penetrate its source, then even if one cultivates merit for a hundred kalpas and refines one’s practice through a thousand lifetimes, it will be nothing but self-exhaustion and suffering, with no connection whatsoever to the truth.

If, however, one deeply clarifies this principle and thoroughly penetrates its source, one will realize that whether moving or still, acting or responding, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—every single instance accords with the Way.
In every thought-moment, one should turn toward the source. Did not the Patriarch say: "Deluded beings are in a state of stillness and turmoil;
when awakened, there is neither good nor evil. Let gain and loss, right and wrong, be cast off all at once. If this is so, who is deluded and who is awakened? Who is right and who is wrong?

It is simply that you people alone give rise to divergent views, observing the great as small, clinging to existence and clinging to non-existence, and though the numinous spirit shines within yourselves, you are unwilling to accept it. Your mind—
The moon is solitary and full, yet it naturally gives rise to contradiction. How is this different from abandoning one’s father at home or forgetting a pearl within one’s robes?
This causes thorns to form a forest upon the path to Bodhi, and misty clouds to obscure the sun in the sky of liberation.

Today, by good fortune, I, this mountain monk, encounter the *pravāraṇā* ceremony of the assembly of monks; the patron has returned to the mountain, and these virtuous superiors have come specifically to visit me. I must not remain silent.
Silence. This is a tangle of complications suited to the times, a slight opening of expedient means. You must all fix your eyes and observe each with careful attention.
If you further hesitate or engage in discursive thought, there will be ten thousand miles of white clouds. Then he took up his staff and said:
"If you can understand this, the assembly on Vulture Peak is solemnly present before your eyes. If it is not yet so, wait for me tomorrow morning."

After seeing Qingyuan, Master Zu’an lived among the thatched huts on Mount Heng for over thirty years without anyone knowing of him.
One day, moved by inspiration, he composed a verse, saying: "A small cauldron boils vegetables while rice steams above; the vegetables are cooked and the rice is fragrant, yet no one is present."
He was hungry. Having once healed the wound of hunger, he had nothing further to do. The next morning, he drew a cat exactly as before.
From this, monastics braved the thickets to seek him out. Lord Zhang Wujin earnestly urged him to open a dharma center, but he did not comply; in the end, he passed away on this very mountain.
Master Jing Shengyin ascended the hall and said: "Though you have traveled throughout the world, you should know that you have never moved a single step.

Though you have exhausted every gate and courtyard, there is no house where smoke is lacking from the hearth. Therefore, with staff over shoulder and sturdy sandals on your feet, you set out on your journey as the inspiration moves you."

Drawing the hook and letting the line sink, he dwells according to his natural disposition. He does not seek out fine lands in his native village; wherever the conditions are ripe, there he makes his home.
Today he takes up whatever comes to hand; how often has he deliberated on this in the past? It is nothing other than the same old pattern.
Each time it is raised, it is new again. For those with clear vision, they turn back at a mere glance; for those who have not yet awakened, recognize this very face.
But tell me, what is this original face? After a long silence, he said: "The flowers bloom on the front stage, yet they are seen from the back stage."
The sound of the bell from the upper realm is heard in the lower realm. [The Master] strikes the meditation seat with his whisk and descends. Ascending the hall, he raised an example:

'Among my great disciples and the fourfold assembly of devas and humans, they have never shown reverence or admiration as I constantly preached the Dharma. I shall now enter...'"
Because he was sitting in retreat during the ninety-day summer rains retreat in the Sandalwood Mortar Room, someone suddenly came to inquire about the Dharma.
[The Master] said, "Wait; I shall explain it for you: all dharmas are unborn; all dharmas are unceasing. Having spoken these words, he closed his room and sat in silence.
The Master summoned the assembly and said, "When Śākyamuni first attained the Way of the Buddha, for the most part, he had no choice in the matter. Just as..."
Having established this community, he immediately gave rise to a mind of weariness and retreat.

Had Shengyin seen him at that time, he would have driven a nail through the door of the room, ensuring he had no way out for the rest of his life, so as to prevent future generations from following his example.
Have you not heard it said: "If one does not transmit the Dharma to save sentient beings, one cannot be called a repayer of gratitude"? (He strikes the whisk.)
The Master (styled Xiyu) descended from his seat.

Master Mici of Dongchan ascended the hall and said: "Opening the mouth is not Chan; closing the mouth is not the Way.

If you are repenting another's sins, that person's sin is not yours; how could you possibly repent for it? The Master was unable to answer, so he subsequently changed his course.

Li was speechless. The Master showed him a verse, saying: "The domestic thief vexes the person—what can be done? Even the thousand sages turn their faculties back for his sake.
Pervading the world and pervading space, yet leaving no trace; Without dependence and without abiding, he is beyond all nets and snares. Thief! Thief! A fierce general, a hero!"
The soldiers could not capture him; they suspected he had killed the old Chan masters of the world. He made the ancient Maitreya in the bustling marketplace laugh to tears.
Enough, enough! There is no need to seek with the mind outward. In a fleeting glance, the thief’s own body is revealed;

caught with the stolen goods, he has no peer in the world. This peerless one is truly worthy of emulation; from now on, he will no longer boast of his cleverness, but will settle peacefully into his home and enjoy his work.
At that time, the myriad phenomena and all things under heaven clapped their hands in unison.

This is the tangle of the distinction between the holy and the ordinary, and between delusion and awakening. Simply by guarding right mindfulness, one accords with the Way;

by turning the emotions away from external objects, karma cannot bind one. Once the maladies of dullness and agitation are completely eliminated, one naturally forgets the intent of question and answer.
Moreover, since the Buddha who dwells in the position of succession is presently within the light of Prajñā, what matter could not be manifested therein? This serves as the preface.

Master Fānghuì of Fǎngqí, belonging to the Nányuè Línjì lineage, was naturally alert and quick-witted from his youth. Upon reaching the age of twenty, he no longer occupied himself with brush and inkstone, instead being registered as a tax collector for trade duties.

Finding himself unfit for his position as the head monk, he fled by night and entered Jiufeng in Ruizhou. There, he felt as if he were visiting an old haunt; filled with affection, he could not bear to leave, and so he shaved his head.
Whenever he read the sutras, his mind merged with them and his spirit attained realization. He was able to humble himself to seek instruction from veteran masters.

Chan Master Baizhang Shouduan studied calligraphy in his youth; at the age of twenty, he received the tonsure under Chan Master Yuru of Chaling.
He subsequently went to visit Yangqi. One day, Yangqi suddenly asked, "Who is your preceptor? The Master replied, "Venerable Yuru of Chaling."
Zhiji said, "I have heard that when Yi fell from the bridge, he attained realization and composed a verse that is truly extraordinary. Can you remember it? The Master recited it:
"I possess a bright pearl, Long locked away by the dust of worldly toil. Today the dust is cleared and the light shines forth, Shining through ten thousand peaks of mountains and rivers.
Zhiji smiled and rose to his feet. The Master was struck with astonishment and could not sleep all night. At dawn, he went to consult him.
He questioned him about it. It happened to be the end of the year. Xuefeng said, "Did you see those who were performing the exorcism ritual yesterday?

He replied, "I saw them. Xuefeng said, "In this matter, you are one step behind them. The Master was again startled and asked, "What is the meaning of this? Xuefeng said, "They love to be laughed at."

"You fear the laughter of others. The Master attained great enlightenment and served as his attendant for a long time. Ascending the hall, he said: "By naturally avoiding what offends the palate, all illnesses are diminished;
yet having many passions cannot avoid occasional toil. Living in poverty, every movement results in either opposition or compliance;
thus one attains the singular height of pure leisure. Although this is so, do not say that a 'mindless' state is the Way; even 'mindlessness' still leaves one at a further barrier."
Addressing the assembly, he said: "The Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm, universally manifesting before all living beings.

Responding to conditions and meeting with stimuli, its grace is never lacking; yet it constantly dwells upon this very seat of Bodhi. How, O Great Assembly, do you explain the principle of responding to conditions and meeting with stimuli?
In the mere snap of a finger, the capacities and karmic roots of all sentient beings throughout the entire world—"
At that time, one should be fully sufficient, yet never move even a single hair’s breadth; this is what is called responding to conditions as they arise while constantly remaining in this seat.
It is just like this mountain monk here: having accepted the invitation for the *Lotus Sūtra* assembly, I shall soon take my leave of the great assembly and depart.
Once I have finished opening the hall within Susong County, I will then return to the monastery. Tell me, have I left this seat or not?

There is no seat. If you say they are separate, that is merely the proliferation of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*). If you say they are not separate, how do you perceive this matter of non-separation?

Is it that the realms of boundless lands have neither self nor other separated by even a hair’s breadth, and that the ten ages of past and present, from beginning to end, are never separate from the present moment? Or is it that all things are without mind, and at once—?
"Vipama! If it is thus, you are truly striking the moon with a falling staff. Reaching this point, you must awaken;

This is the path that does not blind the eyes of the student. If you merely awaken to the head of a dry radish, not only will you blind the eyes of the student, but moreover, as soon as you move, you will first strike your own hand upon the edge of the blade.

Meeting people at a crossroads, yet shaking hands atop a thousand peaks;
meeting atop a thousand peaks, yet shaking hands at a crossroads. Therefore, I, this mountain monk, have often composed a verse:
"I do not dwell where others dwell; I do not walk where others walk. It is not that it is difficult for people to gather together;

rather, it is that the monastic and the lay must be clearly distinguished. This mountain monk, at the moment of departure, has untied the mouth of his sack and scattered its contents all at once before you.
Those with eyes, do not mistake this for something else. Take care! *Kai* (Opening).
The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "In the past, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, the World-Honored One held up a flower, and Kāśyapa smiled.

"What is it like when the bow is broken and the arrows are spent? The Master said: "A scene of utter embarrassment. Ascending the hall, he said: "The Supreme Way is not difficult."
I only regret that you discriminate between the red peach blossoms and the white plum blossoms. Who says that their harmonious blending is but a single color? The warbler speaks, the oriole sings;
who says that their "guan-guan" call is but a single sound? It does not penetrate. You vainly take the mountains and rivers to be the pivot of the Patriarch’s gate, mistaking them for your own eyes.
[He ascended the hall. Holding his staff horizontally, he said: "First illumination, then function. Raising it upright, he said: "First function."
Later, as he was turning back to look, he said, "Illumination and function are simultaneous. He struck the ground once and said, "Illumination and function are not simultaneous.
You people have all been swallowed up in one gulp by my staff; it is simply that you yourselves do not realize it.
If you can utter a phrase of turning back here, you will avoid this bout of stifling frustration. If you cannot yet do so, I, the old monk, have lost today."
[The Master] said, "Li. Inside the Master's quarters were six wooden dice, each face of which was inscribed with the character "one" (幺).
As soon as a monk entered, the Master threw them and asked, "Do you understand? Before the monk could even consider it, the Master struck him out. [Verse]: A monk asked, "What is the Buddha?"
The Master said: "While eating rice, one bites upon grit. [Added from the Supplementary Collection.
Chan Master Foyan Qingyuan of Longmen was reading the *Lotus Sūtra* when he reached the passage:

"This Dharma cannot be understood through thought or discrimination. He took this up to question a lecturer on the sūtra, but the lecturer was unable to answer. The Master sighed, saying: "The study of doctrine..."
"Names and appearances are not the means by which one realizes the great matter of birth and death.

Thereupon, he rolled up his robes and traveled south to attend the Dharma seat of Chan Master Yan of Taiping in Shu Prefecture. While begging for alms in Luzhou, he happened to stumble and fall to the ground.
Amidst his distress, he heard two people cursing each other; one who was admonishing them said, "You are still suffering from affliction! At these words, the Master attained realization.

[The Master] paused. [Verse: Upon returning, whenever anyone asked him a question, Yan would simply say, "I am not as good as you; you will understand it well on your own," or he would say, "I do not know;
I am not as good as you. The Master grew increasingly suspicious and consequently sought a definitive resolution from the Head Seat Yuanli.
Lil took the Master’s ear with his hand and, circumambulating the brazier several times while walking and speaking, said, "You will understand this well enough on your own.

The Master said, "I hope for your instruction; why do you mock me in this way? Lil replied, "Only after you have attained enlightenment in the future will you understand the significance of my words today.
As Taiping was about to move to Haihui, the Master sighed deeply and said, "I..."

Carrying his alms bowl, he was returning home when he again visited a desolate monastery. "How can you hope to investigate and resolve your own matter? [the master] said, and thus composed a verse to bid him farewell.
He spent the summer retreat at Jiangshan, where he happened to meet Chan Master Lingyuan; their friendship grew increasingly deep.
During a relaxed conversation, the Master remarked, "Recently I have seen a venerable elder in the capital whose words and phrases seem to have a karmic affinity with me. Lingyuan replied:
Master Yan was a patriarch of the highest rank in the world. For what reason did he abandon [his post] to travel afar?

What is meant by "having a karmic affinity" is that such a teacher of intellectual understanding corresponds with the original aspiration of the Master. Following his instructions, the Master proceeded directly to Haihui.
Later, he was appointed to oversee the reception hall. Once, sitting alone on a cold night, he poked at the stove and saw a flame about the size of a bean; suddenly, he realized for himself.
Xī said, "Deeply stirring the embers, there is something here; the affairs of my entire life are just like this. He suddenly rose and examined the *Lamp Records* (Denglu) on his desk.
Upon reaching the account of Pòzuò Duò, he attained a sudden great enlightenment and composed a verse:

*Diao-diao the forest birds cry out;* *I pull on my robes and sit through the night.* *Stirring the embers, I awaken to my whole life;* *Exhausting the spirit, I return to the broken hearth.* *The matter is bright, yet people are themselves deluded;* *How could it be that the straight is not as good as the crooked?*
"Who can harmonize with this plainness? Thinking of it, I shall never forget. Few people pass through the gate.
Yuanwu then went to his quarters and tested him by citing the story of Qinglin’s "carrying earth," saying, "No one, past or present, has been able to get out of this. How do you understand it?"
The Master said, "What difficulty is there in that? Wuzhuo said, "As for what he said, 'The Iron Wheel-turning King’s decree throughout the realm'—what is the meaning of this?

The Master said, "I say it is like the proclamation of a general amnesty from within the palace of Śakra. Wuzhuo withdrew and told others, "It is a joy indeed that Elder Yuan now possesses a phrase that brings life to others.
[He] ascended the hall and said: "When a single leaf falls, spring comes to all under heaven. No [further words].
Seeking it along the way, the laughter kills a man. Below is heaven; above is earth. These words do not accord with the minds of the current age.
South becomes north; east becomes west. Movement becomes stillness; joy becomes sorrow. A snake’s head and a scorpion’s tail—one must test them.
A live sparrow in the mouth of a fierce tiger—what kind of talk is this? Return to the hall! [Verse] Ascending the hall: To speak a thousand times or ten thousand times is not as good as—
To see face-to-face is to see directly; even without words, it is naturally clear.

This is like the analogy of the prince’s precious sword, the analogy of the blind men feeling the elephant, the matter of beckoning across the river in Zen study, the matter of meeting at the Wangzhou Pavilion, the matter of being in a desolate place where no one is present, and the matter of being in deep mountains and rocky cliffs—all of these are seen through direct encounter and do not depend on verbal explanation. *Above* (the title of the preceding section).
In the Hall: Su Wu tended sheep; though humiliated, he did not bend. Li Ling gazed toward Han; so joyful was he that he forgot to return.

Whether in a foreign land or one’s own country, among the disciples of the Buddha, there were those whose two feet leaped across a pit, those who danced upon hearing the zither, those whose bodies were buried in dung and soil, and those who reviled the river god.
Are these habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)? Or are they sublime functions? To the utmost...

When Jingcha struck the ground with his staff, or when Shishuang held up his whisk and tapped the meditation bench; when Muzhou kept his door perpetually closed, and Luzu spent his entire life facing the wall—were these acts for the sake of others, or were they not?
One can know for certain that all ordinary people bury their own precious treasures and fail utterly as true men of spirit.
Why do you all not hoist the sails and set the rudder to cast off from the river and reach the other shore? Cease further nailing down stakes and rowing back and forth!
On the day you arrive home, having become a person of Caoxi, you are also a man of the house. Do you still see the affairs of the house?
The Master once inscribed these words on the wall of Yan-shou at Long-men: "The Buddha permitted that those who are ill should receive medical treatment;
there must be places for them to recover. Zen practitioners have several names: some call it 'Nirvana,' which refers to seeing the Dharma-body."

"Permanently abiding" means to realize that all phenomena are unborn. Some say it is "conserving one's practice," meaning to recognize that these adverse conditions all arise from the suffering inherent in conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*).
Others say it is "prolonging life," meaning to sustain the physical body with the life-force of wisdom. In truth, its purpose is to cause people to understand the nature of birth and death.
I have often seen those with little awareness who, upon falling slightly ill, immediately enter this hall; by not stubbornly resisting their condition, they derive great benefit.
When one has been ill for a long time, one longs for one's hometown; yet if one does not cultivate wholesome reflection, one cannot eliminate the root of suffering. As the former sages said:
"Illness is the excellent medicine for sentient beings; if one takes it well, there is none who will not be healed. [Verse] Prince Nala.
"The flesh returns to the mother; the bones return to the father. Only then does he manifest his true body and, exercising great spiritual power, preach the Dharma for his parents.
The Master said: "If the flesh has returned to the mother and the bones have returned to the father, what do you use as a body?

If a student can see into this point, they will clear away the five aggregates and swallow up the ten directions... [Added from another source] (The verse appears in the first volume of the *Lianzhu*).

Chan Master Kaifu Daoning was a man of the Way from his youth. While serving as the bath attendant at Chongguo Temple, one day as he was about to wash his feet, he happened to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Upon reaching the passage, "If this chapter can give rise to faith, and if one takes this as reality," he suddenly forgot all that he knew.
As he lowered his feet into the boiling water, his own realization was illuminated. He addressed the assembly, saying: "The autumn sun shines..."
Vast sky. The autumn river drenches the void in azure; one sighs for those outside the gate, searching everywhere for Maitreya.
Suddenly lifting one’s head along the path, one meets him yet does not recognize him. O Zen practitioners, since you have met him, why do you not recognize him?

Having cut away all the bamboo before the frost, he does not transform into a dragon upon reaching the stream. Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The true command of Mahākāśyapa was not yet free from..."

Rugged and steep. Shaoshi Mountain bestowed its compassion early on, yet his wind-bone frame was soon wounded. With satchel at waist and staff in hand, he betrayed his lifelong dedication to refining his conduct and extinguishing the mind.
To let each other down in this way—how can it compare to a spring rain clearing away the mist, leaving the mountain green? Three clouds, four clouds, drifting white.
The yellow oriole sings once, twice—how can the Great Compassionate One with a thousand eyes look upon it enough? Though Wang Wei was skilled in painting, he could not capture it;
even if one were to simply act thus, one would still be traversing the path. Yet, as for the phrase "not traversing the path," how do you speak of it?
A person comes from Bianzhou, yet receives no news of Dongjing. A monk asked: "What is the meaning of 'the phrase reaching the intent'?"
"Not yet. The Master said, "The auspicious grass has no root from the start; it is used as it is picked up by the hand. [The student] asked, "What is 'the meaning reaches but the phrase does not'?
The Master said, "Receive the meaning on the hook; do not fixate on the zero-point of the scale. [The student] asked, "What is 'both the meaning and the phrase reach'?
The Master said, "The Great Compassionate One does not extend his hand; his entire body is eyes. [The student] asked, "What is 'the meaning...'"?
The words reached neither of them. The Master said, "You head toward Xiangxiang; I head toward Taishan.
Chan Master Nantang Jing (later named Daoxing) of Daisui first studied under Chan Master En of Yong'an, where he gained insight into the story of Linji’s three blows of the staff.
Subsequently, he relied upon various renowned elders, but none satisfied him. Hearing that Wuzu’s pedagogical style was rigorous, he went to him.
Wishing to suppress him, he then went to visit the Patriarch (Nanquan). The Patriarch said, "This place of mine is not like other quarters.

Within my room, I do not require you to advance or retreat, point with your fingers, clench your fists, circle the meditation seat, perform the 'woman's bow,' lift up your sitting cloth, or employ a thousand other tricks.
I only want you to have a decisive, correct realization in a single word; that shall be your point of view. The Master—

He was at a loss. He withdrew and practiced for three years. One day, after the session in the inner quarters had concluded, the Patriarch said to him, "The words you have offered are already ninety percent correct;

try to explain them to me further. The Master then analyzed and presented his understanding. The Patriarch said, "You can indeed explain it well enough—ninety percent—but try to give me a definitive judgment on it.
The Master then passed judgment according to each question posed to him. The Patriarch said, "It is good, indeed it is good; however—"
"This is not something you have ever heard from an old monk before. After the meal, you may come to the site of the Patriarch’s stupa;

there, I shall examine each point with you one by one. When he arrived there, the Patriarch [Baizhang] spoke of "Mind is Buddha," "Neither mind nor Buddha," "Muzhou as a man carrying a wooden board," "Nanquan killing the cat," and "Zhaozhou’s 'The dog has no Buddha-nature' and 'The dog has Buddha-nature.'"

[The Master] spoke. He wove together [the various sayings], and whatever he was questioned about, there was no obstruction whatsoever. When they reached the story of "Zihu’s Dog," the Patriarch suddenly turned his face away and said, "That is not it.
The Master asked, "If that is not it, then what? The Patriarch said, "If this is not it, then everything preceding it is also not it.
The Master said, "I hope the Honored One will show compassion and instruct me. The Patriarch said, "Look at how he says, 'Zihu has one...'"
The dog: it takes the person’s head above, the person’s waist in the middle, and the person’s feet below. Those who enter the gate should observe this well.

As soon as the monk enters the gate, [the Master] says, "Look at the dog! If you could have offered a turning word at the point where [the Master] said "look at the dog," you would have left Zihu speechless and caused this old monk to seal his mouth;
that would have been the place where you attained realization. The next day, when entering the room for instruction, the Master silently began.
When he said this, the Patriarch laughed and said, "I do not say that you are not a man who has reached a definitive conclusion;
however, these words sound exactly like those spoken by my late teacher. The Master asked, "What person am I that I could be like Master Duan? The Patriarch replied, "It is not so.
Although I have inherited his lineage, I say his words were 'clumsy' because he used only the methods of Master Yuanlu to receive disciples."
It is so. For instance, when this old monk was with Master Yuanlu, we walked hand-in-hand with Baizhang, Huangbo, Nanquan, Zhaozhou, and their peers.
As soon as one sees that their words are clumsy, they are deemed unacceptable; yet you, Master, think otherwise, and so you have taken up your staff and crossed the river.
At that time, as the great waters were overflowing, he detained the Fourth Patriarch; his peers urged him to return, and only after another two years did the Patriarch finally grant his consent.

Once, while discussing the past and present, the Patriarch took the Master’s hand and said, "To understand what you say, it must be prompted by me; to understand what I say, it must be prompted by you.
From this day forward, the secret essentials of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and the key points of all quarters shall not escape you."
[He] mastered it. ○ Ascending the hall, after the questions and answers were finished, he said: "Since the time of the Patriarchs, people have misunderstood;
they take mere words and phrases to be the Way of Chan. They do not realize that the Way has no essence—it is because of an essence that it receives its name.
The Way has no name—it is because of a name that its designation is established. It was just like when the Venerable One here came out a moment ago; as soon as he did so—"
Returning to the assembly in this manner—now, does one possess the eye or not? If you say one possesses the eye, as soon as one comes forth in this way, where is that eye?
If you say one does not possess the eye, how could one simply depart in such a manner?
O worthy ones, if you can see this with clear and decisive insight, then you will know that when the Second Patriarch prostrated himself and stood in his place, he truly attained it.

The marrow. Only this much constitutes the life-root of the Buddhas of the three periods, the life-vein of the six generations of patriarchs, and the place where the old monks of the world establish their bodies and lives.
Nevertheless, you must arrive at it personally before you can attain it.
A monk asked, "I pray the Master will directly point out the Patriarchal Heart-Seal. The Master said, "Do you hear the sound of boiling water? The monk said, "I hear it. The Master said, "Just..."
[The monk] said, "I do not hear the cold. [The Master] asked, "Do you, Reverend, hear the heat? The Master said, "I do not hear it. [The monk] asked, "Why do you not hear it?
The Master shook his fan and said, "Because I have this. [The monk] asked, "What is mountain Chan?
The Master said, "In the courtyard, the tender bamboo sprouts its shoots; at the bottom of the stream, the withered pine grows long branches. [The monk] asked, "What is marketplace Chan?"
The Master said: "The bells and drums of the six wards resonate *dong dong*; this very place is a world spread with gold. He asked, "What is Chan in the village?
The Master said: "Thieves and bandits have vanished; silkworms and wheat are ripe; people sing and dance, rejoicing in peace.
An old master offered a statement, saying: "A single thatched toilet is erected at the crossroads, yet it is simply not permitted—"
A person defecates. The monk brought this up to consult the Master. The Master said, "You have already defecated; what more do you want me to make someone else defecate?
Having heard this, Xiu burned incense, gazed afar toward Dawsui, and bowed twice in gratitude.
After Chan Master Wutai emerged from the mountain passes, he traveled extensively among various monastic communities.

Upon arriving at the Fifth Patriarch’s monastery on the day he offered incense, the Patriarch presented him with the story of Zhaozhou washing the alms bowl to serve as his koan for investigation. When it was time for the private interview, the Patriarch brought up this same story and asked the Master, "Tell me, what did Zhaozhou say to that monk?
That monk attained enlightenment immediately. The Master replied, "'Go wash the alms bowl,' he said. The Patriarch remarked, "You..."
"You only know the matters of the road; you do not know the flavor of the road. The Master said, "Since you know the matters of the road, what flavor is there on the road?
The Patriarch said, "Do you not know? He asked again, "Have you ever traveled through Zhejiang? The Master said, "No.
The Patriarch said, "You have not yet attained awakening. From that time on, for five years, the Master was unable to respond. One day, the Patriarch ascended [the seat].
