The Master said to himself, "I have studied Chan for twenty years, yet I have made no entry."
At the head of the road, he again performed this practice, becoming utterly despondent and intending not to practice at all.
His friend Zongyuan scolded him, saying, "It is not that you cannot practice Chan while on the road. Go; I will go with you. The Master had no choice but to proceed.
On the road, he spoke weeping to Yuan, saying, "In my entire life of practicing Chan, I have found nothing at all that has been effective. Now..."
Furthermore, as you are traveling along the road in such haste, how can you achieve resonance with the Way? Yuanyou told him:

"You need only take that which you have studied in various quarters, that which you have awakened to, and that which Yuanwu and Miaoxi have explained for you—you must not concern yourself with any of it."
"Along the way, there may be matters that can be substituted; I shall substitute for you in all of them. There are only five things, however, for which I cannot substitute on your behalf;
these you must attend to yourself. The Master asked, "What are these five things? I wish to hear their essentials. Yuan said, "Clothing."
"Eating, defecating, urinating, and carrying a corpse along the road. At these words, the Master realized the meaning;
unconsciously, he began to dance with his hands and feet. Yuan said, "This time you may send a letter. You should proceed forward; I shall return first.
Yuan immediately returned to Mount Jing, while the Master did not return for half a year. As soon as Miaoxi saw him, he said joyfully, "Jianzhou!"
"Disciple, this time you must not do so. Ascending the hall, he said: "The mind of the Great Sage of the Land of Chu (India) was secretly transmitted from east to west.
What is this mind that was secretly transmitted? After a long silence, he said: "In the autumn of the eighth month, where is there heat?"
When Chan Master De Guang of Yuyang was serving under Dahui, who had taken charge of Yuyang Monastery, the finest talents from all quarters gathered there like scales of fish;
the Master was among them. Within Dahui’s room, Dahui questioned the Master: "To call it a 'bamboo whisk' is to encounter resistance; not to call it a 'bamboo whisk' is to turn one's back on it.
You may not utter a word, yet you may not remain silent. As the Master prepared to respond, Dahui struck him with his staff, and the Master attained sudden enlightenment.
He attained great enlightenment. Initially, he resided at Kuangxiao Temple on Mount Tiantai. A monk asked, "In the midst of vast dust and confusion, how does one discern the master?

The Master replied, "At the very tip of the spire atop Mount Jin. [Verse] While the Master was residing at Lingyin, Emperor Xiaozong of the Song dynasty summoned him for an audience and questioned him:
"When Śākyamuni Buddha entered the mountains, what did he accomplish during those six years? The Master replied, "I thought Your Majesty had forgotten. [Verse]
Xiaozong summoned the Master for an audience, where the Master recited the verse of Lingyun: "Right up until now, there has been no further doubt.
The Emperor asked, "Wherein lies his state of being without doubt? The Master replied, "Empty-handed, he leads a metal ox. (These two cases appear at the end of the sixth fascicle of the *Huìyuán*;
the verse is found in the tenth fascicle of the *Liánzhū jí* under the chapter of Fozhào.)
Chan Master Huazang Dun’an Yan ascended the hall and, picking up his staff, said: "If you recognize this, the task of a lifetime of study is finished.
When the ancients spoke thus, Huazang says it is not so: "If you recognize this, you must still buy straw sandals and travel on foot.
Why? "When you reach the river, the land of Wu ends; beyond the bank, the mountains of Yue abound."
Chan Master Wuyou Quan of Tiantong ascended the hall and said: "Studying the Buddha merely results in saying that 'the True does not stand'; practicing Chan often runs counter to the Way.
Forget the mind and forget the environment; quickly turn back. With no ground and no needle-point, take a step and return. The Buddha is not [it]."
The mind, too, is not it. To directly realize its essence is to transcend all dependence. "For ten thousand ages, the moon in the empty sky reflects in the green depths;
only after repeated scooping and stirring does one finally come to know it.
Chan Master Yiyuan of Yuquan had long relied upon Yuanwu and considered himself free from doubt. At the beginning of the Shaoxing era, he went forth to reside at Xinghua.

Auspicious clouds gathered, and the Dharma assembly was quite flourishing. When Dahui entered Min, he realized that the Master’s realization was not yet definitive; he sent a letter summoning him to come.

The Master delayed, so Dahui held a small session (xiaochan) and severely rebuked him, subsequently posting a public notice for the fourfold assembly. Having no choice, the Master broke the summer retreat to go and visit him.
Dahui interrogated him regarding his realization, and after a while said, "With such a view as yours, how dare you claim to be the successor of Old Yuanwu?"

"Is he a human being? Master Huairang withdrew from the monastery to attend to him personally. One day, while entering the room for instruction, Huairang asked, "I want someone who does not understand Chan to serve as National Teacher.
Huairang said, "I am fit to be the National Teacher. Huairang shouted him out.
Not long after, he said to him, "Xiangyan’s place of awakening was not at the point where the bamboo was struck; Jushi’s attainment was not upon his finger. Master [Huairang]...
Then, it was suddenly clarified.
Master Ben of Jianfu ascended the hall and said: "I would give thirty blows of the staff to one who bows high to Śākyamuni but does not pay homage to Maitreya.
Why? Because such a person only knows how to climb higher step by step, but does not know how to let go from the void. The neighbor to the east..."
Plow! If you pull the plow-handle for the house to the west, I shall give you thirty blows of the staff. Why? Because you only know how to let things drop from the void;
you do not know how to ascend higher step by step. When I, this mountain monk, speak thus, is there any fault in it?
Is there anyone among the assembly who can examine and discern this? If you can so discern it, we shall walk hand in hand beyond the southern flank of Mount Sumeru. If...
Unable to be scrutinized: an old crow in a cloth bag; though alive, it is as if dead.
Zen Master Xing of Lingyan ascended the hall and said: "He has been thoroughly exposed. To let him off by one move is like a patchwork monk’s straw sandals.
To manifest the form of an asura and perform a woman’s bow is the work of a wild fox spirit. To draw a circle is empty space."

A single step backward is the mere trickery of a child. Blocking the cheeks and striking with the palm, then brushing the sleeves and departing—this is precisely the state where karmic consciousness is vast and boundless, with no fundamental ground to rely upon.
Even if one were to suddenly cut it off all at once before the black bean had even sprouted, it would still be so.
No one yet has attained the capacity to partake of the staff of Lingyan. I dare ask the assembly: tell me, where does the essential point for guiding others lie?
Do you understand this thoroughly? Since the spring colors first appeared at Songshao, the thirty-six peaks have remained green to this day.
A monk asked, "What is the body that stands alone? The Master said, "A cat sleeping beneath a peony flower."
When Chan Master Zhizhe of Jiangshan first visited Miaoxi at Huiguan Peak, Miaoxi asked him one day, "Where are you from, Senior Monk?
The Master replied, "I am from Anzhou. Miaoxi said, "I have heard that people from Anzhou are skilled at wrestling;
is this true? The Master immediately assumed a wrestling stance. Miaoxi said, "People of Hunan eat fish; why then do you act like someone from Hubei?"
Someone had a fishbone stuck in his throat. The Master performed a somersault and left. He said with joy, "Who would have known that within cold ashes there was a single bean that burst?

One day, while Chancellor Chen Junqing, the Governor-General, was hosting a tea gathering at Mount Shàn, he raised the *kōan* regarding the phrase "having a word or not having a word, like a vine leaning against a tree" and ordered the monks from various mountains to provide critical commentaries.
All of them offered marvelous words to pay their respects, but the Master’s were the most [profound].
The Master later said: "Zhang Oil-man, Li Oil-man; they do not hit the whole body, but only the head. Chen was greatly pleased.
When Chan Master Shuan of Linyai ascended the hall, he said: "The face-gate is smashed through; heaven and earth are vastly different.
Having penetrated the secure barrier, white clouds stretch ten thousand miles. Even if one cuts off both ends, there is still another way to turn—three lives and sixty kalpas."
"Not even dreamed of," he said, and with a shout, he descended from his seat.
Master Guangxiao Yuan gave a formal discourse, citing the story of the woman emerging from samādhi, and said:

"From of old, beating the drum and playing the lute requires meeting two families who understand one another. When the jade pendants and phoenix bells have finished their song and dance, everything remains as it was before the gate."
The setting sun slants low. Chan Master Yin of Zuian in Lingyin ascends the hall. Five times five is twenty-five; he shatters the drum of empty space.
The great earth cannot admit a needle; throughout the ten directions there is not an inch of soil. What more need be said of spring’s growth and summer’s ripening? The sweet is sweet indeed.
As for "Suffering is suffering":

Master Yuan’an of Zhuyuan had long relied upon Dahui and shared his seat at Xichan Monastery. When Chancellor Zhang Gong Jun was the regional commander of San Shan, he welcomed him with several monasteries, but he did not accept.
He returned to his native village to tie up a thatched hut, naming it "The Garden of Myriad Wonders" (Zhongmiao Yuan), where veteran monks and practitioners gathered.
Now, regarding the request to open the Dharma: [The Master] addressed the assembly, saying: "If you investigate this matter, it is like having lost a key;
you simply keep searching and searching until, suddenly, you strike upon it—*Aha!*—and right here you open the lock.
You will then see your own treasury, where all provisions and enjoyments are fully present, needing nothing from elsewhere. What else could there be?"
[The Master] addressed the assembly, saying: "A person who presides over the Dharma must have a spirit that swallows the universe; he acts as a great Dharma King.
Even if Śākyamuni Buddha or Master Bodhidharma were to appear, I would still command them to join their palms and stand behind me."
To have one's hair stand on end at this moment is still not considered extraordinary. He uttered a *chuyǔ* (a hanging word):
"This little bit is just like running into a murderer; if you do not kill him, he will kill you."
Chan Master Jingjunimi Miaodao was the daughter of Huang Shangshu, a high official of Yanping. On the day she ascended the hall, she said:

"Let the formal questioning cease for a moment. Even if one possessed the eloquence that overturns the ocean and the spiritual mechanism that topples the mountains, it is still of no avail before the gate of the patch-robed monks."
Not a single bit of it is necessary. Furthermore, before the Buddha appeared in the world, there was nothing at all.

Since my ancestor came from the West, many establishments have been founded; the monasteries stand in rows like stars, branching out into various lineages down to this day, continuing through successive generations.
Thus, I, this mountain monk, am compelled to stir up waves where there is no wind before this great assembly of humans and devas, and turn toward the secondary gate of meaning.

A message that penetrates all: it encompasses both speech and silence beyond exhaustion, pervading the vast expanse of the universe. Where words and explanations fail to reach, it is omnipresent throughout the realms of sand.
One’s entire being is eyes; facing the situation directly, it rolls like lightning and rushes like shooting stars—how can one ever grasp it?
Sometimes a single shout possesses the full authority of both life and death; sometimes a single shout leaves even Buddhas and Patriarchs unable to discern it;

sometimes a single shout leaves one vulnerable from all eight directions; and sometimes a single shout leaves one unable to save oneself. Tell me, which shout is the one that possesses the full authority of life and death?
Which shout is the one that Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot discern? Which shout is the one where one is attacked from all eight directions? And which shout is the one where one cannot save oneself?
"Hai! This will not suffice for self-deliverance. If you can realize it here, you will be worthy of repaying the unrepayable debt of gratitude.
If this is not yet so, I, this mountain monk, shall speak a dream while dreaming. Raising his whisk, he said: 'Do you see it? If you see it...'"
Obstructed by the thorn of seeing, he struck the meditation seat and asked, "Do you hear it? If you hear it, you are deluded by the sensory object of sound.
Even if you were to transcend both seeing and hearing, that would still be the minor fruit of the Two Vehicles. Take a step further: cover form while riding upon sound;

let go completely and gather back completely; let host and guest interchange. Therefore it is said: 'If you wish to know the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should observe the conditions of time and season.'"
[The Master] said, "I venture to ask all of you: what season is it right now? The vast breeze of benevolence supports the sagely transformation;
the harmonious and joyful qi assists in the peace and prosperity. He threw down his whisk and descended from the seat. A nun asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said:
"Not Buddha. [The monk] asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "The old trinkets at the bottom of the bone.
Nun Wuzhuo of Zishou was the granddaughter of Chancellor Su Gong, the Chan Master Miaozong.

At about thirty years of age, she grew weary of the world’s transient flow, cast off her worldly adornments, and consulted various elders until she had entered into right faith. She then spent the summer retreat there.
At Jingshan, Dahuì ascended the hall and recounted the story of Yàoshān’s initial visit to Shítóu and his subsequent encounter with Mázū.
Upon hearing this, the Master attained a sudden and thorough realization. After Dahuì descended from the seat, the Layman Fēng Gǔjí, known as Bùdòng, followed him to the abbot’s quarters and said:
"I have understood the kōan you just cited, O Monk. Huì said, "How about you, Layman?
He replied, "'It is not so'—this will not do. *Suru svāhā*. 'It is not not so'—this will not do. *Śiri svāhā*."
"It cannot be either 'thus' or 'not thus. *Suru siri svāhā.*" Huiju presented this to his teacher.
The teacher said, "I once saw Guo Xiang's commentary on the *Zhuangzi*. Those who understand it say that it is actually the *Zhuangzi* that is commenting on Guo Xiang.
Seeing that these words were extraordinary, Huiju further brought up the dialogue regarding the "Rock-Sitting Woman" to question him. The teacher replied with a verse: *A single-leafed skiff.*
Vast and boundless. Paddling oars and dancing rudders, they depart from the notes of *gong* and *shang*. Clouds, mountains, sea, and moon are all cast aside;
thus one wins the long dream of Zhuang Zhou’s butterfly. Huixiu departed. Feng Gong doubted that his realization was not rooted in truth.
Later, when Huixiu passed through Wuxi, Feng invited him onto his boat and asked: "The old woman gave birth to seven sons; six did not meet with a true connoisseur. What about this one alone?"
"It is not acceptable," he said, and immediately threw it into the water. Master Dahui asked, "The Master of the Way understands this principle;
how do you understand it? The Master replied, "All that has been offered above is entirely the truth. Lord Feng was greatly astonished. Next, during Huì’s turn to hang the plaque:
The Master entered the room. Huì asked, "An ancient did not leave his quarters; why then did he go to the manor to eat oil-cakes?
The Master said, "If you, Reverend, let Miao-zong pass, then Miao-zong will dare to deliver a message.
Huì said, "I let you pass; try and say it. The Master said, "Miao-zong also lets you, Reverend, pass. Huì said, "What can be done about this?"
"What is this oil-cake? The Master gave a shout and went out. Thereupon, his reputation spread in all directions.

In the first year of the Longxing era, Zhang Gong Xiaoxiang, a Palace Attendant, came to govern this prefecture and invited Zishou to open the Dharma. Upon entering the monastery, he ascended the hall for the formal address.
When the Dharma-vehicle is proclaimed once, the Three Pitakas cease their explanatory power; when the Patriarch’s command is put into practice, the ten directions are cut off at once.

Upon hearing this, those of the Two Vehicles flee in terror, and even those on the Ten Stages remain doubtful upon reaching this point. If one belongs to the elite stream, they understand before a word is spoken.

Even if one were to employ the skillful means of shifting stars and changing constellations, or apply the mechanisms of seizing the banner and capturing the drum, these would still be but empty fists—how could there be anything else?
The ultimate meaning—the path leading upward—is not transmitted by the thousand sages; students exhaust their bodies like monkeys grasping at reflections.
At Vulture Peak, the entrustment was made in accordance with the timing of the occasion, proclaiming the Three Vehicles according to the various capacities of beings.

Beginning at the Deer Park, the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths was turned, delivering hundreds of thousands of millions of beings. Today, this mountain monk, for this world and all other realms, [is] the Buddha...
Your ancestors—the mountains, rivers, the great earth, the grasses, trees, and forests, as well as the fourfold assembly present here—each turn the Great Dharma Wheel.

Their light intermingles and interlaces like a net of precious threads. If even a single blade of grass or a single tree did not turn the Dharma Wheel, it could not be called turning the Great Dharma Wheel.
Therefore it is said: "Upon the tip of a single hair, one manifests a jeweled kingdom; sitting within a mote of dust..."
He turns the Great Dharma Wheel. Seizing the opportune moment, within that interval he performs immeasurable and boundless, vast Buddha-works throughout the entire dharma-realm.
One becomes many; the many become one. Within the small he manifests the large;

within the large he manifests the small. Without moving a step, he wanders through Maitreya’s pavilion; without turning back his hearing, he enters Avalokiteśvara’s Universal Gate. Sentient and insentient beings—his nature...
The marks are equal; this is neither the wondrous function of supernatural powers nor the natural state of things.

To be bold and clear about this, the imperial grace and the Buddha’s grace are both repaid at once. But tell me, what is the phrase for "repaying the grace"? The heavens are high and the myriad forms are upright;
the ocean is vast and the hundred rivers flow with the tide. Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The Old Man with the Yellow Face has preached sideways and preached vertically."

Whether speaking with expedient means or speaking of the ultimate truth; whether teaching through the Dharma or through parables; whether erecting the banner of the Dharma or establishing the fundamental tenets—to serve as a model for future generations—why then do you say:
"From the Deer Park at the beginning, to the Vārāṇasī River at the end; within these two intervals"?
"I have never uttered a single word. To examine this from the outset, it is much like clutching stolen goods while crying out for innocence.
The mountain monk, being preoccupied with many affairs today, shall let this matter pass for now. He then descended from his seat.

In the autumn of the Ding-si year, the Vice Minister Zhang Jiucheng, the Layman Wugou, saw that National Teacher Dahui was presiding over Mount Jing, and scholars looked up to him as they do at the stars and constellations.
Upon reading his *Essentials of Speech*, Zhang sighed and said, "I now know there is someone in the Chan school who upholds the lineage.

He took this to tell Master Shang (that is, Chan Master Weishang), regretting that he had not yet met him in person. Later, when Zhang served as the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites, he happened to meet Senior Councillor Liu Gong.

He invited Master Hui to preach the Dharma in India. The Duke went there three times but did not meet him. When Hui finally returned his visit, the Duke received him with nothing more than formal greetings of weather and well-being;

Hui, however, silently took note of this. Subsequently, having completed his service at the ancestral shrine, he returned to his home village and arrived at Mount Jing, where he discussed the principle of "investigating things" (gewu) with Official Feng and other gentlemen.
Hui said, "Your Honor knows only 'investigating things,' but you do not yet know 'the transformation of things' (wuge). The Duke—
He was at a loss. Huì laughed heartily. The official said, "Can you provide an explanation? Huì replied, "Have you not seen it recorded in a minor novel?
During the Tang dynasty, there was a man who conspired with An Lushan to rebel. This man had previously served as the Governor of Langzhou, and his portrait was among those on display there."
When Emperor Minghuang visited Shu and saw it, he grew angry and ordered an attendant official to strike the head of the statue with a sword.
At that time, the Governor of Lang was residing in Shaanxi; suddenly, the head fell to the ground. The Master (Zhaozhou) heard of this and immediately grasped its profound meaning.

He inscribed on the wall of the "Immovable Hall": "Zishao [subdues] objects; Miaoxi [attains] the subduing of objects. If you wish to know the 'One Thread,' two fives make ten. Huisi granted him his approval, and later he served as governor.

In Shaoyang, while observing mourning for his father, he passed through Mount Jing and provided a meal for the monastic community. The person holding the reins of government (the Prime Minister) intended to involve Huì in discussions on state affairs;
consequently, Huì was exiled to Hengyang. After the public official had completed his period of mourning at home, he was relocated to Nan’an in the spring of the Bingzi year.

Having received imperial favor, he returned north. While passing through Xigan on his way, Huì happened to arrive there; they traveled together by boat and engaged in an intense discussion on the essentials of the school, never mentioning past events.
In the autumn of the *dingchou* year, he requested leave from his post and took a detour to visit Huì at Yuyang Monastery. The following year...

Huìdé attained the essential meaning [of the teachings] and subsequently took charge of Mount Jingshan. When the Duke visited him at Qingshanyuan, he said, "In my dreams, I invariably recite the *Yǔ* and the *Alì*;

what do you think of this? Huìdé cited the *Yuánjué jīng*, saying, "Because of stillness and silence, the minds of all Tathāgatas throughout the worlds of the ten directions appear therein, like images in a mirror.
The Duke remarked, "Were it not for the Great Teacher, one would never hear such a discourse."
The lay practitioner Li Bing, a Minister of State, whose courtesy name was Hanlao, had long been devoted to the Way of the Patriarchs.

When he heard that Dahui categorized "silent illumination" as heterodox Chan, he felt a mixture of doubt and indignation. However, upon seeing Dahui address the assembly and cite Zhaozhou’s public case regarding the cypress tree in the courtyard, saying:
"The cypress tree in the courtyard—today I raise it once more; break through Zhaozhou’s barrier, for you have gone to great lengths seeking words," [Li Bing’s doubts were resolved].
[The Master] spoke. "I venture to ask the great assembly: since you have already broken through Zhaozhou’s barrier, why do you instead go out of your way to seek words?

After a long silence, he said: "At first I only thought of the length of the thatch; it was only after burning it that I realized the ground was uneven. The Master (Gong) attained realization and said to Huì:
"Had it not been for the Master’s later words, I would have nearly missed it. Later, he sent a letter to inquire for a definitive resolution, saying: "Recently, I..."

In the counting-chip chamber, I was inspired by your exhortation to overcome my dullness and obscurity, and suddenly attained a realization. I pray that you consider how my faculties and consciousness have been dark and obtuse;

all the learning and understanding of my life have fallen into the realm of emotional views. My every grasping and rejecting was like walking through thorny brambles in tattered rags—only to become further entangled.

Now, with a single laugh, my doubts are instantly dispelled; my joy and gratitude are beyond measure. This could not have happened were it not for the Great Master’s compassionate and patient guidance.
Maitreya, how is it that I have come to this? Since arriving in the city, I have dressed, eaten, embraced my children, and doted on my grandchildren;
in every respect, I remain as I was before. Having no feelings of attachment or constraint, nor do I harbor thoughts of anything extraordinary.

Furthermore, my long-standing habitual obstacles have somewhat diminished, and I dare not forget the words of instruction you gave me at our parting. I reflect deeply that I have only just begun to enter the gate.
Yet, the Great Dharma has not yet been fully clarified; in responding to sentient beings and engaging with affairs, I have not yet attained unimpeded mastery.

I hope you will provide further instruction so that I may reach my ultimate destination and, by all means, avoid bringing blemish upon the assembly of the Dharma. Furthermore, in a letter, he wrote: "I have recently received your compassionate reply and have thoroughly understood its profound purport.
I have personally verified this in three ways: first, amidst circumstances—whether favorable or adverse—I respond spontaneously according to conditions without obstruction."
1. Retain it within your breast. 2. If your two-fold habitual tendencies are thick and heavy, they will naturally become light and subtle without the need for deliberate expulsion.
3. Regarding the ancient *gong'an* which you previously found bewildered by, there will be times when you suddenly see through them; this is not something you are unaware of.

My previous remark that the Great Dharma was not yet clear was intended to prevent you from being satisfied with a mere fragment; you should expand and fulfill it—how could you seek a superior understanding elsewhere? Jing.
It is indeed logical that the superior stream of manifestation is not non-existent; how could I dare not engrave this in my heart?
When the lay practitioner Liu Yanxiu, a precious student, was appointed as the Governor of Yongjia, he went to seek the Way from Chan Master Dahui. Dahui said:
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature? Zhaozhou said, "No. Simply look at it like this.
Later, the Master [Dongshan Liangjie] attained enlightenment regarding the cypress tree, composing a verse that says: "Zhaozhou’s cypress tree is truly reckless."
To seek it upon the objective realm is indeed most difficult. At every place, green willows are fit to tether the horse; at every household, beneath the gates, one penetrates Chang’an.
Layman Wu Weiming, Inspector of Justice, long studied under Chan Master Zhenxie Liao and attained the samādhi of self-enjoyment.
After reaching this ultimate realization, he visited Dahuì at the Yangyu Hermitage. He entered the room with the assembly;

when Dahuì brought up the koan of the dog having no Buddha-nature to question him, the Master was about to respond when Dahuì struck him with his bamboo staff. The Master had no reply and remained there to seek instruction.
One day, Dahuì said to him: "There is no need to display your cleverness; you must simply 'snap' and 'break through'. Only then—

The enemy had attained life and death; if one merely displays mere cleverness, what end can there be? He then took his leave and, while traveling along the road at Yanping, suddenly attained awakening.
The layman Huang Yanjie of Mōshi was suddenly liberated from his state of doubt upon hearing Dahuì’s single shout; Dahuì then bestowed his robe upon him.
Lady Jishi Miaozhen of the Qin State cast aside worldly distractions and practiced conditioned dharmas, having been sent by Dahuì.
The Chan master Qian sent a message to his son, Duke Wei. Duke Wei retained Qian and sought to guide him through the ancestral Way.
One day, Zhen asked Qian, "How does the Abbot of Jingshan usually instruct people?
Qian replied, "The Abbot only teaches people to contemplate the 'dog has no Buddha-nature' kōan and the 'bamboo stick' kōan; one must simply not utter a word and must not engage in thought."
[The Master said: "You must not seek the meeting at the place where it was raised; you must not take responsibility at the place where the mouth opened.

'Does a dog have Buddha-nature? It has not. He simply taught people to look in this way. Zhen then came to believe it with deep sincerity. Thereupon, he sat in meditation through the night, diligently investigating the previous dialogue.
Suddenly, everything became transparent and unobstructed. Qian took his leave and returned home. Zhen personally wrote a brief account of his entry into the Way. [He] composed...
He presented several verses to Hui, the last of which read: "Reading the scriptural texts day by day Is like meeting an old acquaintance. Do not say that frequent repetition causes obstruction;
With each recitation, it is renewed."
When Chan Master Tiantong Ying’an Tanhua was residing at Guizong, Da Hui was at Mei Yang.
A monk transmitted to him some verses of instruction by the Master; upon seeing them, Da Hui praised them with great fervor. Later, he sent a verse to him, saying:
"Severing all paths atop the First Peak of the Golden Wheel, A thousand demons and a hundred monsters have all hidden their traces. In recent years, I have received a true report: It is said—"
The true lineage of Yangqi is thus transmitted with such emphasis. ○ He ascended the hall and said: "Those who practice Chan must take care not to apply their minds in error.
To seek to awaken to and clarify the Buddha-nature is to apply the mind in error. To seek to become a Buddha or an ancestral patriarch is to apply the mind in error.

To read sutras or lecture on the teachings is to apply the mind in error. Even walking, standing, sitting, and reclining is to apply the mind in error. Eating porridge or eating rice is to apply the mind in error."

Applying the mind. To apply the mind to defecating or urinating is a mistaken application of the mind. To apply the mind to movement and stillness, or to coming and going, is a mistaken application of the mind.
There is yet another place where the mind is mistakenly applied; Guizong does not dare to reveal it to you all. Why?

"When a single character enters the gates of officialdom, even a team of nine oxen cannot pull the cart out. [Verse] Addressing the assembly, he said: "It is like a fine horse of the world that, upon seeing the whip..."
[The Master] was walking along the shadow. At that time, the monk Chaoguang stepped out from the assembly and said, "One who sees the whip's shadow is not a fine horse.
The Master then desisted. [End of Anecdote] [Verse]: Addressing the assembly, he said: "The phrase that cannot be uttered even with one’s full strength is not at Mount Tiantai;
it must be on Mount Nanyue. [End of Verse] Because the Master was able to refine and temper even the most venerable elders within his quarters, the world called him Dahuì (Great Wisdom).

The Master’s dwelling served as two gates to the nectar of immortality. He once admonished his disciples, saying: "When a monk of our tradition puts on straw sandals and takes up residence in a monastery, how could it be anything less than a serpent clinging to its burrow?"
A monk once brought up the story of Dahui’s bamboo stick to seek instruction from Chan Master Qingliang Tan. The Master showed him this verse:

If one’s faculties and nature are base and inferior, yet one wishes to gnaw upon that which has flavor, and encounters a teacher of the scholastic learning (*yixue*), who locks one in mutual constraints—then even if you can speak with words arising like clouds and appearing like rain, it is still but a frog transforming into a dragon;
in the end, you will remain as before, eating mud and eating earth. What use is such a person? He addressed the assembly, saying: "To contemplate form as emptiness constitutes the Great [Vehicle]."

Because of wisdom, one does not dwell in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Because one contemplates emptiness as being identical with form and thus achieves great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), one does not realize *nirvāṇa*.

Tell me, where do you establish your body and life? Is it not that which is luminous within the space between heart and mind, yet its form cannot be seen; radiant and bright...?

If it is thus, all is merely clashing before the skull. You must know that those who transcend measure possess their own transcendent function.

Where do the flowing yellow leaves come from? An ox, trailing crows in the cold, passes through a distant village. [Verse] Addressing the assembly, he said: "By observing the direction one knows where it has gone;
yet that which goes does not arrive at a direction. When the heel of the straw sandals suddenly breaks, the whole body remains in the Imperial Capital. [Reincorporated]
The Zen Master Yuan’an Ci, a man of wisdom, visited lecture halls to listen to the *Nirvāṇa-samantabhadra-bodhisattva-paripṛcchā-sūtra* (the *Yuanjue jing*).

Upon reaching the passage, “When the four elements have each departed, where then does this illusory body abide? Ultimately it has no substance; it is truly like a magical illusion,” he attained a realization.
He composed a verse, saying: “A single bright pearl is here within me; Touch it or move it, and it emits light that shakes the earth. With this, he presented his realization.
None of the various lecturers were able to explain it. He returned and presented it to his own teacher, who then challenged him with the "dog has no Buddha-nature" koan.
His teacher said, "Even hundreds of thousands of millions of koans do not go beyond this verse.
The teacher considered this insolence and rebuked him, ordering him out. Consequently, he traveled south and stayed at Yuan Tong on Mount Lu. At that time, Wan’an...
While acting as the West Hall attendant, he entered the room for the assembly. He cited a monk’s question to Yunmen: “When one brushes away the dust and sees the Buddha, what then?
Yunmen said, “The Buddha is also dust. As soon as these words were spoken, the Master let out a shout and pointed to his chest, saying, “The Buddha is also dust.
The Master then offered this verse: “Brushing away the dust to see the Buddha— The Buddha is also dust. Question finished, answer finished; In an instant, turn yourself around! He exhorted them thus.
"Please finish one more cup of wine; once you have gone out past the Yang Pass to the west, there will be no old friend left.
Wan’an deeply affirmed this. Later, Chan Master Mugam Yong of Gushan went to visit Lǎn’ān at Yunmen. One day, upon entering the inner room for instruction, Lǎn’ān said:
"I do not ask about words, nor do I ask about wordlessness. When the World-Honored One remained silent for a long time, you must not understand it by way of the World-Honored One’s long silence."
Thereupon he took a drink. Suddenly attaining realization, he prostrated and said, "Had I not asked today, how could I have lost this opportunity before my very eyes?
The Hermit granted him permission. He ascended the hall for discourse. Citing Muzhou’s address to the assembly, which said, "All of you who have not yet attained an entrance must attain an entrance;
once you have attained an entrance, do not forget me," the Master said, "If it were so..."
[The Master] spoke. "How thick-skinned you all are! Wooden Hermit was not like this. As long as you have not yet found a point of entry, you must find one.
Once you have found a point of entry, you must cast that very point away before you can succeed."
Chan Master Baitang Ya of Longxiang ascended the hall. "The great capacity values directness; the great function values sudden manifestation.
Even if there were a 'biting-iron' capacity, it must be struck dead with a single blow. Why? Within the treasury of our King, there is no such blade. He ascended the hall again:
"Purple ferns stretch out their fists as bamboo shoots break through the tips; the willow flowers have flown away, and the green shades interlace. This is clearly the Western Patriarch."
The phrase of single transmission: the yellow oriole sings, the swallow speaks as it builds its nest.

If you can see the truth here and have full conviction, then according to the standards of other quarters, you would certainly be settled beneath a bright window. But in the school of Longxiang, we simply strike them dead with a single blow of the mallet.
Why? It is not that we find it difficult to dwell together with others; rather, everyone must clearly distinguish between black and white.

The Abbot of Fengan at Jianmen followed Lan’an, yet he had not yet attained profound realization. He took leave of his teacher to visit Dayue at Mount Jing. While traveling along the riverbank, he gazed up at the imperial palace and heard the street official shout, "The Minister is coming!

At that moment, he was suddenly and greatly enlightened. He composed a verse, saying: The Great Way is originally vast and open; Why do people labor so hard to seek it? When the Minister comes, the Minister goes; The clouds and mountains are naturally as they are.
For several years, this single matter had hung in his breast; he had questioned all quarters of the land, yet his eyes remained unopened.

At that moment, his liver and gallbladder were utterly shattered as the cry rang out: "The Minister at the River is coming! He then returned directly to Xichan, where Lan’an welcomed him and bestowed upon him the *kāṣāya*.
Chan Master Mituan Jie of Tiantong went to visit Ying’an at Mingguo in Quzhou. Because Ying’an was solitary and rigid, it was difficult for him to gain entry;
he was repeatedly rebuked. [Verse: Ying’an asked, “What is the True Dharma Eye? The Master immediately replied, “A broken sand pot. Ying’an nodded his head in approval. [Ascending the Hall:
He cited the discourse of National Teacher Jinfeng, who addressed the assembly, saying: “Twenty years ago, this old monk had...”
"The grandmotherly heart. Twenty years later, he no longer had this grandmotherly heart. At that time, a monk asked, "What was the meaning of your having a grandmotherly heart twenty years ago?
Feng said, "When asked about the ordinary, I answered as the ordinary; when asked about the sacred, I answered as the sacred.

The monk asked, "What was the meaning of your not having a grandmotherly heart twenty years later? Feng said, "When asked about the ordinary, I did not answer as the ordinary; when asked about the sacred, I did not answer as the sacred."
The Master replied, "Had Wugu seen through it at that time, he would have simply let out two cold laughs.
Had this old fellow suddenly attained sudden enlightenment, he would naturally not have fallen into the conceptual trap of 'saint' or 'ordinary person.'"
Nan Shuji long relied upon Ying’an; regarding the koan of Zhaozhou’s “The dog has no Buddha-nature,” he attained sudden enlightenment.
He composed a verse which said: “The dog has no Buddha-nature; The planet Rāhu enters its destiny. It is not that it kills people;
It is certain to be killed by others. When Ying’an saw this, he rejoiced in his untrammeled liberation.
The Layman Li Hao, a Court Vice-Minister, had read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* since his youth; it was as if he were wandering through an old home, committed to memory and never forgotten.
Later, while serving in office, he visited Mingguo Temple and entered the room to seek instruction. Ying’an struck him on the chest and said, "After you die, Minister..."
"Where are you going? The official was startled, and his sweat broke out. The Hermit shouted, "Go! The official withdrew to reflect. Within ten days, he had ascended to the inner sanctum.
He sent a verse to his fellow practitioner Yan Kangchao, saying: "The gate has the shop of Sun Bin; The house harbors the wife of Gan Zhi.
Sleeping at night and rising early— Who awakens, and who is deluded? When the Hermit saw it, he praised it as excellent.

Chan Master Huarang Yian Quan’s Verse: Once, sitting in meditation through the night until dawn, the monk was about to receive rice gruel. When the server arrived, he forgot to spread out his alms bowl.
A neighboring monk nudged him with his hand, and the Master was awakened to the truth. He composed a verse, saying: "A pitch-black K'un-lun man grips his fishing rod;
The ancient sail is hoisted high as he descends the surging rapids. Amidst the shadows of the reeds, he plays with the bright moon, Drawing the blind turtle onto the fishing boat."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Zen, Zen—without faction, without partiality. When lost, one is separated by a thousand miles;
when awakened, it is right at the edge of the lips. Thus, a monk asked Shishuang, 'What is Zen? Shuang replied, 'A brick for a deer. Again, a monk asked Muzhou, 'What is Zen?
Zhou replied, 'A fierce fire frying oil. Again, a monk asked Shoushan, 'What is Zen? Shan replied:"
"A monkey climbing a tree, its tail trailing behind. O Great Assembly! There is no shortcut on the Way; the place where one stands is solitary and precarious.
These three great elders traveled upon a living path before sound and employed numinous mechanisms beyond kalpas.

Yet, if one were to examine them with the true eye of a monk, there would be no lack of distinction between their excellence and inferiority. One was like Zhang Liang entering the fray; another was like Xiang Yu employing his troops. One...
If a person can discern and clarify this as Zhuge Liang did when gauging the enemy, they may stand shoulder to shoulder with the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Even so, suppose a monk were to come forth and say, "Venerable sir, you have split your words into two pieces!

Just now you said that the Way has no shortcuts, being without factionalism or partiality; yet now you have again divided it into so many distinctions of superior and inferior. How is this? How would you respond?
In response: Have you fully understood? "Holding hands while climbing the mountain, everyone exerts their strength; the breath escaping from the throat is known by oneself.
(A monk asked Shishuang, "What is Chan? Shishuang replied, "A brick for a deer. This exchange is actually the words of Shitou Xiqian; it seems there has been an error here.)
Chan Master Sanfeng Yin ascended the hall and, citing the story of the Wild Fox, said: "Neither falling nor being obscured—this is to falsely accuse another of a crime.
Not obscured and not falling—this is to bind oneself with no rope. How pitiable, the willow catkins following the spring breeze; sometimes they go from west to east on their own."
Chan Master Deshan Yuan ascended the hall and, holding up his staff, said: "Sometimes the person is taken away but the environment is not;

the staff wanders freely in all directions. Sometimes the environment is taken away but the person is not; I, this mountain monk, am sevenfold topsy-turvy. Sometimes both person and environment are taken away;
the staff and I both erase our traces and swallow our voices. Sometimes both person and environment..."
He did not take it. Zuo leaned on his staff and said, "A companion who travels a thousand li with me; one who carries you across ten thousand mountains.

What is it like when you suddenly encounter Great Master Linji? He shouted, "If you have not yet clarified the seal of the mind-ground, it will be difficult to penetrate the barrier of the Patriarchs."
(End of Volume 20 of the *Huìyuán*) End of Volume Ten of the *Zhènzéng zhèngmài*.
